name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Manufactured home park tenants often have no protection when new owners bring new fees
description: On February 28, 2023, Katherine Kilbride logged on to pay her lot rent at her manufactured home park and was startled to see a new charge: $161, with this explanation: “Damage Fee. Cost to replace and install new water meter.” “How am I supposed to pay rent with an extra charge of 161?” she wrote […]
text:
Big Lake Estates, a manufactured home park in Big Lake, Minnesota Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)On February 28, 2023, Katherine Kilbride logged on to pay her lot rent at her manufactured home park and was startled to see a new charge: $161, with this explanation: “Damage Fee. Cost to replace and install new water meter.”
“How am I supposed to pay rent with an extra charge of 161?” she wrote to management a day later. “I never signed a meter agreement or an amended lease.”
She never got an answer. She would spend the next three years asking versions of the same question, in writing, while the park’s payments system turned a charge she didn’t owe into late fees, an inflated balance, and eventually an eviction filing against a tenant who was, the whole time, trying to pay her rent.
Kilbride is a single mother of four daughters. After disability limited her job prospects, she lost her home to foreclosure in 2007. After a series of moves, her family eventually settled into Big Lake Estates in September 2020. Following years of tumult, having just clawed her way back to financial stability, she said the mobile home was the only option she had left. “I wouldn’t live here if I didn’t have to,” she said. 
Kilbride’s story, and the stories of those in similar predicaments, underscore the lack of protections for people who live in manufactured home parks, where people own their home but not the land beneath it. Time and again, management companies find creative ways to exploit residents who feel powerless to do anything about it. 
“Everyone here thinks low income means less rights,” Kilbride said.  
An installation no one permitted
Big Lake Estates is a 124-lot manufactured home community about 45 minutes northwest of Minneapolis in the city of Big Lake. It was acquired in late 2020 by Big Lake MHC LLC, a Delaware-registered entity operated by Sado Management under owner Joel Mazur. Rent began climbing after the sale. 
In the summer of 2022, management added something new: individual water submeters at every home, with water and sewer billed back to residents — including those who had signed leases saying those services were free. 
To install the meters, Mazur hired Clayton Hultman, a local handyman who advertises on Nextdoor as “Clayton from Hultmans Plumbing.”
Big trouble in Little Canada: Water bills at manufactured home park skyrocket after unpermitted work

When Big Lake Estates converted to submetering in 2022, Minnesota law said little about how a park should do it. The Legislature changed that in 2023. State law now requires park owners to provide residents sample bills for three months before utility billing; caps rent for 13 months after conversion for residents whose leases included water and sewer; and requires that meters be installed or repaired only by a licensed plumber, electrician or manufactured home installer. The current law also bars park owners from charging residents any capital or administrative costs of providing utility service, including late fees.
The conversion at Big Lake Estates’ preceded those 2023 reforms. Residents received no sample bills; the first notice Kilbride got was dated one day after billing began. But Kilbride never needed the new law; her lease expressly stated what she owed. In lease documents reviewed by the Reformer, this original version states expectations clearly: section 5 promised water and sewer “at no extra charge,” and Section 18 said any change that substantially modified the lease would not apply to her. No addendum was ever signed, but the park began billing her anyway. 
Lilly Sasse, an organizer with the Manufactured Home Resident Collective with ISAIAH, an ecumenical progressive nonprofit, said this is a common tactic across parks under private investor management: “These new private equity firms come in and set new rules, telling people that they’re supposed to abide by them, even though the lease they signed indicates that they don’t have to.”
Hultman, the plumber, confirmed in a phone interview with the Reformer that Mazur hired him directly and that the job took about two and a half months, working through whatever fittings each home had: SharkBite, PEX, compression, copper. He installed the meters in line between each home’s curb stop and its water line. Once completed, Hultman said he offered Mazur a 90-day warranty on the work. After that, he said, problems belonged to “the park or the tenant.” Hultman added, unprompted: “Joel was sort of cheap about things.”
Hultman holds no Minnesota plumbing license, according to the state Department of Labor and Industry’s licensing database. In follow-up text messages, Hultman told the Reformer he performed the installation under his father’s plumbing license, not his own, noting his father passed away two years ago. He said that he understood how this may have been perceived by residents, but said he “probably had more experience than most plumbers out there” and that “most [manufactured home residents] don’t really take care of their stuff and that’s why they live there.” He also confirmed his assistant was unlicensed and “didn’t hold any specific knowledge” regarding how to complete the project. 
A DLI plumbing inspector, Charles Olson, put the license requirement plainly in a written response to Kilbride: “New installation of a water meter would require a licensed plumber. The city of Big Lake has an inspection department and would issue the permit(s).” 
City Administrator Hanna Klimmek later confirmed to the Reformer that no permits were ever filed. The city has reached out to the park to determine what permit applications should be submitted for work done four years ago.
Joel Mazur and Sado Management did not respond to requests for comment.
None of the homes had electrical outlets near their curb stops, Hultman acknowledged, meaning the heat tape that protects outdoor water lines through a Minnesota winter had nowhere to plug in. Hultman said the park provided heat tape and extension cords, leaving installation to tenants. His offers to install $1,200 heat wrap kits directly to park residents have gone largely unanswered, with only a handful sold. Kilbride says no tape, no cords, and no instruction ever reached her. “There was zero instruction. There wasn’t a policy. I asked for months and months,” she said. 
What’s not in dispute is what happened next. That winter, meters froze, with the park’s own payment portal recording the cause in a February 2023 credit entry: “Partial Water & Sewer credit due to broken meter caused by frozen pipes.” The park knew the meter froze, then credited Kilbride $28.16 for the broken meter, only to turn around and bill her $161 to replace it.
‘How can I pay my rent?’
Over the following months, Kilbride wrote to management again and again seeking resolution, according to logs of the park’s own message system reviewed by the Reformer. She alerted them to correspondence with Hultman, the unlicensed plumbing contractor, who told her he was responsible for installing the now frozen meter, and said she refused to pay for someone else’s mistake. 
In early March, she told them she was unable to pay the accumulated bill.
Minnesota needs a Manufactured Home Park Resident Bill of Rights

That message finally reached the corporate office. The same day, an email went out to on-site staff, later printed and handed to Kilbride with a sticky note attached: corporate had “removed the late charge and moved the damage charge while we work to resolve the meter issue.” She could pay her $580 rent. The handwritten note confirmed the rest: the “$161.00 fee being moved to May 1st 2023.”
Moved — not removed. 
Two days later, the park sent her a ”pay or quit” notice. The payment portal, which doesn’t allow payments below the full balance, kept blocking her from paying the agreed upon $580, insisting on payment for the additional $161. She documented attempt after attempt: February 28, March 27, April 2, April 3, each one a screenshot of the same yellow banner refusing a different amount. The office, per policy stated to Kilbride, wouldn’t take a cashier’s check. Late fees stacked onto rent she was being prevented from paying.
In early April, Kilbride wrote: “You’re bullying a single mother and disabled veteran into paying illegal fees to remain in this poorly maintained community. My pipes didn’t burst. My pipes were never frozen. Your contractor damaged my property.”
That same day, she paid the entire balance: $1,206.40, the disputed fee included. Not because she agreed she owed it, but because it was the only way the system would accept her rent.

The meters were not the park’s only infrastructure failure.

Around the same time, another resident reported sewage bubbling over manholes to state environmental regulators, according to a Reformer public records request. The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency (MPCA) contacted Sherburne County, which dispatched environmental specialist Jerome Doede to visit the property and photograph frozen sewage accumulated around a manhole cover outside the home.
When Doede stopped  by the park office afterward, staff told him something similar had happened “a month ago in the same spot.” Doede issued a formal public health nuisance letter to the park’s owner that day. 
In January 2026, the MPCA fined Big Lake Estates $24,150 for multiple wastewater violations and required corrective action under a stipulation agreement. An environmental specialist described the response: The park “did not make timely attempts to stop the release or clean up the frozen sewage,” and “these releases have been occurring for almost two months.”
In his response to the MPCA before signing the settlement, Mazur said the park was “not aware of the requirement under Minnesota law” to notify regulators of the discharge, and had “reasonably believed” that licensed contractors would handle any state obligations. The agency assessed the full penalty anyway.
This spring, the bill for the park’s sewer problems arrived, addressed to the residents. A May 2026 rent increase notice to Kilbride’s neighbors at 405 Polk raised their lot rent from $660 to $745, citing “a significant wastewater rehabilitation project to address aging infrastructure within the community’s sewer system.” Kilbride’s own rent, $440 with utilities included when she moved in, will reach $795 in August, an increase of more than 80% since 2020 — nearly triple the rate of inflation during that time. A bill at the Legislature this year would have capped the annual increase to 3% but didn’t pass.
Trees line the street at Big Lake Estates, a manufactured home park in Big Lake, Minnesota Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Three evictions on one street
In January this year, Big Lake MHC LLC filed to evict Kilbride for nonpayment. It was the company’s third eviction filing on Polk Street in five months: 407 Polk in September, 408 Polk in December, 416 Polk in January, all through the same law firm, Landlord Resource Network LLC.
Kilbride had fallen behind in December. In January, when she went to catch up, the payment portal was disabled. She documented more than 15 attempts to pay between January 6 and the filing date: online, by phone and in person at an office that accepts no cash, no cashier’s checks, and no certified funds of any kind. 
“Being evicted while actively trying to pay your rent is f*cking wild to me,” she said.
Seventy days before the park filed that eviction, the park had denied her Americans with Disabilities Act accommodation request for an accessible sidewalk between her parking space and her door, citing budget. Her neighbor got a new sidewalk. Then, six days after filing, the park added $1,385 to her bill for court costs, filing fees and “damages.” No court had awarded these fees.
The Minnesota attorney general’s office declined to comment. 
Her two Polk Street neighbors faced their eviction hearings without lawyers, and both settled within weeks. Kilbride was represented by Mid-Minnesota Legal Aid, and her case ran nearly four months, up to the day of an evidentiary hearing at which three park managers were scheduled to testify. The park settled instead. Kilbride paid rent and utilities only; no disputed fees. The court expunged the case in May.
In June 2026, Big Lake sent a formal notice of code complaint to Mazur at Sado Management’s Delaware address, citing five complaints received by city staff regarding conditions at Big Lake Estates: shelter access and emergency preparedness; building code concerns in the park’s common basement; debris and property maintenance; ongoing sewage and environmental concerns; and the unpermitted water meter installations, with some referred to Sherburne County. 
Congress takes notice 
Last month, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan, ranking member of the Joint Economic Committee, sent a formal document request to Mazur at Sado Capital, citing an ongoing New Hampshire attorney general investigation into the company’s rent increases and requesting 14 categories of records about its business practices across manufactured housing communities.
Meanwhile, at Sado-managed Big Lake Estates, Katherine Kilbride documented everything. Her record stands: four years of screenshots, ledgers, portal messages and complaints, most of it from the park’s own systems. Per park policy, she continues to pay rent using the same system that prohibited her payments in the first place.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s GOP says it can win the 5th Congressional District race
description: Republican Chris Shea said he sees an opening with unaffiliated voters which could help him defeat Democratic incumbent Rep. Jahana Hayes.
text:
Chris Shea, the Republican congressional candidate in Connecticut’s 5th District, said he sees an opening with unaffiliated voters which could help him defeat Democratic incumbent Rep. Jahana Hayes, in the general election in November.
Shea remains confident that he will win, even though many political analysts project Hayes will keep the 5th District seat.
“There’s a lot of room to sway people, and a lot of room for people to move,” Shea said.
Shea isn’t the only Connecticut Republican running for Congress.
But several other Republicans and political analysts agree that the 5th District is competitive. This is due in part to voter registration records.
As of 2025, municipalities in the 5th District, like Waterbury, have more unaffiliated voters than registered Democrats or Republicans.
According to the Cook Partisan Voting Index, Hayes’ district doesn’t have as much of an overwhelming advantage for Democratic voter registrations as other parts of the state.
Shea said reaching out to those unaffiliated voters represents one of his best chances at winning.
Shea has also been critical of what he characterized as Hayes’ failures on economic affordability issues. According to Shea, Republicans across the state are unified by that messaging.
But Shea has also used cultural grievances, from trans people’s participation in sports, to stronger immigration enforcement and border security as part of his platform.
“We’re about unity, unifying behind the gubernatorial candidates and everybody down ballot from us, and helping get as many of them across the finish line as we can,” Shea said.
Hayes responded to Shea’s attacks by stating voters are focused on quality of life issues in a statement to Connecticut Public.
“The people of the Fifth District are looking for leaders to address the affordability crisis, cuts to healthcare, endless wars we are engaged in and so many other things,” Hayes said. “I have no comment on the Republican nominee, from what I can see these are the same attacks that have been tried, and were rejected by the voters and failed.”
Shea won a contentious primary, according to previous reporting from the CT Mirror. He has supported much of President Donald Trump’s policies, but says his primary challenger, Jonathan De Barros, spent as much time attacking him and fellow Republicans as he did Democrats.
Mara Suttmann-Lea is a government and international relations professor at Connecticut College. According to them, Republican primary voters reflected internal divisions, even as state Republicans try to minimize the extent of divisions within the party.
“It’s really this question of how do we move beyond, overcome, navigate the tension that is very clearly still there between more establishment Republicans and the MAGA wing of the Republican Party,” Suttmann-Lea said.
Michael Goldstein, a Republican candidate, who is now running against Rep. Jim Himes for the state’s 4th District, has not focused as much on cultural issues as other candidates.
Instead, Goldstein centered his campaign on conventional Republican policies from affordability to helping small businesses.
Goldstein said he is driven by practical concerns not political ideology.
“The grocery bill isn’t Republican or Democratic,” Goldstein said. “Neither is the electric bill. Healthcare costs aren’t partisan. Neither are jobs, infrastructure, housing costs or whether your children can afford to build their lives here.”
But Suttmann-Lea also said the primary didn’t reveal whether Trump-style populism has run its course in Connecticut.
“I don’t think it has anything much to say about the broader trend towards or away from a more MAGA Republican oriented approach,” Suttmann-Lea said.
Ben Proto, who chairs the state’s Republican Party, said one party does have an identity crisis; but Proto said it’s the Democratic Party.
“Are they the party that’s being taken over by DSA, in Connecticut, or are they more traditional Democrats,” Proto said. “I think the answer to that is the former,” Proto said.
This story was first published Aug. 13, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Political Notebook: Layoffs the latest sign of trouble for clean energy
description: The state agency tasked with turbocharging the state's green economy laid off 11 employees, citing a "challenging funding landscape" amid federal headwinds.
text:
CALL IT a sign of the times: Layoffs have hit Massachusetts’s agency aimed at turbocharging the state’s green economy.
The Massachusetts Clean Energy Center has laid off 11 people, a spokesperson for the agency confirmed to CommonWealth Beacon, as it navigates a “challenging funding landscape as the federal administration has disrupted clean energy programs and the industry overall.”
The timing is notable: It comes just a month after Gov. Maura Healey signed a $63.4 billion budget for fiscal year 2027.
MassCEC, a quasi-public agency that boosts clean technologies in energy, buildings, and transportation, receives funding from a variety of sources. But Healey’s budget did it no favors.
The agency was allotted just $8 million in the FY27 budget, down from $10 million last year and $30 million in FY24. That will leave the organization’s new CEO Ben Downing to reckon with a smaller staff as it seeks to pivot from its emphasis on offshore wind supply chain development, given President Trump’s stifling of new such projects.
And the reduced budget speaks to the fiscal pressures facing Massachusetts officials: Even as the needs are greater than ever, including in the clean energy sector that has suffered from whipsaw federal policies and revoked incentives for electric vehicles, solar power, offshore wind, and energy efficiency measures, funding from Washington has also dried up, forcing states to shoulder more costs for core safety net programs like health care and food aid.
Those federal headwinds “have forced both the Legislature and the administration to adjust operating budget proposals in recent years,” the MassCEC spokesperson said.
MassCEC will still be able to collect money from its three remaining federal awards and a small charge on utility bills that generates about $20 million annually.
No matter what, Rollins is on the ballot
Rachael Rollins, the scandal-tarred former Suffolk County district attorney running to reclaim her old job, has been in the spotlight all week amid reports that she filed nomination papers featuring the signatures of several Chelsea city councilors who say they never actually signed. Asked whether she should be removed from contention, Attorney General Andrea Campbell replied during a live radio interview, “If she fraudulently got on the ballot, yes.”
There’s just one catch: At this point in the calendar, Rollins is on the primary ballot — no matter what other facts emerge.
The ballot for the September 1 Democratic primary has already been printed, distributed, and returned by many voters. There is no mechanism by which state elections officials can remove a candidate from consideration after votes have already been cast.
And while the series of stories in the Boston Herald and The Boston Globe have generated significant buzz, the secretary of state’s office has not received any formal complaints about the nomination papers that would prompt officials to refer the matter to law enforcement, according to Deb O’Malley, a spokesperson for Secretary of State Bill Galvin.
Todd Taylor, one of the Chelsea city councilors whose name appears despite saying he did not sign, even went to Galvin’s office in early June — roughly two months before the news stories appeared — to review Rollins’s nomination papers featuring his signature, after which he did not file a complaint, O’Malley said. (Taylor’s signature wound up not counting anyway because he’s a registered Republican and Rollins is running in a Democratic primary.)
The Chelsea city clerk also reached out earlier in the process to Galvin’s office to ask what to do if a local official thought a signature was fraudulent. Unlike the cases of attorney general candidate Michael Walsh and GOP lieutenant governor candidates Anne Manning-Martin and Anne Brensley, in which several town clerks submitted questionable nomination papers to the secretary’s office for review, the Chelsea clerk did not send along any documents with her inquiry suggesting a broader issue, O’Malley said. In those cases, the secretary’s office alerted district attorneys in Plymouth and Norfolk Counties.
“That was an unfortunate breakdown in communication from the Chelsea city clerk to our office, but she did not refer it to us” for further action, O’Malley said.
Plus, Rollins filed a total of 1,606 signatures, easily surpassing the 1,000 she needed to qualify, and the number in question in Chelsea is far fewer than 606.
So the scrutiny — including the latest Globe report detailing how Rollins personally handed in two sheets in question — might impact how voters think about the Democratic primary, but it will not change the list of names from which they will choose.
A $40 million question at Hanscom
The developers of a controversial and high-profile effort to add 17 new hangars for private jets at Hanscom Field airport have closed on a $40 million loan to retrofit one existing hangar, according to a bank document reviewed by CommonWealth Beacon —though progress on the larger project remains stalled.
The developers have finalized the financial transaction with Needham Bank to fund construction of one hangar previously used by the Navy, confirmed Rick Muse, director of operations for the Hanscom redevelopment proposal. That part of Hanscom will be used by Merlin Labs to pilot autonomous flights.
State officials approved that limited “change of use” of Hanscom last year.
The influx of cash reignites questions about when the developers will pursue the larger project to add new private jet hangars at the Massport-owned airport. The state rejected an earlier environmental plan in 2024 and sent it back to the developers to resubmit, which they thus far have failed to do.
Public records obtained by CommonWealth Beacon show a resubmitted environmental impact review continues to face delays as the developers cite shifting customer preferences and even the presence of a rare flower on the site that has caused hiccups.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas State Board of Education starts work on technology use policies for public schools
description: The Kansas State Board of Education is discussing how to help guide local public school districts on use of computers and other technology in classrooms.
text:
Kansas State Board of Education member Jim Porter of Fredonia says excessive use of technology in classrooms is harmful to students. The State Board of Education is working on policies of potential help to local school districts grappling with the complex issue. In this image from July 8, 2025, Porter speaks to colleagues in Topeka. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas State Board of Education is pushing ahead with drafting recommendations for public school districts on use of technology in classrooms and crafting a potential mandate that local school boards implement policies controlling student access to computers.
The 10-member State Board of Education shared a sense of urgency Wednesday for development by November of consensus on boundaries and expectations for laptops and pads that have become common in K-12 schools. That three-month timeframe would enable the state board to implement its version of best practices before the 2027 Kansas Legislature convened in January to consider its own agenda.
Members of the state board expressed a range of personal views on implications of technology in schools while discussing either a recommendation or requirement that districts adopt technology plans that kept best interests of students at the forefront. Concern was expressed by Republicans and Democrats on the state board that too much technology was detrimental to students, especially children in early grades.
“We have to be the leaders to make sure people understand that there are negative consequences,” said Jim Porter, a Fredonia Republican member of the board and a former teacher, principal and superintendent. “There are significant negative consequences. Now that we know that, we have to communicate that.”
There was conversation among board members about imposing a ban on classroom technology until students reached the third grade.
“Screens don’t belong in kindergarten. The end. It’s static. It’s not engaging,” said Melanie Haas, a Democrat from Overland Park on the state board. “I would like to see a ban through second grade.”
The state board could impose a powerful incentive for districts to comply with a ban by including it in accreditation standards applicable to public schools statewide.
Board member Danny Zeck, a Republican from Leavenworth, said the state board’s adoption of meaningful restraint on instructional technology had the potential — however small — to discourage the Legislature from wading into the subject. He said legislators during the 2026 session imposed a near-prohibition on student possession of cellphones during school hours. That controversial bell-to-bell moratorium at public and private schools was signed into law by Gov. Laura Kelly.
“What’s going to happen is we’re going to do a great job, give good guidance and then the Legislature is going to come in and do their stupid stuff,” Zeck said.
Members of the State Board of Education appeared eager to share model policy on technology that could be adapted to needs of individual districts. A one-size-fits-all policy could be difficult because Kansas has districts with enrollments ranging from less than 100 students to more than 45,000 students.
“We do have longitudinal data that paper, pencil and books have given our nation a great education for a lot of years,” said state board member Debby Potter of Garden Plain.
Board member Michelle Dombrosky of Olathe said reliance on technology in classes could reduce student retention and comprehension of information. Excessive dedication to technology has been tied to worsening anxiety and mental health challenges of students, she said.
The board discussed whether limits on technology could require districts to adjust budgets to account for the purchase of more textbooks. In addition, the state board pointed to potential complications of compelling students to perform class assignments with pencil and paper and subsequently making them take standardized assessments online.
Jake Steel, recently appointed Kansas commissioner of education, advised the state board to be careful with regulatory mandates on schools. Technology reform could be enforced by linking policy to accreditation standards, he said, but a less aggressive approach would be to engage in “public shaming” by posting online the school districts that did or didn’t adopt a framework for dealing with student technology.
“We’ve got to be very judicious about what we’re going to put in regulation because it takes forever to get in and it’s not easy to get out,” Steel said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s 1st Congressional District candidates share housing affordability plans
description: Democrat Luke Bronin and Republican Dr. Amy Chai are running to represent Hartford, Litchfield, Middlesex Counties. They have plans to address housing.
text:
For the first time in nearly 30 years Connecticut will have a new member of Congress representing the state’s 1st Congressional District and with the new role comes the opportunity to share new ideas on affordable housing reform.
Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, a Democrat, and Dr. Amy Chai, a Republican, are running for the 1st Congressional District seat, which represents parts of Hartford, Litchfield and Middlesex Counties.
Bronin recently secured his party’s nomination after defeating longtime incumbent Rep. John Larson in August’s primary election.
Bronin told Connecticut Public the federal government can play a larger role in affordable housing development than many realize. He wants the federal government to return to a more involved role in affordable housing development.
“Go back and look at the GI Bill, throughout much of the 20th century, the federal government was a huge part of creating housing opportunity, and in more recent decades, it’s done less and less,” Bronin said.
Revamping existing federal affordable housing finance programs is one of Bronin’s legislative priorities.
“We have to reform and update a lot of the federal housing finance tools,” Bronin said. “There are important tools like Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) that make a big difference. But, first of all, we don’t put enough resources into them, and second of all, I don’t think they’re flexible enough.”
As Hartford’s mayor, Bronin said several areas of the city were revitalized and converted from seas of parking spaces to new housing opportunities.
Chai, the Republican candidate, previously ran as an Independent against Rep. Rosa DeLauro in 2022.
Chai said she has two legislative plans for housing reform and has drafted federal legislation that would expand limits on private equity firms purchasing single family homes.
“I’ve long been interested in stopping some of the private equity abuses,” Chai said. “Because I’m a doctor, I know what it’s done to medicine. I’ve always kind of been anti the scooping up of resources by private equity and sucking us all dry and then spitting it out.”
Chai said she has firsthand experience with private equity’s encroachment on single-family homes. When trying to sell her parents’ home, the top bidder was a private equity firm.
“I sold it to the lowest bidder. That was a young couple,” Chai said. “I’m already making money, I don’t need extra money. I want someone in the neighborhood. That’s nice, but not everybody can afford to do that. People do sell to the highest bidder. Investors are using the low-income housing market for profit on a national level, and I think it’s causing some problems.”
Chai also has plans for a pilot program in Hartford that would construct affordable home ownership opportunities on underutilized properties. If the program were to be a success, Chai said she’d try to get it expanded nationwide.
This story was first published Aug. 13, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Nevada Current
title: Scientists define a new category of heat wave: ‘Snow eaters’
description: This story was originally published by Grist.  Matthew LaPlante doesn’t have to go to a lab to see his research in action. On some mornings, he can just look out his own window in the mountains high above Salt Lake City. After a warm night when the temperature stays above freezing, he’ll wake up and […]
text:
The downtown Salt Lake City skyline is backdropped by fresh snow on the Wasatch Mountains on Monday, January 15, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)This story was originally published by Grist. 
Matthew LaPlante doesn’t have to go to a lab to see his research in action. On some mornings, he can just look out his own window in the mountains high above Salt Lake City. After a warm night when the temperature stays above freezing, he’ll wake up and see that the snow level has dropped by inches, revealing more of the aspens he taps for syrup.
“It feels like a monster came and just in the middle of the night, took a bite out of a snowpack,” said LaPlante, a journalist and climate scientist at Utah State University.
So it’s fitting that scientists have started calling these kinds of heat waves, marked by unusually high temperatures in the spring and early summer, “snow eaters.”
LaPlante was part of a recent study, published in the journal Science Advances, that attempted, for the first time, to identify what conditions exactly make for a “snow eater.” Compared to normal warm spells or heat waves, the researchers determined that these events happen when temperatures stay above freezing through both day and night for multiple days, typically three to five. These events can roughly double the rate at which snow melts, causing flooding and making it challenging to manage water resources.
“Snow eaters” appear to be occurring earlier in the year and becoming more widespread in the Western United States as the climate warms. Since the 1850s, the study found, the area affected by snow eaters has increased by an average of about 40,000 square miles per century, and the first snow eater of the season has been arriving about one month earlier per century.
The term “snow eater” has a murky history. By at least the 1880s, people in the West were talking about “snow-eating” chinooks, warm mountain winds that make snow disappear quickly. More recently, the phrase “snow-eater heat wave” first made headlines in March, when an early heat wave enveloped much of the West, quickly wiping away snowpack in the Colorado Rockies and California’s Sierra Nevada. The scientists hope the catchy, evocative term can help draw more attention to this type of heat wave, since there’s still a lot to learn. The study only looked at the Western U.S., but snow eater heat waves almost assuredly occur elsewhere, LaPlante said.
Solar radiation is a major, but sometimes overlooked, driver of snowmelt, said Noah Molotch, a professor of geography at the University of Colorado Boulder who was not involved in the new study. When it interacts with heat waves, those impacts are amplified. As snow crystals warm up, they lose some of their structure and light-reflecting abilities, causing snowpacks to absorb more sunlight and melt faster. “It’s a little bit of a — no pun intended — a snowball effect,” he said.
Much of the Western U.S. saw record-low snowpack this spring. What was really unusual about it, Molotch said, was how widespread it was. Colorado received less precipitation than normal this winter, while California got lots of precipitation, but in the form of rain instead of snow. But across the region, “the one thing in common was above-average air temperatures,” Molotch said.
These conditions have likely helped fuel exceptionally severe wildfires in the West, from Utah to Spokane, Washington, where hundreds of homes burned earlier this month. “Drought stress for mountain forests around the Western U.S. is heavily dictated by the snow that accumulates each winter and then melts through the spring and summer,” Molotch said. “There is a direct connection there in terms of the water availability and drought stress that can provide one of the important ingredients for increases in wildfire intensity and frequency.”
If scientists are able to better predict what will happen to snowpack, it could help water managers plan for what’s coming. Early or rapid snowmelt poses problems for managing water resources in the West, where snowpack serves as a key source of fresh water in the drier summer months. “Water that would otherwise be stored as snow comes out early, and then we have to deal with it as a hazard instead of a resource at our reservoirs and along the rivers and streams,” said Ben Hatchett, a co-author on the study and a scientist at Colorado State University’s Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere.
Snow-eater heat waves also may pose risks to skiers, hikers, and anyone else on or near mountains. They could be linked to hazards such as avalanches, glacial collapses, and permafrost melt, Hatchett said, though scientists are still investigating those connections. He lives in the Sierra Nevada, and he’s noticed one tangible change over his lifetime: The soundscape has changed.
“At night, it used to be quiet,” he said. “And now it’s not quiet, because everything’s melting all the time.”
This article originally appeared in Grist.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Income taxes. Cleveland.com’s Laura Hancock reports, “DeWine says Ohio has cut income taxes enough, breaking with Ramaswamy.”
Gov. Mike DeWine doesn’t believe Ohio needs to cut income taxes any further, undercutting a key policy of the man who he wants to be his successor.
“I’ve signed four budgets, and (in) every one of the budgets we have reduced the income tax,” DeWine said Wednesday, speaking to reporters. “We’re to the point where the issue of income tax never comes up when we’re talking to businesses.”
• Another lawsuit. The Columbus Dispatch’s Haley BeMiller reports, “Lawsuit says Ohio Rep. Max Miller released nude photo of daughter.”
A new lawsuit accuses Ohio Congressman Max Miller and his attorney of sharing a nude photo of his 2-year-old daughter online as Miller pushes back against domestic violence claims.
The image was included in a trove of documents shared by Miller that are tied to a custody battle with his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, according to the lawsuit filed by Moreno Aug. 12. The photo surfaced in a text exchange between Miller and Moreno and showed their daughter’s genitals, the lawsuit states.
“This child is an entirely innocent victim who has become collateral damage to her father’s political ambition,” said Subodh Chandra, an attorney for Moreno.
A spokesperson for Miller declined to comment.
• Flock cameras. The Dayton Daily News’ Avery Kreemer reports, “DeWine, Ohio AG defend Flock cameras amid public scrutiny.”
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson and Gov. Mike DeWine recently defended the use of Flock cameras by local governments amid growing public scrutiny around the surveillance company’s contracts with law enforcement agencies across the country.
Both Wilson and DeWine noted that, while Flock cameras can be misused, they are hugely valuable to law enforcement officers in Ohio.

name: Nevada Current
title: PUCN denies public session on NV Energy’s data center-driven resource plan, advocates call foul
description: The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada denied an application for a PUCN-led consumer session last week, an unprecedented move advocates say follows a pattern of cutting public input in recent months. Advocates say the denial is another example of utility regulators thwarting public comment on contentious utility issues.  In June, the PUCN delayed and resc[...]
text:
Alexander Simpson speaks during a press conference at the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada's offices in Las Vegas on June 15, 2026. (Photo by Bryan Steffy/Getty Images for People's Action)The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada denied an application for a PUCN-led consumer session last week, an unprecedented move advocates say follows a pattern of cutting public input in recent months.
Advocates say the denial is another example of utility regulators thwarting public comment on contentious utility issues. 
In June, the PUCN delayed and rescheduled key consumer sessions after facing intense public backlash when dozens of attendees were forced to wait outside in triple-digit Las Vegas heat during contentious utility rate hearings.
The PUCN lead consumer session denied last week was requested by the Bureau of Consumer Protection (BCP), which is under the state Attorney General’s office, in order to provide public input on NV Energy’s 2027 Integrated Resource Plan, a proposal outlining the utilities strategy to meet Nevada’s future energy needs. 
The PUCN, which regulates utility companies like NV Energy and Southwest Gas, is not required by law to hold consumer sessions to discuss utility filings, which can be approved or denied on a case-by-case basis. 
However, requests for those consumer sessions for major dockets with the potential to impact ratepayers are common and rarely if ever denied. 
Several advocacy groups signed on in support of the BCP’s consumer session request, arguing it would allow the public to provide input on NV Energy’s 2027 Integrated Resource Plan once it was officially filed with regulators in its final form. 
In its request, the Bureau of Consumer Protection said the session would provide the public an opportunity to discuss the unprecedented load growth driven by proposed data centers described in NV Energy’s  plan. The BOC noted that a joint application by NV Energy documents requests for up to 22 gigawatts of energy from data center developers. 
Making the PUCN’s denial of the session even more unusual, representatives for NV Energy indicated they did not object to the consumer session.
Olivia Tanager, the director of the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter, said the organization had also filed a request for a consumer session on NV Energy’s resource plan, with full expectation it would be approved, and was surprised by the commission’s departure from established practice. 
“Two other consumer sessions were canceled and postponed with very limited notice from the Public Utilities Commission. Now this consumer session is being denied outright, despite the Bureau of Consumer Protection requesting it,” Tananger said. “This seems like a concerted effort to lock the public out of the Public Utilities Commission spaces.”
In denying a public session, the PUCN said consumer-session comments are not evidentiary and that statute does not require a consumer session in every docket.
Regulators at PUCN said it would not be “in the public interest for the Commission to preside over a consumer session” as it “would not create a meaningful opportunity for consumers to effectively participate.” 
“To the extent that the BCP’s motion requests a Commission-conducted consumer session, the motion is denied,” reads the PUCN’s order, adding that the PUCN “strongly encourages the BCP to hold a BCP-sponsored consumer session to hear directly from those consumers whom the BCP represents.”
Peter Kostes, a spokesperson for the PUCN, pushed back on the characterization that the commission denied the inclusion of a consumer session and public participation, saying the BCP was authorized to hold a consumer session of its own.
Kostes said the commission’s order on the motion “facilitates the scheduling of a consumer session where consumers’ input can actually be incorporated into the decision-making process,” by requesting the state’s consumer advocate conduct their own consumer session.”
Tananger, the director of the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter, argued the responsibility to hold consumer sessions related to utility regulation should remain with the PUCN, adding that the BCP is already overworked. 
Angel DeFazio, a regular attendee of PUCN meetings, said commissioners have regularly bristled at the manner in which members of the public participate in commission public comment sessions, adding that the process is already opaque and difficult to navigate. 
As public interest in the PUCN’s activities have heightened, more barriers have been put in place, said DeFazio, including the PUCN’s decision to only hold afternoon sessions, rather than evening sessions when more people are able to attend.
DeFazio also attended the meeting in June that did not provide an overflow room for the large crowd, resulting in people succumbing to heat-illness while waiting outside in triple-digit heat during a general consumer session. 
“The commission does not want to deal with ratepayers, so they denied it,” said DeFazio. “They don’t want to hear from the ratepayers, and that’s the problem. So yeah, this is to be expected.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Stowe Center explores independence in Black abolitionists’ stories
description: Thousands of formerly enslaved Black Americans made individual declarations independence. Hartford's Stowe Center is sharing their stories.
text:
There is the Declaration of Independence Americans learn about in school, the one signed in Philadelphia in 1776 and celebrated every July 4. 
Then there are thousands of more personal, individual declarations of independence that came afterward — from people who had been enslaved and used their stories, writing and activism to demand freedom and recognition of their humanity.
The Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford is putting those stories at the center of its new exhibition, “6,000+ Declarations of Independence.” 
Through original comic art by Connecticut artist Joe Young, the exhibit features the stories of Black freedom seekers and abolitionists including Frederick Douglass, Harriet Jacobs, Sojourner Truth, Josiah Henson and Phillis Wheatley. It asks visitors to look beyond the familiar story of America’s founding and consider what July 4 meant to the millions of people who remained enslaved, and what independence meant to those who had to fight for it.

Lisenn Rielland, from left, her aunt Elisette Hunter and uncle Marc Hunter, all visiting from France, talk  about the 6000+ Declarations of Independence exhibit featuring original comic art by artist Joe Young at the Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford on Friday, August 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

For Erika Slocumb, the Stowe Center’s director of interpretation and visitor experience, the exhibit reflects a broader effort to change how American history is told. 
“We’ve inherited our freedom because of the work that they put in,” Slocumb said.
The idea for the exhibit began in the Stowe Center’s archives, when Director of Collections Kat White discovered an unpublished narrative written by the Rev. William Phillips after the Civil War. In it, Phillips described a Fourth of July gathering where he stood before his community and delivered a speech declaring his freedom. 
White began wondering whether stories like Phillips’ could be understood as their own declarations of independence.
That idea became the foundation for the exhibit’s title, which refers to more than 6,000 freedom narratives identified by historians. Some were written by people who experienced enslavement, others were dictated, and some were preserved through oral traditions. The Stowe Center intentionally uses the term “freedom narratives” rather than “slave narratives” to emphasize the voices and agency of the people telling their stories.

Reproductions of “The North Star” are seen in the Harriet Beecher Stowe House during an “inheriting freedom” tour at the Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford on Friday, August 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

For Slocumb, those stories are also about helping people see themselves in American history. She said she grew up loving Black history but rarely saw those stories reflected in what she learned in school. 
“I hated history growing up because I never saw my story,” she said. 
Now she wants children who visit the Stowe Center to see Black history as part of the broader American story, rather than as something separate. “I want to tell Black history in a way that is relatable, that doesn’t feel separate,” she said.
Young approached that same goal through comic art. The Hartford artist said comics helped him when he struggled in school. He used to call himself “the fisherman,” he said, because his grades were “below sea level.” 
Young said he believes visual storytelling can help young people connect with history in ways traditional presentations sometimes cannot. “Comic art is just so inviting, and it’s fun,” he said.
Young also deliberately centered Black figures, he said, because “they were left out.” He wants the exhibit to highlight both well-known and lesser-known Black individuals whose voices and actions helped shape the country. 

Anna Boers, visitor experience and collections associate, answers questions in the Gallery for Hope & Freedom during an “inheriting freedom” tour at the Stowe Center for Literary Activism in Hartford on Friday, August 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The exhibit comes as America is commemorating 250 years since the Declaration of Independence, but Slocumb said the Stowe Center’s work is about more than marking an anniversary. Over the past two and a half years, the center has reshaped how it presents history, placing greater emphasis on Black freedom seekers and the narratives that helped inspire change. 
Slocumb said she hopes broader understanding can help people recognize the connections between America’s past and present. If everyone understood that history, she said, “I think we would have a less divisive country.”
Young said he hopes young visitors leave with more than knowledge of figures such as Douglass, Truth, Henson and Wheatley. He wants them to recognize their personal connections to the nation’s history. 
“Black folks, we’re part of the whole American story,” he said.
The “+” in the exhibition’s title leaves room for the stories still being discovered in archives, family collections and oral traditions — as well as the declarations that have yet to be written, its curators said.
“Come out and learn about history and be inspired to tell the next story where Black folks are included,” Young said.
The exhibition is on view through December.

name: Nevada Current
title: Buck hitches wagon to defense contractor who schemed to defraud taxpayers
description: When Nevada State Senator and Republican congressional candidate Carrie Buck paraded around Boulder City on the Fourth of July, it was on a truck belonging to a Nevada-based defense contractor who admits he colluded to defraud the U.S. government.   John Buscema, the owner of S.A.F.E. Structure, a Nevada company, and USA Manufacturing, a Florida corporation,[...]
text:
A S.A.F.E. vehicle advertises congressional candidate Carrie Buck's campaign at a 4th of July parade in Boulder City. (Photo courtesy of a parade attendee)When Nevada State Senator and Republican congressional candidate Carrie Buck paraded around Boulder City on the Fourth of July, it was on a truck belonging to a Nevada-based defense contractor who admits he colluded to defraud the U.S. government.  
John Buscema, the owner of S.A.F.E. Structure, a Nevada company, and USA Manufacturing, a Florida corporation, admitted in 2024 that his companies plotted from 2014 through 2023 with another defense contractor to rig bids for military contracts. Buscema agreed last year to pay a $1 million settlement to resolve the government’s False Claims Act suit.. 
Buscema contributed $7,000, the maximum allowed for an individual, to Buck’s campaign for Congress. She’s challenging Rep. Dina Titus, a Democrat, in Nevada’s Congressional District 1. 
Buscema also chipped in an additional $3,000 to GOP Winning Women, a Super PAC that has contributed $28,439 to Buck. 
S.A.F.E. Structure designs and manufactures support equipment and logistics for the U.S. Armed Forces. In addition to the military, it lists Boeing, Airbus, Cessna, and Learject among its clients. 
On his personal website, Buscema “attributes all his success to his Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ…” 
Buscema admitted to assisting in bid rigging by using his companies to make more than 100 bids for contracts he had no intention of winning, according to the settlement agreement. His companies coordinated with NOBLE, a Boston-based defense contractor that provided details to colluders that allowed another vendor to submit a lower bid, though higher than one resulting from a legitimate process.   
Buscema also paid other vendors to submit some 60 false bids so that his companies would win the contracts. 
“As evidenced in this settlement agreement, these contractors gamed the system to line their own pockets. They manipulated and undermined the fair and open bidding process designed to save our military – and taxpayers – money,” U.S. Attorney Joshua S. Levy of Massachusetts said in a news release last year. “Contractors should be scrupulous in dealing with the government, not coordinating with each other to pad their bottom line. When defense contractors collude, rather than compete, they violate the law and the public’s trust.”
Cheating the Dept. of Defense not only wastes taxpayer money, but also compromises the security of troops by supplying the government with inferior or defective weapons. It also deprives the military of revenue that could be used to support the troops. 
Buck has a personal interest in the well-being of U.S. troops. She is the mother of an Army Green Beret and combat medic. 
It’s unknown if she was aware of Buschema’s fraudulent acts when she accepted his contributions. The candidate and her campaign did not respond to requests for comment. 
“This is the height of hypocrisy,” Titus’ campaign spokesman Dick Cooper said in a statement. “She should return the money, just like John Buscema had to pay $1 million to settle the charges against him by the Department of Justice.”
Buscema also did not respond to the Current’s inquiries.

name: Nevada Current
title: Majority of Nevadans support tobacco tax hike, survey says
description: Nearly two-thirds of Nevada voters would support raising the state’s tobacco tax, according to a new survey commissioned by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network. The survey, conducted by Lake Research Partners and The Tarrance Group, comes as ACS CAN and other public health groups push state lawmakers to consider backing a tobacco tax […]
text:
Public health advocates are pushing Nevada lawmakers to raise and revise Nevada's taxes on tobacco products. (Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)Nearly two-thirds of Nevada voters would support raising the state’s tobacco tax, according to a new survey commissioned by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network.
The survey, conducted by Lake Research Partners and The Tarrance Group, comes as ACS CAN and other public health groups push state lawmakers to consider backing a tobacco tax hike. Nevada’s per-pack cigarette tax rate hasn’t been raised since 2015. Advocates argue raising the tax would increase revenue for the state while decreasing the number of smokers, particularly in young and low-income communities.
According to ACS CAN, 63% of likely voters in Nevada indicated they would support a tobacco tax increase whose revenue would be dedicated to programs that prevent tobacco use. 
The survey also found that 59% of likely voters in Nevada are either very (33%) or somewhat (26%) concerned about young people in the community using tobacco products.
ACS CAN Nevada Government Relations Director Jennifer Atlas said in a statement that the survey shows voters “want their lawmakers to pass a meaningful tobacco tax so future generations are protected from the health effects of using tobacco and those who are addicted to tobacco products can quit.”
Advocates made their tobacco tax hike pitch to an interim legislative committee focused on revenue last month. They are pushing to double the cigarette tax and raise the “other tobacco products” tax to keep taxes equitable. That committee is expected to select what bills it will back when it meets later this month.
Recent surveys in other states also found broad support for raising tobacco taxes.
The ACS CAN survey also found 85% of likely voters in Nevada believe it is extremely (53%) or very (33%) important that all Americans, no matter what health insurance they have, should have access to cancer screening and treatment that is close to home and affordable.
It also found that a vast majority — 91% — agreed with the sentiment that “families across the country are feeling squeezed by rising healthcare and insurance costs” and “leaders should focus on making care more affordable and protecting access to health services people depend on.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Jay DeBoyer could help John James avoid a nasty GOP convention fight
description: Lansing legislative experience, support from the grassroots wing of the Michigan Republican Party and a path to a smooth convention vote later this month were all reasons for GOP insiders to be excited about state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) as Republican gubernatorial candidate John James’s running mate in the November general election. James, a congressman [[...]
text:
Michigan House Oversight Committee Chair Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay Township) talks to reporters on continuing allegations of ethics violation by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel. Dec. 16, 2025 | Screenshot Lansing legislative experience, support from the grassroots wing of the Michigan Republican Party and a path to a smooth convention vote later this month were all reasons for GOP insiders to be excited about state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) as Republican gubernatorial candidate John James’s running mate in the November general election.
James, a congressman from Shelby Township, announced Thursday that he had selected DeBoyer, the current chair of the House Oversight Committee.
Several Republican consultants who spoke to Michigan Advance for this story said that was likely a wise choice following James’ tough primary fight against businessman Perry Johnson — who had launched a grassroots opposition campaign against James in the August election, and drove a wedge between him and James with GOP voters across the state.
Jason Roe, who previously served as executive director of the Michigan Republican Party, said DeBoyer has focused his work as chairman of the oversight committee “to highlight  excesses of Democratic leadership, the lack of transparency, and some of the waste, fraud, and abuse within government.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That would make DeBoyer “a very good wingman for John James in terms of reminding people of the failures of Democratic leadership over the last eight years of Gretchen Whitmer.”
Roe said that he believed Lansing legislative experience — which James does not have — was an absolute top priority for a running mate choice. DeBoyer is in his second term in the Michigan House and likely could have an upward leadership trajectory if he chose to remain in the House. As a candidate for reelection this year, DeBoyer was set to defend his 63rd House District seat against Democrat Jamie Sonnenberger.
Gongwer News Service, a Lansing-based statewide political news outlet, noted that DeBoyer would give up his seat if officially nominated at the Michigan Republican Party’s Aug. 22 convention.
Andrea Bitely of Bitely Communications, and the previous spokesperson for Mike Duggan’s suspended 2026 independent gubernatorial campaign, also highlighted DeBoyer’s legislative knowledge, as well as his good reputation in the gun rights and pro-life communities, calling him a “help no hurt” candidate.
Michigan State Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) speaks at a Second Amendment March event outside the Michigan Capitol Building on Sept. 19, 2024. | Photo: Anna Liz Nichols
“He’s not somebody that has, as far as I know, a lot of baggage that he brings to the campaign,” Bitely said. “So he’s going to be theoretically helpful, but he’s not going to create drama for the James team, in any way, shape, or form.”
James came out on the top of a divisive primary against Johnson — as well as former attorney general Mike Cox and Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt, who both suspended their campaigns prior to the Aug. 4 primaries. 
While James enjoyed the backing of much of the party establishment, including President Donald Trump, who endorsed him in June, Johnson rallied significant grassroots support, especially after Nesbitt and Cox dropped out of the race.
“They are working very hard to bring everybody back to the table, and a Jay DeBoyer pick is that,” Bitely said, adding that James might be hoping this will bring Johnson voters back onto his side. “It is uniting, not dividing.”
DeBoyer is also a strategic pick because of his role heading the House Oversight Committee, a role which he has used to investigate and question top Democratic officials, including Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor. 
Both Bitely and Roe said that they expect DeBoyer to act as an “attack dog” for the campaign, with Roe noting, “he probably knows her vulnerabilities as well as anybody in Lansing, and so I think that’s going to be a huge benefit.”



Quotation







There’s always the potential of some mischief at convention and ratifying the lieutenant governor pick. ... I think Jay really puts all that conversation to bed.


– Jason Roe, a Republican political consultant


On the other hand, Dennis Lennox, a Republican public affairs consultant, was more skeptical of DeBoyer as the choice for running mate, noting in a statement, “I would have named a woman because I believe that parties need to balance the ticket, but it wasn’t my selection to make.”
He added that James “chose a governing partner, not a geographic or demographic box-checker” in DeBoyer.
DeBoyer joins James on the all-male statewide Republican ticket, along with former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers as the U.S. Senate candidate, Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd as the attorney general candidate and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini as the secretary of state candidate.
But concerns about the gender makeup of the Republican ticket were not shared by Roe or Bitely.
“I don’t think it’s going to make a difference at all, and I say that as someone who would prefer to have a woman on the ticket,” Bitely said. “I think it matters more on the Democratic side than it does on the Republican side at this point.”
Roe noted that, although it is the first time that Republicans have not had a female candidate on the top of their ticket in decades, he believes that voters are more focused on “competence and a commitment to reforming government.”
Lennox also said that DeBoyer was seen as a potential future leader in the legislature for the Republican Party, but must now give up his House seat to run for the position of lieutenant governor.
DeBoyer ran unopposed in the Republican primary for re-election to his seat in House District 63 this year –- a district which he won twice with over 60% of the vote in the 2024 and 2026 general elections. Republican officials in Macomb and St. Clair counties, which DeBoyer’s district covers parts of, will have to choose a replacement for him on the ballot.
Michigan’s U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township (center right), a Republican candidate for governor, speaks at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump (center) at General Motors Proving Grounds in Milford, Mich. James was invited on stage by Trump, along with former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake (center left), the GOP candidate for the U.S. Senate, US. Rep. Tim Walberg of Tipton (left) and U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain of Bruce Township. July 27, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
All three consultants emphasized the importance of a smooth nominating convention, to be held in Mt. Pleasant later this month, to officially name their candidates in the general election.
“There’s always the potential of some mischief at convention and ratifying the lieutenant governor pick, and there were certainly some smoke signals being sent that there might be mischief at our convention,” Roe said. “I think Jay really puts all that conversation to bed. I think he’s got such broad support within the activist base that he should get approved without any challenge.”
Bitely agreed that James needs an easy convention, and Lennox similarly said there would be “no chance” that DeBoyer’s selection would be derailed at the convention because “malcontents would have to defeat the rules just to put forth an alternative candidate.”
Roe — who is also working with Republican campaigns for U.S. House and Michigan House seats — said that having DeBoyer stumping for incumbent Republicans in down-ballot races, especially his state House colleagues, is very helpful because he can speak about those candidates with authority.
“I also think because of his focus on waste, fraud, and abuse, and transparency, that he brings a very strong messaging resume to the ticket that I think all the candidates in the party, whether they’re at the state or federal level, will be talking about,” Roe said. 
That confidence is a contrast to the type of concerns raised by Lennox both before and after the primary: That James’ nomination as governor might hurt down-ballot candidates, as he had significantly less cash on hand at the end of the primary than Johnson, who almost entirely self-funded his campaign to the tune of around $30 million.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Most of this Utah county’s license plate camera data is searched by out-of-state law enforcement
description: License plate cameras are under scrutiny as questions on misuse and surveillance emerge throughout the country. In Utah, a political action committee is sounding the alarm, after having found that the vast majority of the camera records searches in one county originated outside the state. The records of 10 license plate cameras from the Flock […]
text:
A Flock Automated License Plate Reader on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)License plate cameras are under scrutiny as questions on misuse and surveillance emerge throughout the country. In Utah, a political action committee is sounding the alarm, after having found that the vast majority of the camera records searches in one county originated outside the state.
The records of 10 license plate cameras from the Flock Safety network installed in Weber County streets were searched 5.1 million times between February 2022 and July 2026. Almost 97% of those searches came from law enforcement agencies outside of Utah, an investigation from the Utah Civic Compact found. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The No. 1 searcher of Weber County camera records was the Houston Police Department, which accounted for over a third of all activity.
“When the Flock cameras were proposed, it was pitched to the public as a mechanism by which public safety can be protected, and how technology can make us safer,” Clark Dice, communications director of the Utah Civic Compact said on Thursday. “The more that we dive into this issue, the more we’re learning that these cameras and this technology and the data is being utilized to surveil people who either live, work, or visit Utah.”
It’s not clear how many license plate reader cameras there are in Utah, but the website lprmaps.com has logged 944 in the state, ranking it No. 28 in the nation for total cameras.
The Flock network uses license plate recognition technologies and vehicle data to help law enforcement investigate crimes. According to its website, the company says its platform is currently used to solve about 2,000 crimes per day.
The Utah report comes at the same time as Flock Safety’s announcement of changes to its platform to address privacy concerns and “documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement,” according to a report from the Associated Press.



Let us know what you think...


 


Among the updates set to be implemented next year, all law enforcement customers must establish an audit tool to flag abnormal search behavior. Retention of the data the cameras capture will also be reduced from 30 days to seven, unless it is evidence tied to a case, and law enforcement will need a case number to do a search.
The Utah Civic Compact isn’t alleging any unlawful activity, Dice said. It is possible they have an automatic procedure to use the data available in the network. But that’s unclear so far. The Houston Police Department didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment on Thursday.
However, members of the compact worry about the disproportionate number of out-of-state searches, and wonder what laws those agencies have to adhere to before getting access to Utah data.
Utah law limits searches to active criminal investigations, outstanding warrants, or to search for a missing or endangered person or a stolen vehicle, the Utah Civic Compact said in a release. 
“Save for conducting individual audits of 3,343 agencies (that have searched for Weber County data) there is no mechanism to even know if searches by non-Utah agencies are adhering to Utah’s ALPR search restrictions,” the group said in a release.
The Utah Civic Compact is asking for a legislative audit of the license plate cameras operating in the state, as well as other actions to close the “jurisdictional gap” that happens when out-of-state agencies search for Utah data.
“We want it codified into Utah state law that if you’re going to surveil this very sensitive data, there must be an established process by which you can do it,” Dice said. “Right now, it is our understanding that there’s a bit of a loophole that’s being utilized and we want that to stop as soon as possible.”
