name: Georgia Recorder
title: Potent, mislabeled and easy to buy: Inside Georgia’s kratom market
description: On a chilly night this past February, Andrew Wood died alone in his bed after consuming a kratom product purchased legally at a Brunswick vape shop. He was 24. According to his mother and girlfriend, who found his body, the former Brunswick High School student had been consuming the psychoactive substance for months and thought […]
text:
Carrie Boswell holds a photo of her son, Andrew Wood, who died from an unintentional kratom overdose in February 2026. In Brunswick on April 1, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaOn a chilly night this past February, Andrew Wood died alone in his bed after consuming a kratom product purchased legally at a Brunswick vape shop. He was 24.
According to his mother and girlfriend, who found his body, the former Brunswick High School student had been consuming the psychoactive substance for months and thought it was safe.
Derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia, kratom products are sold widely across Georgia as tablets, powders, drinks and concentrated extracts. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has not approved kratom for human consumption, yet supporters of the $1 billion industry tout such products as a natural alternative for pain relief or opioid recovery. “Some use it as a substitute for coffee,” said Jack Kingston, the former U.S. congressman from Savannah who testified before Georgia state lawmakers in 2025 on behalf of the American Kratom Association.
Yet an investigation by The Current GA suggests a more complicated reality.
Liquid kratom extract, natural leaf powder, capsules, and pressed pills containing 7OH. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
Producers have flooded Georgia with synthetic, highly concentrated products derived from kratom that pose more danger than the plant’s natural form. Additionally, labels for dozens of kratom products post misleading information about the potency of the ingredients, and in some cases, conceal the presence of addictive and potentially lethal compounds, according to lab tests analyzed by The Current.
Despite documenting misleading labeling as far back as 2018, Georgia has not created a regulatory body or funding mechanism for law enforcement agencies to test whether kratom products violate the law — a situation that public health officials and some industry supporters say endangers hundreds of consumers.
Between 2019 and 2025, Georgia medical examiners detected kratom in the systems of more than 740 victims of accidental overdoses, according to state and federal data. However, public health officials say the actual number is likely much higher because only a handful of Georgia’s 159 counties test for kratom alkaloids in standard toxicology screenings. What’s more, they say, many medical examiners across the state are unfamiliar with the synthetically boosted substances in kratom products that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration says are contributing to a third wave of the opioid crisis, let alone with how those substances might interact with common medications such as antihistamines, antidepressants, or alcohol.
“Kratom is an emerging issue that people really don’t know about,” said Heather Trela, the head of operations at The Nelson A. Rockefeller Institute of Government. “It’s really the Wild West out there.”
St. Simons state Rep. Rick Townsend, the main sponsor of Georgia’s current kratom laws, believes that the industry has gotten too big too quickly, but he’s not convinced that all kratom products are harmful. He says he would back tougher regulations that would remove kratom from store shelves and place it behind pharmacy counters.
Law enforcement officers contacted in Georgia’s six coastal counties confirmed that they are not proactively enforcing existing kratom laws.
Carrie Boswell, the mother of Wood, says she is confident that the bottle of MIT 45 Super K found next to her son’s body played a role in his demise. She does not yet have conclusive answers, however.
The initial Glynn County coroner report lists his cause of death as “pending.” Although Glynn County police took the kratom bottle as evidence and listed a previous medical emergency involving kratom, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation did not test Wood’s body for kratom when conducting his autopsy.
Boswell also believes that her son wasn’t trying to harm himself when he drank the product. But that underscores the danger, she said.
“It’s killing people,” Boswell said. “I don’t think it should be sold at all. Period.”
C.M. “Mac” Haddow, the senior fellow on public policy for the American Kratom Association, says that view is misguided. His organization says there is no credible evidence linking natural kratom to any death. Yet he concedes that the synthetically boosted kratom products, which he says dominate about 50% of the market, do pose a threat to consumers. “Those are products that should be banned,” said Haddow, “I think that those products pose a real risk. They are, in fact, opioids, and they have the same addiction profile.”
The Current has spent three months attempting by email and phone to reach each company mentioned in this story, as well as the association that represents the synthetic kratom industry, but received no responses by the date of publication.
Previously, the association that supports the synthetic kratom industry has pushed back on assertions that these products are dangerous. “This isn’t about public health, it’s about power, money, and market control,” said Jeff Smith, National Policy Director for HART. “We are seeing political influence and industry pressure converge around a single narrative: make 7-OH the scapegoat.”
Changing kratom market challenges state regulators
Kratom has been used as an energy supplement and pain remedy in Southeast Asia for hundreds of years, but its use in America illustrates both the complexity and the gray areas of federal and state regulations.
Kratom is illegal to import for human consumption to the U.S., yet products derived from the natural kratom leaf started to become widely available in many states when the opioid epidemic was at its peak. Federal survey data from 2019, the most recent statistics available, estimate that about 1.7 million Americans ages 12 and older used kratom that year, and the most common consumers were males aged 26 to 49.
That’s despite the fact that the FDA classifies synthetic kratom products, which since 2023 have started taking up market share, as the next wave of the opioid epidemic.
The flood of kratom products has prompted states to step into a regulatory vacuum to assert some control of the growing marketplace.
In Georgia, kratom products, both natural and synthetic, are legal to purchase, up to a certain potency, for adults 21 and older. That compares to Alabama, Louisiana, Arkansas and Tennessee, which have banned all kratom due to perceived dangers. The Pentagon, meanwhile, has banned service members from consuming any kratom product.
Georgia’s first kratom laws date to 2019, when state lawmakers passed industry-approved legislation that banned sales to minors and mandated basic labeling.
Still, the market for kratom soared — along with kratom-related poisonings and deaths in Georgia, according to state data.

How does it work?

Kratom’s two main psychoactive compounds are mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, commonly known as 7-OH. These exist in small amounts in the natural plant but are synthetically boosted in many products sold legally in Georgia. These alkaloids act on the same opioid receptors in the brain as morphine and fentanyl. At low doses, these substances can produce stimulant-like effects, such as increased energy and alertness. At higher doses, they can cause euphoria, slowed breathing, loss of consciousness and in some cases, seizures. The FDA says 7-OH is engineered to be addictive.
By 2022, more products were being sold with concentrated 7-OH extracts, according to industry and public health officials. Federal health officials say 7-OH can be 46 times stronger than standard kratom and can be more potent than morphine.
That was the year, according to Rep. Townsend, that Glynn County experienced its first known kratom-related death: Wes Rogers, the 42-year-old former president of the Frederica Yacht Club and member of St. Simons Island United Methodist Church.
Rogers first encountered kratom after a friend suggested the product to help ease the anxiety Rogers had struggled with since his days at Glynn Academy, his mother Anne said.
At first, the family said the substance seemed to help. But the natural plant products were causing signs of addiction, Rogers told his family. He started drinking heavily. At times, his family said, he acted erratically and violently. In late 2021, he checked himself into rehab for kratom addiction.
“Those were horrible times,” Anne Rogers said. “He was never like that before kratom. He was the sweetest boy.”
Anne Rogers holds a photo of her son, Wes Rogers, who passed away in 2022 from an unintentional kratom overdose. On Saint Simons on March 12, 2026.Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
In January 2022, Rogers returned home to St. Simons, began attending Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and stayed clean for two months, according to his mother. In March, he told his family he was going back to kratom to cope with his anxiety.
Four months later, his father found Rogers’ dead body in his shower. More than 40 kratom pills were recovered nearby, his mother said. Those pills contained the natural kratom powder that industry supporters say is safe.
The GBI medical examiner did not perform an autopsy on Rogers or a toxicology test, according to documents obtained by The Current, so kratom was never identified officially as a contributing factor in his death. The GBI did not respond to requests for comment.
Around the same time, Georgia officials and addiction specialists started chronicling higher rates of kratom-related medical emergencies and deaths across the state, causing them to sound an alarm.
“It causes a dependence, just like opioids,” Patrick Filkins, clinical toxicologist at the Georgia Poison Center, said about kratom. “Patients who become daily users are either trying to get off fentanyl, or they start using it for some other purported health care reason. They become dependent on it, and the withdrawal is particularly severe,” he said.
Townsend, meanwhile, began advocating for stronger kratom laws.
In 2023, he sponsored legislation to ban all kratom products, both the natural leaf and the synthetic concentrated products, a move opposed by the American Kratom Association. The effort ultimately failed, as state lawmakers adopted industry-generated draft legislation that kept all products legal while adding another new layer of oversight.
In 2025, the legal age to buy kratom rose to 21, up from 18. Kratom products were moved behind counters or sold from locked cases. Kratom vaping products were banned, and for the first time the state set limits for how much mitragynine and 7-OH could be sold per serving size.
That was considered a compromise between Townsend’s position, which was to ban these synthetic products, and the industry pushback.
By the time the new law took effect, kratom manufacturers and distributors started falling out over the perceived dangers of their products, with the American Kratom Association removing synthetic kratom companies from its membership.
Across Georgia, synthetic kratom products were surging, and those companies evolved marketing strategies to build consumer habit, according to Filkins, while taking advantage of the weakness of Georgia law: a lack of regulation and enforcement.
Packaging and marketing to promote the dizzying array of synthetic kratom products made it difficult for consumers to determine whether they were buying a natural substance or a highly addictive extract, he said.

Lab results raise questions about kratom labels

At the state Legislature, a 2018 state House study came to a similar conclusion. The report by lawmakers found that many kratom products did not accurately list their ingredients and that labeling often omitted risky substances.
Still, legislators did not take action to punish such risky behavior, even as they toughened other parts of kratom laws, according to Eli Cohen, a U.S. Army intelligence officer and former police officer who now works in Atlanta as a plaintiffs’ lawyer.
Cohen spent much of 2025 and 2026 examining whether these kratom industry business tactics endanger consumers. His research has included purchasing a variety of synthetic kratom products in multiple stores in multiple Georgia counties. He then sent them for testing at the University of Florida’s Clinical and Translational Science Institute, the same lab that the American Kratom Association has used for similar work.
The lab results of those products bought across the state, including Coastal Georgia, suggest that most “violate either the content requirements, the content limitations, or the labeling requirements” mandated by Georgia law, Cohen said.
An assortment of kratom-derived products is commonly sold in vape shops and gas stations. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
At the same time, those lab tests show that packaging left off substances that the FDA says are dangerous, leaving consumers in the dark about what they might be ingesting, Cohen said.
Separately, The Current’s own research of kratom products sold in Coastal Georgia suggests marketing language can be inconsistent with state law. Georgia requires servings not to exceed 1 milligram per serving of 7-OH. Several products, however, showed levels higher than that.
Filkins said mislabeling of kratom products in Georgia is driving many of the accidental overdoses. Few people, whether doctors, first responders or consumers, understand how the active ingredients in kratom products interact with other common substances. “What we’re finding is a lot of the deaths involve other substances. So, you know, kratom plus alcohol or kratom plus something else,” Filkins said.
An ongoing lawsuit against a Georgia manufacturer of a synthetic kratom product called Black Liquid Kratom seeks to test liability for misleading packaging. In that multiyear legal battle, a Floyd County family is seeking damages from the company for what it claims was a dangerous product sold without adequate warnings about its potency and risks. Their son, 24-year-old Ethan Pope, died of mitragynine poisoning after consuming kratom, according to court documents.
OPMS, the company that makes Black Liquid, did not respond to requests to comment. The company is a member of the American Kratom Association, and the organization prominently features its brands.
Haddow, the association executive, says that safety concerns are limited to kratom products with higher levels of 7-OH, the compound that the FDA has flagged as a drug of concern.
Some national data indicates that Georgia deaths linked to kratom, as well as a growing number of medical emergencies, have included products that the association classifies as natural, as well as the synthetically boosted products. Last year, the Georgia Poison Center handled 108 cases involving kratom-related products. About 80 of those calls came from health care facilities seeking assistance for patients requiring urgent care.
About 10% of the cases involved children under 5, including a 2-year-old who in August 2025 had to be revived with Narcan after swallowing a 7-OH tablet belonging to a daycare worker in Cobb County. Five Walker County eighth-graders were hospitalized in October 2025 after ingesting concentrated 7-OH gummies.
The trend exists across the nation as well. According to the Centers for Disease Control, poison control centers nationwide have reported a 1,200% increase in kratom-related incidents between 2015 and 2025.
“It’s not all about people dying,” Filkins said. “Some of the outcomes we’re seeing are patients having to get intubated, having to go to the ICU, patients seizing because kratom can cause seizures, especially in patients with any sort of pre-existing epileptic condition or who are on other medications that lower the seizure threshold.”
Meanwhile, Savannah vape shop manager MaCailee Koernig said that kratom products that critics say are more addictive are top sellers at the southside shop where she works.
Most of the people buying such products, she said, are people seeking to treat chronic pain or recovering from opioid addiction. “I don’t think I’ve had a single person that I’ve ended up having a conversation with that wasn’t in opioid recovery,” she said about her customers. “Whether it was someone who did heroin and is struggling now, or veterans who have a lot of pain and the VA is not helping them in the ways that they need.”
Koernig said she and her staff scrutinize products before putting them on the shelves, knowing dangerous products are on the market.
But other vape stores, she said, are actively marketing more addictive products to customers without adequate warning.
A Savannah-area construction company owner in his mid-30s and recovering addict confirmed that assertion. The man, who spoke to The Current on condition of anonymity so as to not endanger his business relationships, said a different Savannah vape shop offered him a synthetic 7-OH tablet as a free sample. He took it gladly, happy to have a pain reliever he believed would be nonaddictive.
He quit using the tablets, however, after he recognized symptoms of opioid dependence, as he didn’t want to endanger his 15 years of sobriety.
A kratom sign hangs in the window of a vape shop in Coastal Georgia. This store was not included in The Current’s investigation. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
In February, lawyer Eli Cohen visited five stores in Chatham County, randomly purchased eight kratom-derived products and sent them to the University of Florida’s Clinical and Translational Science Institute for testing. Lab results analyzed by The Current suggest that six of the eight products violated at least one of the state’s potency laws.
The Current attempted to reach the companies listed on the packaging for comment, but no company responded. Contact numbers for some were not functional.
Back in Brunswick, those who loved Wood, the 24-year-old Goodwill worker, had little information about how dangerous kratom products could be, according to Lindsey Ortiz, his girlfriend of three years.
Ortiz described Wood as a sweet person who was kind to everyone in his life. The two bonded as Ortiz helped Wood recover from a broken jaw in the fall of 2025 that sidelined him from work and forced him onto a liquid-only diet.
Ortiz said her boyfriend received prescription opioids during that recovery. “That really humbled him,” Ortiz said. “He was just very irritable all the time. I think that kind of led to a bad place for him.”
Around the end of 2025, a friend offered Wood a synthetic kratom pill. Wood then researched different kratom products, his mother said, and claimed to know which were safe. Wood began taking the synthetic product to help with pain and at night to help him sleep.
“He said it’s safer than anything else you can get, you can buy it at a gas station,” his mother recalled.
One night in January, after drinking, Wood consumed a new synthetic kratom product, a compound that is even more potent than 7-OH called “pseudo” mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, his girlfriend said. “Pseudo” started appearing in Georgia in late 2025.
Ortiz watched in horror as Wood began slurring his words and suddenly lost consciousness.
“He was struggling to breathe, like he was about to throw up,” she said. ‘I started shaking him and screaming, ‘Andrew, wake up,’ but he wouldn’t respond.”
Ortiz called 911 and followed the dispatcher’s instructions to help him lie flat before attempting mouth-to-mouth resuscitation. Wood’s fingertips had turned blue. Then, as the ambulance arrived at his apartment, he woke up.
Wood told Ortiz he would never take any kratom product again. “I believed him,” Ortiz said. “He was equally as scared as I was.”
A month later, the couple exchanged good-night texts, Ortiz recalled. Wood told her he had to be up early for work. Nothing in his messages suggested anything was wrong, she said.
On Feb. 9, Ortiz received a message from Wood’s store manager saying he had not shown up for work. She went to his house in Calebs Crossing, ran to his bedroom and found his cold body.
A photo of Andrew Wood sits on a table in his mother’s home. In Brunswick on April 1, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America

Three months later, Wood’s mother is still searching for answers about how her son lost his life.
The police officer who responded to his January medical emergency also was the responding officer at the scene of his death. His mother recalled that the officer said he had no doubt kratom was a contributing factor to Wood’s death. In the incident report, the officer cited an empty kratom bottle, as well as the earlier medical emergency.
The Glynn County Police Department declined requests for comment.
The deputy coroner of Glynn County, Justin Thornton, told The Current that he had not been told about the kratom bottle or any past kratom-related use when he ordered Wood’s autopsy.
After learning about that information from The Current, Thornton ordered a new toxicology test.
Four days before Wood’s death, Cohen was visiting Coastal Georgia as part of his kratom industry research. He allowed The Current to accompany him as he bought several kratom products for sale in Chatham County. One of these was MIT 45 Super K — the same product found near Wood’s body.
Cohen sent the bottle to the University of Florida lab for independent analysis of the ingredients. The one-ounce bottle matched the one mentioned in the police evidence log recovered at Wood’s apartment.
Lab testing of Cohen’s Super K bottle showed that it contained 399 milligrams of mitragynine. Georgia law says that the maximum amount per serving is 150 milligrams of mitragynine. While the product label said the liquid was equivalent to 15 servings, normal consumer behavior would be to drink the entire bottle in one swallow, Cohen said, given that its size is roughly half that of popular immunity shots.
Quickly consuming 399 milligrams of that substance could cause seizures, convulsions and respiratory depression, if not cardiac arrest, according to Dr. Andrew Kolodny, who testified before the Georgia House of Representatives study committee about kratom in June.
“What would likely happen in one very large acute dose would be either seizures or a heart attack from sudden cardiac death,” said Kolodny, the medical director at the Opioid Policy Research Collaborative Institute for Behavioral Health at Brandeis University.
Rep. Townsend, whose district includes the neighborhoods where Wood and Rogers both died, led a new House study committee this summer about whether Georgia should further crack down on the kratom industry.
Haddow, the representative of the kratom association, says his group backs the creation of a statewide regulator under Georgia’s Department of Agriculture as a way to rein in bad actors.
For Boswell, the policy debate feels disconnected from her sense of loss.
“This kid was my whole world,” she said. “He’s basically all I had.”
The Current GA used data from the GBI for overdose-related deaths involving kratom in 2019, 2025 and 2026.  Other years come from the CDC’s SUDORS database.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Community air quality monitoring shows periods of ‘unhealthy’ air in Sioux City
description: In 2025, Iowa Environmental Council worked with Woodbury County residents to install air quality monitors in the county. A year later, air quality data shows the county frequently has acute air pollution events.  The council analyzed data from surrounding polluters and found that fossil fuel combustion from local coal-fired power plants, emissions from local[...]
text:
A report from Iowa Environmental Council looks at air pollution in the Sioux City region. (Stock photo by EThamPhoto/Getty Images)In 2025, Iowa Environmental Council worked with Woodbury County residents to install air quality monitors in the county. A year later, air quality data shows the county frequently has acute air pollution events. 
The council analyzed data from surrounding polluters and found that fossil fuel combustion from local coal-fired power plants, emissions from local processing facilities and vehicle emissions caused a “concerning pattern of long-term exposure” in the Siouxland region. 
Exposure to the type of air pollutants measured by the monitors, particulate matter 2.5, or PM2.5, can contribute to “a wide range of adverse health outcomes” including respiratory illnesses and cardiovascular disease, strokes and certain types of cancer. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the report notes multiple pollution sources impacting PM2.5 levels in the region, it also finds correlation between periods of high PM2.5 levels and reported emissions from the George Neal North and George Neal South power plants. 
One of Iowa Environmental Council’s main priorities is pushing for continued transition from coal-powered energy to renewable energy sources like wind and solar. In a news release about the report, council staff members called for a phaseout of the coal plants, which are both owned and operated by MidAmerican Energy Company. 
“Air pollution is an issue across Iowa, but the effects are not felt uniformly,” Jordan Oster, the council’s energy program director said. “The Sioux City community is bearing the health impacts of MidAmerican Energy’s dirty coal plants. We need our utilities to transition away from coal, and until they do so, our utilities should be held responsible for the cost of their pollution.” 
Geoff Greenwood, the media relations manager for MidAmerican Energy Company, said in a statement the report draws “broad conclusions” on the causes of local air quality conditions. 
“To put it plainly, the report encourages readers to focus on a few selected sources while overlooking the fact that many other factors may have contributed to the measured air quality conditions,” Greenwood said. 
What are PM2.5 monitors?
Iowa Environmental Council helped residents install six PurpleAir monitors for PM 2.5 in Woodbury County shortly after the council published a report that listed the county as having the highest rates of asthma in adults over 18, compared to other Iowa counties. 
PurpleAir monitors are wifi-enabled monitors that measure particulate air pollutants and report to a global air quality database to enable citizen-led, near real-time monitoring of air quality. 
Particulate matter is a mixture of solid and liquid particles in the air, like dust, dirt, smoke and other smaller particles. PM2.5 refers to “fine inhalable particles” with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or smaller – about 30 times smaller than the diameter of a single human hair, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. 
EPA holds these smaller particles pose the greatest health problems as the fine particles can be absorbed “deep” into the lungs and even enter the bloodstream. Exposure to these particles, according to EPA, is linked to aggravated asthma, premature death in people with heart or lung conditions, heart attacks and decreased lung function. 
A year’s worth of data from the monitors shows a “highly synchronized, city-wide problem” according to the report. 
“Rather than experiencing isolated local incidents, the entire Greater Sioux City area undergoes simultaneous, acute pollution events,” the report said. 
A sensor installed on Market Street in downtown Sioux City showed a “concerning pattern of long-term exposure” where PM2.5 levels formed a “continuous block of pollution” through the spring and summer months rather than periodic spikes that exceed EPA thresholds for “unhealthy” and “unhealthy for certain groups.” 
A chart from an Iowa Environmental Council report shows a correlation between nitrogen oxides and sulfurdioxide emissions and measured PM2.5 levels. (Graph courtesy of Iowa Environmental Council)
Sources of PM2.5 
Some sources of particulate matter are directly emitted, but most, per EPA, are in the atmosphere as a result of “complex reactions” of chemicals emitted from power plants, industries and vehicles, like sulfur dioxide SO2 and nitrogen oxides, NOx. 
The report tracked a correlation between increased SO2 and NOx emissions and higher PM2.5 levels in the region. This correlation, it argues means a connection between increased coal plant emissions and PM2.5 levels. 
“Although this correlation does not equal causation, it does underscore the coal plants’ role as a key contributor to regional particulate pollution during this timeframe,” the report said. 
It also notes that things like wildfire smoke contribute to regional increases in fine particulate matter and that other local sources, like industrial facilities, commercial operations, transportation “also contribute to ambient air quality.” 
A chart of major local polluters shows that a fertilizer facility actually pollutes more than either of the George Neal power plants, though not more than the emissions of the two combined. 
“Recognizing multiple pollution sources does not diminish the severe impact of coal emissions on community air quality,” the report said. “Instead, the data reveal a layered environment in which coal emissions elevate baseline PM2.5 levels and stack on top of other local sources of pollution.” 
Greenwood with MidAmerican said the report’s conclusions are “based primarily on correlations.” He said the report acknowledges the role that other emission sources have on PM2.5 levels but  “inaccurately attributed air quality conditions to a single source without a comprehensive evaluation of all contributing factors.”
“Some of those factors could have had an equal or even greater impact, but the report does not quantify their contribution,” Greenwood said. “As a result, readers may be left with the impression that these other influences were insignificant when, in reality, the report does not provide the analysis needed to support that conclusion.” 
Greenwood said all MidAmerican facilities “comply with federal and state environmental laws and regulations” and that the company will continue to do so and “invest in cleaner energy resources, and provide the safe, reliable and affordable energy our customers depend on every day.” 
He said the company’s investments into wind energy have related to considerable reductions in carbon dioxide, sulfur oxides and nitrogen oxides emissions. 
“Similar reductions in particulate matter emissions have occurred during the same timeframe,” Greenwood said. 
Health impacts and recommendations 
The report notes that long-term exposure to elevated PM2.5 pollution is linked to increased hospitalizations, chronic illness and mortality. 
Asthma-related emergency room visits have increased in Woodbury County over the past several years, according to the report.
Data from the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, however, show Woodbury County rates of emergency room visits due to asthma are fairly consistent with overall rates for the state. The rate of asthma hospitalizations has been higher in Woodbury County than the state average since 2022, however. 
The Iowa Environmental Council report called for coordinated action to “reduce emissions, improve exposure monitoring, and strengthen public health protections.” 
Recommendations in the report include: expanding air quality monitoring, adding air pollution exposure screenings in healthcare assessments, sending public text message alerts during air quality index spikes, adopting electric vehicles, advocating for emissions controls and clean energy investments. 
The council will host a free presentation and panel on the report and air pollution health effects Thursday from 5:30 to 6:30 at the Sioux City Public Museum.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisianians more interested in politics, less polarized than most Americans, survey finds
description: A new survey on civic life in Louisiana has found that while Louisianians are more interested in politics than the rest of the country, they are less politically polarized.  The Louisiana Common Ground Survey was published Wednesday by the LSU Reilly Center for Public Affairs and the Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana, a nonprofit […]
text:
A voter walks into a polling location at the Zachary Public Library for the May 16, 2026, election (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)A new survey on civic life in Louisiana has found that while Louisianians are more interested in politics than the rest of the country, they are less politically polarized. 
The Louisiana Common Ground Survey was published Wednesday by the LSU Reilly Center for Public Affairs and the Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana, a nonprofit good governance organization. 
“These findings show that Louisianans can disagree on politics while still sharing important democratic values,” PAR president Steven Procopio said. “That broad commitment to free speech, equal opportunity and constitutional principles creates space for more constructive debate and cooperation.” 
Nearly half of Louisianians reported being very or extremely interested in politics, a significant gap from the 28% nationwide found in a 2023 Pew survey. Over half of all respondents said they discuss government and politics several times a week or nearly every day, compared to 45% nationwide. 
“It’s said that all politics is local, and Louisianans not only understand that mantra but live by it, comfortably talking to people they politically disagree with, while steering clear of such talk on social media,” said LSU Reilly Center Director Michael DiResto. 
The survey found that while 70% have had a real-life conversation in the last month with someone with different political views from their own, only 8% frequently post about politics on social media, which the report identified as a possible sign of civic health. 
Researchers also found that Louisianians have a high opinion of democratic norms, with 91% of respondents saying they believe in equal free speech rights, regardless of political beliefs, and 70% saying they believe political violence is never justified. Also, 92% of Louisianians reported they believed individuals deserve an equal opportunity to succeed regardless of race or ethnicity. 
In addition, The results show 81% of Louisiana residents want their elected officials to find common ground with public officials of the opposing party. 
The researchers also measured polarization, the gap between how positively an individual feels about their own party versus how negatively they feel about the opposing party. 
On a scale of 0-100, Louisiana’s polarization rate is 48.2, compared to 49.9 nationwide. But when pollsters asked individuals to imagine a person respondents know that belongs to the opposing party, the state’s polarization score dropped to 38.
The survey also revealed Louisianians’ trust in institutions is low. Survey respondents said their trust in scientists, universities, state, local and federal government, courts and news organizations fell between “not much” and a “fair amount.” Only hospitals and doctors were ranked between a “fair amount” and a “great deal.” 
The most common news sources for Louisianians is local television news and friends and family and the most commonly used social media site is Facebook, the survey found. 
LSU policy researchers conducted the poll from Nov. 29 through March 2 and surveyed 1,046 adults in Louisiana. It has a margin of error of 3.4%.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV DEP approves air quality permit for plastic pyrolysis facility in Belle despite local resistance
description: The state Department of Environmental Protection issued a finalized air quality permit on Wednesday to Clean-Seas West Virginia, allowing the out-of-state company to move forward with the construction of a controversial “advanced recycling” plant in eastern Kanawha County.
text:
Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who is concerned about the proposed Clean Seas project, speaks at the Kanawha County Commission meeting on July 23, 2026. Caruthers — along with several of his neighbors — delivered a petition signed by nearly 1,000 residents opposing the pyrolysis plant to Commissioners Ben Salango and Natalie Tennant. (Photo by Caity Coyne/West Virginia Watch)
The state Department of Environmental Protection issued a finalized air quality permit on Wednesday to Clean-Seas West Virginia, allowing the out-of-state company to move forward with the construction of a controversial “advanced recycling” plant in eastern Kanawha County. 
The permit was approved despite numerous concerns raised by dozens of residents in Belle, West Virginia, where the plant would be located, as well as the Kanawha County Commission and Charleston City Council. In the DEP’s final determination letter, regulators said that the concerns voiced by residents — including the company’s financial instability, the proposed facility’s impact on air quality, the region’s burgeoning tourism economy and its proximity to local schools, among other things — did not violate the state’s set standards for issuing air quality permits.
For locals and advocates who have been organizing in opposition to the facility, the DEP’s permit approval was not a surprise, but was still disappointing.
“This is pretty much what we expected from the DEP,” said Lani Wean, the West Virginia field organizer for the nonprofit environmental group Moms Clean Air Force. “They have a pretty consistent pattern of approving permits like these and essentially ignoring community input and concerns.”
For over a year, Wean has worked alongside Belle residents and other organizers to sound the alarm on the proposed pyrolysis plant, educating people on how it could actually function and what might be at stake if Clean-Seas does begin operations.
The DEP previously granted a draft permit for the facility, which would operate by burning plastic feedstock to create pyrolysis oil, synthetic gas and solid residue to be used and sold for petrochemical manufacturing purposes.
Locals have voiced concerns about the potential emissions that could come, especially as the proposed location sits only a few hundred feet from Riverside High School, Midland Trail Elementary School and  residential neighborhoods. They wonder how the facility, located in the old 84 Lumber building, will affect a new offroad trail system meant to bolster the area’s tourism opportunities and the local economy.
Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who has been heading organizing efforts within his community, said that the stakes are high for him and his neighbors, who will continue to fight against Clean-Seas despite the DEP’s permit issuance.
“The community members that have gotten together to fight this are very passionate and engaged on this, and we are not giving up,” Caruthers said Thursday. “So we’re looking at our next steps, how to strategize, how to continue the fight because even though the permit was approved, we still don’t want it and we’re not going to just let it happen.”
Residents are also wary of Clean Vision Corporation’s (the parent company of Clean-Seas) track record in opening and operating the types of facilities it’s proposing for Belle, and question its overall financial stability. 
According to a report published last month by the Ohio River Valley Institute, the company currently has two operational pyrolysis facilities: one in India and another in Morocco. Since operations began at those locations in 2023, filings with the federal Securities and Exchange Commission show the company has generated less than $614,000 in revenue from pyrolysis activities, with the income shrinking year over year. Meanwhile, it’s accumulated nearly $58 million in deficits due to operational losses and other growing expenses.
And while the company has marketed its plastic pyrolysis process as a “clean” and a “sustainable energy solution” for the world’s ongoing plastics crisis, experts and organizers are doubtful. The technology, they’ve said, is questionable and nothing more than a rebranding of plastic incineration, which is shown to harm the environment and public health while contributing to climate change. 
“(The West Virginia DEP’s) approval of this air permit represents a rollback of critical pollution safeguards put in place to keep families and children safe from the most damaging impacts of waste incineration. In addition to departing from decades of precedent, the decision also dismisses concerns of local residents and county officials,” said ORVI Chief of Staff Tom Torres in a news release. “With this permit, Clean-Seas West Virginia has reached a critical milestone. However, If its parent company’s past performance and the industry’s track record are any indication, the facility likely faces an uphill climb towards successful commercial operation.
Wean said that the DEP’s issuance of the permit will not detract from local efforts to protect the community.  
“If anything, all this does is bolster the passion and drive with which the community will be taking on other avenues to fight against the facility,” Wean said. “Because, like I said, this was expected. So when we can’t rely on our regulatory bodies to represent us … we have to take that into our hands.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC AG Jackson: Duke Energy gave wrong information about rate hike under oath
description: Jackson said Wednesday that he wouldn’t sign onto the latest proposed settlement with Duke Energy.
text:
N.C. Attorney General Jeff Jackson speaks at a Duke University forum  Nov. 12, 2025. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)In the latest volley in a public feud between North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson and Duke Energy, Jackson accused the utility of providing incorrect information under oath. 
Kendal Bowman, North Carolina President for Duke Energy Progress and Duke Energy Carolinas, said during her testimony in front of the North Carolina Utilities Commission on Tuesday that residential customers can expect to pay about 6.8% more over the next two years. The residential rate would rise by 3.7% the first year, followed by 3.1% in the second year, she said. 
However, that’s the number for the average rate increase across all customer classes, including industrial users who pay less, according to independent calculations from Jackson’s office. Residential ratepayers under Duke Energy Progress would actually see a higher increase of 9.3% over the next two years.
“The details matter here, and Duke got it wrong under oath,” Jackson said in a statement on Thursday. “A 6.8% increase was already too high for families, and Duke can’t justify an even bigger increase.” 
Jackson said Wednesday that he wouldn’t sign onto the latest proposed settlement with Duke Energy, just as he refused to agree to an earlier proposal in July.  The agreement of the state attorney general isn’t required for the Utilities Commission to approve a deal, but the AG can take it to court if they object.
NC environmentalists continue pushing back on Duke Energy rate hike

Duke Energy Progress originally asked for an 18.1% increase on residential rates over two years, but lowered its request after months of backlash. 
Last week, Duke Energy Progress announced it had reached a settlement with the Utilities Commission’s Public Staff, a department that represents consumers in regulatory cases. They agreed to an average increase of 3.4% each year for the next two years for all users, but didn’t offer an estimate of how much more the average residential customer would pay. 
State leaders and environmentalists said even 3.4% is still too high.
Dan Crawford, senior director of public affairs at the North Carolina League of Conservation Voters, said during a press conference Tuesday that Duke Energy shareholders made huge profits in 2025.
“Poor, poor Duke. They’re barely scraping by on $5 billion in profits they made last year, and last week, they announced they’re already on track to make even more this year,” Crawford said sarcastically. “Clearly, they need this increase.”
The Utilities Commission is holding hearings on the Duke Energy Progress rate case before it decides whether to approve or reject the proposed settlement. New rates would take effect Jan. 1, 2027. 
A spokesperson for Duke Energy did not immediately respond to NC Newsline’s request for comment.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: The government is spying on its own citizens — again
description: That the federal government secretly recorded conversations, infiltrated Signal chats and obtained financial records of labor unions and progressive groups in Minnesota as part of a surveillance effort during Operation Metro Surge should be repugnant to all Americans.  Citing court documents released Thursday, the Reformer’s Madison McVan reports that, for i[...]
text:
Federal agents on patrol in Minneapolis, Minnesota in January. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)That the federal government secretly recorded conversations, infiltrated Signal chats and obtained financial records of labor unions and progressive groups in Minnesota as part of a surveillance effort during Operation Metro Surge should be repugnant to all Americans. 
Citing court documents released Thursday, the Reformer’s Madison McVan reports that, for instance, “Agents collected the license plate numbers of attendees during a meeting of anti-ICE protesters at Prince of Peace Lutheran Church in Roseville to obtain the names of the attendees. The agents then compiled a dossier including attendees’ names, photos, addresses, vehicle registrations, family and employment information.”
Can’t say I’ve been to Prince of Peace, but I suspect the only threat to public safety there is the over-salted hotdish. Americans are allowed to meet and strategize about how to oppose the policies of their government, especially when agents of the government were openly racially profiling people, snatching them off the street and violating their constitutional rights. It’s sort of an important thing about us. 
In a revolting bit of irony, the investigation began four days after the killing of Alex Pretti, which was about three weeks after the killing of Renee Good. 
Rather than investigate the circumstances of those killings, the Department of Justice began investigating Minnesotans. 
Unfortunately, the use of government resources and intelligence methods to investigate civil society groups engaged in lawful political activism is not surprising. 
Especially if you’re familiar with American history — and specifically the 1976 document, “Intelligence Activities and the Rights of Americans,” i.e., the Church Committee report, named after U.S. Sen. Frank Church, an Idaho Democrat, though the committee and its conclusions were bipartisan. 
The report concludes that the intelligence services and their skulduggery are necessary in a dangerous world and appropriate within strict legal, constitutionally bound limits.
And then Book 2 of the report lays out in detail over nearly 400 pages how the vast apparatus of the federal government was misused to violate the rights of American citizens.
“Whatever opinion one holds about the policies of the targeted groups, many of the tactics employed by the FBI were indisputably degrading to a free society,” the report reads. 
“For approximately 20 years the CIA carried out a program of indiscriminately opening citizens’ first class mail,” the report states. “Since the early 1930s, intelligence agencies have frequently wiretapped and bugged American citizens without the benefit of judicial warrant,” including a member of Congress, congressional staff, journalists and others who didn’t engage in criminal activity. 
“During the 1960’s alone, the FBI and CIA conducted hundreds of break-ins, many against American citizens and domestic organizations.” 
Note the word choice, indicating this was illegal behavior: Break-ins.
The FBI anonymously sent intel about people to their employers to get them fired and anonymously sent letters to spouses of targets to destroy marriages. They falsely claimed targets were government informants, thus exposing them to retributive violence. They provoked IRS audits. 
The geniuses at the FBI’s “Domestic Intelligence Division” decided that Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech, which they called “demagogic” (?!), established King as the “most dangerous and effective Negro leader in the country.”
What followed was a years-long and shameful campaign to discredit the Nobel Peace Prize winner. 
The FBI had King under heavy surveillance, “employing nearly every intelligence-gathering technique at the Bureau’s disposal … about the ‘private activities of Dr. King and his advisors’ to ‘completely discredit” them.” The FBI put their goals in writing. 
The bureau smeared him, the report states, with “executive branch officials, congressional leaders, foreign heads of state, American ambassadors, churches, universities.” 
They secretly recorded King in hotel rooms with women other than his wife and mailed them to him. 
“The tape recording was accompanied by a note which Dr. King and his advisors interpreted as threatening to release the tape recording unless Dr. King committed suicide.”
Back to our mournful present: As the filing states, “The government’s initial disclosures reflect that (Homeland Security Investigations) and the (Department of Justice) embarked on an improper investigation of First Amendment protected activity without any suggestion that the investigation’s targets had committed any crime,” the defense attorneys wrote in their filing Thursday. 
The motion continues: “Indeed, HSI undercover officers seemingly sought to manufacture a basis for prosecution where no crimes had been committed.”
For decades, the American right was obsessed with the overweening power of the federal government, the “jack-booted thugs” who were going to confiscate their guns and their Gadsden flags. I’m sure they’ll eagerly join our effort to expose and neutralize this attack on our Constitution, right? 
We don’t yet know the extent of this despotic activity by the Trump administration, but Thursday’s filing makes clear that if and when the honorable people ever again fill the halls of Congress, we’ll need yet another Church Committee for our amnesiac nation.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Political parties can survive internal struggles over identity
description: In forming opinions about public policy, I always try to look at alternatives, both for and against a proposed course of action. There is one conservative advocate that I read most frequently and that is George Will. Will is the noted Libertarian and conservative author and commentator who has won a Pulitzer Prize, is syndicated […]
text:
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night watch party in Detroit on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)In forming opinions about public policy, I always try to look at alternatives, both for and against a proposed course of action. There is one conservative advocate that I read most frequently and that is George Will.
Will is the noted Libertarian and conservative author and commentator who has won a Pulitzer Prize, is syndicated nationwide and normally writes twice weekly. I like his epistles because they are well reasoned, avoid cliches, slogans and repetitive argument based on platitudes. He also uses historical analogies, which I too enjoy. Will has even written about professional baseball, so he can’t be all bad.
But most recently he seems to have joined a chorus of writers, liberal and conservative, who have chosen to describe the party that they do not favor by the most vocal, outspoken advocates. Thus, there is only the far-right Republican party and those left-wing liberal Democrats.
I remember years ago when the New Frontier staff arrived to join the John F. Kennedy administration. Rep. Sam Rayburn, D-Texas, the speaker of the House, was asked about them. Rayburn allowed how yes, they were bright, young, and energetic, but he added, “I just wish one or two of them had run for sheriff.”
I have a similar wish to that of the former speaker, except that I would like to have those who write about political parties first run for office after having a race in a party primary. Believe me, it Is different and I write that because I’ve done that.
First things first, if you are seeking the party’s nomination for the office, run left if you’re a Democrat and right if the GOP is your party of choice. The wings of a political party vote more heavily than moderates. Wingers are more passionate about issues, follow the proceedings more closely and recruit followers to their side.
However, what recent studies have shown is that there are four to five different reasons for a person following a donkey or an elephant. Some are there simply because the family has always been there, others are motivated by a single issue.   Surprisingly, there are conservatives inside the left and progressive with the movement on the right. Some join or maintain interest in one side or the other because a candidate or a series of candidates brought them on board.
Once the party’s nomination has been obtained, the admonition given to all is “shift to the middle.” The candidate must remember there are independent voters out there who will speak in the fall. A good politician is always trying to form a consensus.
Both political parties will always struggle with their identity and that is a healthy democratic function, not the death cry of a Republican or Democratic organization. History gives us many examples of Democrats and Republicans in disarray and yet they win in the fall.
For example, take the 1952 Republican contest for the nomination for president, Dwight D. Eisenhower versus Mr. Republican, Howard E. Taft. Taft’s wing of the party was traditional conservatism, hated the New Deal, and wanted the U.S. to withdraw from world affairs. Eisenhower was new to the GOP, even considered running as a Democrat and believed in heavy involvement in international affairs. Eisenhower easily won the fall election and went from General Eisenhower to President Eisenhower.
You’d think the silly season is over now that the primaries have passed. Better keep the TV off, the theater of the absurd continues. This week, when U.S. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise came to Des Moines on behalf of Rep. Zach Nunn, he attempted to link the Democrats’ 3rd District nominee, Iowa state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, to socialism and communism, claiming that she was a disciple of New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani and Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Trone Garriott’s campaign said she is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, nor a supporter of its agenda. Scalise’s assertion should fall into the category of scare tactics.
Said and done: Both parties show the strain of different internal viewpoints. A better understanding of party politics might cause correspondents to refrain from announcing the results of a fall election, based on internal divisions within a party, in August. But don’t expect political shenanigans to stop just because it’s general election time. And don’t rely on forecasts based on comments made by party leaders made at campaign events and reported as fact.
As for Mr. Will, be kind to him.  He still thinks that the Washington Nationals could win the pennant in his lifetime.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Hartford awarded $20M ‘innovation cluster’ award
description: The state grant will go toward developing a 100K square foot campus intended to support workforce development around applied AI technologies.
text:
City and state officials, business leaders, and academics gathered in downtown Hartford Thursday morning to celebrate a major milestone: a new $20 million state award intended to jumpstart innovation efforts in Connecticut’s capital city.
The money, which comes from the Department of Economic and Community Development’s Innovation Clusters program, will be used to support the creation of the “Hartford Innovation Center,” a 100,000-square-foot facility intended to support workforce development and education around applied artificial intelligence technologies. 
Aside from the state grant, the project has secured several supporters and financial backers including Hartford HealthCare, The Hartford, Travelers, Nassau, Google and QuantumCT.
The facility will be housed within a portion of the State House Square complex in downtown Hartford, which will be renovated.
Speakers at the Thursday event framed the award as part of a technological transformation that will push Hartford and the state to the front of national innovation efforts.
“You’re not going to need to go to Silicon Valley to use AI in the most effective way possible,” said Gov. Ned Lamont. “You can do it right here in Hartford.”
[RELATED: CT redoubles efforts to equip workforce for AI economy]
When completed, the facility will serve as the flagship campus for workforce development and advanced technology efforts in the city, using technology to support industries from insurance to healthcare. The downtown campus is expected to include a number of labs, project spaces and classrooms, all with the goal of fostering “a dynamic environment where residents, youth, startups, corporate partners, and higher-education researchers develop real-world solutions and accelerate responsible AI adoption across Connecticut industries,” according to a press release. 
Matthew Pugliese, deputy commissioner of DECD, said that the $20 million from the state will be used in two ways. First, $3.5 million of the money will support the operations and the initial activities of the Hartford Innovation Center. The remaining $16.5 million will be used for capital project components tied to the effort. 
Pugliese called it “an investment in people and space focused on collaborative labs, classrooms, and project spaces that will help our capital city and partners succeed in this period of immense technological advancement.”
Innovation in Hartford comes with concerns
City officials said the money will help Hartford claim a position at the forefront of community-oriented innovation efforts in the country. 
“This is a statement about where we are going as a city and how we can control our destiny,” said Mayor Arunan Arulampalam. “It is a statement that the state is fully invested and bought into this vision of who we are and where we are going.” 
Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam speaks during an event announcing a 100,000-square-foot flagship campus for the Hartford Innovation Center at State House Square on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. The $20 million investment comes from the Connecticut Innovation Clusters Program, which is administered by the Connecticut Department of Economic and Community Development. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
The award, he added, comes” at a time when people are more scared than ever before about what this technology means, what it will mean for us, what it will move for our economy, and who’s going to get left behind.” 
That latter point was repeatedly raised on Thursday, with city and state officials using the announcement as a chance to address community concerns about the project. 
Hartford’s innovation cluster was originally pitched as an “applied AI center” that would be located at a former data center site bordering Hartford’s North End, a part of the city that has faced significant disinvestment and still struggles with high poverty rates.
The city’s original applied AI center framing quickly raised concerns in the community, with residents worried the project was data center in disguise. The city has since pushed back on that framing, saying the intention is to help people around Hartford, but particularly its most vulnerable communities, access the skills and training needed to fully participate in the workforce of tomorrow. 
“This is going to allow communities in Hartford, communities that would otherwise be locked out of this economy that is being built, to have full access to these tools that they need to thrive, to grow, to use their skills to make this city better,” Arulampalam said on Thursday.
Jeff Auker, director of the city’s Department of Development Services, said the new innovation center will serve three primary functions: to operate as a marketplace for ideas around innovation and advanced technology; to serve as a front door for community members, students and businesses looking to learn more about AI and the skills necessary to use it; and to support a larger ecosystem around artificial intelligence in the state.
The goal, he said, is to support already strong projects and organizations around the state, while also providing new avenues for innovation and workforce development. 
“This is not to replace or to centralize,” Auker said. “This is to augment.”
Jennifer Widness, president of the Connecticut Conference of Independent Colleges, noted that the Hartford effort, which started a few years ago, has already fueled new educational endeavors. That includes the Connecticut AI Alliance or CAIA, a group of academic institutions and community organizations that are working to establish Connecticut as a key hub for AI innovation. 
“Our colleges and universities have tremendous talent, research, and expertise in AI,” Widness, a CAIA co-founder, said. “But Connecticut will be much more competitive if we find ways to connect those assets across institutions and with, in partnership, employers, government and our communities.” 
“Hartford is an especially exciting place for us to do this,” she added.
Additional organizations will also come online in the coming months to support AI in Hartford. The Trustworthy AI Network (TWAIN), a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that will help manage parts of the innovation center, will be launching later this year, according to the governor’s office. 
A new city joins CT’s innovation clusters effort
The $20 million awarded to Hartford marks the second award from DECD’s Innovation Clusters Program. Announced in 2024, the program is a $100 million initiative that encourages municipalities to partner with a private sector entity or university to propose an economic development initiative that could benefit from state support. 
The program focuses on industries the state wants to see grow because they support highly skilled, high-paying jobs: emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and quantum computing, as well as more established fields like financial technology and advanced manufacturing. It replaces an older initiative known as “Innovation Corridors” that set out to accomplish a similar goal but ended after early struggles.
Speaking with The Connecticut Mirror last year, DECD Commissioner Dan O’Keefe said the Innovation Clusters program has been more intentionally structured. 
“We’re seeking to activate ecosystems. We want to activate private sector dollars. We want to activate stakeholders,” he said. “We want these programs to bring people together and to catalyze investment energy and collaboration in a way that wouldn’t necessarily happen if it weren’t for these programs.” 
Attendees including Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam, center, listen to a speaker during an event announcing a 100,000-square-foot flagship campus for the Hartford Innovation Center at State House Square on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. The $20 million investment comes from the Connecticut Innovation Clusters Program, which is administered by the Connecticut Department of Economic and Community Development. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
In 2025, DECD announced three finalists for the grant: the now-reimagined Applied AI Center in Hartford that would support training in artificial intelligence technology; an AI Innovation Institute in Stamford aimed at new technologies in cybersecurity and fintech; and a Quantum and Bioscience Cluster in New Haven intended to take advantage of local industry and universities to support the expansion of quantum technology. 
Last year, the state announced its first award winner, giving $50.5 million to the city of New Haven. That award also dedicated money to QuantumCT, an ongoing effort to ignite a quantum computing industry in the state. QuantumCT is also involved in the Hartford innovation cluster. 
With the latest award, the state has now given out $70.5 million of the money. DECD has not publicly said how the rest of the Innovation Clusters funding will be allocated or whether Stamford will receive an award.
The Hartford Innovation Center will also share space with a forthcoming $18 million learning center developed by Junior Achievement, an organization focused on promoting youth skills development, financial literacy and economic mobility. For now, the city is using a different space downtown to house its AI innovation efforts. 
The project moves forward as Connecticut continues to stake a claim that it is a national innovation leader, with government, the private market, and education institutions working on a number of interconnected initiatives. 
The state has also adopted new artificial intelligence regulations in the hopes of balancing economic competitiveness with protections for state residents. 
Supporters of those efforts also spoke Thursday, saying the combination of new projects and legislation has put the state in a strong position moving forward.
 “One of the true promises of AI is the ability to democratize access to technology, and that anyone who has an idea can try to make that happen,” said state Sen. James Maroney, D-Milford, a co-chair of the legislature’s AI Caucus. “In this center, that will happen.”
Currently, the city does not have a timeline for when the Hartford Innovation Center will be open to the public. But officials emphasized that when the final space does open its doors, it will be a place capable of supporting more than Hartford — it will be a resource for the entire state. 
“We’re writing a different story, in which our city can be in control and in the driver’s seat of where we are going,” Arulampalam said. “In which innovation isn’t something that happens to us, but something we create, something that we guide.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ, other states sue over Trump demand for commercial drivers’ private info
description: The lawsuit alleges the Trump administration is seeking the information so it can use it for immigration enforcement purposes.
text:
The lawsuit alleges the Trump administration is seeking the information so it can use it for immigration enforcement purposes. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey and a group of other mostly Democratic-led states sued the U.S. Department of Transportation over the federal government’s demands for Social Security numbers and other private information from a cross-state database of commercial driver’s licenses.
New Jersey, 20 other states, and the District of Columbia are seeking to block the release of information from a database managed by the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators that the Trump administration has demanded under threat of withholding $10 million in funding that maintains tools states use to ensure truck drivers are licensed somewhere.
“New Jersey has one of the strongest data privacy laws in the country, and we will not allow the Trump Administration to illegally misuse the private information of our residents,” New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport said in a statement.
The lawsuit was filed Thursday in federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia.
The association maintains the Commercial Driver’s License Information System, a database the Department of Transportation and other federal transit authorities have acknowledged is functionally operated by the states.
Even today, individuals applying for an account that can query the database through a Department of Transportation form are told the data belong to the states, the attorneys general said in the suit.
“AAMVA and the Secretary are neither the owners of the information the States provide nor the ultimate recipients of that information; rather, their sole role is to facilitate the exchanges of information between and among States,” the states said in their lawsuit.
The states argued the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s demand for data is barred by the Privacy Act of 1974, the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act, various state privacy laws, and contractual provisions with states.
The administration had also violated the Administrative Procedures Act by failing to consult with states — or even notify them — before seeking to seize data they owned from a contractor.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to claim vast amounts of personal information Americans have given to governments under legal guarantees of privacy, including when registering to vote or filing their taxes, though courts have routinely slapped those attempts down as unlawful. Last month, a federal judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit against New Jersey Secretary of State Dale Caldwell seeking private voter data.
“We will not allow New Jerseyans’ safety or the employment of our CDL drivers to be jeopardized by yet another unlawful request for private data,” Davenport said.
The states said the federal government’s demand and funding threat would necessarily harm public safety and their economies.
The states query the Commercial Driver’s License Information System or a separate database maintained by the association whenever any individual applies for any driver’s license, and cutting the association’s funding could stunt economies and worsen road safety, the states said.
It could also create licensing delays or force states unwilling to bear increased road risks to stop issuing commercial driver’s licenses altogether.
Moreover, the federal government is lying about why it wanted the data, the states alleged. Though the administration initially told the association it would use the data to verify commercial driver’s licenses, its demand for data coincided with identical demands from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
The states argued that it’s clear the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration intends to share the data it receives with Homeland Security officials “for immigration enforcement purposes.”
Last month, the Department of Transportation said it was teaming up with the Department of Homeland Security to crack down on “fraudulent and illegal practices” at commercial driver’s license schools. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said his department has removed more than 24,000 drivers from the roads for failing to speak English and forced states to cancel more than 28,000 licenses issued to foreign drivers.
