name: Alaska Beacon
title: Head Start could soon be overhauled. Here’s exactly what would change.
description: This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th. Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. The Trump administration is pushing a total overhaul of Head Start that could fundamentally reshape the 60-year-old program that has provided childcare and key support for America’s lowest-income families. A new [[...]
text:
Preschool children line up to go outside at the Ralph Hawley Head Start Center in Emeryville, Calif., in December. The Trump administration has proposed major changes to the Head Start program. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)
This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th.  Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
The Trump administration is pushing a total overhaul of Head Start that could fundamentally reshape the 60-year-old program that has provided childcare and key support for America’s lowest-income families.
A new proposed rule released last week put more than 1,400 regulatory provisions that govern how Head Start is implemented on the chopping block. Across the country, 1,600 Head Start grant recipients provide quality care for disadvantaged children, as well as support for families by connecting them to health insurance, job training, developmental screenings, specialist referrals and postpartum support.
This latest proposal is aimed at cutting red tape and allowing more flexibility in the programs, the administration said.
“There’s 1,600 providers across the country facing different conditions, and our proposed rule will reduce their paperwork. It will streamline duplicative statutory requirements and give them flexibility for things like personnel and workforce decisions, as well as licensing relief,” said Alex Adams, the assistant secretary at the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), on a call with reporters.
But Head Start providers and experts say the proposal may actually make it harder for programs to operate and transform Head Start to look more like commercial childcare than an anti-poverty program.
“Families lose the assurance that Head Start means the same thing everywhere, and taxpayers lose a clear measure of impact that Head Start funding should have,” said Celena Roldan Sarillo, the president of Start Early, a nonprofit that advocates for quality early learning.
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on a call with reporters to announce the changes that “it is important to protect” Head Start, which is administered by HHS and was created in part by Kennedy’s uncle Sargent Shriver during the Lyndon B. Johnson administration. Kennedy wants to see more nutrition and physical activity requirements added to Head Start, and agrees the new rules could streamline it and open seats for more children.
That messaging, however, is misleading, said Yvette Sanchez Fuentes, the senior vice president at Start Early.
“At first glance, these proposed changes might not seem so terrible, but as you dig deeper into it, what we will find is that there really are a lot of changes that will impact what is the heart of Head Start,” Sanchez Fuentes said, adding that the performance standards are not just red tape, “they really are the foundation for how we ensure that programs across the country are supporting children, families and communities in the way that they want best.”
Here is a breakdown of what the administration is proposing to change for Head Start.
 Overall, how is this proposal changing Head Start? 

Fundamentally, the changes would have Head Start operate much more like other childcare centers under state and local rules. Because quality is such an important benchmark in Head Start, its rules are more stringent than the rules governing other childcare options — in many places, those differences would disappear.
“States didn’t design their childcare programs to serve the population that Head Start serves. They design those to regulate private businesses and set a floor for safety, like they regulate hospitals or restaurants, not to prepare a high-need community for school,” said Katie Hamm, who oversaw the Head Start program under the Biden administration.
 Are there any immediate impacts to my child’s Head Start program? 

No. The public has until October 6 to comment on the proposed rule before HHS reviews the comments and issues a final rule. That review process can take time — months or longer — in addition to any legal challenges that may arise, so it’s unlikely, though not impossible, for changes to happen this year.
 How would classrooms change? 

One of the biggest changes in the proposal is eliminating Head Start’s teacher-to-student ratios. One of Head Start’s quality initiatives is that it offers more individualized care — each teacher is in charge of a smaller number of students than in most other childcare settings. The policy is both about safety and support for low-income kids, some of whom need more focused attention.
Under the proposed changes, an estimated 80 percent of children currently in Head Start would be subject to worse ratios. The maximum number of toddlers per teacher would more than double in nine states: Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nevada, North Carolina and Texas.
The proposal also removes the cap on group sizes, so it’s likely classrooms would have more children.
Another big change: All instruction will have to take place in English instead of offering bilingual support to children who are not native speakers. More than a quarter of children in Head Start come from homes where a language other than English is spoken.
The only exception is for Head Start programs on Tribal lands.
 Are there any changes that impact health and safety? 

Yes.
Detailed requirements on how to prevent lead exposure are gone and replaced with a broader requirement that programs prevent children from being exposed to lead in water and paint in however way they see fit.
A requirement that a bus monitor be on board any buses transporting children at all times has also been removed.
Other detailed rules on facilities, safety training, hygiene, disaster preparedness and equipment and materials are also gone; instead programs are instructed to follow state laws in those areas.
 Is discipline changing under the new regulations? 

Currently, children generally cannot be expelled from Head Start. The proposed rule would remove that prohibition and allow programs to set their own disciplinary rules, as long as they align with state and local requirements. Head Start would still need to provide children with any behavioral problems with screenings and referral services.
The administration said it made these changes because when the expulsion and suspension rules were first implemented in 2016, many states did not have their own rules governing those issues. Since then, many states have adopted their own.
“These proposed changes are not an endorsement of suspension and expulsion as approaches to address persistent and serious behavioral concerns; rather, the intent is to allow programs to determine their own discipline policies, within the context of state and local licensing requirements,” the rule says.
 Are there changes related to health support? 

Head Start typically offers a variety of mental health and health screenings as part of its program requirements. For example, within 30 days of enrollment, programs have to check that a family has insurance or ongoing medical care; within 45 days it needs to check for or conduct vision and hearing screenings; within 90 days, it needs to check on whether children have immunizations up to date, have had their well-child pediatrician checkup and had dental visits. Programs also require that children brush their teeth at school. All of those specific requirements are gone under the proposed rule.
Many mental health supports, such as a monthly mental health consultation, would go away.
So while the requirement from the Head Start Act — that programs support families with a comprehensive array of health services — remains, the set rules on how to achieve that, like the timeline requirements, disappear. Advocates say this could lead to inconsistent care and less accountability.
 How does this impact children with disabilities? 

Similarly, the proposed rules require that Head Start programs comply with all applicable federal and state regulations in providing services to children with disabilities, but eliminates much of the structure for how to provide those services.
 What about impacts on unhoused children? 

The proposed rule removes a provision that allows families experiencing homelessness to simply confirm their situation and thus qualify for Head Start. Families that are unhoused may also be in situations where they are living with someone else or in a temporary structure — situations they could rarely prove through documentation.
Under the new rules, families and children would have to provide some documentation.
 Would newborn and pregnancy services be impacted? 

Yes. Early Head Start, which services low-income pregnant people and children under the age of 3, would lose a lot of tailored requirements. Newborn home visits would still be required, for example, but the requirement that they happen within two weeks of birth was dropped.
Also gone is a requirement around addressing racial and ethnic disparities in birth outcomes. Currently, programs must track demographic data on pregnant people, identify any disparities and provide services to close those gaps. The administration said cutting that requirement is in line with its mission to cut back on diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and claims programs said it was beyond the scope of what they could reasonably be expected to do.
 Would parent involvement change? 

Possibly.
The way Head Start works now, parents are actively engaged with much of the decision making at individual centers. Each center is required to have a parent committee that has power in advising the school on activities, policies and services, and the regulations determine how those must function.
Under the proposed rule, those committees would be optional, and the rules that govern how they operate would also be eliminated, which the administration said were designed to give programs more flexibility.
 Are there any new rules being suggested? 

Yes, and they largely have to do with nutrition and physical activity.
Programs will be required to offer 30 minutes of physical activity, ideally outside, for every three and a half hours of classroom instruction. That would expand the existing general requirement that programs “recognize physical activity as important to learning and integrate intentional movement and physical activity into curricular activities and daily routines.”
The current Head Start regulations require that programs generally fulfill a third to a half of children’s daily nutritional needs with meals at Head Start. Three- to 5-year-olds must get healthy meals and snacks that conform to U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) guidelines, and meals should be culturally appropriate as well as developmentally appropriate — infants and toddlers are fed according to their individual needs and readiness.
Under the new proposal, they will also be required to offer nutrient-dense whole foods within the framework of the USDA Child and Adult Care Food Program meal standard, ensuring that “all the meals are aligned with the dietary guidelines,” Kennedy said.
 What is the new addition around “healthy marriage”?

One of the less-talked-about additions the administration is proposing is providing educational material to children that “demonstrates healthy marriage as a positive good,” in concert with new strategies to engage parents in their kids’ learning, and particularly fathers, the rule says.
“This proposed change to current requirements reflects ACF’s commitment to supporting strong families as the cornerstone of a healthy society,” the administration said.
 If the rule is finalized, do programs have to adhere to it? 

It’s unclear.
Adams emphasized that programs can continue to operate as they currently are if they wish to. In the areas where the administration is adding new requirements, however, such as nutrition and physical activity, programs would have to make changes.
“If a program likes its ratio, it can keep its ratio. If a program likes its group size, it can keep its group size. This does not require them to do anything different. As I said, flexibility is permission; it’s not a mandate,” Adams said.
But the actual regulations that would be part of the final rule — the final 13 pages of what was released last week — don’t specify that most of this is optional.
“If they truly mean, for example, a program can decide to keep the ratios that exist in the regulations today, the regulation should say that. It should say programs have a choice,” Hamm said. “It doesn’t say that, and so that’s a problem for a lot of reasons.”
Head Start centers receive grants from the federal government to offer services — it’s unclear what assurance there is that the administration will offer grants to programs that choose to adhere to prior rules.
There’s already some evidence HHS could target programs it deems to be in misalignment with  the Trump administration. Earlier this year, the agency tried to withhold funding to Head Start programs that used words like “women” and “race” in their grant applications, what it perceived to be diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives that have been a target of the administration.
Head Start programs in Illinois, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin sued and a judge granted them a preliminary injunction, blocking the Trump administration from cutting funding while the case is litigated.
“When grants get negotiated or when there are grant competitions, and HHS is selecting a grantee, they have a lot of power in that,” Hamm said. “Oftentimes, a Head Start grant feels like they need to comply with what’s being asked of them.”
 Why is the administration pursuing these changes? 

Since the start of the Trump administration, Head Start has faced upheaval.
Project 2025, the policy blueprint for President Donald Trump’s second term, advised eliminating the program, claiming it lacked positive outcomes and was rife with abuse. A leaked White House budget in early 2025 showed the administration was hoping to eliminate it altogether before massive backlash from Head Start parents and alumni persuaded the administration to change course.
But programs continued to face financial challenges. Funding was cut off at the start of 2025 as part of a government-wide freeze, leading some to close their doors. Then in April of last year, the administration closed five of the 10 regional offices that support Head Start programs.
Last summer, the administration released a proposed rule that would bar undocumented children from Head Start entirely. The proposal is on pause due to ongoing litigation.
Adams said the goal of the proposed rule is to provide flexibility in the program, not dismantle it.
“In broad strokes, what we are trying to accomplish is we built this rule around trusting local leaders to make the decisions that are best for their local communities,” he said.
If the changes were enacted across programs, the administration estimates a savings of $2.2 billion that would be reinvested in the program to open as many as 236,000 new Head Start spots. There is no national repository of waitlist data on Head Start, though programs are required to be filled and maintain an active waiting list.
“We’re trying to ensure that programs have the flexibility not just to meet their community needs, but to start clearing out some of their waitlists, ensuring more children are served,” Adams said.
 How could these changes impact childcare staff? 

The administration is proposing a reduction in how much money programs can spend on administrative overhead, lowering it from 15 percent to 5 percent.
The justification, Adams said, is “so that more money is reaching children and families, and less is going to administrative overhead, like administrator salaries or administrative offices.”
But childcare providers have argued that the reduction will actually mean less money to operate Head Start — money that goes to things like buses and human resources, or to conduct background checks and fix the refrigerator when it breaks.
“Don’t believe that somehow that 15 percent makes our Head Start directors rich. It does not. Everyone I know in Head Start, including myself, has never become rich from being a Head Start employee,” said Lori Pittman, the co-founder of the Washington State Parent Ambassador Program and a former Head Start parent.
By the administration’s own analysis, the changes could lead to a reduction in teaching staff at centers across the country. Other workforces that would be hit: home visit staff, health and mental health personnel, child development specialists and bus monitoring staff.
 Is there any new money for Head Start under the proposal? 

No. Funding for Head Start has remained flat for the past three years — about $12 billion — even though operating costs and inflation have risen.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: ‘Inexcusable’: Georgia man to spend nearly 45 years in prison after shooting SC trooper in the face
description: A judge tacked nearly seven more years onto the 38-year sentence Derrick Gathers is already serving in state prison.
text:
Lance Cpl. B.A. Frazier tells reporters outside the federal courthouse in Columbia, South Carolina, on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026, that he's thankful for the support he received after being shot during a traffic stop in 2023. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A man convicted of shooting a South Carolina trooper in the face during a traffic stop will spend a total of 45 years in prison, a federal judge decided Thursday.
Derrick Gathers, 40, is already serving a 38-year sentence after a jury convicted him last year of attempted murder, possessing a weapon during a violent crime and failing to stop for police.
U.S. District Judge Mary Geiger Lewis sentenced him to 15 more years for illegally having a gun as a felon. However, eight years and four months of that will be served concurrently with his state sentence. So, her decision adds six years and eight months to his prison time.
Once he’s released, Gathers will spend three years under supervision to ensure he doesn’t reoffend.
Lewis gave Gathers a higher sentence than typically recommended under the legal guidelines because the crime was “terrible,” she said.
“Unbelievable,” she continued during the hearing. “Shocking. Inexcusable. Unfathomable, really.”
What happened
The charges stem from April 2023, when Lance Cpl. B.A. Frazier, a state Highway Patrol trooper, pulled Gathers over about 3:30 a.m. for speeding through rural Bamberg County at 90 mph, or 35 mph over the posted speed limit. Gathers was driving on U.S. Highway 78 just outside the town of Denmark, according to court documents.
At the time, he lived in Augusta, Georgia, roughly 75 minutes away at legal speeds.
While running Gathers’ driver’s license, Frazier noticed the photograph didn’t seem to match Gathers’ appearance. As he returned to the driver’s side of the car to check whether Gathers was the person in the picture, Gathers took out a stolen handgun and shot Frazier point-blank in the right cheek, according to court filings.
Gathers led police on a high-speed chase, covering about 18 miles over 11 minutes before crashing his car in a person’s front yard. The car, which had a passenger inside, flipped several times before coming to a stop.
Why Gathers shot Frazier during what was otherwise a routine traffic stop remains unclear, said prosecutor Lamar Fyall. Gathers probably would have spent the night in jail for driving with a fraudulent license before being released pending charges, Fyall said.
“That’s a crazy reason to shoot a law enforcement officer,” Fyall said.
Law enforcement officers understand a certain amount of risk comes with their jobs, Lewis said. But they should be able to know they’re safe during a routine traffic stop, she said.
“All these people go out there every day to do that, and they need to know they’ll be safe,” Lewis said.
Frazier survived and is back on the job as a state trooper. About a dozen of his colleagues, as well as the commander of the state Highway Patrol, came to support him during the hearing Thursday.
“I do have my days,” Frazier, who didn’t speak in court, told reporters after the hearing. “But, hey, as long as I can get back to work, man, I’m going to be OK.”
Recognizing the need for experienced officers, this year’s state budget includes $1.7 million to fund pay increases for state troopers who stay with the Department of Public Safety for more than a year.
At 18 months, an officer can become a trooper first class, which has a minimum salary of nearly $62,500, and at three years, they can make close to $64,000 at a minimum, according to the agency. The money will also give phone operators, who take and direct emergency calls, a 5% raise, according to budget documents.
‘Demons he needed to conquer’
Gathers was high at the time of the shooting and says he doesn’t remember what happened, said attorney Jeremy Thompson, his public defender.
“These are demons he needed to conquer before he got in the car that night, and he didn’t,” he said.
Gathers is generally a pleasant person, Thompson said. Every time they’ve spoken, Gathers has been “polite and kind and intelligent and interesting,” which makes his crime all the more inexplicable, Thompson said.
“I stand here baffled at why we are here,” Thompson said during the hearing.
Gathers declined his chance to address the judge in court Thursday. In a letter to the court, Gathers’ sister, Darlene Williams, asked Lewis not to add any additional time to his sentence.
Gathers has two daughters, one who is 23 and one who is 3, as well as an 8-year-old granddaughter, Williams wrote.
“My brother is a foundational pillar for our family across three generations,” Williams wrote.
Criminal history
Gathers’ previous criminal record swayed Lewis toward a harsher sentence, she said.
While this is his first conviction in South Carolina, Gathers’ history of run-ins with the law dates back to 2002, including both federal and state charges of assault, possession of drugs and illegally owning weapons.
He wasn’t allowed to own a gun because of previous federal convictions in New York of rape, criminal impersonation and illegal weapon possession, according to court filings.
Gathers’ most recent stint in prison was in New York, also for criminally possessing a weapon. It ended in 2020, three years before the shooting, according to court documents.
And he lost privileges last year while imprisoned in South Carolina for being caught with drugs, a cellphone and a weapon, according to his inmate record.

Lewis said those charges suggested Gathers clearly hasn’t learned his lesson while in prison.
“Violence, violence, violence,” she said to him. “I don’t know what kind of sentence does deter you. It doesn’t seem like anything would deter you.”
In her 14 years as a federal judge, Lewis has presided over many violent and terrible crimes she struggled to understand, she said. Even so, Gathers’ case stood out for its seeming randomness, she told him.
“I see a lot of bad things in this courtroom, but this is impressive,” Lewis said. “It really is.”
Lewis asked Gathers to imagine the worst case scenarios of his actions. He could have easily killed Frazier when shooting him, she said. He could have hit another driver while speeding away from the crime. He could have caused another officer to crash during the high-speed chase he led, or killed the other person in the car with him, who wasn’t identified in court documents.
Only luck allowed everyone to get out of that situation alive, Lewis said.
Because of that, Gathers’ prison sentence was meant to keep law enforcement officers and the general public safe from Gathers’ erratic behavior, she said.
“I’m not saying you’re a bad person,” Lewis told him. “That’s between you and the good Lord. I’m just trying to keep everybody safe.”

title: Ethics panel clears Braun administration official to join construction firm, lobby lawmakers
description: The Braun administration’s top contract-oversight official can immediately begin lobbying Indiana lawmakers for a construction company after an ethics panel Thursday waived a one-year restriction on such work. The Indiana State Ethics Commission unanimously approved the waiver for Department of Administration Commissioner Brandon Clifton, who plans to become[...]
text:
Indiana Department of Administration Commissioner Brandon Clifton talks about government efficiency and savings at a news conference on Wednesday, Aug. 27, 2025. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Braun administration’s top contract-oversight official can immediately begin lobbying Indiana lawmakers for a construction company after an ethics panel Thursday waived a one-year restriction on such work.
The Indiana State Ethics Commission unanimously approved the waiver for Department of Administration Commissioner Brandon Clifton, who plans to become director of government affairs for Hagerman Group.
Clifton has led the agency since appointed by Gov. Mike Braun in January 2025. It is responsible for reviewing and approving thousands of state contracts each year.
In his new position, Clifton will serve as Hagerman’s primary liaison to local governments, the Indiana General Assembly and industry associations. His work will also include business development, according to filings submitted to the commission.
Clifton said Thursday that lobbying will be a significant part of the job.
“That will be a critical component of the job, especially with the Legislature and shaping construction informed policies going through,” Clifton said. “I would expect to register as a lobbyist in that capacity, as well.”
Indiana ethics law generally bars former state employees from registering as executive-branch lobbyists or lobbying the agency for which they worked for 365 days after leaving government. The commission’s action waives that “cooling off” restriction for Clifton, although he remains subject to other post-employment rules.
Story continues below.
Clifton
 
IDOA General Counsel Jennifer Jansen told commissioners that Clifton rarely reviews or approves contracts himself because those duties generally fall to the agency’s legal division. 
Clifton said he has personally approved one contract during his tenure — an Indiana Department of Correction agreement handled by him because of a conflict elsewhere in the agency — and it did not involve Hagerman.
Hagerman has no active state contracts, according to the waiver request. The company’s only state agreement during Clifton’s tenure was a $22,883 Department of Natural Resources contract to install a shooting-range baffle at the Roush Lake Fish and Wildlife Area. The four-month contract expired June 30.
Clifton did not know about, review or sign that agreement, state filings said.
After Clifton entered employment negotiations with Hagerman, IDOA imposed an ethics screening barring him from exercising official duties or participating in decisions involving the company.

The screen, executed July 28, also prohibits him from helping a future employer with matters in which he personally and substantially participated while working for IDOA.
Clifton said Hagerman has historically focused on local government work and is not expected to pursue the state as a significant source of business. His new duties will largely involve local capital projects and construction policy before the General Assembly.
“The primary responsibilities will be working with local units of government on their capital projects, on their vertical construction opportunities,” Clifton told commissioners.
The commission separately approved a post-employment waiver for Indiana Department of Transportation Deputy Commissioner Roland Fegan, a 42-year agency employee who plans to become a construction project director for engineering firm Butler, Fairman & Seufert.
Commissioners additionally approved updated rules for limited personal use of Indiana Criminal Justice Institute property, expanding the policy to cover contractors with state-issued equipment
The panel also determined that former Department of Child Services official Justin Litman must remain recused from work involving the Jay County Family Resource Center in his new role with Firefly Children and Family Alliance. 
In a separate case, commissioners said technology consultant Anthony Vespa can continue serving on the State Workforce Development Board but must file updated ethics disclosures as new state contracts involving his company arise.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV chemical plant didn’t require workers to wear respirators during deadly incident, CSB report says
description: A Kanawha County chemical plant where two employees died and four others were critically injured in April after a highly toxic hydrogen sulfide gas was released did not require workers to wear respirators, according to a report released Thursday by the U.S. Chemical Safety Board.
text:
Station 80 Nitro Fire Department assisted Institute Fire Rescue with operations at the chemical leak at Catalyst Refiners in Institute, West Virginia, on Wednesday, April 22, 2026. (Photo by Nitro Fire Department)A Kanawha County chemical plant where two employees died and four others were critically injured in April after a highly toxic hydrogen sulfide gas was released did not require workers to wear respirators, according to a report released Thursday by the U.S. Chemical Safety Board.
The incident happened around 9:31 a.m., April 22 at Catalyst Refiners Inc. in Institute, West Virginia.  
Employees at the plant told investigators that because the facility was transitioning from normal production to decommissioning, workers were not required to wear respirators, and the company did not provide personal gas monitors to workers or contractors, the report said. 
Chemical Safety Board investigators found four full-face respirators at the facility, but they were not equipped with filters that would protect against hazardous gases such as hydrogen sulfide, the CSB said.
“This tragic incident underscores the need to have clear procedures and safely manage the serious chemical hazards that can arise during facility decommissioning,” CSB Chairperson Steve Owens said in a news release. “Although the CSB’s investigation is still ongoing, we are concerned that Catalyst Refiners did not require employees to wear respirators during decommissioning and also never provided or required workers to use personal gas monitors that might have alerted them to the presence of the highly toxic hydrogen sulfide gas.”
In a statement Thursday, Ames Goldsmith, owner of the facility, said it appreciates the assistance of the Chemical Safety Board and Hazard Investigation Board and other agencies as they investigate the deadly incident. 
“We have reviewed the CSB update and understand it reflects the significant efforts of the CSB to date in its investigation,” the statement said.  “As the CSB works toward a final report, we will continue to cooperate fully with its investigation, as well as with all other agencies involved. Our thoughts are always with our Catalyst Refiners colleagues and their families.”
After the incident, 18 personnel — including seven first responders — were decontaminated and transported to local medical facilities for evaluation, according to the report. Twenty-two personnel, including four responders, were decontaminated at the site.
On the day of the incident, plant employees pumped roughly 80 gallons of A-50 and 275 gallons of M-2000A from their storage containers into a wastewater receiving tank, according to the report. Then they started pumping diluted nitric acid from a tote into the same tank.
As the nitric acid was being pumped into the wastewater tank, workers observed a chemical reaction occurring and a fog forming over the tank. The employee operating the pump stopped the flow of nitric acid into the tank. The employee went outside to get some fresh air, passed out and then regained consciousness.

A supervisor was notified about the issue with the chemicals, approached the tank area and also lost consciousness, the report says.
Two more employees also entered the area to assist. One of these employees pulled the unconscious supervisor away from the tank area. The supervisor recovered, but the employee who had come to the supervisor’s assistance, as well as the one who also had entered the area, were overcome by the gas emitting from the tank and later died, the report says. ​
The facility was used to manufacture silver catalyst. The incident caused a shelter in place for residents in the area.
West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection’s Environmental Enforcement teams also launched a full investigation into the facility, the state announced after the incident.  
The Chemical Safety Board is continuing to investigate the deadly incident, it said in the report.The board does not issue fines or safety citations, but makes safety recommendations to companies, labor groups and regulatory agencies.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Jay Collins says GOP voters need to rally around him to stop Byron Donalds
description: Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins says it’s now a two-person race for the Florida GOP nomination for governor, and that Republicans still skeptical about front-runner Byron Donalds should choose him in Tuesday’s primary. “Byron Donalds has been in the race for 18 months, give or take, right? Far longer than anybody else,” Collins told reporters […]
text:
Lt. Gov. Jay Collins in his office in the Florida Capitol. (Photo by Livia Caputo/Florida Phoenix)Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins says it’s now a two-person race for the Florida GOP nomination for governor, and that Republicans still skeptical about front-runner Byron Donalds should choose him in Tuesday’s primary.
“Byron Donalds has been in the race for 18 months, give or take, right? Far longer than anybody else,” Collins told reporters Thursday in a virtual press conference. “There are still 15, 20, 25% who remain undecided. That means those 15, 20, 25% of people have had 18 months to not choose him. I think Byron Donalds has gaps.”
Donalds, now serving his third term in Congress, has dominated the Republican race for governor in polls and fundraising since Donald Trump endorsed him before he entered the contest in February 2025. However, about a quarter of voters polled remain undecided.
Donalds leads Collins by an average of around 37 points, according to RealClearPolitics. That same polling also shows, however, that about 27% of the electorate remains undecided.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.The 50-year-old Collins began his remote press conference with a detailed presentation of his agenda that lasted nearly 25 minutes.
“Life will get easier,” he said, if he gets past the primary and wins in November. “Things will get cheaper. We will be safer. It’s not rhetoric. That is a statement and a standard. Florida can be one of the cheapest states to live in without sacrificing the quality of life or safety. We’re not choosing between affordable and free.”
Start in politics
Collins served for more than two decades in the U.S. Army Special Forces, deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan. In 2019, he moved to Florida and began working for Operation BBQ Relief, a disaster relief nonprofit.
His political career began in 2021, when he initially filed to challenge Democratic U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor, but he pivoted to running for a Hillsborough County state Senate seat in 2022 that previously was held by Democrat Janet Cruz. Collins ended up winning the seat by nearly 10 points.
A year ago, Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed him lieutenant governor during a press conference that appeared to many observers an annointment as the governor’s chosen successor. The governor noted at the time that Collins had recently traveled to the Middle East to help Floridians return to the United States during a military conflict between Israel and Iran.
“He was in these countries during the middle of a war, personally helping to rescue his fellow Floridians and fellow Americans,” DeSantis said. “Sen. Jay Collins is the Chuck Norris of Florida politics.”
That endorsement never came, however.
Collins maintains his selection as lieutenant governor proves DeSantis believed he could be his successor.
“Last time I checked, there were 23.5 million people in Florida,” he said. “I’m the only one who was hand-picked to be the lieutenant governor. What he said on Day One is still factual, functional, and true. I am Day One ready. I’m ready to lead the state of Florida. I don’t need training wheels. I don’t need a time to warm up in the bullpen. I’m running to make sure that we continue what we built.”
‘He doesn’t connect’
While the polls suggest the GOP race to succeed DeSantis is a lopsided affair, political observers note that public polling has fallen short throughout the country this summer, and Collins says those surveys in Florida don’t reflect what he’s seen on the ground.
“When I’ve gone door to door to door, people feel like he doesn’t connect. That he doesn’t understand what they’re going through. I’ve heard numerous times, ‘Well, he really hasn’t been here. Where was he during the storms? Where was he on these issues. Why didn’t he weigh in on these primary issues?’”
The statement that Donalds “hasn’t been here” echoes the criticism DeSantis himself issued last year when he announced he wasn’t backing his run for governor. Speaking in Tampa in February 2025, DeSantis said Donalds “hasn’t been a part of the victories that we’ve had here over the left over the last few years. He’s just not been a part of it.”
It should be noted that Donalds endorsed Donald Trump for president, and not DeSantis, when the two men competed for the Republican nomination for president in 2024.
“Byron puts himself above the people,” Collins said Thursday, adding that he himself has been told by voters, “You seem like one of us.”
Donalds’ decision not to participate in any debates with his GOP opponents still rankles Collins.
“The fact that he wouldn’t get out there and debate for the primary, and he thought it was about him, me, or the other candidates, that tells you exactly that he’s out of touch,” Collins said. “Debates aren’t about the candidates, they’re about the people.”
“There are no participation trophies in politics,” Donalds’ communications director Gates McGavick said in June. “It is not Byron’s job to legitimize campaigns that have failed to gain meaningful support. Republicans are united behind Byron Donalds on defeating Democrats in November.”
While Collins was addressing reporters on Zoom, Donalds was in Crawfordville with GOP U.S. Sen. Rick Scott. Saturday in Tampa, he’d campaigned with Florida’s other U.S. senator, Ashley Moody, along with Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson and CFO Blaise Ingoglia, each a statewide elected top state official.

title: ‘Our focus is on Hammond’: Bears keep stadium sights on Indiana
description: The Chicago Bears are continuing to look at two Northwest Indiana sites as potential locations for the team’s new domed football stadium, but team officials declined to fully commit to the move across the border in a much-hyped press conference Thursday. “Our focus is on Hammond,” team Chair George H. McCaskey told reporters. “That’s where […]
text:
The Chicago Bears say they remain focused on Hammond for the team's new domed football stadium. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)The Chicago Bears are continuing to look at two Northwest Indiana sites as potential locations for the team’s new domed football stadium, but team officials declined to fully commit to the move across the border in a much-hyped press conference Thursday.
“Our focus is on Hammond,” team Chair George H. McCaskey told reporters. “That’s where we’re advancing our efforts, and that’s where the bulk of our time, attention and resources are being devoted.”
The team’s board of directors voted in June to advance the stadium project at possible locations in Hammond — mere minutes from the Illinois border.
The decision follows legislation signed into law by Gov. Mike Braun in February directing potentially $1 billion or more in taxpayer dollars toward infrastructure projects near the stadium site, where officials intend to develop a mix of retail, restaurants, hotels and residential to compliment the stadium.
Bears President and CEO Kevin Warren said Thursday the team is “working diligently” to finish topographical, geographical and environmental studies of sites at Wolf Lake terminal, one of two sites under consideration.
The team already determined the Lost Marsh site in Hammond is a viable location for the stadium project, Warren said, suggesting the team may use both locations for its mixed-use development if the Wolf Lake site is viable.
Porter County splitting on planned taxes for Bears stadium in Hammond

“It’s reached the point now where we’re starting to get some clarity,” he said. “And the moment we finish our due diligence and have the appropriate capital stack and financing together, we are looking forward to making a decision so we can break ground and get our project going forward.”
Still, Warren told reporters the team has held occasional meetings with Illinois officials, though he said the state has not presented anything in writing to counter Indiana’s offer.
The Bears leaders did not provide a timeline for when the team will reach a decision on the stadium site, nor did they formally rule out the possibility building the stadium on team-owned property in the northwestern Chicago suburb of Arlington Heights. Neither, however, appeared optimistic they could reach a deal with Illinois.
“We were waiting to see whether there would be some substantive action taken,” McCaskey said of discussions with Illinois officials.
“We felt we had presented a pretty compelling case that a stadium in Arlington would be beneficial not only for the village of Arlington Heights, but for the community and the entire state—tremendous driver of economic activity, job creation, tax revenue, sales revenue,” he said. “Ultimately, that argument was unsuccessful.”

title: Without Holocaust education, Vermont students can’t understand Israel
description:
A letter from a Vermont teen showed what's missing when schools skip Holocaust education.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Without Holocaust education, Vermont students can’t understand Israel.
text:
Dear Editor, 
Vermont Friends of Israel is deeply concerned about the state of education in Vermont schools that allowed 14-year-old Zoya Bianchi to become so certain of her moral clarity regarding the world’s most complex conflict and so convinced of the evils of America’s closest ally. This is a failure by the adults and institutions that have shaped her understanding.
However, it comes as no surprise. Vermont is one of only eight states nationwide and the only one in New England that does not require Holocaust education, without which neither Israel nor the dangers of modern anti-Zionism can be understood.
That missing foundation distorts students’ view of Israel’s seven-front war against terrorist organizations openly committed to destroying the world’s only Jewish state. Bianchi, for example, ignores more than 40,000 rockets launched at Israeli civilians since 2001, Hezbollah weapon caches the Israel Defense Forces says are embedded in civilian infrastructure and their extensive terror tunnel network. Instead, she cites a biased United Nations with its own long history of failure in Lebanon.

READ MORE

An education that omits context robs our children by replacing critical thought with dogma and pressure to conform to fashionable causes, inviting students to take their cues from influential adults. Sen. Bernie Sanders, for example, recently devoted more than 400 words to decrying the situation in Gaza without once mentioning Hamas’ refusal to disarm as required by the ceasefire agreement. He also called for the immediate release of Mohsen Mahdawi, a Vermont-based Columbia University student facing deportation over allegations of antisemitic conduct through leading pro-Palestinian protests and calling for Israel’s destruction. Despite Mahdawi’s denials, the federal government also revived additional claims in recent court proceedings that Mahdawi told a Vermont gun-shop owner that he used to build submachine guns to kill Jews and told another person, “I like to kill Jews.”
Bianchi herself once wrote that empathy begins with listening to those with whom we disagree. Vermont’s educators and elected leaders should take her advice. With antisemitism rampant in Vermont, including in our schools, how much longer can we look away?
Mark TreinkmanAthens, Vt.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas sticks with ‘scientific evidence’ for vaccine schedule, despite Trump order
description: TOPEKA — Kansas won’t change its vaccine schedule to match the executive order from President Donald Trump but instead will continue to “trust in scientific evidence” and follow recommendations from major health organizations, a spokeswoman said.  In an executive order, Trump recommended separating the measles, mumps and rubella vaccination — although there[...]
text:
Kansas health officials aren't changing the state's recommendations for childhood vaccinations, despite an executive order from President Donald Trump that makes numerous changes, including the number of vaccines recommended for all children. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas won’t change its vaccine schedule to match the executive order from President Donald Trump but instead will continue to “trust in scientific evidence” and follow recommendations from major health organizations, a spokeswoman said. 
In an executive order, Trump recommended separating the measles, mumps and rubella vaccination — although there aren’t separate vaccines available — and that all vaccines should be given in separate doctor’s visits. 
The order also separated vaccines into three categories, delineating vaccines for all children, those in certain high-risk populations and several “based on shared clinical decision-making.”
Jill Bronaugh, spokeswoman for the Kansas Department for Health and Environment, wrote in an email that vaccines are one of the most effective tools for preventing serious infectious diseases. 
“Decades of rigorous studies have shown they are safe and effective,” she said. “We remain committed to supporting clinical guidance and recommendations that provide the most accurate, credible and transparent information available for health professionals and Kansas families.”
KDHE currently follows immunization guidance from the American Academy of Family Physicians, American Academy of Pediatrics, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, Bronaugh said. 
“We continue to review and assess the most current and accurate information before making any changes or issuing additional guidance or educational materials as it relates to current vaccine schedules and recommendations,” she said. 
When Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was appointed to head the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, he was well-known for disseminating inaccurate information about vaccines that wasn’t based on scientific studies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention called for changing the vaccine schedule in January, and at the time Bronaugh said the state wouldn’t follow the recommendations. 
The Kansas Legislature inserted a provision in the state’s budget bill that would have forced the state to follow CDC vaccine recommendations. Gov. Laura Kelly used her line item veto authority to reject the idea. 
Bronaugh said parents or caregivers with questions about current Kansas immunization schedules should talk to their medical providers.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Planned Parenthood begins offering procedural abortions in the Missouri Ozarks
description: Abortion access in Missouri continues to expand under the constitutional amendment voters approved in 2024 — less than three months before they’ll be asked to undo it. The latest expansion is in Springfield, where Planned Parenthood began offering in-clinic procedural abortions Thursday. Just a few weeks earlier the clinic began prescribing abortion medicati[...]
text:
The Planned Parenthood clinic in Springfield began offering procedural abortions in addition to medication abortion on Thursday, just weeks after the clinic resumed abortion access in the area for the first time in 21 years (photo submitted).Abortion access in Missouri continues to expand under the constitutional amendment voters approved in 2024 — less than three months before they’ll be asked to undo it.
The latest expansion is in Springfield, where Planned Parenthood began offering in-clinic procedural abortions Thursday. Just a few weeks earlier the clinic began prescribing abortion medication, returning abortion access to the Missouri Ozarks for the first time in 21 years.
The Springfield clinic will offer procedural abortions up to 12 weeks into pregnancy, Planned Parenthood Great Rivers said in a press release. 
Krissy Durant, a spokesperson for Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, which operates the clinic, said appointments are already fully booked for this week. For now, the clinic will offer both medication and procedural abortion appointments every couple of weeks, she said, but that is subject to change as clinic staff work out a longer-term schedule.
Prior to July, Missourians in the area had to drive hours to reach a Planned Parenthood clinic where they could end a pregnancy. Reproductive rights advocates point to limited paid time off, childcare access and lack of transportation as barriers to accessing abortion outside a person’s hometown.
“After decades without abortion care nearby, we have seen patients right here in Springfield, and they are relieved to find the care they need within reach of where they live,” Dr. Margaret Baum, chief medical officer of Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, said in a statement. “We know abortion care is on the line in Missouri, and that’s exactly why we are expanding. We won’t back down. We are standing proudly in solidarity with our patients who want, who need, and who voted for access to abortion care.”
The Springfield clinic is the fourth Planned Parenthood in the state to offer in-clinic procedures after Missourians passed a constitutional amendment in 2024 protecting abortion up to the point of fetal viability. Planned Parenthood clinics in Kansas City, Columbia and St. Louis restarted procedural abortions in 2025. 
Missourians getting abortion pills by mail from out-of-state providers quadrupled since 2023

All four clinics, along with the Planned Parenthood in Gladstone, offer medication abortion following a June court ruling that struck down dozens of abortion regulations challenged under the 2024 amendment.
The judge in that case upheld only a few of the challenged abortion regulations, including a requirement that patients meet with a doctor in-person before being prescribed medication abortion and a requirement that only physicians can perform abortions. Durant said these laws affect Planned Parenthood’s ability to offer more appointments at this time.
Planned Parenthood officials have advocated for patients’ ability to choose which abortion method is best for them. 
Medication abortion is the most common method for ending a pregnancy in the U.S. It typically involves taking mifepristone — which in Missouri must be administered at a clinic — followed later by misoprostol. The Food and Drug Administration has approved the regimen for use through 10 weeks of pregnancy. 
Procedural abortions, which can be performed later in pregnancy, take place in-clinic using various methods and are completed much faster than medication abortion.
This November, Missouri voters will decide whether they want to reinstate an abortion ban. The proposed constitutional amendment, which will appear on the ballot as Amendment 3, would ban the procedure with limited exceptions for survivors of rape and incest and for medical emergencies. It would also write a ban on gender-affirming care for minors, already prohibited under state law, into the state constitution.

title: South Dakota board approves nearly $500,000 in state loans and grants for business projects
description: A South Dakota board approved a total of $481,199 in state loans and grants Wednesday for businesses in Rapid City and De Smet. The Board of Economic Development approved a $300,000 loan for Chemistry Distilling, a Rapid City company founded in 2024. The money will help the company purchase and renovate an industrial facility to […]
text:
A page on the South Dakota Governor's Office of Economic Development website in August 2026. (Photo by South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota board approved a total of $481,199 in state loans and grants Wednesday for businesses in Rapid City and De Smet.
The Board of Economic Development approved a $300,000 loan for Chemistry Distilling, a Rapid City company founded in 2024. The money will help the company purchase and renovate an industrial facility to manufacture and store high-purity ethanol. 
The company’s Sam Papendick said in a statement to South Dakota Searchlight that Chemistry Distilling is taking existing ethanol and putting it through an additional purification process to “remove trace impurities and water to produce very high-purity, 200-proof ethanol that can meet specifications for higher-value markets.”
Papendick said those markets include pharmaceutical and laboratory applications, food and flavor processing, personal care products, extraction and other specialty chemical uses. 
“We also have a beverage side of the business, where high-purity neutral spirits can become the base for products like vodka and other distilled beverages,” he said in the statement.

The loan comes from the SD Works Program, which provides low-interest financing for eligible business projects. The Governor’s Office of Economic Development said the project is expected to create seven full-time jobs over five years.
Dakota Evergreen received a $90,000 loan from the same program to purchase a chiropractic clinic in De Smet. The loan is expected to help retain four full-time jobs and keep the clinic operating. A press release from the Governor’s Office of Economic Development said it is the only chiropractic provider in a 35-mile radius.
“These projects strengthen local communities, support good-paying jobs, and build a strong, diverse economy that is ‘Open for Opportunity,’” said Gov. Larry Rhoden in the release. 
The board also approved a grant of up to $91,199 through the South Dakota Jobs Program for Innovative Materials & Processes to expand its Rapid City operation with a new building and manufacturing and warehouse equipment. The jobs program provides grants tied to qualifying business investments and job creation.
The defense contractor and research firm was founded in 1999, and researches and manufactures explosives, pyrotechnics and more for the U.S. Army and Navy. The state release said the expansion is expected to create 18 to 24 jobs.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Private equity firm returns $13.3M to PNM’s parent company following criticism
description: The private equity firm seeking to acquire New Mexico’s largest electric provider has returned more than $13 million in dividends it earned from a stock sale that state utility regulators in July determined to be illegal, recent filings show.
text:
Regional bulk transmission lines crisscross the area between Golden and Madrid along New Mexico Highway 14. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)The private equity firm seeking to acquire New Mexico’s largest electric provider has returned more than $13 million in dividends it earned from a stock sale that state utility regulators in July determined to be illegal, recent filings show.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission in July voted 2-1 to rule that a $400 million stock transaction between a Blackstone Infrastructure affiliate and TXNM Energy Inc., which owns PNM, violated state law, in part because the companies did not first obtain PRC approval.
The commission ordered the companies to undo the sale, rendering it “void and of no effect.”
Critics of the proposed $11.5 billion merger between Blackstone and TXNM were quick to point out that, in subsequent regulatory filings, Blackstone’s attorneys revealed that the private equity firm held onto about $13.3 million in dividends created by the stock sale after undoing the stock sale.
“They complied with the ‘void’ part, but not the ‘of no effect’ part,” Mariel Nanasi, executive director of the Santa Fe-based clean energy advocacy organization New Energy Economy, told Source NM. “If it never happened, then you can’t be making profit off of it.”
Opponents to the overall merger took aim at the $13.3 million in dividends at a recent public comment hearing that the PRC held on the University of New Mexico campus in Albuquerque late last month.
New Mexico residents turn out to UNM campus to weigh in on proposed private equity takeover of PNM

In a regulatory filing this week, attorneys for Blackstone wrote that the firm repaid the $13.3 million to TXNM on Aug. 7, “after consultation” with PRC regulatory staffers.
Blackstone did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment.
Last month, Blackstone and TXNM agreed to extend the deadline for the pending acquisition, which still needs state approval, to mid-2027. Company leaders have long said that a cash infusion from a firm like Blackstone would be the best way to invest in New Mexico’s aging power grid.
“We appreciate the NMPRC’s careful review of this case and look forward to further demonstrating why this partnership will strengthen the grid, support long-term investment and deliver meaningful benefits for customers and communities across New Mexico and Texas,” TXNM Energy President and CEO Don Tarry wrote in a statement at the time.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lexington alderman guilty of harassing and stalking city clerk
description: Alderman Charlie Earl Simmons (left) is pictured alongside Mayor Percy Washington and City Clerk Casshondra Pitchford at a Lexington Board of Aldermen meeting on Jan. 6, 2026
text:
A Lexington alderman allegedly bullied and harassed Deputy Clerk Brenda Powell to the point that she required anti-anxiety medication. She also accused him of recording video of her and stalking. She said tint was applied to a teller window near her desk at City Hall to deter future video recording.
Another city employee also accused Charles Earl Simmons, who was reelected last year, of simple assault. Yet another accused accused him of stalking. The incidents occurred earlier this year, court records show.
On Aug. 5, Justice Court Judge Abraham Gates found Simmons, who did not appear for the hearing, guilty in absentia of harassing, stalking and assaulting city employees. Court records indicate Simmons had proper notice of the hearing.
Gates ordered Simmons to pay $2,675 in fines and assessments. Gates also ordered Simmons to stay at least 100 feet away from Powell and to stop calling her unless for official city business.
Simmons’ alleged abusive behavior in the small community just outside the Mississippi Delta stretches back years, coinciding with several lawsuits and a Department of Justice probe into unfair policing practices and harassment by police officers. 
Alderman Charlie Earl Simmons is seen at the Lexington Board of Aldermen meeting on Jan. 6, 2026. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Simmons’ harassment and stalking were “constant,” according to court records and testimony from Powell.
Simmons did not respond to a request for comment. Lexington Mayor Percy Washington declined to comment.
Lexington public officials’ abuse, particularly of Black residents, has been well documented in court records and a 2024 federal probe. The Justice Department investigated the Lexington Police Department and city government for subjecting Black residents to excessive force, unlawful searches, retaliatory arrests and detention without due process. 
In 2022, the Lexington Board of Alderman voted to fire Police Chief Sam Dobbins, who is white and was at the center of the DOJ investigation, after an audio recording leaked of him using multiple racist and homophobic epithets and bragging about shooting a Black man 119 times.
Simmons, who is Black, voted to keep Dobbins as police chief. They were friends, according to a 2022 civil rights lawsuit filed by Lexington locals against police leadership and the city. The same lawsuit alleges Simmons requested that Lexington police officers harass his neighbors.
Simmons abused his position as an alderman to “retaliate against organizers who worked to correct LPD’s constitutional violations,” the lawsuit read.
Powell, the deputy clerk who filed a criminal charging affidavit against Simmons, said the harassment started in 2019. She accuses Simmons of making inappropriate sexual advances and vulgar comments about her appearance.
As a deputy clerk, Powell was in close proximity to Simmons, who was elected city alderman in 2021, and reelected last year. At city hall, she works from the front desk behind a teller window. The board room for aldermen meetings is adjacent to the clerk’s office in the same building.
Powell said the city eventually installed tint on the teller window because Simmons would linger in the foyer of the city clerk’s office with glasses that recorded video of her. Simmons would also make disparaging remarks toward other city employees until residents stopped by the clerk’s office to pay bills and fill out paperwork. Then he would leave.
Simmons would also yell for work orders and other documentation for city hall meetings at the teller window, and demand them “because I’m an alderman,” Powell recalled. He would sometimes call the office between three and five times per day, she said.
When she reported his actions to city officials in 2024, the mayor and Board of Aldermen restricted Simmon’s access to City Hall, Powell said. Simmons continued to stalk and bully her at work, Powell detailed in written testimony shared with Mississippi Today.
“I think the board has tried to do everything they could to keep him away, but he does what he wants to do,” Powell said.
Powell eventually filed an affidavit against Simmons because, she said, her other formal complaints were unsuccessful despite multiple witnesses including city officials.
On Dec. 2, 2022, Gates found Simmons guilty of stalking. Gates also dismissed two charges of aggravated assault and a charge of simple assault against Simmons that day.
Removing from office a local elected official found guilty of a serious crime requires state involvement. The attorney general’s office must submit a motion for removal to the local circuit court. The circuit court judge then orders them removed. MS Code § 25-5-1 
Jill Collen Jefferson, an activist and attorney, remembers hiring a security team after Simmons continued to harass an organizer she worked with. Simmons took photographs of cars outside the organizer’s home and stalked and harassed her, according to a 2022 civil rights lawsuit Lexington locals filed against police leadership and the city. Simmons also called the organizer’s employer to get her fired, the lawsuit alleged.
Bonita Streeter, who also organized on behalf of city police reforms, said Simmons tried to run her off the road with his pickup truck in 2022. She said she believes it was retaliation for advocating on behalf of victims of police harassment. She said she still tries to avoid him for her safety, but that’s difficult in a community of fewer than 1,500 people.
Bonita Streeter speaks at a Lexington Board of Aldermen meeting on Jan. 6, 2026.
Removing from office a local elected official found guilty of a serious crime requires state involvement. The attorney general’s office must submit a motion for removal to the local circuit court. The circuit court judge then orders them removed. MS Code § 25-5-1 
Simmons could have been punished for up to one year in the county jail for guilty verdicts on both stalking charges. Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office did not immediately respond to a question about whether her office is filing a motion to remove Simmons.
It was difficult for Powell to tell her husband about the harassment she endured at work.
“I had to go to him,” Powell said, “and I had to literally break down and cry and tell him some of the things I had been going through and some of the nasty things that were being said to me.”
Powell said she’s worried of retaliation or more aggressive harassment or bullying. She has asked colleagues to sit with her at the city clerk’s office for protection. Judge Gates mentioned that Simmons could appeal the verdict, Powell said.
“I have been flipping myself on the inside, too, worried about the next step that he’s going to take,” Powell said of Simmons. “No matter what they tell him to do or what restrictions he has, he doesn’t obey them.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma students head back to school with focus on literacy
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Hundreds of thousands of Oklahoma children returned to school this week for their first academic year under strict new literacy laws. It will be their final school year before reading scores carry even higher stakes. More than 21,100 Oklahoma third graders, or 44%, scored below a basic level on statewide reading tests […]
text:
Families enter Adelaide Lee Elementary on Tuesday, the first day of school, in Oklahoma City Public Schools. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Hundreds of thousands of Oklahoma children returned to school this week for their first academic year under strict new literacy laws. It will be their final school year before reading scores carry even higher stakes.
More than 21,100 Oklahoma third graders, or 44%, scored below a basic level on statewide reading tests this past spring, according to state Department of Education data. Future third graders, starting in the 2027-28 school year, would risk being held back a year for scoring below basic, which the state defines as failing to demonstrate even partial mastery of grade-level expectations.
District leaders are pouring over students’ literacy data as state laws now require extra help for low-scoring readers. Some schools have increased class time spent on reading instruction, knowing the gravity third-grade reading tests will have in the near future.
State leaders enacted more rigorous reading laws this year in hopes of emulating Mississippi, which progressively rose in national academic rankings after implementing similar regulations. 
Mississippi, though, retained only 6% of its third graders in the 2024-25 school year, according to the most recent data available. The Magnolia State held back 8% of its third graders, or 3,000 students, in its first year of retentions in 2014-15.
A sign is posted on a classroom window at Hills Elementary in Santa Fe South Charter Schools while students take a start-of-year reading assessment on Aug. 4 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The fact that Oklahoma could have significantly more students at risk of retention indicates that “our state tests are not the same” as Mississippi’s, said Chris Brewster, superintendent of Santa Fe South Charter Schools. That’s a signal Oklahoma might have more work to do on its methods of assessing students, he said.
“There are certain schools where the vast majority of all of their third graders, historically speaking, haven’t met that standard,” Brewster said of the potential statewide impact. “I don’t know if that’s the intent of the law, but it seems very punitive to children and not really a way to progress the work.”
Brewster, though, said he’s not at all against holding schools accountable for ensuring all children learn to read. His charter district, based in south Oklahoma City, had 46% of its third graders score below basic in reading in 2026, but he said he’s optimistic about future growth.
How are schools accelerating learning?
This past spring, 66% of Santa Fe South’s first graders, who will be among the initial third graders to take the high-stakes literacy test, scored at or above their grade level in reading on districtwide benchmark assessments. 
That’s the result of six years of steady improvement since spring 2020, when 34% of the district’s first graders performed near or above their grade level, Santa Fe South leaders said. Rather than making significant changes this year, they plan to continue with the methods behind that success.
Santa Fe South students, many of whom come from low-income and non-English-speaking homes, take a mix of assessments that test specific reading skills. 
Once students’ weak points are identified, they begin a three-week cycle of daily small-group instruction focused on the skills that need improvement, said Missy Stotler, Santa Fe South’s content and curriculum coordinator for early childhood. That’s in addition to daily class time dedicated to literacy.
“It’s the idea of short bursts of intense, very focused work with a group of kids, and then quickly assessing, ‘Did they move the needle? Where are the needs now?’ And then, quickly putting them back into new groups that meet their new need of learning,” Stotler said.
Key pieces of reading law still undefined
Still, “there’s a lot of question marks” for schools about the new reading laws, said Meg Wheeler, executive director of elementary education at Santa Fe South. Right now, the number of students scoring below basic is one of the only clear indicators school leaders have of how many of their students might face retention, she said.
Third graders take a start-of-year reading assessment at Hills Elementary in Santa Fe South Charter Schools on Aug. 4 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Under the new law, students would have to score below basic on state reading tests and fail a second literacy assessment to be held back in third grade, unless they meet limited criteria for an exemption. State officials haven’t decided yet what that second test will be. 
Also, all districts will have to implement the same reading screener to check students’ literacy levels and determine how much intervention each child needs. The universal screener hasn’t been chosen yet, either.
“For schools who have not previously used that screener — (it) could be us, we don’t know — we won’t have any historical data to pull from,” Wheeler said. “We don’t get very much information (from state tests) about why a student is scoring at below basic at the third grade level, and we don’t know that we’re going to have any historical data from the screening assessments to help us understand what is happening with a student. 
“So, there’s a lot of blindness in the data that I think we have some fear of right now.”
Districts prepare for high-stakes testing
The question in Edmond Public Schools Superintendent Josh Delich’s mind, he said, is how training and staffing can support the literacy initiative — and whether the state will help with the cost of educators’ professional development.
The state already began rolling out teacher academies for educators who want to earn a reading specialist credential. The state Department of Education’s team of literacy coaches also offered summer workshops.
Edmond schools continue to focus on building teachers’ capacity for literacy instruction, Delich said. A major emphasis has been the quality of general classroom reading lessons, which are provided to all students in a class regardless of their performance level.
Thirty percent of Edmond third graders scored below basic in reading, according to 2025-26 state test results.
“What is that first level of teaching and learning instruction that students receive in the classroom, and how do you support that?” And then through that, you look at how do you spiral in learning objectives that students may struggle with. How do you reteach areas and content in which students are struggling?” Delich said. “We want to make sure we’re moving every single student through individual growth.”
A student writes on a worksheet at Adelaide Lee Elementary in Oklahoma City on Tuesday. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma City Public Schools found reason for optimism during the 2025-26 school year when nearly a quarter of its first graders demonstrated a year’s worth of reading growth after only the fall semester. Adding a second reading curriculum on top of the district’s original lesson plans helped accelerate learning, administrators said.
But, “there are many students who would fall in that retention window,” said Jason Galloway, the district’s chief of academics.
Sixty-six percent of third graders in the district scored below basic, according to state test results.
So, Oklahoma City schools made further changes following the new reading law.
Daily reading instruction time has increased to 150 minutes in many elementary schools from the previous standard of 90 to 120 minutes, said Alisha Suffield, Oklahoma City’s chief of schools.
The district also added more reading interventionists, paraprofessionals and teaching aides to work with students in small groups, Suffield said. All kindergarten and first grade classes will be staffed with a certified teacher rather than someone holding an emergency certification, who might not have traditional classroom training.
“Emergency certified teachers have a very valuable place in our system, but we don’t want them to be placed in those early primary reading years of kinder and first grade,” she said. “So (we’re) just trying to protect those reading spaces and ensure that our kids get the strongest start possible with a certified staff person.”
Reporter Emma Murphy contributed to this report.

name: WyoFile
title: In secretary of state race, Republican candidate Short spends nearly 10 times more than competitors
description:
Notable Wyoming Republican figures have backed Short with campaign donations. 
The post In secretary of state race, Republican candidate Short spends nearly 10 times more than competitors appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Republican secretary of state candidate Robert Short, a Converse County commissioner, has outspent his competitors by about $360,000 ahead of Tuesday’s primary election, campaign finance reports show. 
Short has so far raised a whopping $429,521 for his campaign, $401,645 of which he has already spent. His largest expenditures paid for consulting services, advertising and polling. 
This amount of money is unusual for a secretary of state campaign. That being said, the last election cycle in 2022 also saw a jump in spending in the race for the state’s elections chief. Current Secretary of State Chuck Gray reported more than half a million in contributions ahead of the primary election in 2022, while his main opponent, Tara Nethercott, reported more than $300,000 in contributions. 


Short raised $122,870 through individual donations, including from notable figures like Wyoming Treasurer Curt Meier, former Wyoming Secretary of State Max Maxfield, former Wyoming GOP Chairman Diemer True and billionaire philanthropist Molly Hughes, who donated $500, $1,000, $500 and $2,500, respectively. He also received an in-kind donation — a non-financial contribution — from Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson for catering at fundraisers. 
About half of Short’s money comes from $221,600 in loans. 
Short grew up in Glenrock and studied electrical engineering and computer science. He has built businesses across the energy, agriculture, retail and tourism sectors. Short first served as a Converse County commissioner in 2014 and has also been the vice president of the Wyoming County Commissioners Association.

Secretary of state candidate Rachel Williams of Park County gives her speech during the Wyoming Republican State Convention on Saturday, April 25, 2026, in Douglas. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)

Trailing Short, secretary of state candidate Rachel Williams, a Cody Republican and head of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, reported raising $44,590 and spending $41,195. Williams has represented Park County in the Wyoming House since 2021. She was the main sponsor of two major anti-abortion bills, both of which were struck down in court. Williams, a retired cop, supports banning “ballot harvesting” — the practice of gathering and submitting absentee or mail-in ballots. Gray and wealthy donors from Teton County such as Carleen and Daniel Brophy and Karen and John Kemmerer have backed Williams with donations of $250, $5,000 and $4,800, respectively. 

Republican candidate for Wyoming Secretary of State CJ Young on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, during a candidate forum at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

Meanwhile, CJ Young, a Cheyenne Republican and the former Elections Division director under Gray, reported $45,097 in contributions and spent $39,242. Young, who grew up in Carbon County and earned a law degree and master’s in public administration from the University of Wyoming, worked as the policy planning manager for the Wyoming Department of Corrections before joining Gray’s office in 2023. He left that post in 2025 to work as a field representative for U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman. Young left that position in May to run for secretary of state. 

Republican candidate for secretary of state Qwenton Eagle Oviatt on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, during a candidate forum at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

Lander Republican Qwenton Eagle Oviatt, an academic advisor at Central Wyoming College, reported $2,156 in contributions and overspent that amount by $1,356. Oviatt earned bachelor’s degrees in psychology and environment and natural resource management from the University of Wyoming. After college, he worked in Antarctica supporting scientists. He later became an entrepreneur, founding his own contracting and painting firm and another company with his father that manufactured flare stacks and waste gas burners.
Whoever wins Tuesday’s primary will face Bryan McCarty, the Democratic candidate for secretary of state, in November’s general election. McCarty is unopposed in the primary election. His campaign finance report wasn’t posted on the secretary of state’s website before publishing time. The primary election is Aug. 18 with early voting already underway.
