name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT worker unions to test gubernatorial contenders on key issues
description: Union leaders are making an early push to frame negotiations over CT state employee retirement benefits with Gov. Ned Lamont and Ryan Fazio.
text:
With a rare window opening next year allowing Connecticut to negotiate the terms of state employee retirement benefits, union leaders are making an early and unusual push Thursday with Gov. Ned Lamont and his Republican challenger, state Sen. Ryan Fazio, to frame those talks.
The governor, who won a Democratic primary Tuesday by a 2-1 margin and is favored in early polling to win a third term in November, and Fazio are meeting with representatives of 45,000-plus unionized state employees at a closed-door forum at Charter Oak International Academy in West Hartford.
Previous contracts establishing long-term benefits have been set in increments of 10 or even 20 years, raising the stakes for labor and the state. 
Coming after the primary and as the general-election campaign takes center stage, the event has the trappings more of a political and lobbying effort than collective bargaining. The unions are offering limited press coverage at the start of the event before the doors close and talks begin.
The fiscally moderate governor has frustrated labor steering by $11 billion since 2020 into debt reduction and away from spending on current services. And while most employees have enjoyed annual raises averaging 4.5% for most of Lamont’s tenure, he repeatedly challenged them this spring to roll back flexible work-from-home rules established during the COVID pandemic.
Fazio will not be offering labor any leverage to make Lamont more generous or pliable.
The state senator from Greenwich says Lamont has been too loose with state budget policies and should have generated even more savings to ease Connecticut’s debt burdens. The GOP nominee said Wednesday that state employee retirement benefits, which have been scaled back three times in the past 17 years via concessions deals,  need to be tightened further.
“Connecticut’s state workforce keeps our roads and bridges safe, cares for children and families in crisis, protects our air, water and food, staffs our colleges and universities, administers critical health and safety programs and provides hundreds of other services that residents rely on every day,” the State Employees Bargaining Agent Coalition wrote in a statement this week advancing Thursday’s forum. “Few elected officials have more direct influence over those services than the governor.”
SEBAC, which represents all major employee groups except the state police troopers, faces a crucial test during the first six months of the next gubernatorial term, which begins in January.
The coalition will try to negotiate a new contract that will preserve or revise the pension and retirement healthcare benefits workers have enjoyed for decades.
Gov. John Rowland, a Republican, and the coalition struck a controversial deal in 1997 that guaranteed these benefits for 20 years, limiting the bargaining power of his successors.
Gov. Dannel P. Malloy, a Democrat, extended that system for another decade, from mid-2017 through June 30, 2027. It was the price labor extracted for ratifying concessions packages in 2011 and 2017 that delivered the multiyear wage freezes and benefit cutbacks Malloy needed to balance budgets during the protracted fiscal crisis following the 2008 recession.
Unions also approved a 2009 agreement with Gov. M. Jodi Rell, the Republican who served between Rowland and Malloy, that increased worker contributions toward retirement healthcare.
In talking with labor on Thursday, the governor and his challenger will be keeping two audiences in mind: the union members, who eventually will vote on a new contract, and the voters who will choose between Lamont and Fazio in November.
Lamont noted that the billions he has saved during his first two terms have bolstered cash-starved pension funds for state employees and for municipal teachers, easing pressures on seeking further concessions.
“It also means they have a pension they can count upon,” Lamont said. “They weren’t sure about that eight years ago.” The average annual state employee pension in 2025 was $44,961, according to the state comptroller’s office’s OpenPension website.
Connecticut amassed tens of billions of dollars in pension debt by not saving for these benefits for more than seven decades prior to 2011. Future generations not only had to make up these missing deposits but also the massive investment earnings that could have been achieved. The state still owes more than $30 billion in this area, a burden expected to pressure state finances well into the 2040s.
Fazio has criticized Lamont for not saving even more to shrink this hefty debt. And given that, and the high state and municipal taxes many households and businesses face, Fazio added, Connecticut should tighten retirement benefits again before extending them next summer.
“I think it would be fair to see there needs to be reforms or changes made to make the long-term state of the state more sustainable,” Fazio said, adding that Connecticut must be fair to its taxpayers and to its employees.
The Republican nominee also said the work agreements that allow many state employees to perform their jobs remotely need reform as well.
Fazio said his administration would look closely into key positions that necessitate work be performed in-office and on-site, such as social workers responsible for monitoring child abuse cases.
“They clearly need some changes,” he added.
Lamont said Wednesday he still believes “We [can] talk about that a little bit going forward” about limiting some remote work rules.
But the governor expressed confidence that the issue is manageable.
“Two-thirds of our people show up in person day day,” he said. “Some people can work very efficiently remotely, so we’re trying to get that balance right.”
The governor added he believes most state employees “do amazing work” and validated some union leaders’ concerns about staffing levels. “In some categories, we need more people. So please, if you want to be a state employee, here’s a pretty good time to apply.”
Fazio  expressed disappointment that Thursday’s forum would be closed to the public and to most of the media. The union coalition said one news photographer and one videographer would be allowed in for a few minutes prior to the forum’s staff to capture images and scenes and then would have to leave. The coalition also said its leaders would be willing to discuss the forum with the media after the event.
But Fazio said those restrictions wouldn’t stop him from attending. “I have an attitude,” he added, “that you go everywhere and you listen to everyone and you talk to everyone, whether they’re inclined to vote for you or not.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Cancer patients deserve peace of mind when it comes to medication
description: Cancer patients should never have to question whether the medicine intended to help them is safe and authentic — particularly when health, and sometimes life, hangs in the balance.
text:
Medications are stored on shelves at a pharmacy in Los Angeles. The U.S. Supreme Court heard a case April 29, 2026, that could have major implications on the price of generic drugs. (Photo by Eric Thayer/Getty Images)For more than two decades, I’ve worked with people living with cancer in Louisiana and witnessed thousands of families confront fear and uncertainty that follow a diagnosis.
Patients are thrust into a frightening “new normal” while being asked to absorb an overwhelming amount of information and place extraordinary trust in their physicians, nurses, pharmacists and the medicines that become part of their care.
Amid this uncertainty, they should never have to question whether the medicine intended to help them is safe and authentic — particularly when health, and sometimes life, hangs in the balance.
Cancer medicines are complex, and with that complexity comes unique challenges within the pharmaceutical supply chain: drug shortages can disrupt treatment, manufacturing often spans multiple countries and patients frequently have few alternatives. Every treatment plan is carefully developed around a patient’s diagnosis and needs, making confidence in the quality and integrity of those medicines essential.
Many people assume counterfeit or falsified cancer medicines are a problem that happens elsewhere in the world. But in reality, these products have already reached U.S. clinics, and reports of counterfeit cancer medicines increased 60% worldwide between 2021-23.
While these incidents remain relatively uncommon, they underscore why protecting the integrity of cancer medicines matters so much.
I applaud some legislative and regulatory solutions already underway. The proposed Safeguarding Americans from Fraudulent and Experimental (SAFE) Drugs Act and the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy’s efforts to strengthen adverse-event reporting and information sharing are important steps toward improving medication safety. Greater transparency, clearer labeling, stronger oversight of large-scale compounding and more consistent reporting can help regulators identify unsafe practices and emerging risks earlier.
These reforms should preserve access to legitimate, patient-specific compounding while making it harder for unapproved, poor-quality, or deceptively marketed products to reach patients without appropriate safeguards.
Regulation and reporting alone, however, are not enough. Reports often surface only after someone has been harmed. Patient education must be a central part of any safety strategy, so people understand exactly what they are receiving, including whether a medication is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, compounded for an individual clinical need or sold through an unregulated or illicit channel.
Patients should be encouraged to ask who manufactured or compounded the product, why it is being recommended, whether FDA has evaluated it for safety, effectiveness and quality, and how to report an adverse reaction. No patient should discover only after experiencing harm that a medication was not FDA-approved or that its purity, potency, sterility or dosing had not been independently reviewed.
That education is especially important as patients become more engaged in their healthcare decisions while navigating an increasingly complex information environment. Telehealth platforms, online pharmacies, direct-to-consumer advertising and the inconsistent use of terms such as “FDA-approved” and “compounded medication” can make it difficult to distinguish reliable medical information from marketing.
Many patients understandably assume that every prescription medication reaches them through the same review process, but that is not always the case. This confusion has become so widespread that more than eight in 10 physicians report caring for patients who do not realize compounded medicines are not FDA approved.
That distinction should not diminish the legitimate and essential role of compounding in patient care. When an FDA-approved medicine cannot meet a patient’s specific medical needs, a pharmacist may prepare a customized medication for that individual. For some patients, these preparations are necessary, but they follow a different regulatory pathway than FDA-approved medicines.
Patients and families can take simple steps to protect themselves by asking physicians or pharmacists whether a medication is FDA approved or compounded, why it was selected, who made it and where it came from. They should be cautious of medicines offered through unfamiliar websites or social media and speak with a trusted healthcare professional before making any changes to their treatment.
Most importantly, they can report unexpected reactions or concerns promptly. Taking these steps is an important part of making informed decisions during the biggest health battle a patient will face.

title: More Than Helping Hands: Angela Williamson Is Building a Better Way to Volunteer
description: For nonprofits, volunteers can expand capacity, relieve pressure on staff and help organizations serve more people. For volunteers, Williamson believes the rewards can be equally significant. By John Riddle For Angela Williamson, volunteering is about much more than filling an empty shift, helping at an event or adding another name to a nonprofit’s roster. I[...]
text:
Photo Courtey of Volunteer Engagement Accelerator. Created with AI on 8/13
For nonprofits, volunteers can expand capacity, relieve pressure on staff and help organizations serve more people. For volunteers, Williamson believes the rewards can be equally significant.
By John Riddle
For Angela Williamson, volunteering is about much more than filling an empty shift, helping at an event or adding another name to a nonprofit’s roster.
It is about belonging.
Williamson, founder of Volunteer Engagement Accelerator (VEA), has spent nearly two decades working in volunteer engagement and nonprofit leadership. Today, she helps mission-driven organizations develop stronger systems for attracting, supporting and retaining volunteers, while helping those volunteers find meaningful ways to contribute.
“As a consultant, I help nonprofits create places where people belong, and I focus on volunteer engagement,” Williamson said. “Volunteer engagement is where people give of their time, their talents, their heart, their passion and their donations because they want to make their world and the nonprofit a better place to be.”
Williamson holds the Certified in Volunteer Administration credential, or CVA. She is a past president of the Delaware Association of Volunteer Administrators and received the AL!VE Impact Award in 2022. She has presented at conferences, appeared on podcasts and serves as an instructor for NOVAA 101, helping volunteer administrators develop stronger leadership skills.
Her passion for volunteering, however, began long before it became her profession.
As a child, Williamson watched her parents volunteer in many different capacities. One of her earliest memories involves volunteering at the Delaware State Fair, where she helped pick up litter and received concert tickets in return.
“I thought that was the best, most amazing thing ever as a kid,” she recalled.
Those childhood experiences also taught her something about the importance of making people feel included.
“I’ve always had that heart, I think, of helping the ones that don’t feel belonging, because I have felt left out before,” Williamson said. “As a kid, feeling left out, I think my heart grew for those people who did also feel left out.”
That desire to create connections remains at the heart of her work.
“I love volunteering because it helps people. It helps the community,” she said. “I get to grow, others get to grow, and it just builds a better world, a better community and better people along the way.”
Volunteering Is Changing
While the desire to help remains strong, Williamson says the way people volunteer has changed.
“I think volunteering has changed in what and how and when, but the passion and the desire to help others of volunteers is still deep-seated,” she said.
One challenge is that people are busy and often reluctant to make long-term commitments. Some prefer to decide at the last minute whether they are available, while nonprofits may need to know well in advance if someone will fill a particular shift.
Williamson believes organizations need to adapt by reconsidering what volunteers can do, how much time they need to give and even where the work takes place.
“We do need to, as a nonprofit field, adapt and change and create different volunteer roles and responsibilities and times and places,” she said.
That could include shorter assignments, one-time opportunities, virtual volunteering and skills-based projects.
Williamson also believes volunteering can help address another challenge facing many people today: a need for greater human connection.
“By volunteering and getting out into the world, doing things that are good for the world and connecting with people, people’s mental well-being can be supported and encouraged toward a more positive view,” she said.
Finding the Right Fit
For someone interested in volunteering, Williamson recommends starting by understanding what kind of experience best matches his or her personality.
“Know your personality,” she said.
Do you prefer working behind the scenes or interacting with people? Do you like structure or flexibility? Would you rather work independently or as part of a team?
“There are so many options,” Williamson said. “Sometimes a bad fit isn’t great. Even though you want to help, maybe it’s not the best fit for you. So, find the best-fit volunteer role for you, and you will flourish and do great, and the nonprofit will appreciate it.”
Opportunities can include one-time events, ongoing assignments, direct service, behind-the-scenes work, skills-based volunteering, leadership positions and board service.
And not having much free time does not necessarily rule out volunteering.
“You might not think you have time to volunteer, but sometimes it’s just an hour,” Williamson said.
Virtual and at-home opportunities can provide additional flexibility.
Once someone finds the right opportunity, Williamson emphasizes some basics that can make a big difference: Show up when promised, communicate if plans change, ask questions and speak up if something is not working.
When the Nonprofit Doesn’t Call Back
What happens when someone wants to volunteer, contacts an organization and never hears back?
Williamson says not to give up too quickly.
“If you’ve had a ‘bad’ experience or an organization did not get back to you, please be patient and ask them again,” she said. “Maybe give them three tries. Three strikes and you’re out, maybe. But not all volunteering is like that.”
Ironically, the reason a nonprofit does not respond may be the same reason it needs volunteers.
Staff members are often juggling numerous responsibilities with limited time and resources. An organization may desperately need additional help while lacking an effective system for recruiting and onboarding the people offering it.
That is one of the problems Williamson created Volunteer Engagement Accelerator to address.
“That’s where, as a consultant, I go in and help nonprofits organize themselves better so that they can respond more quickly and in more efficient ways,” she said. “I like helping nonprofits build that bridge toward volunteers and understanding to get people more involved.”
For nonprofits, volunteers can expand capacity, relieve pressure on staff and help organizations serve more people. For volunteers, Williamson believes the rewards can be equally significant.
“When you volunteer, you feel great because you’re making a difference in a cause, a movement, somebody’s life, a pet’s life, whatever that is, whatever the nonprofit mission is,” she said.
People looking for opportunities can contact nonprofits directly or explore resources such as AARP Create the Good and Idealist. In Delaware, Williamson points potential volunteers toward Volunteer Delaware, United Way of Delaware and Delaware Difference Makers.
And for anyone who thinks volunteering is simply about giving away valuable time, Williamson offers another way to look at it.
“It can be a résumé builder. It can be the reason and purpose to get out of bed in the morning,” she said. “It can be all sorts of things to all sorts of people, but it’s all beneficial.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Juneau residents grapple with whether to stay or flee as glacial outburst floodwaters rise
authors: Alix Soliman, KTOO, Clarise Larson, KTOO, Corinne Smith
description: As the Mendenhall River swells with glacial outburst floodwater, hundreds of people living in the suburban valley below spent Tuesday night and Wednesday preparing to evacuate or hunker down. The National Weather Service predicts the flood will crest Thursday. Officials managing the flood response recommended residents evacuate by 3 p.m. On Marion Drive, Ann[...]
text:
Ann Lind looks out from her balcony on Marion Drive at the Mendenhall River as it rises on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Clarise Larson/KTOO)As the Mendenhall River swells with glacial outburst floodwater, hundreds of people living in the suburban valley below spent Tuesday night and Wednesday preparing to evacuate or hunker down. The National Weather Service predicts the flood will crest Thursday.
Officials managing the flood response recommended residents evacuate by 3 p.m.
On Marion Drive, Ann Lind plans to watch the flood from her second-story balcony overlooking the Mendenhall River.
“I got lawn chairs up there, and we’ll just be sitting there, and that’s where I’ve been every year,” she said.
Lind said her crawl space flooded last year when water leaked through the HESCO barriers and a drainage pipe failed. She said she’s staying again this year to protect the property.

Ann Lind secures sandbags at her house on Marion Drive on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Clarise Larson/KTOO)
“Because if I wouldn’t have stayed last year, I never would have known that I was flooding back there, and the flooding would have been way worse,” she said. “Within 30 minutes of me calling for help, I had nine guys and five pumps back there.”
She said she’s more confident her home won’t flood this time after the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers placed an industrial-sized pump just beyond her lawn to send water that leaks through the flood wall back into the river.
Although she plans to stay behind with her 17-year-old daughter, she said her other kids and pets will evacuate – heeding official advice.
Downstream from Lind’s place, on Meander Way, Locke Brown said he and his wife are optimistic about flood protection this year. Last year, the pair’s crawl space and garage flooded.
“If we had these pumps on the roads sitting here last year, I think we probably wouldn’t have had any water in the house,” he said.

Locke and Melissa Brown sit on their porch at their home on Meander Way as the Mendenhall River rises on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Clarise Larson/KTOO)
They said they’re grateful for the pumps and bolstered flood wall provided by the Army Corps this year — but they’re not taking any chances. They said that once the water rises high up on the barriers, they plan to evacuate to a camper they have set up outside of the flood zone.
Locke is retired from the U.S. Coast Guard and his wife still works for the Coast Guard.
“We’ve made our living saving people when they know they should have left,” he said.
Locke said the prudent thing is to leave since there’s a possibility the barriers could fail.
“It’s one of those unknowns. You just — what do they say? — Prepare for the worst and hope for the best,” he said. “We just feel like, at this point, we’re just driftwood. Whatever happens is gonna happen, and we’re just gonna have to deal with it when it’s over.”

HESCO barriers installed along the Mendenhall River on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Clarise Larson/KTOO)
Just a few blocks over, on Gee Street, Benson Bullock said he’s not too worried. He’s patching a pair of waders in his garage, but not for walking through floodwaters.
“Hopefully, if it’s not too crazy, I’ll be going fishing,” he said.
Bullock had a few inches of water in his garage during the catastrophic flood in 2024, but his house has never flooded. Bullock says he plans to put sandbags in front of the garage before the flood crests.
“We have stuff moved and cleaned up,” he said. “We moved my boat, we’ll move my wife’s truck, and we’ll just have my truck here in case we decide to leave.”
On View Drive, many residents say they’re planning to stay to try to protect their property and look out for their neighbors.
View Drive is a forested cul-de-sac that forms a peninsula jutting into the Mendenhall River. It’s been hit the hardest by past floods. For a second year in a row, the street has been left without the protection of the flood wall constructed by the City and Borough of Juneau and the Army Corps. Officials have said in the past that the street has porous soil and have doubts that the homes could be protected.

The Mendenhall River surrounds homes on View Drive in the Mendenhall Valley on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Clarise Larson/KTOO)
Mandy Mallott lives at the end of the cul-de-sac. She bought the house from a family she babysat for when she was growing up in Juneau. It looks out over Stroller White Mountain, where her father died in 2005.
“It’s a very spiritual place to us,” she said. “It’s a private place, and we’ll do what we can to protect it.”
She and her family spent Tuesday evening moving their belongings up onto shelves in their garage. Last year, she worked with her neighbors to have contractors put up their own HESCO barriers around a few properties, and she said her home didn’t flood.

Mandy Mallott points over HESCO barriers to the Mendenhall River from her home on View Drive on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Clarise Larson/KTOO)
Although a federally sponsored buyout for her home and others on View Drive might be on the table — Mallott said she’s emotionally tied to the place, and sees a long-term solution designed by the Army Corps as her best option.
“That emergency tunnel fix gives us all a lot of hope,” she said.
Mallott and her family are tribal citizens, and she said she’s grateful for the dozens of sandbags that the Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska dropped off on Tuesday.
Residents of the Riverview Senior Living facility were about 50-50 split on whether to evacuate on Wednesday afternoon, said its Executive Director René Bryant. This year, new HESCO barriers are now standing between the Mendenhall River and the two-story assisted living and memory care facility.
She said the roughly 70 residents have a choice whether to stay or evacuate, and they are providing transportation to a nearby emergency shelter at St. Paul’s Catholic Church after an early dinner on Wednesday evening. Bryant said additional transportation to evacuate will be provided Thursday if needed.
“We are respecting everybody’s rights, while contacting family members to make these decisions as well,” Bryant said.
See the latest flood updates on the KTOO live blog.

title: Democrats push nearly 250 state bills opposing federal immigration efforts
description: Democratic lawmakers proposed nearly 250 bills in state capitols this year seeking to limit federal immigration efforts as they sought to push back against what they view as federal government overreach.  In a new report tallying 2026 action, State Futures, a nonprofit coordinating hundreds of Democratic lawmakers across the states, tracked 242 pieces of suc[...]
text:
Colorado state Sen. Mike Weissman, a Democrat, speaks at a February news conference about immigration enforcement-related bills at the Colorado Capitol. Democratic lawmakers nationwide proposed nearly 250 bills this year in statehouses seeking to limit federal immigration enforcement efforts. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Democratic lawmakers proposed nearly 250 bills in state capitols this year seeking to limit federal immigration efforts as they sought to push back against what they view as federal government overreach. 
In a new report tallying 2026 action, State Futures, a nonprofit coordinating hundreds of Democratic lawmakers across the states, tracked 242 pieces of such legislation introduced across 32 states. About a fifth of them passed. Most of the measures address the ramped up immigration enforcement efforts that have defined President Donald Trump’s second term. 
Some of those bills have faced Republican opposition and White House challenges. But Democratic governors have also raised concerns and even vetoed some measures, saying they supported their aims, but worried they could have unintended consequences and invite litigation.
The bills sought to ban the masking of immigration officers, protect against immigration enforcement in sensitive places such as schools and hospitals and enact new zoning regulations on private detention facilities, among other issues.
State Futures said 50 bills passed in 17 states this year, though several were vetoed or still await action from governors. Many of those bills face legal review as courts weigh the limits of state authority to regulate federal action.
Democrats, Republicans alike focus on states’ rights as a way out of America’s political woes

But lawmakers say those numbers underscore the left’s growing embrace of federalism — the division of power between federal and state governments — that has gained traction during the second Trump presidency.
Rhode Island state Sen. Tiara Mack said many Democrats, including herself, have been wary of championing states’ rights, an ideology that evokes odious memories of slavery and segregation. But she said constituents are demanding action from state leaders to oppose the White House’s hardline immigration arrest and deportation efforts.
“This new landscape requires legislators to really own the narrative and own the reality that federalism is something that we can use as a tool to strengthen protections for our state,” she said, “and we have to work with states across the country.”
Mack is a co-chair of State Futures’ federal response working group that shares legislative ideas with state lawmakers across the country. This year, she was among those sponsoring Rhode Island legislation that seeks to protect people from immigration arrests while attending court proceedings. Signed into law in June, that law says violators of the protections can be held in contempt of court and can face a lawsuit from those arrested without a judicial order or warrant. 
Virginia Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger vetoed a similar bill that would have prohibited immigration enforcement in courthouses, schools and hospitals. In her veto message, the governor said she appreciated the intention of the bill but worried it would put security guards and law enforcement in the “untenable position” of choosing whether to break federal or state law. 
Another Delaware measure is currently awaiting action from Democratic Gov. Matt Meyer.  
Mack said lawmakers are increasingly coordinating across state lines, learning from legislative wins and failures in other capitols. As an example, she pointed to a California law aimed at banning federal and state agents from wearing masks.
A judge blocked that law earlier this year because it exempted state law enforcement, saying it therefore discriminated against federal agents. A similar proposal in Rhode Island, which was held in committee this session, seeks to stop all law enforcement officers from concealing their identity.
Oregon governor signs slew of bills protecting immigrants amid federal crackdown

Oregon Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek signed eight laws this April seeking to defend immigrant rights. Those laws protect against enforcement efforts in schools and hospitals, ensure individuals’ data remains confidential from the feds and allow people to sue the federal government for violating the law.
In Colorado, lawmakers this year expanded the health department’s authority to inspect immigration detention facilities and required compliance with state health and safety standards and reporting rules. That law is currently being challenged by a private prison operator as state officials demand more access and information regarding at least one tuberculosis case among detainees.
Colorado state Sen. Mike Weissman, one of the sponsors of that measure, said he’s worked with Democratic colleagues across conservative and liberal states more than ever before to oppose federal government efforts.
“We all talk because we all have the same concerns,” he said, “and that is to protect the basic freedoms of our people from an absolutely out of control federal regime.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

text:
Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) speaks at an election security event in Lansing, Michigan on June 5, 2024 (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)U.S. Rep. John James, a Republican congressman from Shelby Township who is the GOP nominee for governor, has selected state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) to serve as his lieutenant governor should he be elected in November. 
James made the announcement on Thursday morning, saying that DeBoyer would help him “lead the fight against corruption, fraud, waste, and abuse, protecting core services while fixing what’s broken.”
DeBoyer is in his second term in the Michigan House and serves currently as the chair of the House Oversight Committee, where he has made a point to investigate and question top Democratic officials, including Attorney General Dana Nessel and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is the Democratic nominee for governor.

“I am choosing Jay DeBoyer as my running mate because he has run a business, served in local government, and overseen elections. He knows how to work with both parties in the Legislature to get things done,” James continued in a post on X. “He will lead the fight against corruption, fraud, waste, and abuse, protecting core services while fixing what’s broken.
DeBoyer is a staunch conservative in the state legislature, and his selection was celebrated online by groups such as Great Lakes Gun Rights and fellow Republicans, including Senate Minority Leader and former gubernatorial candidate Aric Nesbitt and U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) 
Jamie Roe, a Republican consultant, also expressed his support for James’ pick in a post on X, writing, “Jay DeBoyer is a great leader and public servant. Through his work on oversight he knows the problems facing our state can help the future James administration fix them.”
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel, however, said James picking DeBoyer as his running mate came out of pressure to choose “the most MAGA candidate possible.”
“DeBoyer has voted in lockstep with Republicans’ extreme agenda in Lansing, peddled disproven election conspiracy theories, received thousands of dollars in campaign cash from the DeVos family, and even refused to open an investigation into Jeffrey Epstein’s connections to a Michigan school,” Hertel said in a statement. “A James-DeBoyer administration would be a rubber stamp for Trump’s agenda of cutting healthcare, stripping away fundamental rights and freedoms, and putting corporations and special interests first.” 
Republican Party delegates will officially nominate a candidate for lieutenant governor at their annual convention on Aug. 22.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Seeing the future? Massachusetts wants to see your license
description: It would be easy to assume that most psychics, tarot card readers, and mediums want to do away with the red tape, but that isn’t necessarily the case. Salem licenses more fortune tellers than any other community in the state, and many say although the archaic statute may have been rooted in distrust and prejudice, there are tangible benefits of the law today[...]
text:
IT’S NO SECRET that Massachusetts suffers from an abundance of red tape, outdated laws, and obsolete regulations. One law still on the books requires at least three bells to be attached to horses drawing sleighs or sleds.
So, it shouldn’t come as a surprise that even fortune telling is a licensed job in the Bay State, right along with barbering, teaching, and nursing. 
State law says no person shall “tell fortunes for money” unless they have been issued a license by a local licensing authority. The law also states that a fortune teller must reside continuously in the city or town in which they wish to practice for at least 12 months before they can receive a license. The licensing fee, set by the municipality, must cost at least $2 but not more than $50.
The statute dates back to 1963 and was likely established to prevent grifters from passing from town to town. But lawmakers haven’t forgotten about it – or at least some of them haven’t.
State Rep. Susannah Whipps of Athol introduced legislation in 2025 for the second time that would repeal the 12-month residency requirement for fortune tellers. A previous version of the bill passed out of the Joint Committee on Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure but never made it to the House floor for a vote. The current version sits in legislative limbo and is likely to face the same fate.
“To be honest, there is not a very active or powerful fortune-teller lobby in the state that I know of, so there hasn’t been a big push to get this over the finish line,” Whipps said. “My interest is just to remove an outdated law.” 
There have been numerous attempts to repeal the residency requirement over the years, yet none have been successful. In 2000, for example, then-state Sen. Stan Rosenberg filed the legislation after being asked by the city of Northampton to challenge the law. An applicant there had been denied a license because of the rule. Whipps said she was similarly asked by a former Greenfield city employee to file the legislation after someone reached out to the city wanting to provide fortune-telling services. 
It would be easy to assume that most psychics, tarot card readers, and mediums want to do away with the red tape, but that isn’t necessarily the case.
Nowhere do people have more opinions on the topic than in Salem, which licenses more fortune tellers than any other community in the state. Many say although the archaic statute may have originally been rooted in distrust and prejudice toward marginalized communities like the Romani people, there are tangible benefits of the law today.
“I don’t think there’s anything wrong with trying to regulate and monitor to make sure that there aren’t fraudulent people,” said Leanne Marrama, co-owner of Pentagram, a psychic shop in Salem. “A lot of people have a certain amount of fear in regard to this industry. The world, unfortunately, is filled with jerks, and this is supposed to weed out the jerks.”
So, what differentiates fraudulent fortune telling from genuine fortune telling? Don’t worry, there’s a state law for that too, though it prompts more questions than answers. It states that whoever fraudulently obtains money from another person “by a game, device, sleight of hand, pretended fortune telling, or by any trick or other means by the use of cards or other instruments” shall be charged with larceny.
But what is “pretended” fortune telling?
Marrama, 56, is a licensed psychic who has practiced in Salem for 25 years. She said psychic readings are meant to empower customers and “show people a map of their life” rather than tell them a “fortune.” Fraudulent fortune tellers take advantage of people’s fears and hopes and may promise someone a quick fix or a future outcome for a hefty price, she said. They also might purposely instill fear or desperation in a customer or tell them a grim fortune that only they can correct for money.
“A lot of people don’t know what it is. They think I’m going to tell them when they’re going to get married or how many kids they’re going to have,” said Marrama, who also describes herself as a witch. “If you want to change the map of your life, you change your actions in the world. There’s no crystal ball or candle that’s going to fix everything.”
Leanne Marrama, a licensed psychic and self-described witch, stands outside of Pentagram, a psychic shop in Salem that she co-owns. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
The licensing process provides psychics, mediums, and other magical practitioners with some degree of credibility in a field that is often met with skepticism and suspicion, Marrama said. Bad actors could threaten the entire industry in Salem.
“When one of us turns around and acts a fool, then all of us are going down with them,” she said. “A lot of our clients come in October, and they want to be sure that these people have been vetted. We get to say that all of our psychics have been vetted by the city.”
Lorelei Stathopoulos, the owner of the Crow Haven Corner shop in Salem, is a licensed psychic reader, as well as a “love witch.” She said the licensing and residency requirement ensures that when Salem experiences a massive tourism boom in October because of Halloween, those who don’t typically practice in the community cannot simply set up shop on the street and take business away from psychics who have been working in the city for years.
Salem city ordinance defines a fortune teller as anyone who forecasts futures or reads the past “by means of any occult, psychic power, faculty, force, clairvoyance, cartomancy, psychometry, phrenology, spirits, tea leaves, tarot cards, scrying, coins, sticks, dice, sand, coffee grounds, crystal gazing, or any other such reading, or through mediumship, seership, prophecy, augury, astrology, palmistry, necromancy, mindreading, telepathy, or other craft, art, science, talisman, charm, potion, magnetism, magnetized article or substance, or by any such similar thing or act.”
In other words, it covers almost anyone in the supernatural industry who charges money for their services. It even includes aura photographers, who capture and interpret visual representations of a person’s energy field.
Old Town Hall in Salem (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
At any given time in Salem, there are between 80 and 100 active fortune-telling licenses, according to the licensing department. That includes individual practitioners, store owners, and sub-licensees providing fortune-telling services in stores. Licenses expire after two years and cost $50, mostly to cover the price of a background check. By comparison, Boston, which only offers individual licenses, currently has just five licensed fortune tellers.
The application asks for a five-year employment history, educational background, and a brief description of the nature of the services to be provided.
Marrama’s business partner Timothy Reagan, who is also a psychic, holds the store license for Pentagram. Marrama lives in Revere and does not have to meet the residency requirement herself because she is sub-licensed under the store. Only individual fortune tellers who do not work in a licensed store in Salem have to meet the 12-month residency requirement.
City ordinance allows licensed fortune-teller shops to have up to five sub-licensees practicing at a time – a restriction that limits how many readings and services they can offer in a day and ultimately reduces profits, according to Reagan. But overall, he is happy with the licensing process.
“It is kind of a pain in the butt, and it costs us money,” Reagan said. “But it protects our profession from anybody off the street just wanting to make a couple of extra bucks who has never done this or studied or trained in this.”
In 2022, Reagan, a Salem resident, successfully challenged a fortune-telling ordinance in Beverly that placed a residency requirement on store owners. After spending nearly $200,000 on the construction of a new psychic shop in the city, Reagan was denied a license because he was not a resident of Beverly. The requirement was later overturned by the city council.
In order to receive a fortune-telling license, Salem also requires at least 75 percent of a store’s revenue to derive from the sale of “metaphysical products,” defined as “ritual tools or materials used in the study or practice of Witchcraft, Wicca, Pagan, New Age, Occult, or other spiritual belief.”
“If you are selling sandwiches, you can’t just be like, ‘I’m also going to offer psychic readings,’” Marrama explained.
Christian Day, a self-described warlock and one of the most well-known figures in Salem’s magical community, said the metaphysical requirement is almost impossible to evaluate and enforce.
“I can take out a bag of Doritos and do a reading. It’s the same as using tea leaves,” he said. “You can see signs and omens in just about anything, so what the hell is a metaphysical product?”
In 2007, Day was at the forefront of a controversial but successful effort to remove a city ordinance that said only five fortune-teller shops could be licensed at any given time. Many of the psychics who practiced before the restriction was lifted were not happy about the new competition.
Downtown Salem (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Day said he sees the benefits of the licensing process when it comes to background checks, but he is otherwise against the red tape.
“I don’t like overregulation of things, and when you’re overregulating psychics, you’re overregulating people from a variety of minority and often persecuted religions like witchcraft, voodoo, or spiritualism,” Day said. “Do I agree with the 12 months? No. Do I agree with the 75 percent metaphysical requirement? No. I think those things level themselves out anyway. How many pizza parlors are really going to want to get into this business?” 
Just weeks ago, when asked what he would put on his legislative “fun agenda,” House Speaker Ron Mariano jokingly told reporters that fortune-telling policy would make the list.
Some have questioned why lawmakers have repeatedly tried to repeal only the 12-month residency requirement rather than the entire law.
“We have never discussed removing the requirement to have a license,” Whipps said. “I believe it might be an industry that could be exploited for trickery or scams. At least with a licensing process, a town knows who is performing this kind of work and could do a background check to make sure they are on the up and up.”
But when it comes to regulatory overreach, if there’s a political will, there’s a way. In 2021, for example, Massachusetts eliminated licensing for natural hair braiders in a bond bill signed by former Gov. Charlie Baker. The move was celebrated by immigrants and women of color who said the licensing requirements were a major employment hurdle.
Whipps isn’t so confident that fortune-telling regulations will garner the same attention. 
“If I were to make a prediction, this bill will not move forward, although I would like to see it come for a vote,” Whipps said. “If only I had a crystal ball.”
