name: Rhode Island Current
title: Guckian and Pelino trade accusations over resumes and radio comments in first TV debate
description: It didn’t take long for the first face-to-face of Rhode Island’s Republican gubernatorial candidates to turn combative. Elaine Pelino didn’t finish her first sentence of the Wednesday debate, hosted by NBC 10 and Coastal ABC, before turning to fellow GOP candidate Aaron Guckian to ask for an in-person apology. Pelino’s request was cut off by […]
text:
NBC10 News Anchor Gene Valicenti (left foreground) moderates a live, televised debate between Republican gubernatorial candidates Elaine Pelino  and Aaron Guckian Wednesday. (Screenshot)It didn’t take long for the first face-to-face of Rhode Island’s Republican gubernatorial candidates to turn combative.
Elaine Pelino didn’t finish her first sentence of the Wednesday debate, hosted by NBC 10 and Coastal ABC, before turning to fellow GOP candidate Aaron Guckian to ask for an in-person apology. Pelino’s request was cut off by moderator Gene Valicenti, who redirected Pelino to his question about Gov. Dan McKee’s Supreme Court nominee.
But the tension lingered and intensified over the course of the hourlong forum in the lobby of the Providence Performing Arts Center and livestreamed on both local broadcast stations.
Ideological differences have separated the Republicans since the race began. Guckian, 50, a former aide to Gov. Don Carcieri who also ran for lieutenant governor in 2022, launched his 2026 campaign as a “compassionate conservative” focused on affordability and government efficiency. Pelino, 72, a first-time candidate, proudly proclaims herself as the “only MAGA candidate” in the primary, promising to keep the left-leaning state from continuing down a path toward “socialism.”
Guckian won the GOP’s endorsement at its state convention in June, and has roughly 10 times more campaign cash than Pelino as of June 30. But Pelino had a 25-point lead over Guckian in a University of New Hampshire poll published June 30. 
One day after the unfavorable polling information for Guckian was released, he made disparaging comments about Pelino’s age and appearance in a WPRO interview.
Pelino on her campaign social media sites in a radio interview on WPRO. Pelino quickly denounced the comments as sexist and agist. A day later, Guckian called back in to radio host Tara Granahan’s show to apologize. But, as Pelino noted Wednesday, he had not yet apologized to her in person despite several close interactions since the comment.
“I ran into him a couple times, and I was waiting for him to say something,” Pelino said.
After Guckian tried to return the focus to policy as the topic voters most wanted to hear about, she added, “and they want to know if their governor has good moral character, too.”
Credentials in question
Pelino never got the “sorry” from Guckian she wanted. But she had more accusations ready to lob at her opponent, calling him a “flip-flopper” on conservative social issues like gun rights and abortion, and later, insinuating he exaggerated his role in Carcieri’s administration.
Guckian also took aim at Pelino’s resume, specifically a claim mentioned in her campaign social media post that she served as chief of staff for financial services giant Cantor Fitzgerald. The position was first reported by The Providence Journal. 
Pressed by Valicenti on this role, which is not mentioned on Pelino’s LinkedIn or other public credentials, Pelino flashed a badge from the company to the cameras.
“Just because you have a badge from Cantor Fitzgerald doesn’t mean you were chief of staff,” Guckian said.
Pelino, whose extensive resume also includes a bit role in “Terms of Endearment,” a stint as a Houston Oilers cheerleader and publisher of a women’s magazine, never directly responded to questions about her position at Cantor Fitzgerald.
“I had the highest security you could get,” she said, adding she also served as an executive assistant to firm founder B. Gerald Cantor, and worked on the firm’s charitable foundation.
Guckian, who admitted in a previous Ocean State Media interview that his job for Carcieri was primarily as a driver and special assistant, continued to emphasize his credentials in government and relationships with public and private sector leaders as top qualifications. Guckian most recently served as executive director of the Rhode Island Dental Association, stepping down when he launched his run for governor.
“You can’t teach experience,” Guckian said. 
He also pledged to use his party affiliation to secure more support from the Trump administration, including federal funding for satellite health services centers and to offset the lost revenue from the still-shuttered state truck toll program. Neither Guckian nor Pelino supported reactivating the gantries despite a federal appellate court decision in 2024 allowing Rhode Island to revive the truck toll program with some restrictions.
The two GOP rivals also espoused similar conservative talking points about increasing government efficiency and accountability while reducing state spending and taxes. But Guckian’s campaign hinges on a plan to work with unions and government employees to incentivize ways to trim unnecessary government spending, while Pelino said working with organized labor was not a top priority.
Immigration enforcement
Pelino took a stronger position on immigration, promising a first-day-in-office executive order that would clarify the state is not a sanctuary for undocumented residents — though that official designation does not exist now — and ordering state police to work with federal immigration agents to remove undocumented residents.
“A big thing that would help us is if we would take the illegals out of Rhode Island,” Pelino said, alleging proof, though not cited, that undocumented residents’ use of social service and welfare programs was edging out veterans and other documented recipients. Undocumented immigrants do not qualify for many safety net programs including Medicaid and federal food assistance.
Guckian stressed the importance of cracking down on “violent offenders” — who statistically are more likely to be U.S. citizens than undocumented residents — while also creating pathways to citizenship to support the workforce needs of major employers.
“You want a socialist state,” Pelino said of Guckian’s response, which she contrasted with the desires of conservative residents. “Rhode Island wants to be a capitalist, free enterprise state. We want a chance to buy a home, afford a home, buy a car we want, and not have all these crazy green energy standards.”
Yet, as Valicenti noted, even a Republican governor will have to work with a Democratic-led legislature, which controls the state pursestrings and major policy decisions.
Guckian acknowledged the need to work across the aisle, while staying within the bounds of the governor’s authority. Pelino’s take?
“If I can’t change it or fix it, I can actually podcast at night and expose what they’re doing,” she said of state lawmakers.
Back to the bridge 
Pelino also engaged in a heated back-and-forth with Valicenti during a segment devoted to the Washington Bridge. Valicenti, who frequently hosted former Rhode Island Department of Transportation Director Peter Alviti on his own WPRO radio show, grilled Pelino after she remarked that she hoped Alviti was “in witness protection right now” to avoid being investigated by her proposed “department of accountability” for his role in the bridge debacle.
“I’m not offended by it, but I’m using your words,” Valicenti said. “You sort of bought the narrative that wasn’t the state’s fault. They hired inspectors and construction companies that failed them. Alviti is the state, failed him. Why do you want to pivot on him?”
Guckian also took issue with the witness protection comment, despite Pelino characterizing the remark as a joke.
“Oh, Aaron, grow up,” Pelino said to the 6-foot-7 rival beside her, later adding “Forgive me honey.”
“Now you’re calling me honey,” Guckian noted.
A second gubernatorial debate featuring Democratic candidates McKee and Helena Buonanno Foulkes was set to air at 7 p.m. on NBC10 and Coastal ABC, with both events also available on the station’s YouTube channel.
Early voting begins Aug. 20 ahead of a Sept. 9 primary.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Medicaid fraud panel discusses ways to solicit more fraud tips, engage public
description: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Iowa can find ways to be more “proactive” in collecting and responding to Medicaid fraud tips as the Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force held its second meeting Wednesday. The task force was convened by Gov. Kim Reynolds in July. The 11-member group will draft recommendations for the state […]
text:
Lee Grossman, right, Iowa Medicaid director, updated Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, left, and members of the Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force about efforts to collect data and instances of fraud and abuse within Medicaid spending at a Aug. 12, 2026 meeting. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Iowa can find ways to be more “proactive” in collecting and responding to Medicaid fraud tips as the Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force held its second meeting Wednesday.
The task force was convened by Gov. Kim Reynolds in July. The 11-member group will draft recommendations for the state Legislature on how to stop instances of fraud within Medicaid. It was created in response to an executive order from President Donald Trump creating a federal task force with a similar goal, headed by Vice President JD Vance, that came with an announcement that each state’s Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCU) would undergo a new evaluation before being recertified to receive federal funding.
The state task force was given the directive of crafting a “comprehensive statewide strategy to eliminate Medicaid fraud, waste, abuse” and finding ways to leverage federal funding resources to assist Iowa’s existing MFCU.
State leaders overseeing the departments of Public Safety, of Management and of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing, as well as Iowa Medicaid and the Iowa Medicaid Fraud Control Unit within DIAL, shared updates at the Wednesday task force meeting about work being done by their groups to find ways to better identify and address instances of waste, fraud and abuse within the state’s Medicaid system. When the task force met for the first time, members said they planned to create a website where individuals can submit concerns about suspected Medicaid fraud alongside finding ways to make the state’s MFCU more efficient.
These discussions continued at the second meeting, as leaders talked about ways different state entities can collaborate and more efficiently tackle issues related to fraud and abuse. Bird told reporters after the meeting that currently, Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit works through a “referral-based system” — and that system could be expanded to draw from more sources.
“What can we do to be more proactive, to make sure that we are getting those those fraud tips, and we’re not (just) eliminating Medicaid fraud, not letting it happen — either preventing it, or when it does happen, holding those wrongdoers accountable?” Bird said.
While members of the task force spoke on new areas to expand efficiency, critics — including Dean Lerner and Kevin Techau, who served as directors of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals under Democratic governors Tom Vilsack and Chet Culver — have called the task force “political theater” because the state is not fully funding the state’s existing MFCUs.
Bird said the task force has also found the state’s MFCU is doing well and has “detected more fraud” and taken on more complaints in recent years.
“I think we see that our Medicaid Fraud Control Unit that we have here in Iowa is doing well, it is very efficient,” Bird said. “I think that is very encouraging. Also, we believe that you can take something that’s good and still make it better. And so, one of the great things about today is how the work group members and the task force members were bringing up ways that, even though we are very efficient and we are doing a good job, what can we do to make that better in Iowa? What can we do to eliminate Medicaid fraud?”
Larry Johnson, the principal deputy director for the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, suggested Iowa can look to other states that have made changes to their MFCU and programs in recent months that can better help connect residents with resources to address instances of fraud.
“I would say, looking across the nation, probably six months ago, I would have said Iowa has some of the best resources available,” Johnson said. “But due to the Vice President Vance’s emphasis and focus on this, that other states have really improved some of their resources. So while we have FAQs that are good, I would say other states have FAQs now that are more specific, more interactive and engaging, so that way people know exactly what to look for. And so, there are some of those that the group has identified that I think implementing and adopting those would be of great benefit to the state.”
The discussion on Medicaid fraud also comes as Iowa and many other states are seeing deficits in state Medicaid budgets. Earlier this year, Reynolds signed into law a retroactive increase on premium taxes for HMOs, a type of Medicaid Advantage plan offered by private companies, from a rate of 0.925% to 3.5% between Jan. 1 and Sept. 30, 2026 to help fill the expected funding gap.
The task force plans to hold meetings in September and October before eventually finalizing recommendations for state lawmakers to consider. Bird said in the coming months, work groups within the task force will continue to look into ways to improve Iowa’s Medicaid fraud units.

title: South Dakota attorney general plans to introduce ‘safeguards’ for license plate readers
description: South Dakota’s top law enforcement official announced Thursday that he plans to propose state legislation limiting the use of automatic license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, to “legitimate law enforcement purposes.” Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley said it’s important to have “reasonable safeguards” statewide, while allowing uses that help s[...]
text:
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley speaks during a press conference on Dec. 19, 2025, in Sioux Falls. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ALPR-legislation-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
South Dakota’s top law enforcement official announced Thursday that he plans to propose state legislation limiting the use of automatic license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, to “legitimate law enforcement purposes.”
Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley said it’s important to have “reasonable safeguards” statewide, while allowing uses that help solve criminal investigations.
He said the technology was “instrumental” in finding a 9-year-old girl who was abducted in Clark County in 2023 and in the investigation into the disappearance and death of 14-year-old McKenna Wendel, of Sioux Falls, which is the subject of an ongoing prosecution.
“I think this is, because of really what’s happened nationally, something that I think deserves legislative attention and proper legislation that allows law enforcement to use vital tools and has safeguards for private, individual privacy,” Jackley said.
Worried about surveillance, states enact privacy laws and restrict license plate readers

National groups including the American Civil Liberties Union have raised concerns about how the data collected by Flock cameras is used. In other states, police officers have been accused of abuses such as using the technology to track romantic partners or exes.
Jackley said he believes there’s bipartisan support for using the technology to solve serious crimes.
“But if you’re doing that, you need to safeguard our privacy, we take that very seriously in South Dakota,” he said, adding “let’s put in the safeguards, put it in the law so that everybody knows what those safeguards are.”
Sioux Falls and Madison are among the South Dakota cities already using the technology. Earlier this year, law enforcement in those cities said the technology helps find criminal suspects. The cameras capture images of license plates on passing vehicles, which can be checked against databases of reported crimes.
Decisions on how the technology is used, how records are kept and where the cameras are placed are all up to local authorities, Jackley said. He said the goal of his legislation would be to ensure data from license plate readers may only be collected, accessed or used for law enforcement investigations into criminal activity, and to require that any information gathered must be protected and deleted within an established period of time unless it is directly relevant to an ongoing criminal investigation.
Jackley said he’s engaging groups like the state’s attorneys association, the sheriff’s association and the police chief’s association, as well as other states’ attorneys general to learn about how other states regulate the cameras.
The attorney general in South Dakota can ask lawmakers to sponsor bills on his behalf. Jackley’s term as attorney general ends in January, the same month that the annual legislative session begins. Jackley is running for the U.S. House rather than for reelection as attorney general.
Jackley told South Dakota Searchlight he plans to involve Lance Russell, the unopposed Republican nominee for attorney general, in conversations about the legislation. Russell did not immediately respond to a message from Searchlight.

name: VTDigger
title: How Amanda Janoo, a progressive political outsider, won Vermont’s Democratic primary for governor
description:
“She represented a more authentic version of change, to enough voters, to give her the victory,” one observer said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  How Amanda Janoo, a progressive political outsider, won Vermont’s Democratic primary for governor.
text:
Candidate for governor Amanda Janoo speaks during a Democratic Party unity rally in Burlington on Wednesday, August 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Amanda Janoo seemed to have none of the typical advantages on her side going into Tuesday’s Democratic primary for governor of Vermont.
She had both raised and spent less campaign money than her opponent, Aly Richards. She had fewer endorsements from current and former lawmakers. And compared with Richards — the former head of a prominent childcare lobbying organization — she’d spent far less time in the Statehouse and rubbing shoulders with political insiders.
But Janoo, an economist who until this year had never run for office, eked out a win that even she acknowledged Tuesday was “a long shot.” As of Wednesday afternoon, she had 49.1% of the vote to Richards’ 46.5%, according to unofficial results, setting her up to face Republican Gov. Phil Scott in the general election this fall. 
So, how did she do it?
By her own telling, Tuesday’s win was a result of talking to voters in no uncertain terms about the biggest challenges facing the state and the country. Democrats were hungry for a candidate who spoke plainly about economic inequality and criticized the power of big technology companies, she said, refrains that featured heavily in her campaign.
At the same time, Janoo said she was the only candidate who offered solutions that would make the kind of structural changes many voters wanted. Those include proposals to enact new taxes on wealthy households and on tech firms to pay for universal primary care and other initiatives, as well as reducing the state’s reliance on federal funding, she said.
“When we try to advocate for just maintaining, tinkering, stabilizing these existing systems, people aren’t going to be excited. They’re not going to mobilize, and they’re going to be, sort of, frustrated,” she said in an interview Wednesday morning. 
“It was really about, like, how do we expand the political imagination? How do we bring people together?” she said of her campaign. “How do we make it irresistible to want to be part of a movement for justice, together?”
Matthew Dickinson, a professor of political science at Middlebury College, agreed that Janoo’s success was due to how she met voters where they were. Democrats across the country are eager for change after a year and a half of a second Trump administration they don’t like, he said — and Janoo did a better job reflecting their concerns.
“She represented a more authentic version of change, to enough voters, to give her the victory,” Dickinson said.
Aly Roberts left, chats with Amanda Janoo at a Democratic Party unity rally in Burlington on Wednesday, August 12, 2026. Janoo defeated Roberts in Tuesday’s primary to become the party’s candidate for governor. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Richards also described herself as the “change” candidate, said Chris Graff, a former longtime Vermont political reporter. But while she drew a contrast between herself and Scott, he said, Janoo came off more clearly as a change from politics as usual. That led to Richards getting cast as the “establishment” candidate in the race.
Richards had arguably stronger credentials to lean on, Graff said — she also worked in former Democratic Gov. Peter Shumlin’s administration — but Janoo “was just pushing change, change, change.” That was the right strategy to build support in a primary, which typically draws the most ideology-motivated voters to the polls, he said. 
“She really did retail politics well. She carried crowds and got them excited,” Graff said. “And she really, effectively, reached the smaller universe of voters that were most likely to participate.”
In addition to her campaigning, Janoo was able to extract some advantage, near the finish line, from an infusion of money into the race by a pro-Richards political action committee. 
The PAC blanketed the internet with more than $200,000 worth of ads urging people to vote for Richards in the final weeks of the race. The organization was not affiliated with her campaign but was supported by donors that had ties to Let’s Grow Kids, the childcare lobbying and advocacy group Richards led for a decade.
Most of the PAC’s money came from people or sources outside the state, according to financial disclosures filed with the Vermont secretary of state’s office. 
Some voters may have been put off by this infusion of out-of-state PAC money into the race, especially because Richards had publicly disavowed PAC money, Dickinson said. But the funding also gave Janoo a chance to reinforce the distinctions she was already trying to make, he said, even as the ads it paid for likely boosted Richards’ name recognition.
“That contributes to the perception that you’re the candidate of the establishment. You’re not the candidate of change,” he said, referring to Richards. “It allowed Janoo to argue that she was more authentically a grassroots candidate mobilizing Vermont voters.”
Richards herself raised about $440,000 ahead of election day and spent more than $375,000, according to the latest campaign finance reports. Janoo, in comparison, raised about $305,000 and spent about $260,000, filings show.
That means pro-Richards spending, including from her campaign and the unaffiliated PAC, was double the pro-Janoo spending in the race.
Looking at the town-by-town results of the race, it’s difficult to find broad geographic patterns that explain Janoo’s win, according to Graff. Those results were still unofficial as of Wednesday afternoon but included all but two towns.
Janoo’s win does not cut clearly across urban and rural divides, he said, noting both she and Richards had different pockets of strength across the state that nearly balanced each other out. The tipping point, though, may have been in some of the deepest-blue pockets of Chittenden County.
In the state Senate district that spans much of Burlington, all of Winooski and Essex Junction, part of Essex Town and a sliver of Colchester, Janoo bested Richards by about 2,000 votes. That’s roughly her overall margin of victory in the race, Graff noted. 
Janoo bested Richards by 16 percentage points in Burlington and by 40 percentage points in Winooski, unofficial results show.
“The election was close everywhere else in the state, but she built up this huge margin in Burlington and Winooski, and that saved the day for her,” Graff said.
Janoo’s grassroots-focused campaign worked well for a primary election, where there are a relatively small number of voters to reach, Graff and Dickinson said. At least 88,500 people voted in Tuesday’s election, according to data Wednesday afternoon from the secretary of state’s office. That’s more than the 52,000 who voted in the 2024 Democratic primary for governor, though it pales in comparison to the 373,000 who cast a vote for governor in the 2024 general election, data shows.

 
Amanda Janoo, who won Tuesday’s Democratic primary for governor of Vermont, speaks to fellow Democratic nominees and party officials at a celebration in Burlington Wednesday morning. Video by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger

It remains to be seen whether Janoo can replicate her success on that larger scale — and against a popular incumbent in Scott, they said. The governor’s job approval rating has slipped in recent months, according to polling from the University of New Hampshire, though he continues to have the approval of many Democrats. And according to polling from the firm Morning Consult, he remains the most popular governor in the country.
“Most Vermonters have, for a number of election cycles, voted for Phil Scott. Now, you have to persuade them that they were wrong to do that — or that they’re wrong to do it today,” Graff said. “And that’s a really big sell. That’s a hard sell.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA revenue officials: Income tax will bring in more money than first expected
description: A new analysis from the state Department of Revenue shows Washington’s high-earner income tax will be paid by thousands of additional households and produce hundreds of millions of dollars more than previously assumed — if voters don’t ditch it this fall. These larger figures will be in front of voters as they decide whether to […]
text:
The state Capitol in Olympia, Washington on Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)A new analysis from the state Department of Revenue shows Washington’s high-earner income tax will be paid by thousands of additional households and produce hundreds of millions of dollars more than previously assumed — if voters don’t ditch it this fall.
These larger figures will be in front of voters as they decide whether to repeal the tax in the Nov. 3 election. If voters uphold the tax, it could mean lawmakers need to make fewer cuts to balance the next two-year budget.
When Gov. Bob Ferguson signed legislation creating the income tax in late March, he and lawmakers counted on it to generate $2.7 billion for the next budget and $6.9 billion for the following two-year fiscal cycle.
Now, three months before an initiative to repeal the tax appears on ballots statewide, the department has revised its numbers, predicting this new levy will bring in $3.1 billion in the initial fiscal year and roughly $8.3 billion in the 2029-31 biennium.
The new estimates appeared without notice last month, tucked into a chart in the online statement describing the potential fiscal consequences of Initiative 645. The revenue agency did the calculations and the Office of Financial Management wrote the document, which will be in voter pamphlets in October.
Initiative 645 seeks to repeal the 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million a year, which is slated to take effect Jan. 1, 2028, with payments due the following year. 
Because a “yes” vote on I-645 would eliminate the tax, the projected collections are portrayed as losses in the online statement.
The Department of Revenue analysis also found that 25,000 households would pay the income tax, up from 21,000 discussed during the last legislative session. That information is not in the fiscal statement prepared for voters.
Ferguson, a vocal opponent of the initiative, oversees both the Office of Financial Management and Department of Revenue but was not involved in the development of the document, officials said.
Narrower budget gap?
The added dollars would be welcome for Ferguson and lawmakers who expect to wrestle with a strained budget in the next legislative session. The governor has warned of a shortfall for a third straight year and asked agencies to take a hard look at spending.
But the money can’t be counted on quite yet.
Operating budgets must be based on official revenue forecasts prepared by the state’s chief economist and adopted by the Economic and Revenue Forecast Council. 
For his June forecast, chief economist Dave Reich followed past practice and used the Department of Revenue estimates in the extensive fiscal note for the income tax legislation. That meant he assumed 21,000 filers and tax collections of $2.7 billion for the next budget.
The September forecast will be the first to potentially include the higher sums calculated by Ferguson’s revenue office.
“We will be taking a look at how they forecasted the tax but our forecast may or may not match depending on our assessment of the method, risk, etc.,” Reich said in an email.
An updated forecast won’t matter if voters pass Initiative 645 in November. And even if the measure fails, a legal challenge to the tax’s constitutionality could stanch this revenue stream.
The revenue department’s statement makes no mention of its earlier estimate that was part of the June forecast or what it could mean if the chief economist does not assume the new, larger figures in the next forecast.
Nor is there much explanation for why the figures are so much higher.
“What a shock,” Initiative sponsor Brian Heywood said sarcastically. “Why would you trust anything that comes out of Olympia because there’s been a consistent pattern of factually inaccurate releases from the administration.”
Just estimates
A Department of Revenue spokesman stressed that the new fiscal estimates “are just that, estimates.”
“We do not have any actual collections to inform this question, so we estimate the impact using a variety of data sources that are in turn influenced by the most recent economic forecast,” said Mikhail Carpenter, communications director for the agency.
Providing estimates, he said, is routine. There was no decision on which numbers to use. It was determined by economic modeling, he said.
When the legislation was signed into law, the estimated tax collections were based on the November 2025 forecast. Figures used in the fiscal impact statement are derived from the June forecast and are higher because they reflect improved economic conditions.
“Specifically, dividend income, stock income, personal income, and wages grew from the November to June forecasts, which has a positive effect on the number of taxpayers and the amount of Washington taxable income, increasing both,” Carpenter said.
That is why the department now thinks more households will pay the tax. State revenue analysts plugged in numbers and concluded that 4,000 households just below the $1 million threshold now will be above it by the time the tax kicks in. 
Also, analysts predict those already earning more than $1 million will be wealthier and thus pay more. The combination of more filers and greater household wealth is why revenue estimates rose, he said.
The numbers are not static. Had the June forecast been negative, it would have been reflected as a decline in the numbers for this estimate, he said. Numbers could improve again based on the September forecast. But the fiscal impact statement won’t be edited or updated regardless of the information.
Heywood, leader of the politically conservative Let’s Go Washington, questioned the calculations because they assume a static population. “They think nobody is going to leave because of the tax. They’re wrong,” he said.
Other figures, like the number of filers, need a closer look, he said. “Next month it’ll be only 40,000. Then, after that, it will be 100,000. To some extent they’re just making it up.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana wildfires expand, Maverick Mountain Ski Area burns
description: In the face of tragedy, and with a growing number of wildfires spreading across Montana, Gov. Greg Gianforte found a few bright spots.  Calling it a “big victory,” Gianforte said on Wednesday morning that the state’s largest wildfire — the Sand Creek Fire burning near Polaris — had not destroyed any structures while making a […]
text:
The plume of the Sand Creek Fire seen from Wisdom on Aug. 11, 2026. (Courtesy InciWeb)In the face of tragedy, and with a growing number of wildfires spreading across Montana, Gov. Greg Gianforte found a few bright spots. 
Calling it a “big victory,” Gianforte said on Wednesday morning that the state’s largest wildfire — the Sand Creek Fire burning near Polaris — had not destroyed any structures while making a 10,000- acre run and jumping a fire line at Maverick Mountain in the last day.
“It blew through Maverick Mountain Ski Area and through a subdivision, but as of this morning, they haven’t lost a single structure,” Gianforte said at an event in Alberton. “Frankly, I haven’t said this very often, but the Forest Service is doing a good job. They’re throwing everything after it.”

The fire, which started Aug. 1, was estimated Wednesday at more than 27,000 acres burning throughout the Pioneer Mountains. 
Structure protection was done on the Maverick Mountain lodge and nearby Elkhorn Hot Springs, and fire officials said Wednesday morning that initial reconnaissance of the hot springs revealed “damage was minimal after the fire moved through.”
Posts on social media showed an outpouring of support for the owners of the two beloved properties, as well as property owners in the Grasshopper Valley, which is under evacuation orders. 
The evacuation status includes Mountain View, Highway Drive, the subdivision where Ma Barnes Country Store is located, Sawtooth Road and Clark Creek Road, according to the Beaverhead County Sheriff’s Office. 
At Maverick Mountain, The Montana Standard reported that while the lodge is still standing, a ski patrol shack and the chairlift have burned.
Just a few miles to the north, the Bobcat Lakes fire has grown to more than 9,000 acres, and firefighters are working on structure protection along the Pioneer Mountains Scenic By-Way. 
Between the two blazes, 527 personnel are committed, including 27 engines, 10 crews and seven pieces of heavy equipment.  
Gianforte added that seven helicopters have been on the fire over the last week. 
Community meetings will be held on Wednesday at the Jackson School at 6 p.m. and on Thursday at the Wise River Community Building at 6 p.m. Meetings will be recorded and posted to the Beaverhead-Deer Lodge National Forest Facebook page. 
United Way of Beaverhead County said on Wednesday that a fire relief fund has been set up with a $10,000 matching gift from Stockman Bank to help those impacted by the Sand Creek Fire. 
“Our community has always come together to support one another in times of need, and I know that spirit will continue through this crisis,” said Ashly Cottom, executive director of the organization. “The United Way Board is honored to help connect resources with those who need them the most. 



				To donate, call United Way at 406-683-4269; visit any Stockman Bank location across Montana, or mail a check to United Way of Beaverhead County, PO Box 263, Dillon, MT 59725 and indicate your donation is for the Fire Relief Fund. 			


Around the rest of Montana, the Department of Natural Resources and Conservation reports that 12 new fires have sparked in the last 24 hours — nine classified as “large” — with nearly 100,000 acres burned in the state this fire season. 
After the two fires in the Pioneers, the next largest is the Moose Fire, burning more than 5,000 acres east of Hamilton, with 151 personnel on it, and the Skillet Fire, which was estimated at 3,375 acres on Wednesday morning. 
The Skillet Fire has 566 personnel working on the blaze, which is 32% contained, according to the latest incident report. 
While closure orders are still in place for sections of the Flathead and Kootenai national forests, evacuation orders have been downgraded for areas close to the burn. 
Fire officials said containment efforts are progressing on all portions of the fire, with a focus along the southern and eastern edge. 
An additional large fire, the Silvertip Fire, is burning more than 6,500 acres in the Bob Marshall Wilderness.

name: VTDigger
title: Incumbents largely hold on in Vermont’s legislative and statewide primaries
description:
While Democrats selected a progressive political newcomer as their nominee for governor, leaders in both parties expressed satisfaction with the success of incumbents.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Incumbents largely hold on in Vermont’s legislative and statewide primaries.
text:
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Deputy State Auditor Tim Ashe held off newcomer Nick Graeter. Ashe is pictured here in August 2020. File photo by Mike Dougherty/VTDigger
As Vermont voters went to the polls for Tuesday’s primary election, they sought change, citing concerns such as tax policy, education reform and wealth inequality.
But while Democrats selected a progressive political newcomer and self-described “long shot” candidate as their nominee for governor in Amanda Janoo, incumbents across Vermont in legislative and statewide offices largely survived their primaries.
Gov. Phil Scott and Lt. Gov. John Rodgers were both unopposed in their Republican primary bids and will face Janoo and Democratic lieutenant governor nominee Molly Gray in November’s general election. State Treasurer Mike Pieciak, Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas and Attorney General Charity Clark each secured another Democratic nomination unopposed.
Tim Ashe, who currently serves as deputy state auditor and who was formerly president pro tempore of the Vermont Senate, beat political newcomer Nick Graeter to the Democratic nomination for his office’s top job. Longtime state auditor Doug Hoffer did not run for reelection. 
H. Brooke Paige, a businessman and frequent Republican candidate in Vermont, received the GOP nominations for state treasurer, attorney general, state auditor and secretary of state. He told Vermont Public this summer he planned to drop out of all but the secretary of state contest, challenging Copeland Hanzas in November.
In a moment of transition for the state Senate as current President Pro Tempore Phil Baruth, D/P-Chittenden Central, exits his seat, no current senator lost a primary bid for reelection. Two Democratic House members — Rep. Jim Masland, D-Thetford, and Rep. John Bartholomew, D-Hartland — did lose their primaries, while Republican members all held on, according to party leaders Wednesday morning. 
Paul Dame, who chairs the Vermont Republican Party, said in an interview that the success of GOP incumbents — and their relative lack of challengers across the primaries — was both an endorsement of recent legislative work and a signal of party unity. Democrats, he argued, struggled to showcase the same level of togetherness, as their incumbents saw more difficult tests at the polls.
“I think Republicans are feeling very energized, very motivated to support the folks who have served us for the last two years,” he said.
In the coming days, Dame said, he’ll focus on filling in gaps in the ticket, such as the race for the Rutland-6 House seat, where no major party mounted a candidate for the primary. Looking to November’s general election, he added, the GOP will focus its message on affordability with an emphasis on issues like tax relief and housing.
Lachlan Francis, the state’s Democratic Party chair, pushed back on Dame’s takeaways from Tuesday’s results, pointing to the near-total success of the party’s incumbent candidates for both legislative and statewide offices. Vermont Democrats are unified and “moving forward,” he said Wednesday, adding that assertions to the contrary are “a little rich” given recent conflicts within the GOP’s Senate caucus.
Sen. Ginny Lyons, D-Chittenden Southeast, added Wednesday that for her, strongly contested primary elections signify strength for Democrats.
“I welcome that kind of competition,” she said. “I think it’s extremely healthy.”
Lyons held her own Tuesday evening in a contested Chittenden Southeast primary, alongside fellow Democratic Sens. Kesha Ram Hinsdale and Thomas Chittenden. Challengers Elizabeth Ann Hunt and Joanna Grossman finished fourth and fifth, respectively, in the three-seat district.
“I think that was an affirmation of the work that we have been doing,” Lyons said, emphasizing her recent focus on addressing healthcare costs. “We each bring valued experience, leadership — and we’re getting results.”
Meanwhile, the hard-fought and well-funded Chittenden Central Senate primary saw progressive newcomer Nikhil Goyal, an adjunct professor at the University of Vermont, take first place in the three-seat district. Incumbent Sens. Tanya Vyhovsky, a Progressive/Democrat, and Martine Gulick, a Democrat, fended off a robust challenge from former county planning commissioner Elaine Haney. 
“We have a resounding mandate for bold structural change,” Goyal said in an interview Wednesday. His intensive canvassing model allowed him to reach some voters who have historically skipped primaries, he said, which may have accounted in part for his decisive success Tuesday.
Incumbents also prevailed in a crowded Windsor County Senate primary, which saw Rep. Elizabeth Burrows, D-West Windsor, gain the nomination for the seat previously held by the outgoing Sen. Alison Clarkson, D-Windsor. Incumbent Democratic Sens. Becca White and Joe Major staved off three other challengers.
Masland and Bartholomew, who lost their House seats in Tuesday’s primary, each came third in the two-seat Windsor-1 and Windsor-Orange-2 districts. Bartholomew said Wednesday that personal issues had kept him from campaigning as vigorously as he has in the past, but also that lawmakers have failed to adequately address education reform in recent years.
“We keep coming up with plans that are going to extend into the future, and they just don’t happen fast enough,” he said.

title: Rob Sand proposes raising minimum wage, expanding farm income streams
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand released policy priorities Wednesday to support Iowa farm and rural economies. Part of Sand’s priorities included raising the state minimum wage to $12 an hour, ending Iowa’s privatized Medicaid program and investing in programs to diversify the family farm.  Sand, in a statement announcing his “Opportunities for A[...]
text:
A farmer in Carroll County preps his field for planting. (Photo by Jared Strong/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand released policy priorities Wednesday to support Iowa farm and rural economies.
Part of Sand’s priorities included raising the state minimum wage to $12 an hour, ending Iowa’s privatized Medicaid program and investing in programs to diversify the family farm. 
Sand, in a statement announcing his “Opportunities for All” plan, said he never felt a lack of opportunity growing up in a small town. 
“But today, our small towns and main streets are struggling, young workers and families are leaving for better opportunities in other states, and the Iowa way of life is becoming a thing of the past,” Sand said. “I want to change that.”
Sand is running for governor against Republican candidate Zach Lahn, who has also shared ideas on protecting Iowa land ownership and diversifying farm income.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sand’s policy proposal contains four main objectives: invest in Iowa’s economy and workforce, save the family farm, protect rural healthcare and build more housing.
In an effort to keep Iowa’s workforce in the state and in rural communities, Sand proposed raising the minimum wage from $7.25 to $12 to be more in line with neighboring states. As governor, Sand said he would also allow state employees to work from any of the 99 counties, provided the position allows, rather than just Iowa’s capital city.
He also called for expanded high speed internet access in rural areas and to streamline applications for programs that support small businesses. 
More farm opportunities
The policy proposal said “it’s not the farmers who need to work harder – it’s the farms that need to work smarter.”
Farms can work smarter, the policy proposal says, if they can implement multiple revenue streams, through things like agritourism, value-added commodities or equipment rentals. The policy also called for “more enterprises” that allow farmers to turn manure into “valuable bio-based products” like renewable natural gas. 
These policies align with suggestions that former governor and former U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack has said would support small and mid-sized farms. 
Sand’s policy also called for greater support of renewable energy production and local and regional food production efforts. 
The Democrat, currently serving as Iowa’s state auditor, said he would also establish a first-of-its-kind Office of Rural Prosperity, if elected governor, to give rural communities a “direct contact” and to “ensure an understanding of rural issues” across state departments. 
Lahn calls for anti-trust enforcement
Lahn has said he would bring anti-trust lawsuits toward “big ag” corporations to help farmer incomes. On an episode of the Iowa Podcast Wednesday, Lahn said he wanted to bring companies to Iowa that would support farmers who want to follow more regenerative farming practices.
“We’ve watched as for decades, things have not gotten better for the actual producers,” Lahn said. “I’m trying to provide other diversification options to actually add farm income to these producers.”
Lahn also advocated for a centralized food system that allows for things like on-farm butchering and direct sales.
Healthcare, housing
Iowa’s Medicaid population is currently managed by three managed care organizations — Iowa Total Care, Molina Healthcare of Iowa and Wellpoint Iowa inc. Sand has been critical of the state’s privatized Medicaid system and said in the policy proposal he would reverse the privatization of the system “day one” of his administration. 
Sand’s final pillar of the policy proposal would establish a rural housing task force to analyze new ways to build affordable housing in rural areas. The policy also calls for a higher tax on out-of-state landowners and to ban “hedge funds and LLCs from buying up too much Iowa land.” 
Lahn has also called for a higher tax on “institutional investors” buying Iowa property, confiscating Iowa land owned by China and giving exemptions to Iowans “living and farming the land.”
“We have problems right now and the biggest problem we have is that we don’t know who owns our farmland,” Lahn said on the Iowa Podcast.
In addition to land access, Sand said he would push for simplified permitting, fees and inspection processes to cut red tape to support building more housing and more types of housing. Sand said he would also ban landlords from using artificial intelligence algorithms to “price fix and raise rents.”
“This is personal to me – I’m raising my kids here, and I want them to have more opportunities than I had growing up, not less,” Sand said. “That’s why I’m releasing these new policies to support Iowa families, protect Iowa family farms, and ensure that communities across our state not just get by, but thrive.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: The Democratic race for CD 25: Jared Moskowitz vs. Oliver Larkin
description: Progressive Democrats have seen a string of victories in other parts of the nation, but one of the stiffer tests of their sales pitch is likely coming in Florida. South Florida Democrat Rep. Jared Moskowitz has been a reliable and at times sarcastic critic of Republicans and President Donald Trump, but he worked once for […]
text:
Jared Moskowitz (left) and Oliver Larkin (right) face off in the Democratic primary for the CD 25 race. (Photos: YouTube screenshot and Larkin for Congress campaign)Progressive Democrats have seen a string of victories in other parts of the nation, but one of the stiffer tests of their sales pitch is likely coming in Florida.
South Florida Democrat Rep. Jared Moskowitz has been a reliable and at times sarcastic critic of Republicans and President Donald Trump, but he worked once for Gov. Ron DeSantis and has been a strong supporter of Israel since first elected in 2022.
Moskowitz’s old congressional seat was completely overhauled in the redistricting pushed by his one-time boss and he is now running in Florida’s 25th Congressional District. It now covers a coastal area running from Palm Beach County to Miami-Dade County and leans Republican. National Republicans have targeted him for defeat this year, but before that moment comes he has to clear a Democratic primary featuring outspoken progressive union organizer Oliver Larkin.
Larkin has been endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America and supports Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, abolishment of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and to end U.S. aid to Israel.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Larkin has constantly assailed Moskowitz and contends he is out of step with Democratic priorities during a time when Republicans, in his view, pose an “existential threat to democracy.”
“This is someone who had the political establishment backing him and who’s had all the special-interest and corporate money and he’s just never had to work for it before,” Larkin said in an interview with the Florida Phoenix. “So I think he’s always taken voters for granted. … We’re in a moment where voters are no longer accepting that.”
Larkin added about Moskowitz that “he’s got one mode and that’s bipartisanship. And I don’t think Democratic voters are looking for bipartisanship with an administration that is gutting our civil and constitutional rights.”
Larkin’s campaign has touted some of his endorsements and the amount of door knocking and campaigning done face-to-face. Moskowitz has largely avoided interacting with Larkin so far. In an interview with the South Florida Sun-Sentinel, he contended Larkin was “running against me solely on my religion.”
Moskowitz did not respond to the Phoenix’s request for an interview.
 He is a former state legislator who attended Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School and helped push to pass a sweeping bill dealing with firearms in the aftermath of the 2018 Parkland shooting. After DeSantis was elected governor, he tapped Moskowitz as the state’s emergency management chief and later appointed him to the Broward County Commission.
Moskowitz’s connection to DeSantis has been used against him in the past. Larkin has criticized him for it, as well. Progressives have toppled more moderate Democrats in several states, including last week in the Michigan Senate primary. 
Matt Isbell, a Democratic data consultant who focuses on redistricting, is skeptical about whether Larkin can defeat in Moskowitz in the primary. He understands there is a lot of ‘left wing anger” at Moskowitz but pointed out demographics of the district including that it has a large number of Jewish voters.
“I do not expect him to win the primary because the primary in this area is much older and I think moderate than it was like in a place like Denver or New York City,” Isbell said. “So, it’s a different type of electorate.”

description: LINCOLN — Registered nonpartisan Mark Cohen of Lemoyne will appear on the ballot for Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District. He’s the second independent to qualify for a Nebraska congressional race this year. The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office confirmed Wednesday that Cohen had at least 2,207 valid signatures across the district, enough that local elect[...]
text:
The full slate of candidates challenging U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith, R-Neb., center, as he seeks an 11th term for Nebraska's 3rd Congressional District in Congress. His challengers, from top left, clockwise, are Macey Budke of North Platte, a registered nonpartisan write-in candidate; Mark Cohen of Lemoyne, a registered nonpartisan who petitioned to appear on the ballot; Democrat Becky Kelly Stille of South Sioux City; and David Else of Overton, nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)LINCOLN — Registered nonpartisan Mark Cohen of Lemoyne will appear on the ballot for Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District. He’s the second independent to qualify for a Nebraska congressional race this year.
The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office confirmed Wednesday that Cohen had at least 2,207 valid signatures across the district, enough that local election officials could stop validating petition signatures. State law allows nonpartisans to petition to appear on the general election ballot. In this case, Cohen needed at least 2,000 signatures across the sprawling 3rd District.
Election officials can stop signature validation once a petition exceeds 110% of the requirement.
Cohen began petitioning in November. On July 30, he submitted about 3,680 signatures. His deadline was Aug. 3.


Election officials validated signatures for Cohen across 46 of the 80 counties in the 3rd District, according to county-specific data from the Secretary of State’s Office.
The geographic breakdown of Nebraska’s three congressional districts. (Courtesy of the Legislative Research Office)
The most signatures per capita came in Box Butte (4.8% of 6,831 registered voters as of Aug. 1) and Dawes (4% of 4,972 registered voters as of Aug. 1), in the Panhandle. Both counties were also among the top five in counting all validated signatures. That list consists of Box Butte (14.9%), Buffalo (11.2%), Dawson (10.9%), Gage (10.6%) and Dawes (9.3%).
A former Air Force judge advocate and former special assistant U.S. attorney for Nebraska, Cohen officially joins the race against 10-term incumbent U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith, R-Neb.; Democrat Becky Kelly Stille of South Sioux City; and David Else of Overton, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. Macey Budke of North Platte is also running a write-in campaign.
The 3rd District is one of the most conservative in the nation, with about 76% of voters backing President Donald Trump in 2024. Smith won reelection that year with 80.4% of the vote.
Cohen is the second nonpartisan to be certified for the Nov. 3 ballot, following Dan Osborn in his race against U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb. Local election officials have not yet announced the results of signature validation for former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, for governor.
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: VTDigger
title: Part-time Vermonters aren’t the enemy
description:
Property taxes from nonresident homeowners fund Vermont schools and communities. Blaming them for the housing crisis misses the bigger picture.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Part-time Vermonters aren’t the enemy.
text:
Dear Editor,
Housing is a complicated issue. My husband and I have been coming to Vermont to ski and recreate for well over 50 years. He was a part-time ski instructor, so we could afford to ski. He paid Vermont income tax on his salary. 
In anticipation of retirement and after putting our sons through school, we were finally able to afford to buy a home in Vermont 16 years ago. Along with our growing family, we have loved being part-time Vermonters. 

READ MORE

Since when did paying property taxes, mainly for schools, as non-homesteaders make us the enemy? Where is the balance in this situation? We did not cause this housing situation because we have a well-used vacation home. We do not rent it out as a short-term rental. Friends and family come and use it. We all contribute to the Vermont economy.  
No one is owed a house. Vermont needs to do something to encourage industries to come to the state, but they won’t if there are no employees who are trained and ready to work. Three cousins moved to Vermont full-time more than 40 years ago and had eight children. None of these well-educated offspring live in Vermont.
I am a Democrat. I am a taxpayer who cannot vote in Vermont. Stop blaming and alienating people like me. Vermont’s economy needs all kinds of people, including those who can afford to live here part-time.
Donna Brown
Pittsfield, Vt.

title: New Mexico Republican lawmakers host panel on reforming state child welfare agency
description: Five Republicans in the New Mexico state Senate convened an hourslong “task force” hearing Wednesday focused on reforming the state’s troubled child welfare agency.
text:
Five Republicans in the New Mexico Senate — from left to right: Sen. Rex Wilson (R-Ancho), Sen. Larry Scott (R-Hobbs), Sen. Nicole Tobiassen (R-Albuquerque), Sen. David Gallegos (R-Eunice) and Sen. Jay Block (R-Rio Rancho) — convened a task force focused on reforming the state Children, Youth and Families Department at the Central New Mexico Community College Montoya Campus on Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Five Republicans in the New Mexico state Senate convened an hourslong “task force” hearing Wednesday focused on reforming the state’s troubled child welfare agency.
The lawmakers heard from former Children, Youth and Families Department employees and a child currently under state care and the recently confirmed head of the state’s new independent oversight office.
How to manage CYFD has become a key point in New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, particularly after reports that agency staffers earlier this year took a New Mexico teenager out of foster care, dropped him off at the U.S.-Mexico border in El Paso and instructed him to walk alone into Ciudad Juárez to reunite with his estranged mother.
“This is not a department with a few rough edges. It’s a system in crisis,” Sen. Nicole Tobiassen (R-Albuquerque) said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Wednesday’s task force meeting came just one day after Democrats in the state House of Representatives unveiled their child well-being plans for the upcoming legislative session, including a proposal to implement a three-person commission to oversee CYFD. Many of the Democrats’ proposals mirrored the dozens recently recommended by the New Mexico Department of Justice.
“I appreciate the Democrats coming out yesterday and finally talking about this,” Sen. Jay Block (R-Rio Rancho) said during the hearing. “However, the Democrats keep silencing our voice by not hearing our bills in committee.”
A former CYFD employee also spoke before the panel of Republican lawmakers. Evan Sena, who left the agency in 2024 and recounted his experiences in the state attorney general’s April investigative report, said he was alarmed by the lack of structure provided to kids in state custody.
“I’ve been exposed to drugs, been threatened, I’ve had way too many kids in my caseload,” Sena said. “There was an amount of turmoil that I’ve never seen in a state agency or any agency or workplace I’ve been to.” 
In New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s investigative report, Sena is quoted as referring to CYFD office spaces, which controversially functioned as overnight homes for some kids in CYFD custody, as “third world.” 
In January, Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham banned the practice of overnight office stays, saying in an announcement that “children who have experienced trauma deserve safety, stability and dignity — not sleeping in offices.”
That same month, Lujan Grisham appointed Dawn Walters to lead the state Office of the Child Advocate. Walters spoke before the panel of Republican lawmakers Wednesday and told them that she believes many of New Mexico’s issues with child well-being extend beyond CYFD.
New Mexico House Democrats announce plans to overhaul CYFD in 2027 legislative session

The child welfare and foster systems as a whole, she said, can be difficult to navigate for the family members of children in them. She laid out several major observations from her first several months on the job, including that there is no one-size-fits-all approach for family reunification and that family members are often contacted inconsistently or too late into the process.
She said she often hears that the system is “not only extraordinarily difficult to navigate…but it’s also extremely traumatic.”
The Office of the Child Advocate, which is administratively attached to the New Mexico Department of Justice, is a relatively new form of oversight for CYFD. In fact, Wednesday marked the 135th day of “building a new government office, essentially from the ground up,” Walters told lawmakers.
Its nascency led to some questions over who Walters reports to and how to correct course if the office ever had an ineffectual leader.
“Don’t take this the wrong way — I’m just curious,” Block said to Walters, “How do we remove you?”
After reminding Block with a laugh that “it’s only day 135,” Walters said the state attorney general has the authority to remove anyone in her position for violating certain provisions of the 2025 law that created her office.
Walters’ term is currently set to run through 2031.
“My goal is to build an office that is credible, thoughtful and relentlessly child-focused,” she told lawmakers.

title: North Dakota governor lifts ban on TikTok from state devices
description: North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Wednesday lifted a ban on TikTok for state-owned devices, citing a change in ownership for the social media company. The TikTok ban for state government devices had been in place since a 2022 executive order from then-Gov. Doug Burgum. The prohibition aimed to safeguard the state’s cyber infrastructure and […]
text:
A woman uses the TikTok app. (Photo by Thicha Satapitanon/Getty Images)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Wednesday lifted a ban on TikTok for state-owned devices, citing a change in ownership for the social media company.
The TikTok ban for state government devices had been in place since a 2022 executive order from then-Gov. Doug Burgum. The prohibition aimed to safeguard the state’s cyber infrastructure and citizen data from the China-based technology company ByteDance, which owned TikTok. 
Armstrong’s office announced he is rescinding that order because the app has come under the control of a majority-owned, American-led consortium. TikTok announced the U.S. operations joint venture in January, including company ownership stakes and members of its majority-American board of directors. Armstrong’s executive order also cites a July U.S. Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel opinion that related to federal government employees using TikTok.
Requests to access TikTok on state-owned devices must go through the North Dakota Information Technology’s review process, but the department has determined the app “no longer presents an unmitigated or unique cybersecurity threat to state operations,” according to Armstrong’s office.
Separately, the North Dakota University System has its own policy that blocks TikTok from being accessed from public college and university networks or devices. Students, staff and faculty are able to access the app through personal devices not connected to a college or university network.
Armstrong’s order will not affect the TikTok policy for state colleges and universities. 
The State Board of Higher Education could consider changes to the policy at a future meeting, said Billie Jo Lorius, a spokesperson for the North Dakota University System.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Death row inmate seeks order against execution based on paralysis
description: Attorneys for a Tennessee death row inmate filed a request Wednesday to stop his execution, saying the man could be physically incapable of going through the state’s lethal injection protocol. Darrell Hines’ legal counsel filed motions in U.S. District Court for a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction to prevent him from being executed, based[...]
text:
Attorneys for Darrell Hines, set to be executed Thursday by the State of Tennessee, have said his physical condition may render him incapable of going through the lethal injection protocol.   (Photo by Joe Raedle/Newsmakers)Attorneys for a Tennessee death row inmate filed a request Wednesday to stop his execution, saying the man could be physically incapable of going through the state’s lethal injection protocol.
Darrell Hines’ legal counsel filed motions in U.S. District Court for a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction to prevent him from being executed, based on his condition, mainly rigidity in his left arm, after suffering two strokes in December and January.
The filing seeks to forbid the state from “attempting to forcibly straighten Mr. Hines’ stroke-affected left arm or unclench his left fist for the purposes of his execution.” Hines is paralyzed and partially blind on his left side following the strokes and unable to unclench his left fist or extend his left arm, according to his attorneys.
Tennessee death row inmate seeks U.S. Supreme Court review

Tennessee’s execution protocol requires members of the Department of Correction restraint team to “secure the inmate’s arms to arm extensions on the gurney,” according to the filing, which contends Hines is “sure or very likely to experience severe pain and suffering” if his arm is straightened.
“A feasible, readily available alternative … exists that would completely eliminate the risk of Mr. Hines’ experiencing severe pain and suffering due to TDOC’s forcible extension of his left arm – namely allowing Mr. Hines to be strapped to the gurney with his left arm at his side and placing the peripheral IV-lines in his non-stroke-affected limbs,” the complaint says.
The filing says “spasticity and pain” in Hines’ left arm should have been evident to medical personnel in the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution infirmary where he has been housed since the second stroke in January. The filing also includes a declaration by Dr. Gail Van Norman, a cardiothoracic anesthesiologist, who determined the rigidity in his arm will likely make it more difficult to insert a needle and establish an IV for the lethal drugs.
Attorneys for Hines, who was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 stabbing death of motel maid Catherine Jean Jenkins in Kingston Springs, also asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene in the case, claiming he could suffer cruel and unusual punishment, a violation of his Eighth Amendment rights, because of an “under-skilled” physician. The attorneys argue that the doctor likely to oversee the execution is unqualified to insert the IV to administer the lethal drugs after botching the execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers in May.
