title: West Nile Virus confirmed in Montana, health department says
description: State and local health officials confirmed the first detections of West Nile virus in Montana for summer 2026, the Department of Public Health and Human Services said Wednesday in a news release. Two mosquito pools tested positive for West Nile Virus in Roosevelt County, and health officials said the virus will likely spread across the […]
text:
Mosquito. (Provided by the Department of Public Health and Human Services)

State and local health officials confirmed the first detections of West Nile virus in Montana for summer 2026, the Department of Public Health and Human Services said Wednesday in a news release.
Two mosquito pools tested positive for West Nile Virus in Roosevelt County, and health officials said the virus will likely spread across the state.
They are urging all Montanans to take increased precautions against mosquito bites, although no West Nile infections have been reported in humans or horses yet this summer, the news release said.


“Detection of WNV in mosquitoes is an early indicator that activity is increasing within the state, elevating the risk of human illness,” the news release said.
West Nile Virus can cause illness in humans, and the increased risk of transmission to humans is expected to continue through October or as long as mosquitoes remain active in the state.


“The risk of severe illness is a serious concern,” said DPHHS vectorborne disease epidemiologist Devon Cozart in a statement. “Every year, some Montanans experience neurological complications that can cause permanent disability or death.”
Health officials recommend people use insect repellent and take other measures to prevent bites.

The “4 Ds of Mosquito Bite Prevention” include the following, the news release said:


DEET: Use insect repellent containing effective ingredients such as DEET or picaridin. To verify the effectiveness of insect repellent, go to the EPA’s website: www.epa.gov/insect-repellents.




Drain: Drain standing water around the house to prevent mosquito breeding.




Dawn/Dusk: Mosquitoes are most active during dawn and dusk. Stay inside or take extra precautions to prevent mosquito bites during these times. If doors or windows are left open in the summer, make sure they’re fitted with screens to keep mosquitoes out of the house.




Dress: When possible, wear long-sleeved shirts and pants to protect against bites.





There is no vaccine or targeted medication for West Nile Virus in humans, the news release said. One-in-five people experience mild symptoms, including headache, rash, body aches, joint pains, fatigue, vomiting and diarrhea, according to the health department. One-in-150 infections results in severe disease and can cause neurological symptoms, including disorientation, stupor, coma, paralysis, vision loss and convulsions.

Horses can also be infected with West Nile Virus. Horse owners may contact their veterinarian to obtain an annual vaccine to protect against the virus.
Contact your local health department or visit https://dphhs.mt.gov/publichealth/cdepi/diseases/WestNileVirus for more information about protection and surveillance activities.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Judges grill DeSantis administration attorney over Medicaid termination letters
description: A trio of federal judges Wednesday grilled an attorney representing the DeSantis administration over how the state terminated people from Florida’s Medicaid program in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. Florida was first sued three years ago over how it disenrolled people from the safety net health care program — a process known as an […]
text:
Shands Hospital in Gainesville. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)A trio of federal judges Wednesday grilled an attorney representing the DeSantis administration over how the state terminated people from Florida’s Medicaid program in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Florida was first sued three years ago over how it disenrolled people from the safety net health care program — a process known as an “unwinding” — which resulted in hundreds of thousands of people losing benefits.
After losing before a lower court, the state appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit, a court that Gov. Ron DeSantis has pointed out often sides with him and his Republican administration.
That may not happen in this case, as lawyers representing the state got an earful from skeptical judges, with one judge even offering the comment, “This is pretty bad.”
Andy Bardos, representing the state health care agencies that have been sued, tried to defend the state’s handling of Medicaid termination notices, arguing Florida only needed to adhere to minimum due-process requirements. Those included notice of the intended action, the date when that would occur, and a statement of the reason why.
“With nothing else?” U.S. Circuit Court Judge Adalberto Jordan asked.
“We think that’s the minimum requirement of due process,” Bardos answered.
Jordan said the state perhaps could have included additional information in the notices steering people to a website where they could input their annual salary and any other source of income, their expenses, and the number of children they have. 
They could be told whether they qualify for Medicaid and, if not, how much they earned above the qualifying threshold.
But the state didn’t offer that and didn’t include the information in letters to beneficiaries.
“This is pretty bad,” Jordan said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Skeptical judges
U.S. Circuit Court Judges Barbara Lagoa and Robin Rosenbaum also seemed skeptical.
“If you don’t tell me what the basis is of the income determination that you’ve made, what you believe is the income, then how would I know what to challenge?” Judge Barbara Lagoa asked Bardos.
Lagoa, once a DeSantis appointee to the Florida Supreme Court, said “it’s clear” Medicaid notices must provide the recipient with meaningful notice and the opportunity to be heard.
“You cannot be heard if you don’t know what you’re objecting to,” Lagoa told Bardos. “Because, by the way, I don’t think you would like a trial judge to issue an order just telling you ‘denied’ and not tell you the basis. Correct? Because you wouldn’t be able to have meaningful appellate review.”
Rosenbaum grappled with the idea that the state wouldn’t provide the information it used to determine beneficiaries were no longer eligible.
“What is the whole point of hiding this information?” she asked.
State-federal program
Medicaid is jointly administered and paid for by the state and federal governments. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal government increased by 6.2% its contributions. The increased funding came with the requirement states couldn’t disenroll people during the pandemic.
Congress agreed the continuous eligibility requirement would end March 31, 2023, and that, post-pandemic, states could unwind their Medicaid programs to their normal operations. 
Florida started Medicaid unwinding on April 1, 2023, and by the following year the Department of Children and Families redetermined the eligibility of more than 4 million people.
Attorneys for Florida Health Justice Project and the National Health Law Program filed the lawsuit in Jacksonville in 2023 on behalf of people who erroneously lost benefits. 
U.S. District Judge Monica Morales Howard agreed to certify the lawsuit as a class action in 2024 and in 2025 issued a 273-page ruling finding that termination letters issued by the state were “vague, confusing and often incorrect and misleading” in violation of federal law.

title: Trump press secretary Leavitt to leave White House
text: WASHINGTON — White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her position at the end of August to spend more time with her family, President Donald Trump announced on social media Wednesday.In a post on Truth Social, the president praised Leavitt, the youngest person to serve in the role, as one of his closest aides in the White House and said she will move to an adviser role outside of government.“Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect!” Trump wrote.“Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections,” he added.When asked whether the White House had chosen the next press secretary, a spokesperson pointed States Newsroom to Trump’s and Leavitt’s social media posts and did not provide additional comment. In a nearly 500-word statement on the social media platform X, Leavitt thanked the president “for granting me so many extraordinary opportunities,” which she said included spending “countless hours” in the Oval Office and meeting foreign leaders and Americans “from all walks of life.” “Most of all, I am thankful to the President for entrusting me with the distinct privilege of speaking on his behalf at the White House podium. I have spoken with great pride about the many historic accomplishments of this Administration, and I have relished holding the liberal media accountable and ensuring the American people hear the truth about President Trump’s successes,” said Leavitt, who was at times combative with journalists during routine press briefings.Leavitt gave birth to her second child on May 1, and held her first briefing following parental leave less than a month ago. She described her decision to leave “one of the most demanding jobs in the world” as “bittersweet.”Leavitt said she will “always remain a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party” and suggested she’d continue antagonizing the president’s political opponents.“Our country is facing an existential threat from an increasingly extremist Democrat Party that seeks to destroy everything great about America, and I believe it is incumbent upon all of us who care about this country to fight back against that threat,” she wrote.Leavitt credited White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who co-managed Trump’s 2024 re-election bid, for initially hiring her during the campaign.Leavitt was 27 years old when she assumed the role of press secretary in January 2025.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Study pegs median net wealth of Massachusetts families at $370,000
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: A survey sent to 32,817 randomly selected Massachusetts addresses and yielding 5,018 responses highlighted long-standing racial wealth gaps.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS FAMILIES HELD a median net wealth of more than $370,000 last year, according to a new study that found this metric varies dramatically across key factors like race, age, educational attainment, homeownership, and place of residence.
Just over a third of families also said they would be unable to cover a $400 emergency expense such as car repairs or an illness with cash or “its equivalent” in 2025, according to the report released Wednesday by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston. 
The Boston Fed worked with The Boston Foundation — plus the Barr Foundation, Eastern Bank Foundation and the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce — on the Massachusetts Economic Conditions and Household Opportunity Survey that captures household assets and debts, and whether Bay Staters have sufficient wealth reserves to cope with “unstable prices or unexpected expenses.” Sent to 32,817 randomly selected Massachusetts addresses, the survey yielded 5,018 responses. 
The survey highlighted long-standing racial wealth gaps.
White families had an estimated median net wealth of $549,200, compared to $305,000 for Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander families. Median net wealth was just $1,200 for Hispanic families and $7,800 for Black families. About 41 percent of Hispanic families and 31 percent of Black families held zero or negative net wealth.
“Having wealth is the ability to financially navigate an unexpected job loss, a serious illness, or buy and/or maintain a home,” Barr Foundation CEO Ali Noorani said. “It is the difference between one’s ability to live to their fullest potential and a trajectory that mires them in debt.”
Noorani said the swath of families who cannot afford a $400 emergency expense is “a clear indication to us that economic inequity is so deeply rooted that solutions can only be found in collaboration.” The wealth gap can be alleviated, he said, as “sectors and ideologies” work to remove barriers and boost access to capital.
In Greater Boston, 33.4 percent of families said they could not pay an unexpected $400 expense. That figure climbed to 50.1 percent for families in Gateway Cities. There are 26 Gateway Cities with populations ranging between 35,000 and 250,000 people, and  median household incomes and average educational attainment rates that are below the state average, according to the report.
Researchers examined various financial assets that contribute to net wealth, including checking, savings, and money market accounts; certificates of deposits, stocks, bonds, and mutual funds; workplace retirement accounts; IRA and Keough accounts; annuities and trusts; and cash value of life insurance. Non-financial assets include primary residence equity, other real estate equity, vehicle equity, and business equity. For debts, researchers assessed credit card debt, student loan debt, medical debt, legal debt, loans from relatives and friends, and other installment loans.
The report found the estimated median family net wealth was $374,000, but the 25th percentile was just $10,000. That means a quarter of the commonwealth’s population had wealth at or below $10,000. Meanwhile, the 75th percentile was $1.09 million.
Nearly 16 percent of respondents reported no wealth or “negative” wealth, in which their debts exceeded the value of their assets.
High wealth was associated with factors like higher education levels, homeownership, and families with older adults. For families in which a respondent or spouse/partner held a graduate degree, the median net wealth was $947,400. As for homeowners, median family net wealth was $790,500. Families in which the respondent or spouse/partner was 65+ held median net wealth of $702,500.
Median net wealth was only $11,000 for families in which neither the respondent or spouse/partner earned higher than a high school diploma or GED. Renters held only $1,500 in wealth and younger families — in which the respondent or spouse/partner was under 45 — had $97,000.
The report found median family wealth was highest in rural parts of Massachusetts ($465,000), but trailed closely by wealth in suburban areas ($447,100). In cities, the median family wealth was $110,000 and roughly a quarter of families held zero or negative net wealth.
About a third of Massachusetts families had a will or estate plan, according to the report. 
“This well-designed, far-reaching, and rigorously documented survey by the Boston Fed allows us to face the challenge of equity with new vigor and knowledge that our work to strengthen homeownership, improve educational outcomes, and support small businesses can and will over time strengthen the economic well-being of people across the Commonwealth,” Boston Foundation CEO Lee Pelton said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Reporters end suit seeking LSU revenue records after state law changes
description: Three media outlets that sued LSU to obtain records that detail how its athletics department spends public money on student-athletes have agreed to end the case now that a new state law shields that information from disclosure. Louisiana Illuminator’s Piper Hutchinson, Chris Nakamoto with WAFB-TV and Todd Horne of Tiger Rag filed suit earlier this […]
text:
LSU’s Memorial Tower on Monday, March 20, 2023, on Tower Drive in Baton Rouge. (Matthew Perschall for Louisiana Illuminator) Three media outlets that sued LSU to obtain records that detail how its athletics department spends public money on student-athletes have agreed to end the case now that a new state law shields that information from disclosure.
Louisiana Illuminator’s Piper Hutchinson, Chris Nakamoto with WAFB-TV and Todd Horne of Tiger Rag filed suit earlier this year against the university, which had rejected public records requests from the journalists. They sought  records showing how LSU uses the revenue its athletics programs generate, legally considered state dollars, from sources such as ticket sales, media deals and corporate sponsorships, to pay student athletes
Division I college athletics departments like LSU are part of a federal court settlement that allows them to share their self-generated revenue with student-athletes. This money stream is separate from the name, image and likeness deals players make with sponsors, which are private arrangements already exempt from Louisiana’s public records law.
Once the journalists’ lawsuit was filed, state lawmakers advanced legislation to prevent public access to self-generated revenue records. Act 818, sponsored by Rep. Tehmi Chassion, D-Lafayette, went into effect June 8 with Gov. Jeff Landry’s signature. In the final days of the legislative session, lawmakers added a retroactivity clause to the bill. While the reporters and their attorney believe this clause is unconstitutional, it essentially neutralized their lawsuit. 
Scott Sternberg, a First Amendment attorney representing the reporters, said LSU agreed to cover their court filing costs in exchange for the plaintiffs dropping their lawsuit.  
“In Louisiana, our constitution preserves the right of access to public documents, but in this case, taxpayer money would be wasted if we continued on, and so the suit is being dismissed,” Sternberg said. 
In court filings, lawyers for LSU argued the revenue records being sought were covered under the NIL exemption to the state’s public records law and protected under federal student privacy law. If the revenue-sharing information was made public, LSU’s teams would be put at a competitive disadvantage in the student-athlete marketplace, the attorneys said. 
Federal student privacy laws do not provide an exception for all student records. LSU has in the past provided student records in response to reporters’ requests, including student-athlete information. 
The university has also previously made public information on how much it pays its coaches and top administrators without mentioning any competitive concerns.
Historically, the state has treated self-generated money from its universities as public money subject to wide scrutiny. Lawmakers are required to approve how these resources are spent.
Throughout the course of the lawsuit, the plaintiffs and their legal team were subject to a harassment campaign on social media. The messages included violent threats, some sexual in nature. One plaintiff was physically assaulted and another had their property vandalized after the lawsuit was filed. 
The threats became prevalent enough for Chassion to condemn the behavior in a floor speech seeking support for his legislation.
Act 818 is the latest in a string of new exemptions to Louisiana’s public records law in recent years. Most recently, state lawmakers have voted to withhold details on the governor’s schedule and travel, economic development negotiations and higher education leadership candidates.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer's badge and weapon are seen during a vehicle checkpoint on Georgia Ave. in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 30, 2025. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)On Oct. 18, 2025, ICE arrested and detained Jose Pedro Hernandez Lupercio in Brethren, Mich., along the Manistee River — and both records and official statements indicate that Michigan Department of Natural Resources officers were involved in the operation. 
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, said that the arrest was made “during a targeted operation led by the USFS in conjunction with the DNR,” referring to the U.S. Forest Service and the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, respectively.
Lawyers from the Southwest Detroit Immigrant and Refugee Center said that Hernandez Lupercio was out on a fishing trip on the Manistee River when he was stopped by DNR agents for what appeared to be a routine fishing license check, but which eventually resulted in Hernandez Lupercio’s arrest.
“This stop was a pretext. It was a coordinated, targeted operation by Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” a post from the center’s website states. “Instead of simply verifying a license, the encounter resulted in immediate detention.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The account described by the attorneys and DHS is also consistent with the account contained in a habeas corpus ruling from federal Judge Paul L. Maloney in the Western District Court of Michigan that led to Hernandez Lupercio, a native and citizen of Mexico, being released on bond in February.
“Petitioner  was  stopped  by  agents  of  the  Department  of  Natural  Resources (DNR) . . . while fishing with his sons in the Manistee River,” the ruling states, quoting from Hernandez Lupercio’s petition for a writ of habeas corpus. “‘When [Petitioner] could not prove to the DNR agents that he was legally present in the United States,’ the DNR  agents contacted ICE, and ICE took Petitioner into custody.”
Other legal filings in Hernandez Lupercio’s habeas corpus plea, including a supplemental brief from his legal team and a response from U.S. Department of Justice attorneys, similarly reference his arrest and mention DNR presence.
Despite those statements, the Department of Natural Resources has repeatedly denied their officers facilitated the arrest.
“Michigan DNR conservation officers were on site at the location that day conducting fishing license checks, but the person who contacted Mr. Lupercio worked for the U.S. Forest Service,” a spokesperson for the Department of Natural Resources wrote to the Michigan Advance. “The DNR did not initiate this action, but officers were present as backup when the U.S. Forest Service officer determined the subject had an active warrant. U.S. Forest Service coordinated with ICE for the exchange. DNR was only involved as backup for safety reasons.”
When asked by the Advance to clarify the DNR’s role, department spokesman Ed Golder said their officers were “conducting a joint enforcement operation with the U.S. Forest Service related to natural resource enforcement,” and they were “not present to enforce federal immigration laws and did not arrest or detain anyone in relation to immigration.” 
Nessel launches form to report immigration actions, pushes best practices for local law enforcement

Michigan state agencies are not prohibited by law from collaborating with or working alongside federal law enforcement agencies, including ICE and other immigration authorities, as the state is not a “sanctuary state.” 
The incident in question comes as Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has been highly critical of collaboration between local and state officials and federal immigration authorities. At a roundtable event in February, she emphasized the potential liability that local law enforcement agencies face in cooperating with federal immigration enforcement.
“Local municipalities don’t necessarily have the same defenses that the state government has, or the federal government has,” Assistant Attorney General Josh Smith said at that time. “If you’re entering a partnership with the federal government, and you’re executing certain actions with the federal government, those agents and those federal agencies have certain defenses that you as a municipality and your individual officers don’t.”
Nessel’s office deferred comment on Hernandez Lupercio’s arrest and the involvement of state officials to the Department of Natural Resources.
Christine Sauvé, the policy, engagement, and communications manager for the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center, also expressed concern about the details brought to light in the habeas corpus ruling.
“I’m sure this will surprise many people because immigration enforcement is not the job of DNR officers. This man was fishing with his family. No one should be worried about being separated from their family when they go out to enjoy nature and spend time with loved ones,” she wrote in a statement. “State and local law enforcement have no business enforcing immigration law – they are not trained to do this, and it is a misuse of taxpayers dollars who expected in this case the DNR officer to be protecting natural resources and checking for fishing licenses.”
Sauvé added that it was disappointing to see such instances happening in Michigan, noting that there is no formal cooperation agreement between state law enforcement and ICE that would have required state officials to take these actions.
The U.S. Forest Service also wrote to the Advance that the department “does not conduct immigration enforcement operations,” deferring to DHS, and did not respond to questions about the DHS statement that the Forest Service led the operation that resulted in Hernandez Lupercio’s arrest.
“Like all Executive Branch departments and agencies, the Forest Service complies with Executive Orders and Administration Policies directing cooperation with agencies tasked with immigration enforcement,” a USDA Forest Service spokesperson said. “Forest Service law enforcement is dedicated to keeping the national forests safe and secure for the American people. While our law enforcement officers have no authority to enforce immigration law, they collaborate with other federal and local law enforcement agencies.”
Hernandez Lupercio was detained at the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Mich., the largest ICE detention facility in the Midwest that is privately owned by GEO Group and contracted to ICE, until he was released on bond. His case remains active and pending. Hernandez Lupercio, who lives in Detroit, is married and has three U.S. citizen children, one of whom is a minor.
According to government data provided by ICE in response to a FOIA request, processed by the Deportation Data Project, and analyzed by the Advance, Hernandez Lupercio’s bond was set at $7,000. The data lists no convictions or pending criminal charges against him.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine immigrant detentions outside court, at airport follow national trends
description: People in Cumberland County have been detained outside court and at the airport in recent weeks, following a national trend of federal immigration authorities employing new tactics to boost arrest numbers.  Federal immigration agents arrested more people in July than in any previous month of President Donald Trump’s administration. On Tuesday, the Maine Immi[...]
text:
Federal immigration officers were at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on March 23, 2026, to help with airport security during the shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)People in Cumberland County have been detained outside court and at the airport in recent weeks, following a national trend of federal immigration authorities employing new tactics to boost arrest numbers. 
Federal immigration agents arrested more people in July than in any previous month of President Donald Trump’s administration.
On Tuesday, the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition received a report through its hotline indicating that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained a married couple of African descent outside the Cumberland County Courthouse around 12:10 p.m. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment.
The coalition has received other reports of ICE activity near that courthouse in Portland and the Lewiston District Court this year, which the group warns can discourage victims and witnesses from reporting crimes or participating in legal proceedings.
The reported detentions come shortly after ICE detained MaineHealth nurse Debora Kapisha on July 30 at the Portland Jetport (not Logan Airport in Boston, as originally stated by her union). Kapisha, an asylum seeker from Zambia, was released last week, following public outcry. 
According to a Homeland Security document obtained by MainePublic, two ICE officers were conducting “targeted surveillance” at the Jetport by the security checkpoint, where they identified Kapisha with assistance from TSA and then took her into custody. 
With new tactics, ICE reaches new high in monthly arrests

A May 2025 agreement finalized information-sharing between TSA and ICE, made known late last month through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit from American Oversight. 
Over the past two weeks, the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition said it has received reports of at least five detentions at the jetport. ICE and DHS did not respond to requests about how many detentions have occurred there. 
The coalition is advising people with temporary or uncertain immigration status to consult a qualified immigration attorney before flying. 
Homeland Security said that last month it arrested an average of 20-40 people per day at airports, as federal agents targeted passengers with expired visas. Arrests based on expired visas are likely to accelerate in September when a new rule takes effect that sets stricter time limits on visas for students, exchange visitors and foreign media.
In addition to surveilling courthouses and airports, immigration agents have conducted roadside checks in several other states. For example, last month in North Carolina, immigration agents set up a checkpoint at a creek in a National Forest popular with Hispanic residents.
While ICE and DHS did not respond to questions about the recent detentions in Maine, the agencies have in prior instances, such as the large-scale operation in the winter, said they are targeting “the worst of the worst.” 
Less than a third of current detainees have a criminal conviction and 40% have never been accused of anything but non-criminal immigration violations, according to statistics reviewed by Maine Morning Star’s sister outlet Stateline through early July.
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson contributed to this story.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico food banks describe significant increase in demand after federal food aid cuts
description: Officials from New Mexico food banks say recent changes to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, as well as rising grocery costs, have dramatically increased demand at community food distribution centers across the state.
text:
Food bank leaders told U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) during an Aug. 11, 2026, roundtable that they are seeing significant increases in demand, which they attribute to inflation and also New Mexicans losing their federal food assistance benefits. (Photo by Julia Goldberg/Source NM)Officials from New Mexico food banks say recent changes to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, as well as rising grocery costs, have dramatically increased demand at community food distribution centers across the state. 
A leader of Roadrunner Food Bank, the largest food bank in New Mexico, told U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) during a roundtable Tuesday that demand increased 79% at the food bank between January 2025 and January 2026, which is the most-recent data available.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Luján convened a group of state and nonprofit leaders in Albuquerque’s South Valley to discuss food-access impacts of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” President Donald Trump signed into law last July. The law imposed new work requirements on SNAP recipients and also threatened huge financial penalties for states, including New Mexico, that have high rates of errors administering the federal food assistance program. 
Luján’s visit comes on the heels of a recent Center on Budget Policies and Priorities report that found more than 10,000 New Mexico children have lost SNAP benefits since the law went into effect. Also, Luján, a member of the Senate’s Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry Committee, tried unsuccessfully to convince majority Republicans to delay the imposition of error rate penalties on states during a Farm Bill markup session last week. 
Katy Anderson, Roadrunner Food Bank’s vice president of strategy, partnerships and advocacy, told Luján that she believes the increased demand at the food bank comes both from those who recently lost SNAP due to the federal spending bill and also from those who aren’t eligible for SNAP but still need free food due to rising grocery costs. 
“It’s a challenging landscape for a lot of folks in New Mexico right now,” she said. 
Ari Herring, executive director of the Rio Grande Food Project, a smaller food bank serving the Albuquerque area, said  her organization also saw  a significant demand increase between January 2025 and 2026. Recipients made roughly 5,600 visits to the food bank in January 2026, she said, marking a 23% increase from the previous January. 
A Wednesday inflation report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics found that food prices nationally increased 3% in July over a year ago, continuing a trend of rising grocery prices since July 2024. Inflation across all consumer spending categories increased 2.7% in the Mountain region, which includes New Mexico, the new data shows.
New Mexico to impose new federal food aid document requirements to reduce errors

Anderson said Roadrunner Food Bank has largely been able to fill demand, thanks in part to state funding the Legislature approved during a special session last October convened to stave off the most-damaging effects from the federal spending bill to SNAP and Medicaid, as well as other benefit programs. 
The Legislature approved $8 million specifically for food banks. The funding was intended to help the banks, which lost federal funding early in Trump’s second term from programs such as The Emergency Food Assistance Program, meet an anticipated demand increase due to SNAP cuts. 
Few other states used their own funds to help food banks prepare for the increase in demand, Luján noted.
“Everything that was eliminated in the ‘Big Beautiful Bill,’ the state during the special [session] said, ‘Well, we can do this for a year or two,” Luján said. “It’s a patch. I don’t know what happens after that.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Northwest Arkansas airport officials seek federal loan to support terminal expansion
description: Officials at Arkansas’ busiest airport are hopeful they’ll be the first in the nation to secure a federal infrastructure program loan for a terminal expansion they say is needed to meet growing demand. Northwest Arkansas National Airport has spent nearly a year applying for the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act program, which provides[...]
text:
Build America Bureau Executive Director Morteza Farajian (right) speaks to reporters while U.S. Congressman Steve Womack (far left) and Northwest Arkansas National Airport CEO Aaron Burkes listen on Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Officials at Arkansas’ busiest airport are hopeful they’ll be the first in the nation to secure a federal infrastructure program loan for a terminal expansion they say is needed to meet growing demand.
Northwest Arkansas National Airport has spent nearly a year applying for the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act program, which provides credit assistance for qualified projects of regional and national significance, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. 
The $1.2 trillion infrastructure law signed by then-President Joe Biden in 2021 expanded the program to airport-related projects.
The program has previously supported the construction and acquisition of three ferry boats and redevelopment of two ferry terminals for New York’s Staten Island, and the extension of a Dallas Area Rapid Transit line in Texas.  
Proponents say the program generates significant savings because it offers a low, fixed interest rate, financing up to 49% of eligible project costs and a flexible repayment period.
The program is overseen by the transportation department’s Build America Bureau whose executive director, Morteza Farajian, met with airport officials and U.S. Congressman Steve Womack Wednesday morning. 
FAA leader highlights importance of airspace modernization in Arkansas visit 

After their meeting, Farajian told reporters that Northwest Arkansas National Airport applied for the program’s rural rate, roughly 2.25% to 2.5% — half the regular rate. The lower rate often helps loan recipients expedite their projects, he said.
“What they save in financing costs is so much more than what they pay in construction cost escalation if they wanted to wait and build their projects later,” Farajian said. 
Because the loan hasn’t been closed, Farajian didn’t have exact numbers, but he estimated the program would save the airport tens of millions of dollars. 
Officials should make a decision on the loan in a month or two and if it’s awarded, Farajian said it would be the first TIFIA loan for an airport terminal expansion in the country.
Airport CEO Aaron Burkes said the loan would support a new concourse whose construction is expected to begin this fall. Bids are due next week for the project, said Burkes, who estimated it will cost $80 to $120 million to build seven new gates to meet the region’s rapid growth. 
During the first half of 2026, the airport saw nearly 32,000 more passengers than the first six months of 2025, officials announced last month.
Burkes estimated the loan could save the airport around $30 million. Airport officials are also looking at using the loan program next year to build a new parking garage for rental car operations, he said.
“It’s a tremendous savings for us and will allow us to go ahead and get these projects done and funded a little faster than we would otherwise be able to,” Burkes said. “It’s a tremendous help to us.”
There will always be facility needs when you’re in a growing area, said Burkes, who noted officials in 2021 identified about $620 million in projects that need to be funded. The airport is not even halfway through those projects, he said. 
Womack, a Republican who serves as chairman of the Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Subcommittee, praised airport officials for planning ahead.
“They’re projecting this airport beyond the current line of sight to be able to see what a generation or two from now this place is going to look like,” he said. “And getting ahead of those projects early on, getting ahead of that change, I think is very important.”
All six Republicans in the state’s congressional delegation, including Womack, voted against the 2021 infrastructure funding measure that included an expansion of the loan program.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Larson lost to a younger challenger. Could Blumenthal face a similar test?
description: After U.S. Rep. John Larson was soundly defeated by the younger Luke Bronin, CT's aging members of Congress face similar questions.
text:
Hours after celebrating the decisive win of a popular incumbent governor, U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal was back at work.
Standing out in the sun in front of a Ukrainian Catholic church in Hartford, the three-term Connecticut senator told a small group of supporters about the Senate’s recent passage of a wide-ranging Russia sanctions bill he helped get across the finish line. Shortly after, he headed to New Britain’s farmers market to meet with farmers.
Blumenthal, who isn’t on the ballot this year, has an unrelenting work ethic, regardless of whether he’s up for reelection. He typically packs his days in Connecticut with multiple events. When the Senate is in session, he squeezes in whatever he can on Monday mornings before heading back to D.C. 

U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal spoke to reporters at St. Michael the Archangel Ukrainian Catholic Church in Hartford on August 12, 2026. Blumenthal joined Ukrainian Americans to celebrate the passing of a bill the senator championed, bringing sanctions against purchasers of Russian gas and oil.   Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Still, after a high-stakes primary in which his colleague U.S. Rep. John Larson, was soundly defeated by a younger challenger, it could be hard for Blumenthal — and other aging members of Connecticut’s congressional delegation — to dodge questions about age and the calls for generational change that are sure to play a role in future campaigns.
So far, the 80-year-old senator seems undeterred.
“Age is always a state of mind, not just a time of life,” said Blumenthal, a third-term senator who has been on Connecticut’s ballot for several decades. “The energy and excitement are impressive, and I hope to carry it forward myself.”
Blumenthal is up for reelection in 2028 when he will be 82. He hasn’t confirmed what he’ll do in two years, but he said he’s taking the steps to prepare for another campaign — in the event he runs again.
“I’m focused on this November, electing Democrats to the United States Senate so we take back a Democratic majority and that’s my focus,” he said. “I have a campaign committee. I haven’t announced anything. I’m raising money, but my focus is on November.”
Age and seniority have become pressing topics in Congress, hitting a fever pitch in 2024 after a groundswell of calls from Democrats for Joe Biden to drop out of the race. Biden initially declined to pass the torch, but then suspended his presidential reelection campaign months before the race after a disastrous debate. Since then, Democrats have been less inclined to wait for older lawmakers to retire.
Larson became the seventh Democratic incumbent in the House to lose a primary this year. The reasons challengers prevailed have varied — some were ideological and others generational. The four-way primary for Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District was about the latter.
The 14-term congressman lost to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, who mainly campaigned on the need for new voices and new energy in Congress, without needing to lean much on age at all. Bronin called his victory a “political earthquake in Connecticut.”
Luke Bronin celebrates his Democratic primary victory in Hartford on August 11, 2026.
That raises questions and speculation about whether an appetite for change will carry into the 2028 election cycle, when all five U.S. House seats in Connecticut will be up again, along with the U.S. Senate seat held by Blumenthal.
Democrats have wondered, most privately out of a desire not to offend Blumenthal, if Bronin’s run against Larson offered a template for someone to similarly challenge the senator.
The former Hartford mayor hewed to a simple, unchanging message. He made no attacks, praised Larson’s record — and argued it was time for a change after 28 years.
At a church on the Sunday before the primary, Bronin said, “I respect the person I’m running against. I do. But to every thing, there is a season.”
Younger challengers didn’t prevail across the board in Connecticut Tuesday. Gov. Ned Lamont, the older of the two candidates, easily won the Democratic nomination, prevailing over 41-year-old state Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden, who waged a primary challenge from the left.
“Ned Lamont was the older of the two, and he won by a 2-to-1 majority. So clearly age has always been a consideration. When I started, I was the youngest,” Blumenthal said. “But age I think is not going to be a determinant in the outcome of any election on its own.”
U.S. Rep. John B. Larson address supporters as he concedes to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin during a primary election watch party at Connecticut River Academy at Goodwin University in East Hartford on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
There has been little turnover in Connecticut’s all-Democratic congressional delegation in recent years. U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, 83, has been there the longest and is on track to win another term in November. If she prevails, and if Democrats take back the House this fall, she’ll reclaim the gavel of the influential House Appropriations Committee.
Larson was the only member of the five-member delegation to face a primary this year.
But after Bronin and two other challengers took on a sitting lawmaker, a deep bench of Democrats in Connecticut who are waiting to ascend the political ladder both at the state and federal levels might not be willing to wait for retirements.
The question around Blumenthal’s political future came up at one of the congressional debates. In a lightning round, the four candidates in Connecticut’s 1st District were asked about it. Larson’s three challengers answered affirmatively that Blumenthal’s current term should be his last.
Much like Larson’s own defense for seeking another term to Congress, he replied: “It’s up to him.”
In the race for the 1st Congressional District, Bronin was not the first to announce against Larson. Ruth Fortune, a Haitian immigrant and mayoral appointee on the Hartford Board of Education, went first. Seemingly overnight, Larson was facing four opponents, one who would drop out.
Roy Occhiogrosso, who was the campaign strategist for Gov. Dannel P. Malloy’s two successful runs for governor, said the political class sometimes is too quick to draw lessons from the most recent election.
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal spoke at Arch Street Tavern in Hartford on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Blumenthal celebrated Gov. Ned Lamont’s victory in the Democratic primary.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
“I think people make the mistake of watching an election result and then immediately determining there is a trend or a model that can be applied another race. I’m not sure that’s true,” Occhiogrosso said.
He noted that a 78-year-old congressman had been denied the nomination to another two-year term, but a 72-year-old governor cruised to victory over a challenger 30 years his junior the same night.
“It’s usually each race is unique and decided by its own factors,” Occhiogrosso said. “That was a good reminder.”
Age aside, the unprecedented primary challenging Larson may offer a template for future candidates who are looking to navigate Connecticut’s strict ballot access laws. Fortune made the primary ballot through the unconventional and logistically challenging process of qualifying through petition signatures.
“I think we won’t wait until things are so broken again. When we overcome this current nightmare that we’re in, people will challenge their representatives more frequently. And I hope that becomes more of the norm,” Fortune said in the days leading up to Tuesday’s primary. “I’m hoping it’s the straw that breaks the camel’s back.”
“If nothing else, I think we’ll see more grassroots candidates willing to do the petitions because they see that it’s been done,” she added. Fortune has said she’s going to work with the Connecticut General Assembly on trying to take up ballot access reforms.
Charlotte Patterson, 11, of Hartford, shows Ruth Fortune, Democratic Candidate for the 1st Congressional District, her “Chain of Shame,” made from election mailers, outside the polling place at Hartford International University for Religion and Peace on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney agreed that it could open the door to more candidates. He pointed to Fortune’s unlikely but ultimately successful path to qualifying for the August primary ballot.
Courtney’s own primary challenger, Kyle Gauck, didn’t meet the threshold at nominating convention to make the ballot. And he didn’t qualify through the petition process either. Courtney was ultimately uncontested without a primary on Tuesday. 
“I think Ruth Fortune’s success, in terms of getting on the ballot, is really one of the more underappreciated stories of this election. It was really defying all the conventional wisdom,” Courtney said at Larson’s election night party. “I’m sure people are really looking at this as an example. I think her race in some ways was going to be the one that actually has the most sort of enduring appeal and inspiration for people.”
Another nearby race centering around age and seniority is the Sept. 1 Democratic primary in Massachusetts between U.S. Sen. Ed Markey and U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton. Markey is 80 and if he wins again, he’d be 86 at the end of another six-year term.
Moulton, 47, has made age a centerpiece of his campaign even more than Larson’s challengers did. The Massachusetts congressman has a similar profile to Bronin. They’re the same age and both veterans who were endorsed by the Democratic group VoteVets, which is seeking to elect more military veterans to office. Moulton is a Marine Corps veteran who served in Iraq; Bronin is a Navy veteran who served in Afghanistan.
And in a similar vein to Connecticut’s own congressional primary, the incumbent is looking to make it more of an ideological race. As a progressive senator, Markey has focused on Moulton’s more moderate record since coming to Congress in 2015.
Blumenthal argued that it’s not all about age: Democrats need to give voters a reason to vote for them. He’s hopeful that’ll bode well for them in November’s midterms.
“There’s no magic about age. It’s about energy, new ideas, a commitment to fighting, and outreach and connection with people,” Blumenthal said. “It’s what we need to do as Democrats in this election. We need to convince people we’re on their side.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey, in new letter, urges MWRA to meet the ‘pressing needs’ of Quabbin Reservoir communities
description: Healey, through her letter to the head of the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority, is wading into an escalating battle between small towns along the Quabbin and the quasi-public agency that uses that water to serve 2.7 million residents in 61 communities mostly in and around Boston.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY is calling on Greater Boston’s water provider to offer more robust support for struggling rural towns near the Quabbin Reservoir in central Massachusetts, writing in a new letter Wednesday that the agency should “more fully recognize” those communities. 
Healey, through her letter to the head of the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority that was shared with CommonWealth Beacon, is wading into an escalating battle between small towns along the Quabbin and the quasi-public agency that uses that water to serve 2.7 million residents in 61 communities mostly in and around Boston.  
“Every day, these watershed communities provide an invaluable public service to the communities served by the MWRA system,” Healey wrote. “They continue to help protect the watershed’s natural resources while navigating infrastructure constraints, including limitations on their own water supply and economic development.” 
A CommonWealth Beacon report published last week chronicled the tensions bubbling between state officials and the Quabbin communities.  
Gov. Maura Healey fields questions from reporters during a crowded scrum on July 15, 2026. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
Despite living alongside the Quabbin, a water body whose very creation about 100 years ago involved the flooding of four towns, these communities do not get their water from the reservoir. Instead, they rely on smaller municipal and private wells that have suffered in recent years from contamination and dry conditions. 
An ongoing drought has only heightened tensions around water access, when Quabbin communities have at points been under more strict water restrictions than communities that receive Quabbin water in some cases from nearly 100 miles away. 
These towns are also struggling financially, dealing with meager budgets as they are forced to lay off municipal staff, consolidate resources with other nearby towns, and ask their own residents to raise their property taxes. Healey’s top environmental official, Secretary Rebecca Tepper, heard these concerns directly at an MWRA board meeting last month in Belchertown, one of the Quabbin municipalities.  
A loose coalition of local officials known as the Quabbin Stewards has now formed to coordinate a push for Beacon Hill to do more, including proposals in an environmental bond bill for a permanent seat for the region on the MWRA board and a new trust fund to pay for services like infrastructure and public safety. 
They are also seeking increased payments in lieu of taxes from the state, or PILOTs, to compensate the towns for the state-owned land that bars economic development to preserve the Quabbin. 
Five of the seven Quabbin “host communities” have received the same amount in PILOT payments in each of the past five fiscal years – essentially a decrease when adjusted for inflation – laying bare a sizable difference between what these towns earn per acre through state aid and what they generate per acre through property taxes on developed non-Quabbin land. 
The MWRA has so far resisted those efforts. The agency’s advisory board opposes these proposed reforms, and the agency’s interim executive director, Stephen Estes-Smargiassi, previously warned in an interview with CommonWealth Beacon that meeting those demands would trigger hefty water rate increases for its customers.  
The MWRA did not immediately return a request for comment on Healey’s letter. 
In her letter to Estes-Smargiassi, Healey urged the MWRA to step up support for municipal police and fire departments on the front lines of protecting the Quabbin and provide technical expertise for these towns’ water needs.  
She also wants the agency to convene a new body to “serve as a forum for voicing significant concerns and collaborating on productive solutions” and for MWRA localities to implement necessary water restrictions for “equity.” 
“I am confident that a dedicated, collaborative effort by MWRA, working hand in hand with the Quabbin communities, will help them thrive while more meaningfully recognizing their essential role in protecting a clean and reliable water supply for millions of people in Massachusetts,” Healey wrote.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Which CT towns had the highest voter turnout for the primaries?
description: About 23% of CT's registered Democrats voted in Tuesday's primaries, less than in the 2018 primary, according to the Secretary of the State.
text:
About 23% of Connecticut’s registered Democrats voted in Tuesday’s election, according to early unofficial results from the Secretary of the State.
The big Democratic races saw former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin upset 14-term incumbent U.S. Rep. John Larson in the 1st Congressional District and Gov. Ned Lamont beat challenger Josh Elliott.
Results for some towns were still pending Wednesday afternoon.
Turnout this year was lower than for the last gubernatorial primary, when Lamont faced a challenge from Bridgeport’s Joe Ganim in 2018. For that primary, 29% of eligible Democrats came to the polls.
But in some towns, Democrats showed up. Turnout was above 41% in Bethlehem, Hartland and West Hartford, a town with traditionally high engagement that delivered 6,150 votes for Lamont, 5% of his total, and 4,369 or 14% of Bronin’s.
The state house primary in Enfield was postponed until Sept. 1 due to a court ruling last Thursday that placed challenger Tom Tyler on the ballot.
Lamont picked up his largest number of votes in West Hartford, Hartford and Stamford, winning a majority against Elliott in all towns but three: Scotland, Chaplin and Woodstock.
Republican turnout was lower, with only 10% of registered Republicans in towns with a primary turning up to the polls, according to the Secretary of the State.
Turnout was higher for Republican primaries in the 5th Congressional District and in General Assembly races than in the 4th District race, which covers Fairfield county.
The 5th District saw more than double the amount of votes cast in its Congressional primary than in the 4th, and the gap in support between candidates was much more decisive.
Most towns saw a decrease in Democratic turnout compared to 2018, but towns with competitive Congressional or state Democratic primaries were more likely to see an increase. 
The State Elections Enforcement Commission reported it received 79 calls to its hotline on Tuesday, according to Senior Counsel Joshua Foley.
Hamden, Southington and Norwich reported issues with tabulators, but registrars handled it “properly,” Foley said. There had been no reports of voter fraud. 
CT Mirror reporters Sasha Allen and Mark Pazniokas contributed to this report.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT joins multistate lawsuit over federal mortgage escrow rules
description: Lawsuit argues that new rules incorrectly preempt states’ powers to regulate how interest generated by mortgage escrow accounts is handled.
text:
Connecticut has joined a coalition of states suing over federal rules that protect national banks from state laws dictating how interest generated by mortgage escrow accounts is used.
The lawsuit, filed in Oregon on Tuesday, challenged a pair of rules issued in May by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, an independent bureau within the U.S. Treasury Department. The OCC is tasked with regulating and supervising national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches and agencies of foreign banks.
The lawsuit argued that the new rules incorrectly preempt states’ powers to regulate how the interest generated by mortgage escrow accounts is handled. Currently, each state has the power to determine its own rules, with many states opting to return a portion of the interest generated back to homeowners.
Under the OCC’s changes however, national banks are only subject to federal rules, potentially allowing them to keep the interest from these accounts, even if they operate in a state with a law that requires borrowers receive a portion of the interest.
That’s something the plaintiffs want to change. In a statement released on Tuesday, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong said the rules “would strip states of their authority to require national banks to pay interest on homeowners’ mortgage escrow accounts.”
“Homeownership is out of reach for too many families already and the last thing they need is another rule that helps big banks profit off their hard-earned money. This new rule will put banks first, families last, and strip states of yet another tool put in place to help consumers,” he said. 
New federal rules are creating issues for states
The federal rules in question were first proposed last year and were finalized in May. They revolve around state “interest-on-escrow” laws, state laws explaining how banks are allowed to manage interest accrued on the accounts that hold funds for property taxes and homeowners insurance.
Because mortgage lenders often require these accounts to hold far more money than a single upcoming payment, these escrow accounts often carry large positive balances. Banks then collect interest on these balances, earning money from the accounts.
States however, have stepped in to regulate what banks do with that interest, with several states requiring that a portion of the interest generated from mortgage escrow accounts be returned to the homeowner paying into the account. In Connecticut for example, a mortgage lender is required to pay interest to a borrower at an adjustable rate. According to the lawsuit, this rate cannot be less “than the average of the national rates for savings deposits and money market deposits for the prior year”.
Other states set a specific percentage of interest that must be returned to borrowers. In California, the percentage is 2%. In Minnesota it’s 3%. Some states rely on a formula to determine exactly how much money gets returned to borrowers. 
But no matter the amount returned, states have held that their specific rules apply to banks lending within their borders. 
The OCC rules change this, with the agency making two arguments to support the shift. 
The first is what the agency has called its “escrow powers rule,” which argues that national banks have the power to set their own terms on escrow accounts. The OCC has said that preserving this power is necessary so that banks have “the flexibility to make the business decisions that adapt to local circumstances and other relevant considerations.” 
The second rule is the “preemption rule”. This rule finds that because national banks — which are regulated by the federal government — have the power to set their terms, only the federal government can weigh in on those terms. Because of this, the federal government has the power to preempt state regulations that would impact a national bank, specifically calling out its right to preempt regulations in New York on the grounds that the state’s requirements “restrict[s] a national bank’s . . . flexibility to decide whether and to what extent to pay interest or other compensation on funds placed in escrow accounts.” 
The rule then added that this preemption also applies to a dozen other states and two U.S. territories, with the OCC saying the regulations are similar to the regulations used in New York. Connecticut was one of the states listed in this rule. 
The agency hasn’t clearly explained how it determined that the other state regulations are similar. The OCC did not respond to a request for comment before publication. 
Debates over federal preemption are fueling tension between states and the federal government
That lack of explanation is one key issue raised in the lawsuit, with the attorneys general arguing that the OCC is required to challenge each state regulation individually and cannot lump a group of states together and preempt all of them at once. 
In doing so, the plaintiffs argued, the OCC is acting beyond the powers given to the agency. 
“Congress has not delegated such boundless authority to the OCC,” the attorneys general wrote in the lawsuit. “To the contrary, Congress placed strict substantive and procedural limits on the OCC’s ability to make preemption determinations.” 
The suit noted that several U.S. Supreme Court decisions, as well as the Dodd-Frank regulations approved by Congress after the 2008 financial crisis, all support states’ ability to pass regulation. 
The challenge comes as the Trump administration and state governments continue to disagree over preemption, with the federal government arguing that it has the power to overrule a number of state laws while states argue the opposite. 
On this issue, legal rulings have been mixed. A previous challenge to New York’s interest-on-escrow law was pushed to the Supreme Court, but was later sent back down to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. 
In May, the Second Circuit ruled that New York’s law was preempted by federal regulations, specifically the National Bank Act. The court found that the New York law “affects a broad federal grant of power to set the terms of mortgage-escrow accounts and it impedes national banks’ ability to offer those accounts efficiently.”  New York homeowners are currently asking the Supreme Court to take another look at the issue. 
In the meantime, the OCC has argued that the new rules are vital to “reducing unnecessary burden, enabling local and national prosperity, and unleashing economic growth,” according to a press release from earlier in the year. 
The plaintiffs, including Tong, see the issue differently, arguing that “Congress has not delegated to the OCC freestanding power to issue regulations for the purpose of preempting state laws.” 
The states of California, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Vermont have joined Connecticut in the lawsuit.

name: National
title: Federal agency blocks Medicaid coverage of kids’ gender-affirming care
description: A new federal rule will end Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming hormone therapies and procedures for kids under age 18. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced Tuesday a rule that prohibits state Medicaid plans from covering gender-affirming procedures for minors and using federal Medicaid dollars for such care.  The rule also prohibits Chi[...]
text:
A new federal rule is ending Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming hormone therapies and procedures for young people. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)A new federal rule will end Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming hormone therapies and procedures for kids under age 18.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced Tuesday a rule that prohibits state Medicaid plans from covering gender-affirming procedures for minors and using federal Medicaid dollars for such care. 
The rule also prohibits Children’s Health Insurance Program, or CHIP, funds from being used for kids under 19. CMS is defining such care to include puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgical operations. The policy takes effect Oct. 13.
The Trump administration asserts that gender-affirming care is dangerous for kids, while many medical groups say it’s safe and can improve the mental health of children and adolescents. Surgical gender-affirming care operations are very rare for children.
Court ruling limiting adult gender-affirming Medicaid coverage could have national impacts

For kids on Medicaid and CHIP who are currently on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the agency said state plans may continue to use federal money up to six months from now. Funds can still be used for mental health care for kids, the agency said.
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asserted in a new release that gender-affirming procedures “carry serious risks and can cause irreversible harm.”
In response to several Trump proposals on gender-affirming care, many of the nation’s leading medical associations, including the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics, have affirmed the safety of care that aligns with a child or teen’s gender identity.
“These rules are a baseless intrusion into the patient-physician relationship,” Dr. Susan Kressly, then president of the academy, said in a December statement. “Patients, their families, and their physicians — not politicians or government officials — should be the ones to make decisions together about what care is best for them.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

title: DeSantis takes aim at AOC, says it’s not time to let Dems off the hook for ‘Woke 1’
description: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has joined the chorus of conservatives taking exception to a prominent Democratic lawmaker’s weekend comment regarding policy positions taken by progressives in 2020 that are now seen as out of the political mainstream. Speaking on ABC’s This Week, New York Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez defended her previous advocacy[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) speaks at a get-out-the-vote event at Solidarity House in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2024, days before the presidential election. (Photo by Anna Liz Nichols/Michigan Advance)Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has joined the chorus of conservatives taking exception to a prominent Democratic lawmaker’s weekend comment regarding policy positions taken by progressives in 2020 that are now seen as out of the political mainstream.
Speaking on ABC’s This Week, New York Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez defended her previous advocacy for “defunding the police” by saying, “When we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime in bringing crime down.”
She joked about what she said a local city councilman described as ‘Woke 1.’
“Oh, that was just Woke 1. It was crazy.’ Like really?” DeSantis said during a press conference in Pensacola. “You’re really going to just say that it was a mulligan or something like that? Like, people were actually attacking law enforcement. They wanted to defund the police. You did have candidates and still have candidates who talk about abolishing prisons.”
The governor never uttered Ocasio-Cortez’ name, instead describing her as “one of the big lefties.” He went on to say, “You got swept up in that frenzy. Not me. Not Florida. We were the first state to fight back, and we fought back very quickly. But you got swept up in that frenzy. You don’t get to say, ‘Oh, that was yesterday, let’s just move on.’ If you’re embracing things like abolishing law enforcement? Abolishing prisons? “
Many Democratic candidates running for political office in Florida in 2020 were tagged by Republicans with supporting a “defund the police” position although few, if any, did. Many Florida Democrats running for office this year have advocated defunding ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement), including U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon.
The governor derided Democratic Socialists of America candidates on police and prisons. “They start talking about social workers and stuff like that. You know … someone breaking into your house, sending social worker is not going to help you. You need law enforcement.”
In the aftermath of the protests over the homicide of George Floyd by Minneapolis police, St. Petersburg created a program that sends social workers, and not police, to non-violent 911 calls involving mental health crises, suicide intervention, truancy, homeless complaints, and neighborhood disputes.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Judge dismisses lawsuit from RNC challenging Nebraska voter law
description: A Republican National Committee-led lawsuit challenging a law allowing certain overseas voters to vote in the Cornhusker State is over.
text:
A voting booth at the Lancaster County Election Commission office on April 24, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A lawsuit led by the Republican National Committee challenging a Nebraska law allowing certain overseas voters to vote in the Cornhusker State is over.
Lancaster County District Judge Ryan Post ruled Wednesday that there was at least one constitutional application for the challenged law. As such, Post dismissed the challenge from the RNC and two Lancaster County voters with prejudice, meaning the RNC and the voters could not bring the same challenge again.
Lancaster County District Judge Ryan Post. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Judicial Branch)
State law allows U.S. citizens who have never resided in Nebraska but have a parent registered to vote in one Nebraska county to register in one county. It would be a felony to register or vote in multiple states or counties.
To succeed, the RNC would have needed to establish that “no set of circumstances exists” which would allow the act to be valid, Post said.
“A statute is presumed to be constitutional, and all reasonable doubts are resolved in favor of its constitutionality,” Post wrote in a 13-page order.
The RNC and two Lancaster County voters, Jack Riggins and Pam Dingman, the elected Lancaster County engineer, argued the law “dilutes the votes of lawful Republican voters” and violates Article VI, Section 1 of the Nebraska Constitution, which defines a qualified voter as a U.S. citizen who “has resided within the state and the county and voting precinct for the terms provided by law.”
Attorneys for the RNC, Riggins and Dingman had no immediate comment Wednesday.
Post said attorneys for the RNC and Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen correctly identified an 1895 Nebraska Supreme Court case where the justices generally accepted that “residence” was synonymous with “domicile.”
Post also pointed to arguments from the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office on behalf of Evnen in walking through at least one hypothetical instance where the law is constitutional.
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen. June 6, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In the hypothetical scenario, a U.S. citizen, “Joe,” is the son of missionaries who call Saunders County home but moved to South America, where Joe was born. The family continued to live in the foreign country and maintained a home in Saunders County, always with the intent to return home. The family did not change their domicile over time either.
“Under the foregoing authorities, Joe remains a Nebraska resident and domiciliary for voter qualification purposes under the state constitution, and he is ‘eligible to register to vote and vote in’ Saunders County under Neb. Rev. Stat. § 32-939(2),” Post wrote.
As of July, 116 overseas Nebraska voters were registered under the targeted statute, six of whom voted in the May primary, according to data from Evnen’s office.
During the May 12 primary election, there were 1,256,903 registered Nebraska voters. A total of 358,538 voters came out to vote, or 28.5%.
Special ballots must be mailed to some overseas voters registered to vote under the challenged law by Sept. 3. The deadline to certify the general election ballot this year is Sept. 11. Finalized ballots are then mailed to all other military and overseas voters by Sept. 18.
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: VTDigger
title: Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George prevails in hotly contested primary race
description:
Candidates also advance around the state in closely watched law enforcement-related races – sans embattled incumbents.  
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George prevails in hotly contested primary race .
text:
Chittenden County States Attorney Sarah Fair George speaks during a press conference in Burlington on Monday, June 13, 2022. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George has held off a challenger in the Democratic primary race for the top prosecutor post in the state’s most populated county.
Voters also decided Tuesday other races in countywide law enforcement posts in Vermont. 
George garnered 15,931 votes in primary balloting, finishing ahead of challenger Bram Kranichfeld, who collected 14,923 votes, according to unofficial results from Vermont Secretary of State’s Office. 
No candidates filed in the Republican or Progressive party primaries, appearing to clear the way for George to earn a third, four-year term in the office.
George has made headlines during her tenure with her push for progressive criminal justice reform policies. Kranichfeld campaigned on the need for both compassion as well as greater accountability when handling criminal cases.
Kranichfeld currently serves as the Franklin County state’s attorney. He opted not to run for that post this year, throwing his hat in the ring for the state position in Chittenden County where he resides. 
Neither George nor Kranichfeld could immediately be reached Wednesday morning for comment. 

Doug Hall, center, chats with incumbent Sen. Pat Brennan, R-Grand Isle, outside the polls at Coclhester High School on Primary Day, Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Also in Chittenden County primary election results, as VTDigger reported Tuesday night, incumbent Chittenden County Sheriff Dan Gamelin, a Democrat, fended off a primary challenge from Kevin Bloom, who runs a music studio and works for an audio software company. 
The two candidates campaigned on different visions for the department. Gamelin touted his experience in the department while Bloom pitched reforms to how law enforcement work is done.
According to unofficial results from the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office, Gamelin had 15,876 votes, compared to 12,135 votes for Bloom.
Like the Chittenden County state’s attorney race, no candidates filed for either the Republican or Progressive primaries. 
In other closely watched countywide law enforcement-related races Tuesday night, Claude Weyant prevailed in a three-way Democratic primary race for the four-year sheriff’s post in Windsor County. 
Weyant has been the chief deputy of the Windsor County Sheriff’s Department. He is currently running the day-to-day operations of the office. 
Sheriff Ryan Palmer stepped back from overseeing the day-to-day operations of the department earlier this year following his arrest on several charges, including lewd and lascivious conduct and soliciting prostitution. Palmer has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Palmer did not seek reelection.
Weyant collected 3,666 votes in Tuesday’s balloting, besting Christopher Norton, a Windham County Sheriff’s Department sergeant, who had 1,726 votes, and Joshua Lake, a Bellows Falls Police Department patrolman, who had 1,563 votes, according to unofficial results from the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office.
Just days before Tuesday’s primary election, the village of Bellows Falls placed Lake on administrative leave from his job in Bellows Falls after a letter was issued by both the WIndham County State’s Attorney and Vermont Attorney General’s Office raising questions about the reliability of statements by him. 
Weyant, of Windsor, now faces Republican Richard King, of Springfield, a lieutenant in the Windsor County Sheriff’s Department, in the November general election.
In Franklin County, there was a three-way race in the Republican primary to serve as the next sheriff. 
Chad Miles, a lieutenant in the department, garnered 1,057 votes, finishing ahead of Andre Labier who had 589 votes and James Lynch with 318 votes, according to the unofficial results from the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office.
Incumbent Franklin County Sheriff John Grismore did not seek reelection. Grismore had his law enforcement certification revoked in 2023 over a use-of-force policy violation. 
Grismore had also been criminally charged in connection with that incident with simple assault for allegedly kicking a person in custody. However, following two mistrials with jurors unable to reach unanimous verdicts, the prosecutor dropped the case. 
No candidates filed to run on the Democratic or Progressive sides on the ballot, appearing to clear the way for Miles in the general election in November.
