name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Historic plantation among 1,700 acres in conservation projects SC considers buying
description: One purchase state officials are considering could let people camp across the street from a public shooting range.
text:
Harbison State Forest is among properties state agencies are looking to expand with new land acqusitions. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A historic plantation in Richland County could become part of a state-owned nature preserve, according to a funding request to a legislative oversight committee.
All told, nearly 1,700 acres of land are under consideration for purchase by the state across conservation agencies. Some would expand existing nature preserves, while others would establish new ones. One would potentially open a new campsite for visitors at the state’s largest public shooting range.
Goodwill Plantation
The largest project under consideration would expand the Wateree Heritage Preserve and Wildlife Management Area in Richland County by 736 acres.
The 4,459-acre preserve is best known as the home of Cook’s Mountain, a 372-foot-tall peak in an otherwise low-lying area.
The Department of Natural Resources is still in the early stages of evaluating the property and deciding whether it would be a good fit for the nearby nature preserve, according to agency documents.
A large part of the property is the Goodwill Plantation, established in the 1790s and listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1986. Part of the neighboring heritage preserve already includes a portion of the plantation, including graves, ditches and dikes dating back to the 1800s.
Originally owned by the prominent Huger family, Goodwill was purchased in 1858 by Edward Barnwell “Barney” Heyward, grandson of Nathaniel Heyward (South Carolina’s wealthiest rice planter), and father of Duncan Clinch Heyward, South Carolina’s governor from 1903 to 1907.
As many as 976 people were enslaved at Goodwill during the Civil War. Richland County tax records indicate Heyward’s relatives sent slaves from their Lowcountry plantations to Goodwill to “wait out the war.” When it was over, Heyward employed former slaves as day laborers, according to National Register documentation, which doesn’t specify further.
Largest conservation easement project in SC history underway with $50M grant

The property includes a millpond and canal irrigation system built in the 1820s, which is one of the first known attempts to farm on low-lying land in the state, according to the state Department of Archives and History.
Several buildings dating back more than 150 years still survive on the piece of land DNR is considering buying.
The oldest of those, the overseer’s house, was built in 1857. Other buildings that still stand include two slave cabins built in 1858, a blacksmith shop dating back to 1865 and the main house, from 1890, according to oversight documents. A second house was built on the property in 2010.
The Department of Natural Resources doesn’t plan to renovate any of the existing buildings or build new ones, according to the oversight documents.
If state officials find no problems with the property, The Conservation Fund, a conservation-based nonprofit, plans to donate the land to expand the nearby heritage preserve.
The state’s Conservation Bank already chipped in $12.6 million to help the nonprofit buy the land, which was priced at a total $13.8 million.
New conservation areas
Another major project under consideration would create a new, 650-acre wildlife management area in Clarendon County.
The property, which is near Lake Marion, is “one of the most valuable inland wetland tracts available in South Carolina today,” according to the agency documents.
Operating as a duck hunting club, the area’s many ponds and dams create an ideal spot for migratory birds to stop in the winter, according to agency documents.
Because the property is already in use for hunting, DNR wouldn’t have to build new roads, trails, water control structures or storage buildings, as is typical in conservation projects, oversight documents read.
All of that together means the property’s “value for waterfowl conservation is immediate, substantial, and difficult to match elsewhere in the state,” the agency wrote in its request. The land’s owner offered to donate the property, with the state paying $50,000 for land surveys and other preliminary work.
For 30 days, a nonprofit leads hikes and floats across SC. The goal is conservation.

DNR is also looking to add a new nature preserve in Pickens County.
The 106 acres, which the agency is planning to buy for $475,000, would join more than 70 heritage preserves statewide, a network of sites protecting significant ecological and historical areas.
The property would become part of the existing 33,000-acre Jocassee Gorges Wildlife Management Area and is near 37-acre Wadakoe Mountain Heritage Preserve.
The area has “a diverse array of wildlife, including some of the most abundant salamander and black bear populations in the southeast,” according to oversight documents. The untouched land, which includes properties attractive to developers along Eastatoe Creek, is part of the scenic views from Highway 11, the agency wrote.
Visitors would be able to fish, hunt or hike a series of trails, according to agency documents.
Other expansions
Harbison State Forest near Columbia could expand by 71 acres under a Forestry Commission request.
The property, which was clearcut in 2017, would allow the agency to expand the 18-mile trail system already in the 2,200-acre state forest, according to the agency’s request.
“This property and surrounding area are in (imminent) danger of being lost to development,” agency documents read.
Congaree Land Trust, a Columbia-based nonprofit, is planning to buy the land for $1.4 million before selling it to the state for the same price.
Paris Mountain State Park could get nearly 88 acres bigger with a purchase the state parks department is considering.
The Altamont Pass in Greenville County sits between the 1,700-acre state park, as well as land owned by the Department of Transportation and conservation nonprofit Naturaland Trust. The land trust has offered to donate the property to the state.
Proposed campsite
Visitors to the state’s largest public shooting range could have a chance to stay overnight across the street.
The Department of Natural Resources is considering buying 114 acres across the road from the shooting complex, which opened last year. The land is owned by the Love family, which sold the land for the shooting range to the state.
SC opens new state-owned skeet and trap shooting range

If the state decides to buy the property, which has an expected value of $1.3 million, the land would create a buffer between the shooting range and other nearby properties, keeping the area private, according to oversight documents. The agency could also open up the property for camping, fishing and “aquatic education,” the request reads.
The forested land includes a 13-acre pond, which the owners say is 12 feet deep, as well as a small stream. That makes the area ideal for common species of fish and birds, such as bass and pileated woodpeckers, according to the agency.
Officials must still determine whether the land is fit for use by the state.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC counties are dropping Sundays from early voting plans
description: Sunday voting is declining in North Carolina, with counties that had some Sunday hours during early voting for the 2022 midterm elections deciding to eliminate them this year.  The state Board of Elections approved early voting plans for 80 counties where local boards voted unanimously on days and hours. Of those, about a dozen had […]
text:
Voters trickle into the Durham County Main Library to cast their primary ballots on the first day of early voting on Feb. 12, 2026. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)Sunday voting is declining in North Carolina, with counties that had some Sunday hours during early voting for the 2022 midterm elections deciding to eliminate them this year. 
The state Board of Elections approved early voting plans for 80 counties where local boards voted unanimously on days and hours. Of those, about a dozen had early voting hours on Sunday in the 2022 general election but dropped them this year. 
Not all county early voting plans are set, and there may yet be more Sundays eliminated in more counties. 
The state Board of Elections will meet to decide early voting plans in 20 counties where local boards were divided over voting days or polling locations. In most of those counties, Sunday voting is at issue. 
Republicans hold majorities on county boards of election and all have Republican chairs. Republicans are less inclined to support Sunday voting hours. They’ve objected to Sunday voting for various reasons: that people should be in church; that Sunday voting stretches election staff, and that it’s not cost effective. 
Dallas Woodhouse, the former elections liaison in state Auditor Dave Boliek’s office, encouraged county election boards to drop Sunday early voting hours. 
Sunday voting is important to Black voters because Black churches hold Souls to the Polls events on Sundays.
By eliminating Sunday voting hours and making voting inconvenient for college students, the state Board of Elections is sending the message that they don’t want Black, brown, or young people to vote, said Brian Kennedy II, policy director at Democracy NC. He said it’s part of a pattern.
Guilford Board of Elections declines to adopt 2026 early voting sites at NC A&T, UNC Greensboro

The Wake County Board of Elections voted to move an early voting site out of the student union at N.C. State University and to the edge of campus. The vote was unanimous after Republicans shot down Democrats’ move to keep the student union site.
In Guilford, the county elections board split on whether to have polling sites on the campuses of NC A&T State University and UNC-Greensboro. Guilford is one of the counties where the state board will set the early voting plan.
“The effort is to suppress the vote,” Kennedy said. “Advocates are pushing people to vote early, cast ballots, whether or not Sunday is an option.” 
In at least one of the counties that unanimously approved a plan that dropped Sunday voting, Democrats put up a fight. At the Brunswick elections board meeting last month, the board’s Democrats voted to approve two plans that included Sunday hours. But those plans were voted down by the Republican majority. 
When the board’s Democrats were reminded that the Republican-led state Board of Elections decides early voting plans when local votes are not unanimous, the Democrats agreed to a plan without Sundays. 
Brunswick had polls open on both Sundays during the 2022 early voting period. Brunswick elections staff provided data for 2022 that showed turnout was lowest on Sundays.  
Still, speakers urged the Brunswick board to keep Sunday hours. Gary Kozlusky of Sunset Beach asked the board to consider what would be best for voters and recommended the board open voting on both available Sundays. 
“Not everyone has the flexibility to vote during the week,” he said. ”Some people have longer, irregular hours, others work Saturdays caring for family members. No single schedule works for everybody.”
Brunswick elections board Chair Randy Pelton said weekend voting has been an issue every year going back to when he first started serving on the board in 2013.
“Every year, it’s the same thing,” he said. “I don’t think money is the issue at this point.”
Republican member Joe Myers said the 17-day early voting period is too long. 
In an interview Tuesday, Kozlusky, who is a poll worker, said that Brunswick does a good job with election planning. But Republicans have always opposed Sunday voting, he said.  
“There are just so many little things going on everywhere in North Carolina,” he said. “It’s almost like you can see that there’s a strategic movement against Sunday voting.”
Deborah Maxwell, president of the NC NAACP,  predicted voters will still find a way to cast ballots despite Sundays disappearing from early voting schedules. 
“They can try all the suppression tactics they want, but we’re still going to vote,” she said. “Our lives depend on it.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: US Rep. Leger Fernández, NM attorney general announce proposal aimed at unreleased Epstein files
description: A member of New Mexico’s congressional delegation and state Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Wednesday announced newly proposed legislation that they say will help law enforcement agencies across the nation file legal challenges against the U.S. Department of Justice when it refuses to release documents related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
text:
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), left, spoke alongside New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Aug. 12, 2026, to announce newly proposed federal legislation that would make it easier for attorneys general to file legal challenges against the U.S. Department of Justice for not releasing files related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)A member of New Mexico’s congressional delegation and state Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Wednesday announced newly proposed legislation that they say will help law enforcement agencies across the nation file legal challenges against the U.S. Department of Justice when it refuses to release documents related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At a news conference in Torrez’s downtown Albuquerque office, U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) said she began working on the legislation — titled “Epstein Files Transparency Act II” — with U.S. Reps. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) and Ro Khanna (D-California) after seeing the federal government refuse to release some 3 million documents related to Epstein and make redactions on other publicly released documents.
If passed, the proposed bill would empower state attorneys general to file a legal challenge against the federal government alleging an unlawful withholding, redaction or removal of Epstein-related documents and investigative materials.
“If transparency is not transparency, then justice is not justice,” Leger Fernández said.
Torrez sued the U.S. Department of Justice earlier in August and accused it of impeding his criminal investigation into Epstein and his New Mexico property, Zorro Ranch, by refusing to release the relevant, unredacted files.
Torrez told reporters Wednesday that the lawsuit was a “novel” approach, as he had never before encountered a federal administration that denied a law enforcement agency’s requests for documents that could be useful for litigation. The proposed legislation, Torrez said, would give agencies like his an easier path to challenge the federal government’s withholding of documents.
“It is a prerequisite for justice that we have all the facts,” he said.
A dispute over the state’s Epstein investigation
While disputes play out regarding the federal government’s handling of Epstein files, infighting similarly broke out among members of the New Mexico House of Representatives subcommittee charged with investigating the late sex offender’s time in the state.
The subcommittee — known informally as a four-member truth commission with two Republicans and two Democrats from the state House — last week published its first report on its investigation. While lawmakers on the commission acknowledged that their report did not break new ground, they said it put what’s known about Epstein’s time in the state in a single document.
Days later, the commission’s Republican members said they were excluded from final decisions in the report’s creation.
In a joint statement Tuesday, Reps. William “Bill” Hall (R-Farmington) and Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) said they didn’t receive a draft of the commission’s report until 11:30 p.m. the night before they were scheduled to present it to the public at the state Capitol.
They said they subsequently learned that it omitted references to Deb Haaland, the former U.S. Interior secretary and current Democratic nominee for New Mexico governor. Ahead of the June primary election, campaign ads accused Haaland of flying on an Epstein-owned jet in 2014, when she was running on former state Attorney General Gary King’s gubernatorial ticket as a candidate for lieutenant governor. However, publicly available documents show that the plane did not belong to Epstein and that King had requested Epstein’s help in chartering a flight.
Nonetheless, Hall and Reeb said that their fellow commission members had agreed to include reference to Haaland’s flight in the recent report.
“This commission is supposed to be about finding the truth, wherever it leads,” Reeb wrote in a statement. “This is unacceptable. We must be able to assure the public that political considerations are not influencing what is included, or excluded, from this investigation.”
Commission Chair Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) in a statement said she was “shocked to hear of these concerns through the press, as every committee member weighed in on the report and was included in all plans as they were developed.” 
“Our commission came to a collective decision not to name survivors, victims or the countless parties with tangential interactions, unverified claims or fractional reporting and to keep our interim report and ongoing work rightly focused on perpetrators and enablers,” Romero wrote. “All of our members worked with our legal team to compile a draft report with the agreed-upon content, and it was the responsibility of every member to ensure the report reflected what we wanted to convey.”
Romero said commission leaders would “improve our internal processes to ensure all members are on the same page going forward” and will focus on “the important work in front of us, not the headwinds of the day or attempts to politicize or pursuit of justice for victims.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Why super PACs are suddenly spending big on Alaska’s US Senate underdogs
description: In the days leading up to Alaska’s primary election, two super PACs have poured nearly $2 million into the U.S. Senate race. The twist: Alaska’s unusual election format is likely to negate the spending campaigns’ efforts to tear support away from the front-runners. With Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola comfortably […]
text:
Mailers from Fair Deal Alaska, a PAC that is spending to promote U.S. Senate candidate Carol Hafner over former congresswoman Mary Peltola, are showing up in Alaskans' mailboxes in August 2026. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)


In the days leading up to Alaska’s primary election, two super PACs have poured nearly $2 million into the U.S. Senate race.
The twist: Alaska’s unusual election format is likely to negate the spending campaigns’ efforts to tear support away from the front-runners.
With Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola comfortably leading in both fundraising and polls ahead of the Aug. 18 primary, outside groups are directing much of their cash toward secondary candidates in an apparent attempt to manipulate Alaska’s top-four ranked-choice system before the general election in November.
“People are kind of trying to pull the wool over their eyes,” said Deb Otis, the senior director of research and policy at FairVote, a nonprofit that advocates for ranked-choice voting and proportional representation.
Outside groups have become “pretty sophisticated” in the level of “gamesmanship” they deploy, she said. While those tactics often work in states with conventional election formats, Alaska’s system is built differently and may be harder to exploit.
“In most elections around the country, it really is effective,” Otis told OpenSecrets. “If you can prop up a lesser known candidate, they really can take away votes and deny the election to a front-runner. But with ranked-choice voting, when voters get a backup choice, the possibility to alter the outcomes is much narrower, so I think they’ll be disappointed with the impact here.”
All of the spending by the two super PACs took place in July and August, after the Federal Election Commission’s pre-primary reporting cutoff. And because Alaska’s anti-dark-money law doesn’t apply to federal races, voters won’t learn the original sources of most of that money until well after ballots are cast – if ever.

Fair Deal Alaska formed July 28 and within days began spending, dumping more than $768,000 into the race through Aug. 8. Most was spent in support of two frequent candidates from out of state: the Green Party’s Richard Grayson – who told OpenSecrets that running for public office is merely a “hobby” – and Democrat Carol Hafner.
Another super PAC, Right For Alaska, poured $1.2 million into the race between July 30 and Aug. 7, with much of it backing two other minor candidates.
“I think it’s a waste of money,” said Grayson, the beneficiary of more than $300,000 in outside spending by Fair Deal Alaska. Citing rules that prevent super PACs and candidates from coordinating, he added, “I can’t call them and tell them to stop it.”
In a clear sign of their broader strategic motives, Fair Deal Alaska also spent nearly $152,000 on negative ads opposing Peltola while Right For Alaska spent nearly $574,000 to oppose Sullivan. The race, which Democrats view as central to their aim of claiming control of the Senate, is rated as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.
“I wonder if these tactics are just being carried over from organizations that have worked in other states, where this is a more well-established tactic,” Otis said.
None of the candidates supported by those super PACs reported any significant fundraising activity to the FEC. That leaves the money race dominated by the two heavyweights: Peltola raised $18.5 million and held $4.6 million in cash on hand, while Sullivan took in $11.7 million with a war chest of nearly $7.3 million, according to pre-primary filings through July 29.
How top-four voting complicates super PAC strategy
Alaska operates under a nonpartisan top-four system, placing all primary candidates on a single ballot regardless of party affiliation. The top four advance to the general election, which uses ranked-choice voting. In that system, voters rank candidates by preference. If no candidate earns an immediate majority, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated and that person’s votes are redistributed to the voters’ next choice until a candidate clears the majority threshold.
The super PAC surge is intended to foster strategic vote-splitting. The more candidates on the ballot who appeal to the same ideological base, the greater the potential to dilute a front-runner’s support.
“The Republicans – I don’t guess, I know – they would like to see Sen. Sullivan on the ballot with Mary Peltola and two Democrats or two liberals,” Grayson said.
Such a maneuver typically doesn’t work as well in a ranked-choice system, Otis said.
“If one of these lesser-known candidates makes it into the top-four candidates and goes on to the general election, it looks like the hope here is that those lesser-known candidates will siphon votes away from one of the front-runners,” she said.
But, Otis continued, voters who place an underdog No. 1 on their ballots tend to favor a more prominent candidate as a second or third choice.
“Even if you do get your candidate into the general election, and you get some substantial share of voters to vote for them, most of those voters will rank a front-runner as a backup choice,” she added. “You’re not taking votes away in the same way that gamers can do in other states.”
Late spending keeps donors hidden
That hasn’t stopped the super PACs from pouring in big bucks in a relatively short period of time: During the 10-day window between July 30 and Aug. 8, Fair Deal Alaska and Right For Alaska combined to spend nearly $2 million.
Fair Deal Alaska began its spending spree two days after it formed as a quarterly filer with the Federal Election Commission. That timeline matters. Under FEC rules, quarterly filers must submit a pre-primary report covering spending through the 20th day before the primary that wasn’t included in the previous quarterly report.
For the Aug. 18 Alaska primary, the 20-day cutoff was July 29 – the day before the group’s first expenditure. While the super PAC must file 24-hour reports for its independent expenditures that aggregate $1,000 or more after that day, it will not have to identify its funders until well after the election.
And while state law requires disclosure of the “true source” of contributions greater than $2,000 within 24 hours, that requirement does not apply to federal races, which operate under FEC rules.
“It certainly is [timed] so they don’t have to release their donors ahead of the election,” Otis said.
Fair Deal Alaska is headquartered in a Wasilla office building that also houses a gun shop and two medical training facilities. A sign in a window visible on Google Street View advertises virtual office and mail services. OpenSecrets reached out to the super PAC’s treasurer and custodian of records, Sam Praytor, but did not immediately receive a response.

A bit more information exists about the money behind the other super PAC spending heavily on the race’s underdogs: Right For Alaska formed March 23 and is based in Hudson, Wisconsin. Its only disclosed contribution so far is a $100,000 donation on March 30 from William Harris, a retiree in Lexington, Mass. The address Harris listed in FEC records matches one used by the William H. Harris Foundation, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that supports higher education and medical research and disbursed $3.6 million in 2024, IRS filings show. OpenSecrets reached out to the super PAC’s treasurer, Thomas Datwyler, and to the email address listed in the foundation’s IRS filing for comment but did not immediately receive responses from either. Datwyler has served in a similar role for numerous other political entities, has been fined thousands of dollars for breaking FEC rules and was accused of being the “shadow treasurer” for the re-election bid for former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.). FEC records also show a Thomas Datwyler of Hudson, Wisconsin, as a frequent donor to Republican-aligned groups.
Of Right For Alaska’s $1.2 million in spending through Aug. 7, nearly $574,000 went to oppose Sullivan with $410,000 backing Republican Gerald Heikes and nearly $219,000 to support Earl “Skip” Southworth of the Alaskan Party – the successor to the right-leaning Alaskan Independence Party. An Earl Southworth of Dutch Harbor, Alaska, donated to Democratic nominee Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign in 2024 and to Democratic state Sen. Forrest Dunbar a decade earlier, FEC records show. OpenSecrets reached out to Heikes and Southworth but did not immediately receive responses from either.
Fair Deal Alaska started spending on July 30, pouring roughly $17,000 into mailers supporting Grayson and Hafner along with $34,000 into those opposing Peltola. Its largest expenditures came the next day: a $275,000 investment in media placement and production that consisted of $137,500 to back both Grayson and Hafner. In a statement to OpenSecrets, Hafner said she was “totally unaware” of any super PAC interest in her candidacy prior to the spending, adding that she has no involvement in its messaging, which she hypothesized was taken from her website without her knowledge.
Grayson said he has fielded calls from residents blaming him for mailers sent by Fair Deal Alaska, with one leaving a voicemail demanding removal from his mailing list “because my postcard has lies in it.”
He also shared a video ad to YouTube produced by the group that includes an image of him with Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) alongside text saying he “will stand with Bernie and AOC” followed by an image of a red X covering President Donald Trump’s face. He characterized it as a “bizarre AI video ad” from a “mysterious” super PAC.
“There’s no false claims in it,” Grayson said. “The ad was not false advertising. I guess it’s the kind of advertising I would put if I were a serious candidate and had money.”


This article was originally published by OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that tracks money in politics. View the original article.

name: Delaware
title: Walk, Run the Monster Mile: Breast Cancer Coalition Takes Fundraiser Onto Dover Speedway Track
description: Oct. 11 event adds a distinctly Delaware experience to Breast Cancer Awareness Month, giving families and survivors the chance to walk or race on the famed Dover Motor Speedway track DOVER, Del. — Breast Cancer Awareness Month is recognized across the country each October, from community walks and fundraising campaigns to highly visible displays of pink thro[...]
text:
The Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition will hold its 17th annual Monster Mile Walk for a Cause & 5K from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 11, turning one of Delaware’s best-known sports venues into a gathering place for breast cancer survivors, families, supporters and runners from across the state.
Oct. 11 event adds a distinctly Delaware experience to Breast Cancer Awareness Month, giving families and survivors the chance to walk or race on the famed Dover Motor Speedway track
DOVER, Del. — Breast Cancer Awareness Month is recognized across the country each October, from community walks and fundraising campaigns to highly visible displays of pink throughout professional sports.
This year, Delaware will add an experience with a distinctly First State twist: the chance to walk or run on the Monster Mile at Dover Motor Speedway.
The Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition will hold its 17th annual Monster Mile Walk for a Cause & 5K from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 11, turning one of Delaware’s best-known sports venues into a gathering place for breast cancer survivors, families, supporters and runners from across the state.
The event comes during a month when breast cancer awareness receives national attention, including throughout the sports world. The NFL and its teams have long used the October football season to highlight cancer awareness, screening and early detection, helping make the month one of the most recognizable health-awareness campaigns in the country.
Against that national backdrop, the Monster Mile event gives Delawareans their own unusual way to participate — by stepping directly onto the same concrete oval where some of the biggest names in auto racing have competed.
From Race Cars to Runners
Instead of watching race cars circle the one-mile track, participants will take to the racing surface themselves.
The traditional one-mile walk returns this year, while DBCC is adding a timed 5K for the first time, opening the event to more serious runners as well as families and casual walkers.
“The Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition is delighted to bring the 2026 Monster Mile Walk for a Cause & 5K back to the iconic Dover Motor Speedway, where our community will unite to honor, remember and support those impacted by breast cancer,” DBCC CEO Francesca Vogel said.
“Whether you choose to participate in our traditional 1-mile walk or take on our new timed 5K race, every step you take helps fuel DBCC’s life-saving mission,” she said.
For families, the event offers an opportunity to participate in one of October’s signature causes while experiencing a Delaware landmark from a perspective normally unavailable to race fans.
A Community Celebration
The day will extend beyond the walk and race, with music, face painting, food vendors, family activities and local vendor booths planned around the speedway.
Participants are encouraged to form teams, raise money and bring some personality to the track.
Awards will recognize the highest team fundraiser, highest individual fundraiser, best team costume and best dog costume. Special Monster Mile medals also will be presented.
DBCC also is seeking businesses, corporations and community organizations to sponsor the event. Sponsorship packages include event visibility, participant registrations and opportunities for company branding on event shirts and signage.
Every Step Supports Delaware Programs
Money raised through the Monster Mile directly supports DBCC programs throughout Delaware, including breast health education, access to screenings, personalized patient navigation, survivorship services and emergency financial assistance for people and families facing a breast cancer diagnosis.
The coalition also works to reduce financial, cultural and other barriers that can prevent Delawareans from receiving screenings and treatment.
Headquartered in Wilmington with offices serving Kent and Sussex counties, DBCC provides breast health education and support programs throughout the state.
Its programs include community health fairs, breast health presentations and a Peer Mentor Program that helps connect patients and survivors with support and resources.
Breast Cancer Awareness Month brings the issue to national attention every October. On Oct. 11, Delawareans will have the opportunity to make that observance local — and do it on one of the most recognizable tracks in American auto racing.
To Go

What: 17th Annual Monster Mile Walk for a Cause & 5K
When: Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Where: Dover Motor Speedway, Dover
Why it’s different: Participants get to walk or run on the famed Monster Mile racing surface as part of Delaware’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month activities.
What to expect: One-mile walk, new timed 5K, music, food vendors, family activities, face painting and community vendors.
Who benefits: Proceeds support Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition screening, education, patient navigation, survivorship and emergency assistance programs.
Register, form a team or become a sponsor: give.debreastcancer.org/ge/monstermile2026
Learn more: debreastcancer.org

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Four Democratic AG candidates’ records go on trial in first TV debate
description: Most states have district attorneys to prosecute the highest crimes that happen in their jurisdictions — but not Rhode Island. Instead, felony prosecutions are the duty of the state’s attorney general, an office not quite judge, jury and executioner but one which holds more power than in other states. And with that power, as the […]
text:
Rep. Jason Knight, far left, answers a question during a debate for Democratic attorney general candidates at the Roger Williams University School of Law for a debate Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. Left to right next to him are Joseph Solomon Jr.; Keith Hoffmann and Kim Ahern. (Photo by Corey Welch/WPRI 12)Most states have district attorneys to prosecute the highest crimes that happen in their jurisdictions — but not Rhode Island.
Instead, felony prosecutions are the duty of the state’s attorney general, an office not quite judge, jury and executioner but one which holds more power than in other states. And with that power, as the saying goes, comes more responsibility. 
Rhode Island’s four Democratic candidates for attorney general — State Reps. Jason Knight of Barrington and Joe Solomon Jr. of Warwick, former Assistant Attorney General Keith Hoffmann and former Cannabis Control Commission Chair Kim Ahern — have sparred before. They’ve even bickered before an audience. But before Tuesday night, they had not yet slung arrows before a live television studio audience — the studio in this case being a classroom at the Roger Williams University School of Law in Bristol.
The classroom, designed to serve as a mock appellate courtroom for law students, proved an appropriate setting for WPRI 12 reporters Tim White and Ted Nesi to pursue an interrogative line of questioning about the candidates’ respective records. The event marked the sixth time AG hopefuls met for a debate or forum.


Watch the debate
The full, unedited debate is at available at wpri.com.


The attorney general is “one of the most important elected offices in the state,” Nesi noted at the debate’s opening. White and Nesi spent much of the next hour testing how each candidate’s record had prepared them to lead its roughly 120 attorneys.
The four are competing in the Sept. 9 Democratic primary, and early voting begins Aug. 20. The Democratic nominee will face Republican Alan Gordon in the Nov. 3 general election.
Kim Ahern: About that murder trial
A near-decade of prosecutorial experience has provided Ahern a plush cushion on which to rest her campaign messaging. But “it’s not an unblemished record,” White said Tuesday night, opening the debate with a close examination of one line in Ahern’s résumé: a high-profile murder trial in 2017 in which a Superior Court judge declared a mistrial, faulting Ahern and another prosecutor over failures to disclose evidence to the defense.
“He killed his girlfriend. He went to jail, and then he got out and he killed his next girlfriend,” Ahern said. “I’m not ever going to apologize for anything with respect to Andrew Jett, who should never get out of jail.” 
“Did you make a mistake?” White asked.
Ahern did not answer directly and kept circling back to the horror of the crime, including that Jett had “killed his intimate partner by stabbing her 14 times.” 
White pressed again: “I understand the crime. My question to you is: Did you make a mistake in this case, where it led to a mistrial?”
Nesi, meanwhile, had questions about her tenure as the first chair of the Cannabis Control Commission, noting Ahern had said in 2023 that she hoped retail licenses would be issued in 2024.
Those licenses still have not been awarded and regulations written under Ahern’s leadership became the subject of litigation.
“Why should voters give you a promotion when all that went wrong in your last big state job?” Nesi asked. 
It was a new state agency operating under complicated laws and in service of an “extremely litigious industry,” Ahern noted.
“We were sued,” Ahern said of the law which created the commission. “The state was…sued several times related to the law that was passed by the General Assembly.”
Solomon countered that Ahern had ”bragged” about a bill she drafted while working in the governor’s office, “a bill that essentially created a position for the chair of the cannabis commission to earn $200,000 per year,” Solomon said. 
“And while she was in that office three years, she got zero retail licenses passed during that time frame, so I’m surprised that she’s blaming the General Assembly because all we heard was crickets that there was an issue with the law.”
Knight agreed that the Cannabis Control Commission “has not delivered for Rhode Island” what the General Assembly intended. 
“The bottom line is performance matters, and delivering results matters,” Knight said. 
“If the General Assembly wanted the quickest cannabis market in history, that was not the way to do it,” Ahern countered. 
Keith Hoffmann: No criminal trial track record
Hoffmann faced a problem inverse to Ahern’s: A lack of criminal trial experience.
As a former assistant attorney general, Hoffmann accrued plentiful experience in civil cases, White noted. But has he ever prosecuted a capital case like murder or rape? White wondered. 
“No,” Hoffmann replied.
How about a narcotics case? That was also a no from Hoffmann, who then pivoted to point out that U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse had worked on the office’s civil side, and that former AG Peter Kilmartin was not a criminal prosecutor when he ran for and ultimately won the office.
Questions about specific case experience were too narrow to encompass all the job’s duties, Hoffmann said.
“I think that that leadership experience is what sets me apart from the others up here tonight,” Hoffmann said. “I’m the only candidate with any level of leadership experience within this office as a unit chief and on the executive team.”
As far as outgoing Attorney General Peter Neronha is concerned, Hoffmann is also the chosen one. The term-limited Neronha endorsed Hoffmann as his successor early in the primary race. 
Speaking of Hoffmann’s boss: What did the candidate think of criticism that Neronha had gone too far in publicly releasing and commenting on the findings of the AG-led investigation on Gov. Dan McKee’s involvement in a less-than-ideal procurement process for a 2021 education services contract with the ILO Group? The probe brought no criminal charges but Neronha released it to the public in late 2024, telling reporters he was surprised by the “ham-handedness” of the affair.
Ethics probe could be next chapter in ILO saga

Hoffmann said releasing the information was important to the public and he defended Neronha’s at-times bluntness in doing so. 
“I think that’s a good thing that a public official is able to speak their mind and be honest with people,” Hoffmann said. “You know, my social media is a little bit more boring, but I think that’s the core issue here of transparency.”
Jason Knight: Too soft on crime?
After four years as a state prosecutor, Knight became a criminal defense attorney, representing people accused of crimes ranging from drug dealing and domestic violence to homicide, White noted.
White wondered if that would make Knight “soft on crime.”
“The Constitution of the United States demands that any person accused has a fair trial, and in order to get a fair trial, they must have competent counsel,” Knight said. “And if they don’t have that, the entire system falls apart.”
Knight was the first to invoke Trump during the debate, which prompted White to interject and ask what Trump had to do with the AG’s prosecutorial duties.
Knight brought it back around to Neronha’s office — which has filed or joined so many lawsuits against the Trump administration that it started an online tracker — and said the office’s criminal division “needs a little TLC.”
“You simply can’t, while you’re pursuing the Trump administration, you can’t take your eye off the ball on this critical function of office,” Knight said, citing overturned cases, mistrials and acquittals.
“It cannot be a backwater the way it is today,” he added later.
Ahern essentially agreed that the criminal division, which she called “the bread and butter work” of the AG’s office, needs some more love. There are too many cases assigned to each prosecutor, she said, and that unit chiefs are tasked with supervising “too many young attorneys.”
“Baby lawyers, as we call them,” Ahern said.
Left to right, Democratic candidates to be Rhode Island’s next attorney general Rep. Jason Knight; Joseph Solomon Jr.; Keith Hoffmann and Kim Ahern stand behind podiums at the Roger Williams University School of Law for a debate Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Corey Welch/WPRI 12)
Joe Solomon Jr.: Legislative record invites scrutiny
“Mr. Solomon, you’re the only person in this debate who has not worked a day in the Attorney General’s Office, yet you want to lead roughly 120 lawyers who have more experience in this space than you do,” White remarked early in the debate. “Why do you see the Rhode Island Attorney General as an entry-level position into this office?”
Solomon rejected the premise, relying on a record he cited at both the debate’s beginning and its end.
“I’m also the only person standing up here who’s seen the justice system from every angle as a prosecutor, as a bail commissioner, and as a legislator,” he said. 
“So you don’t feel like you would need to learn on the job?” White asked. 
“I don’t need to learn on the job. I’ve been doing this my entire career,” Solomon replied.
Still, a lengthier legislative record also meant more fodder for Solomon’s opponents. 
A particular vulnerability was the 2025 semiautomatic weapons ban in the state legislature, which Knight sponsored in the House and which Solomon voted against.
More specific laws — like Rhode Island’s red-flag law, designed to “take guns out of the hands of people having a mental health crisis” and legislation disarming domestic abusers — work better than broader bans on semiautomatic weapons, Solomon suggested.
“It ultimately is probably going to encompass more guns than was originally anticipated,” Solomon said, noting the bill’s definition of “assault weapon” has a stricter definition in Rhode Island’s new law than did the 1994 federal ban. 
Nesi then asked Knight about criticisms from detractors of the law he wrote, which cleared the State House not intact but only after substantial revisions from the Senate.
“I could not disagree more,” Knight replied.
“I respect Joe’s service, but I have to tell you that it’s just plain wrong. This bill and all the other bills that we passed save lives, and I voted yes for every single one of them. And I didn’t pick and choose.”
Solomon’s vote against an updated safe-storage law also came within Knight’s range of attack. Solomon countered that Rhode Island already had a safe storage law, which he supported. 
“What we need to do is we need to go towards education because we can pass as many laws as we want, but that’s not going to help the problem,” Solomon said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Breaking down petition signatures for Nebraska Working People Party, America First Party
description: LINCOLN — As Nebraska’s fledgling Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party navigate dueling lawsuits, new data indicates where supporters gathered signatures in pursuit of the November ballot. According to data from the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office, each party well surpassed the minimum number of signatures needed to move on to the next[...]
text:
A woman signs a Support Our Schools petition in Omaha. July 8, 2024. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — As Nebraska’s fledgling Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party navigate dueling lawsuits, new data indicates where supporters gathered signatures in pursuit of the November ballot.
According to data from the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office, each party well surpassed the minimum number of signatures needed to move on to the next step of formation, which is filing governing documents. Under state law, signature verification can cease after officials validate at least 110% of the signatures needed — 6,728 signatures in this case.
Supporters needed at least 2,262 signatures in Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District, 2,200 in the 2nd District and 2,266 in the 3rd District. The threshold is based on 1% of the number of votes cast for governor in 2022.
Across the congressional districts, just two counties are split. Parts of Polk County are in the 1st and 3rd districts, while Sarpy is in the 1st and 2nd districts. Election officials did not have exact counts of gathered signatures per district because of the split counties. Still, both proposed parties surpassed 110% of the signature requirement in each district, even excluding Polk and Sarpy.
Signatures were due by July 15.


In the end, supporters for the two parties got conditional approval to move ahead with formation, pending legal action, after each gathered valid signatures from just 0.7% of all registered voters this year. Not all voters turned out in 2022, and there are more voters now than four years ago.
Local election officials validated signatures across 87 counties for the Nebraska Working People Party and 63 counties for the America First Party. 
Of the 89 counties with signatures validated, the Nebraska Working People Party had slightly more signatures than the other proposed party in 65 counties, while the America First Party had slightly more in 18 counties. Six counties had the same number of signatures for each party.
The four counties with no signatures validated were Blaine, Dundy, Grant and Rock.
A breakdown of the official signature results from the Secretary of State’s Office:
Nebraska Working People Party
The Nebraska Working People Party is led by Robin Richards of Ralston. She is a Democrat who ran as a write-in candidate for Legislative District 12 this spring. She was the runner-up for the same district in 2022.
Robin Richards of Ralston, former 2026 write-in candidate for Nebraska Legislative District 12. (Courtesy of Richards campaign)
Richards filed petition language June 25 and turned in signatures July 14. The Secretary of State’s Office said organizers estimated they turned in 8,000-12,000 signatures.
Petitions said the party’s purpose is to give voters an organization “dedicated to advancing the interests of working families, middle-class Nebraskans, rural communities, small businesses, farmers, ranchers and individuals seeking practical solutions to improve economic opportunity, strengthen communities and promote responsive and accountable government.”


The party had a broader canvassing approach than the America First Party, with the most voters per capita in Lincoln County (3.7% of 23,061 registered voters as of July 1). North Platte is the county seat. The county accounted for about 9.5% of all valid signatures.
About 60% of the party’s valid signatures came from the state’s most populous counties: Douglas (28.5%), Lancaster (21.7%) and Sarpy (9.5%). An additional 12% of signatures came from the fourth and fifth most populous counties, Hall (7.5%) and Buffalo (5%) in central Nebraska.
Petitioners had greater success in rural parts of Nebraska, including the Panhandle and Sandhills, which tend to be more conservative.
The Nebraska Democratic Party, alongside the national Working Families Party, is suing to stop official formation of the Nebraska Working People Party.
America First Party
The America First Party is led by John Cartier of Lincoln. He is a registered nonpartisan who had been registered with the Nebraska Democratic Party for about a decade before briefly joining the Legal Marijuana NOW party in the 2024 election cycle, according to voter data from the Lancaster County Election Commission. He returned to the Democratic Party by spring 2025 and ran for a seat on the Lincoln Public Schools Board of Education. He switched to nonpartisan sometime between May 2025 and May 2026.
Omaha Tribe of Nebraska Attorney General John Cartier. (Photo courtesy of John Cartier)
He is also the attorney general for the Omaha Tribe of Nebraska and serves as treasurer for Legal Marijuana NOW’s U.S. Senate nominee Mike Marvin.
Cartier filed petition language July 1 and turned in signatures July 15. The Secretary of State’s Office said organizers estimated they turned in more than 15,500 signatures.
Petitions said the party’s purpose is to give voters an organization “committed to putting Americans and Nebraskans ahead of all others by cracking down on out-of-control government spending and wasteful foreign aid, getting tough on illegal immigrants, standing up against abortion and rigidly defending the Second Amendment.”


The party had a narrower canvassing approach than the Nebraska Working People Party. The most voters per capita came in Hall County (3.5% of 32,792 registered voters as of July 1). Grand Island is the county seat, and the county accounted for about 13% of all valid signatures.
About 69% of the party’s signatures came from the state’s most populous counties: Douglas (30%), Lancaster (29.5%) and Sarpy (9.3%). Another 18% of signatures came from the fourth and fifth most populous counties, Hall (13%) and Buffalo (5.5%) in central Nebraska.
Petitioners had greater success in urban parts of Nebraska, including the metropolitan area around Omaha and the state’s capital of Lincoln, which tend to be more liberal.
The Nebraska Republican Party is suing to stop the official formation of the America First Party.
Pending legal fights
Lancaster County District Judge Darla Ideus has been assigned the dueling lawsuits from Nebraska’s largest political parties, the Republicans and Democrats, seeking to block the new parties. Each contends the new parties seek to mislead voters and damage existing candidates. 
If the parties do move ahead, voters could register and party candidates could still join the November ballot. It’s unclear what races, if any, party leaders would target.
Ideus has temporarily blocked Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen from certifying any governing documents for either new party, if or when leaders turn them in.
About 49.3% of Nebraska voters were registered Republicans as of Aug. 1 compared to 26.1% Democrats. An additional 1.4% of voters are Libertarians, and 0.8% are affiliated with the Legal Marijuana NOW party. About 22.4% of voters are not registered with any political party.



Party purpose statements

Nebraska Working People Party: “Dedicated to advancing the interests of working families, middle-class Nebraskans, rural communities, small businesses, farmers, ranchers and individuals seeking practical solutions to improve economic opportunity, strengthen communities and promote responsive and accountable government.”



America First Party: “Committed to putting Americans and Nebraskans ahead of all others by cracking down on out-of-control government spending and wasteful foreign aid, getting tough on illegal immigrants, standing up against abortion and rigidly defending the Second Amendment.”

title: Trump vaccine order takes aim at states that limit exemptions
description: A largely overlooked part of the executive order President Donald Trump issued this week scaling back the schedule for childhood vaccines threatens legal action against the four states that don’t allow personal or religious exemptions to school vaccine requirements. Those states — California, Connecticut, Maine and New York — are among the states with the […[...]
text:
An executive order President Donald Trump signed earlier this week says the attorney general will take legal action against states that do not provide “religious and medical exemptions from childhood and adolescent immunization requirements.” (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce for the Virginia Mercury)A largely overlooked part of the executive order President Donald Trump issued this week scaling back the schedule for childhood vaccines threatens legal action against the four states that don’t allow personal or religious exemptions to school vaccine requirements.
Those states — California, Connecticut, Maine and New York — are among the states with the highest immunization rates, and they are among those that have been most successful in controlling the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades.
All 50 states and the District of Columbia require students to have certain vaccines before attending public school. All allow exemptions for children who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons. Forty-six states plus the District of Columbia also allow exemptions for religious and/or personal beliefs.
Trump’s order, which he signed on Monday, says the attorney general will take legal action against states that do not provide “religious and medical exemptions from childhood and adolescent immunization requirements.”
Some health officials said that Trump’s order, which has questionable legal authority, is unlikely to prompt the states without nonmedical exemptions to change course. And any legal action would take years to wend its way through the courts.
But they criticized the executive order, and its legal threats, for contributing to the misinformation and skepticism that have lowered vaccination rates nationwide.
“It puts a lot of misinformation and a lot of fear and doubt in parents’ minds,” said Dr. Thomas Lew, clinical assistant professor at the Stanford University School of Medicine. “It clouds the conversation around vaccines and their importance and their safety.”
Measles cases have reached a 35-year high

Dr. Molly O’Shea, a pediatrician who practices in suburban Detroit, warned that nonmedical exemptions “increase the number of parents who opt to forgo one or more vaccines for any list of reasons.”
“The learning environment is then more fragile because of the risk of disruption by infectious illness,” she said.
At the same time, O’Shea said, public health requires empathy with parents who are sincerely worried about their children’s well-being and may have been misinformed about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines.
“Families who are opting not to vaccinate are doing it from the same place that we’re recommending vaccines. They want their children healthy and well,” O’Shea said. “Just because we come to the opposite conclusion doesn’t mean we didn’t start with the same values.”
In response to Trump’s order, political leaders and health officials in many states, including California, Connecticut,  Maine and New York, vowed to maintain their vaccination rules.
California currently has 52 measles cases, Connecticut has two, Maine has five and New York has 10. All four states have vaccination rates higher than 95%, considered critical to “herd immunity” that can protect the unvaccinated to some degree.
“Maine will continue to follow the science and the facts, and our approach to vaccines remains unchanged by yesterday’s executive order,” Maine Democratic Gov. Janet Mills said in a statement published Tuesday.
Measles, whooping cough spike amid low vaccination rates

As of early August, measles cases were at their highest level since 1991. The states with the highest numbers were South Carolina (670), Utah (524), Pennsylvania (216), Texas (216) and Virginia (176). All of those states allow families to opt out of the school vaccine requirement for personal or religious reasons.
Of the five states with the most cases, only Virginia has a school vaccination rate of more than 95%.
Virginia’s statewide rate was 95.6% for 2024-25, but the measles outbreak was in two rural counties west of Richmond, where measles vaccination rates are less than 75%.
Deaths from another vaccine-preventable childhood illness, whooping cough, also are on the rise. Last year, there were 32 whooping cough deaths, the most since at least 1999. Before vaccines became available in the 1940s, as many as 200,000 children contracted whooping cough every year and 9,000 died.
Whooping cough death statistics for every state were not available, but Kentucky reported three whooping cough deaths last year, its first fatalities in five years, while Louisiana reported two deaths.
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

description: SIOUX FALLS — A farmer who formerly served in the Legislature emerged Wednesday as the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor of South Dakota. text:
Steven McCleerey speaks to the media on Aug. 12, 2026, in Sioux Falls after being announced as the running mate for the Democratic nominee for governor of South Dakota, Dan Ahlers. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — A farmer who formerly served in the Legislature emerged Wednesday as the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor of South Dakota.
Steven McCleerey, 73, of rural Sisseton, served six years in the state House of Representatives from 2015 to 2020. He said his approach as lieutenant governor would be focused on cooperation rather than partisan conflict.
“We’re here to help solve problems, not cause problems,” McCleerey said.
Party will not replace withdrawn US Senate candidate, SD Democratic official says

He will be the running mate of another former legislator, Dan Ahlers, of Dell Rapids, who is the Democratic nominee for governor. 
Ahlers said McCleerey’s legislative experience, including serving as assistant House minority leader, taught McCleerey how to earn support from Republicans, given that Democrats do not have the numbers in Pierre to pass a bill on their own. 
McCleerey raises crops and cattle and said he has served about 20 years on his local hospital board, along with serving on a nursing home board. Ahlers said those experiences make McCleerey a useful adviser on agricultural, rural health and long-term care issues.
Ahlers is challenging Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden, who is seeking his own full term after being elevated from lieutenant governor when Gov. Kristi Noem resigned last year to accept a job in President Donald Trump’s administration. Rhoden’s running mate is Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen.
Ahlers and Rhoden have accepted invitations to participate in two September debates. Venhuizen preemptively challenged Ahlers’ running mate to a debate, before Ahlers announced his pick.
McCleerey said he is open to facing Venhuizen, but would prefer a “roundtable discussion” or an open forum where the audience asks the questions. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

title: Trump administration urges Supreme Court to rule soon on limiting vote-by-mail in midterms
text: The Trump administration on Wednesday renewed its request to the U.S. Supreme Court to quickly decide a case over an executive order restricting voting, a day after a Massachusetts federal judge expanded an injunction on the order nationwide.The Tuesday order from U.S. District Judge Indiria Talwani that blocked President Donald Trump’s executive order from taking effect anywhere in the country makes the administration’s request to the Supreme Court more urgent, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. “The district court’s new order confirms the urgent need for this Court to grant the stay of the permanent injunction and to explain its rationale for doing so,” Sauer wrote. Election Day is Nov. 3, less than three months away.Decisions in two cases at district and circuit courts have reached different conclusions about whether the rulemaking could continue in the lead-up to this fall’s elections. That means the Supreme Court’s decision, now on its emergency docket, will likely determine whether the executive order can move forward. A decision could come any day.The Trump executive order would limit vote-by-mail, the primary method of voting in several states, especially in the West. It would require states to send the federal government lists of voters who intend to vote by mail ahead of the election and restrict the U.S. Postal Service from delivering ballots to or from people not on the list, among other things.The administration has sought to focus arguments on the narrow legal question of whether an executive order can be challenged before an agency, in this case the U.S. Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security, issues a final rule. The government argues that the executive order only instructs the agencies to issue rules, and those rules are not yet final, and therefore cannot be challenged.Trial court orderTalwani’s memorandum and order on Tuesday rejected that argument, and she expanded a previous injunction from just the 23 states and the District of Columbia that brought the suit to be effective nationwide. Talwani said — in her order published just 12 weeks before Election Day — she was only blocking the order with respect to the “fast-approaching” midterms. Further arguments over the merits of federal voting regulations could still happen, but federal law requires the status quo to be preserved this close to an election, she said. Because of the tight timeline and the assumption that a final rule will be similar to a June 2 notice of proposed rulemaking, Talwani said she could rule simply on the constitutionality of the executive order. It was an easy call, she said.“The executive branch has no authority to regulate elections,” she wrote, citing the Constitution.The administration has not shown how blocking the executive order would harm the public, as it has not documented any “illegal or fraudulent absentee voting,” while the voting rights organizations challenging the order have shown that voters with disabilities, in rural areas, who need translation help, attend college outside their home states and in other circumstances would be harmed, she said.In fact, the organizations showed their members in states across the country are already being harmed by the uncertainty around what rules will govern the midterm elections, said Talwani.“Where the (executive order) is presently causing confusion and threatening both increasing chaos and an erosion of trust in our democracy, the court finds that enfranchisement heavily outweighs the executive’s attempt to unconstitutionally insert itself into the domain of election regulation,” Talwani wrote. The proximity to Election Day “underscores the critical need for an injunction to prevent Defendants from changing election rules on the eve of the election.”The Federal Voter Registration Act also prohibits states from purging voter rolls within 90 days of an election, Talwani wrote.DOJ’s double bindThe nature of the argument puts Sauer and the U.S. Department of Justice in a seemingly difficult legal position, arguing both that the executive order cannot be challenged because it is not enforceable and that the administration must be allowed to put an enforceable rule in place before Election Day.Sauer asked the court Wednesday to rule for the government and “make clear” that it was doing so “based on the uncertainty concerning the government’s future actions.”But in the next paragraph, he said implementing the executive order was crucial to the public interest.“In all events, it is critical that the Court act promptly on the pending stay,” Sauer said. “Otherwise, the district court’s erroneous orders will effectively run out the clock on the government’s ability to implement Section 3 of the Executive Order for the federal elections in November, thereby causing irreparable harm to the federal government, the public, and election integrity.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Stein signs four bills, criticizes ‘petty’ limits on governor’s office
description: Earlier this week, Stein withdrew Jeff Smythe’s nomination as secretary for the Department of Public Safety.
text:
Gov. Josh Stein signed a bill approving $319 million in Medicaid funding on April 30, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein signed four bills into law this week, calling out one of them for imposing “petty provisions” on his office’s power. 
House Bill 268 makes technical corrections to the 2026 budget. 
Stein praised the legislation for strengthening disaster relief, teacher workforce pipelines, and economic development programs. 
However, the bill also includes a provision that requires a member of the governor’s cabinet to vacate their office if the Senate does not confirm their nomination. Under the measure, the cabinet member’s acting term expires when the General Assembly adjourns sine die or at the end of the legislative biennium. 
“I regret that the General Assembly saw fit to include some petty provisions that undermine the executive branch and impede the work of government on behalf of North Carolinians,” Stein said in a statement. 
Earlier this week, Stein withdrew Jeff Smythe’s nomination as secretary for the Department of Public Safety, an appointment he originally made Jan. 1. Senate Republican leaders declined to hold a hearing on Smythe’s appointment, citing concerns about his track record as Burlington’s police chief.
Veto coming on the GOP’s big elections bill, NC Gov. Stein says

Stein appointed Smythe as his senior adviser for homeland security instead, a position that does not require approval from the legislature. The governor also appointed Department of Public Safety Chief of Staff Casandra Hoekstra to replace Smythe as interim secretary.
“By failing to consider his nomination or even hold a single public hearing, the Senate abdicated its responsibility, disrespected Jeff and law enforcement, and undermined the safety of the people of North Carolina,” Stein said in a statement Monday. “Their failure to do their jobs is unacceptable. 
On Tuesday, Stein also signed Senate Bill 445, the Regulatory Reform Act of 2026. The legislation tackles a variety of issues related to the environment, housing, and public safety, and passed both chambers with bipartisan support. 
It attempts to expand housing, requiring cities with more than 50,000 residents to allow homeowners to build accessory dwelling units, sometimes called “granny flats” or “in-law suites.” Examples include backyard structures or attached apartments.
Stein highlighted the need to build more housing units of all types, driving down rents and mortgages. 
“This bill cuts red tape to help produce more houses and apartments and deliver results for North Carolinians,” he said in a statement. “It also makes it easier for families to install solar panels or battery systems to save on their utility bills.”
Stein also signed House Bill 562, more technical corrections to the state budget, and House Bill 834, which makes administrative changes to the state board of elections. 
Lawmakers left Raleigh last week. Their next meeting on the legislative calendar is Aug. 31, but leaders of both chambers have said they do not anticipate holding official voting sessions again until after the November elections. 
There are two bills remaining on Stein’s desk.
House Bill 377 makes changes to court processes. Democratic senators said they worried the measure makes the judicial branch too political. 
The remaining legislation, House Bill 958, is also controversial. It’s an election law bill that Democratic senators have called a “power grab.” 
The bill includes provisions to reduce early voting periods, require state Auditor Dave Boliek to conduct post-election audits of county election systems, and use federal databases with known problems to identify people who have died but remain on the voter rolls. 
Stein has already said he intends to veto the elections bill. He could sign the other bill, veto it, or allow it to become law without his signature.

title: Judge sets trial date for Missouri redistricting referendum, initiative petition amendment
description: The fate of two proposed ballot measures —- a referendum on Missouri’s gerrymandered congressional map and a constitutional amendment limiting legislative power to alter laws passed by initiative — will go on trial next week, a Cole County judge decided Wednesday. Circuit Judge Daniel Green ordered back-to-back hearings for the two measures Secretary of Stat[...]
text:
The Cole County Courthouse in downtown Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).The fate of two proposed ballot measures —- a referendum on Missouri’s gerrymandered congressional map and a constitutional amendment limiting legislative power to alter laws passed by initiative — will go on trial next week, a Cole County judge decided Wednesday.
Circuit Judge Daniel Green ordered back-to-back hearings for the two measures Secretary of State Denny Hoskins blocked from a statewide vote. He also allowed the Republican National Committee, the National Republican Congressional Committee and the Missouri Republican State Committee to intervene in the redistricting case. 
Both of the cases are moving quickly because state law sets a Sept. 8 deadline for court orders adding questions to the ballot. Missouri Supreme Court Chief Justice W. Brent Powell sent Green letters about each case, Green noted in court Wednesday morning, asking him to move them quickly to give time for appellate review.
In the referendum case, the committee seeking to overturn the congressional map, People Not Politicians, is challenging Hoskins’ assertion that redistricting plans are not subject to a statewide vote. People Not Politicians submitted more than 305,000 signatures in December to force the statewide vote and local election authority reports compiled by the campaign show it has enough signatures to qualify for the ballot.
In the lawsuit over the proposed amendment, the committee promoting it, Respect MO Voters, argues Hoskins is wrong in his assertion that the proposal contains too many subjects. If enacted, it would block lawmakers from altering a law or constitutional amendment passed by initiative unless 80% of lawmakers agree and the changes are ratified in a statewide vote.
No complete report has been compiled for the proposed amendment, but a spot check of local reports on the secretary of state’s website shows it also has enough signatures to qualify for the ballot.
If Green orders a statewide vote, it would be Amendment 6 on the Nov. 3 ballot.
The only drama in the hearing Wednesday was whether Green would grant the Republican committees the right to intervene in the referendum case.
Marc Ellinger, a Jefferson City attorney arguing to be allowed to intervene, said Republicans have a direct interest in making sure the gerrymandered map drawn by lawmakers in 2025 is the one used in the November election. At the insistence of President Donald Trump, the General Assembly muscled the new map through with the goal of taking the 5th District from Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
The primary election that nominated state Sen. Rick Brattin of Harrisonville was conducted in the 15-county district drawn in 2025 that stretches from Kansas City to Jefferson City. That district heavily favored Republicans in past elections, while Cleaver has always been a strong candidate in the districts as they were drawn previously.
Ellinger said his clients want the new map to be used. Six of Missouri’s eight districts were altered as the map was changed.
“If the old maps are used, it’s particularly egregious because you have candidates that will now campaign in different districts,” Ellinger said. “In some cases, slightly different districts. In some cases, completely different districts.”
Republicans need to know whether it is worth it to spend money to defeat Cleaver and whether it must dedicate money to the Missouri referendum, Ellinger said.
“It affects strategy and organizational challenges and decisions on where to deploy resources, in what races to deploy resources, in what ballot measures to be involved in or not be involved in,” Elllinger said.
Chuck Hatfield, attorney for People Not Politicians, argued that the questions facing Republicans also face Democrats and that is not enough to qualify to intervene.
Hatfield also said he worried Ellinger’s interest is in delaying the case so that no decision is rendered by Sept. 8. One way to do that is to seek a change of judge.
“I offered to consent to intervention if they would agree not to take a change of judge,” Hatfield said. “They declined.”
After the hearing, Ellinger said he had no plans to seek a change of judge or delay.
The trials will be held Tuesday, with the referendum issues argued at 1:30 p.m. and the constitutional amendment case will start at 3 p.m.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida prepares to execute the 32nd person in the past 20 months next Tuesday
description: The spiritual adviser to Florida death row inmate William Silvia made a plea Wednesday for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to personally view Silvia’s execution, scheduled to take place Tuesday at Florida State Prison near Starke at 6 p.m. “If you’re going to sign it, watch it,” the Rev. Dr. Jeff Hood said. Silvia was convicted […]
text:
The Rev. Dr. Jeff Hood holds a photo of Florida death row inmate William Silvia during a Zoom conference call on Aug. 12, 2026.The spiritual adviser to Florida death row inmate William Silvia made a plea Wednesday for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to personally view Silvia’s execution, scheduled to take place Tuesday at Florida State Prison near Starke at 6 p.m.
“If you’re going to sign it, watch it,” the Rev. Dr. Jeff Hood said.
Silvia was convicted in 2008 in Seminole County for the first-degree murder of his estranged wife, Patricia Silvia, and the attempted first-degree murder of Patricia’s mother, Betty Woodward.
On Sept. 22, 2006, Silvia purchased a shotgun and went to his mother-in-law’s home, where Patricia was living and while they were having a cook-out, according to court records. After attempting to reconcile with Patricia, Silvia returned to his truck and retrieved his shotgun. He shot Betty Woodward in the face. He then fatally shot Patricia in the head.
The jury recommended by a vote of 11-1 that he be sentenced to death.
The state of Florida has carried out 12 executions by lethal injection already this year, with two taking place on the same day last month. That was the first double execution on the same day in Florida in more than 50 years. Seven executions have taken place elsewhere in the United States this year.
The rapid pace of executions in Florida began last year, when the state held 19, accounting for roughly 40% of all executions in the country and more than doubling the previous modern record of eight executions in both 1984 and 2014.
Hood is founder of the Execution Intervention Project. He said in a Zoom conference call Wednesday that there have been so many executions over the last year-and-a-half that they are becoming “an afterthought” in Florida. And, as he did in the case of recently executed inmate Dennis Sochor, Hood called on the governor to personally attend Silva’s execution.
“What is going on when the person who is most responsible in government for these executions, the person who signs the warrant, does not even have the courage to show up?” Hood asked. “We’re talking about a dozen of executions in recent years. And Gov DeSantis does not even have the courage to show up? Why? Does he not care? Is he oblivious to these executions happening?
Hood previously served as adviser to two recent Florida death row inmates who have been executed: Dusty Spencer and Sochor.
Silvia’s case is before the Florida Supreme Court, and litigation is expected to land before the U.S. Supreme Court. Silvia realizes his execution will likely take place as scheduled, Hood said.
“The reality is most people in Florida won’t even know it happens next Wednesday,” he said. “It doesn’t have to happen. It is my prayer that we have enough courage to step back from the brink and not execute William Silvia.”
‘I don’t take any joy’
DeSantis recently spoke about the surge of death warrants he has signed since January 2025. Speaking at the Florida Sheriffs Association summer conference near Miami July 28, the day of the double executions, the governor said, “I don’t any joy in doing that. It’s a weighty thing.”
He went on to say the legal process from the time a person is sentenced to the death in Florida and the time of the execution is “way too long,” and that he doesn’t intend to let up on death row warrants in his remaining four months-plus in office.
“I think we’ll probably end up having done more [executions] than any administration in the history in the state of Florida. And I’m not like taking any pride in that, because it’s a weighty thing, but to me as we move through those and bring justice, that makes a big difference for a lot of people out there who suffered really, really serious tragedies. So, we’ll continue to do that.”
Since he gave that speech, DeSantis has signed warrants scheduling execution of two more inmates.
Harold Gene Lucas is scheduled for execution on Sept. 1 for the 1976 murder of Jill Piper, and Tuesday, the governor signed off on scheduling the execution of Daniel Conahan Jr. for Sept. 10. Conahan was sentenced in the 1996 murder of Richard Montgomery in Charlotte County.
