title: Points Race Returns to Dover Motor Speedway in 2027
description: Dover Motor Speedway announced that it will hold its 109th NASCAR Cup Series event on May 16, 2027, as well as host the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series race on May 15.    Dover Motor Speedway announced that The Monster Mile will hold a 400-mile points race on Sunday, May 16, 2027, as a part of NASCAR’s 2027 regular season, ... Read More
text:
A picture of the Monster Monument outside of Dover Motor Speedway. Photo Courtesy of Dave Reeder.
Dover Motor Speedway announced that it will hold its 109th NASCAR Cup Series event on May 16, 2027, as well as host the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series race on May 15. 
 
Dover Motor Speedway announced that The Monster Mile will hold a 400-mile points race on Sunday, May 16, 2027, as a part of NASCAR’s 2027 regular season, according to a news release on the Dover Motor Speedway website. 
Dover returns to being a points race after hosting NASCAR All-Star Race Weekend this past season. Denny Hamlin won the 2026 NASCAR All-Star race during Dover Motor Speedway’s first All-Star Race weekend, but said after that he’d rather have the venue host a points race. 
“There’s no other track like this on our schedule, and it is so unique, and it requires such a unique style of driving, far different than any oval that we go to, that it just can’t lose tracks like this in our points schedule,” Hamlin said after winning the 2026 NASCAR All-Star race. “I just think it’s too valuable, and the fans really, really are passionate here.”
Hamlin will get to compete for his fourth consecutive win at The Monster Mile in a points race next May. No driver has ever won four consecutive races at Dover Motor Speedway, according to the release.
The 2027 race weekend will also feature the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series BetRivers 200 on Saturday, May 15, and the return of Dover Motor Speedway’s fan zone. 
(To see pictures of the Fan Zone during last year’s All-Star weekend click here)
“Whether it’s a points race, an All-Star Race or a Chase race, one thing never changes—we work for the fans,” said president and general manager of Dover Motor Speedway, Mike Tatoian, via the news release. “They are the heart of everything we do, and we’re constantly looking for ways to make every visit to The Monster Mile more entertaining than the last. Our goal is to create memories that last a lifetime, and we can’t wait to welcome everyone back next spring for another outstanding weekend on and off the track.”
The start time for the races have not been announced yet. The NASCAR Cup Series race will be televised on FOX Sports and the O’Reilly Auto Parts Series will be televised on The CW, according to an article on NASCAR’s website.
To learn more about acquiring tickets check out Dover Motor Speedway’s website here.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota primary breaks turnout record with over 1.1 million ballots cast
description: Over 1.1 million Minnesotans voted in Tuesday’s primary election, or a quarter of eligible voters, setting the record for most votes cast in a primary, Secretary of State Steve Simon announced Wednesday. Primary election participation is lower than November general elections, where Minnesota has sometimes reached turnout as high as 80% in presidential years[...]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at Webster Town Hall in Webster, Minnesota during the primary election Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Over 1.1 million Minnesotans voted in Tuesday’s primary election, or a quarter of eligible voters, setting the record for most votes cast in a primary, Secretary of State Steve Simon announced Wednesday.
Primary election participation is lower than November general elections, where Minnesota has sometimes reached turnout as high as 80% in presidential years and 60% in non-presidential years.
Tuesday’s record-breaking turnout was likely driven by competitive races for Minnesota governor on the Republican side and the U.S. Senate on the Democratic-Farmer-Labor side.
President Donald Trump’s first midterm election also drew a heavy turnout. In both 2018 and this year, voters in the Democratic primaries drove the big numbers. 
“Minnesotans value democracy and they’ve proved it once again by showing up to vote in record numbers,” Simon said in a statement. “My call to Minnesotans now is to make their plan to vote on Nov. 3 so we can once again lead the nation in voter turnout.”
Minnesota’s last primary voter turnout record high was in 2018, with 925,554 ballots cast, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
In 2024, just 543,982 ballots were cast in the primary — about a 13% turnout. In recent years, voter turnout in primary elections has varied from 7% in 2016 to 24% in 2018.
Minnesotans in 1966 set a record-high turnout with nearly 40% of eligible voters casting a ballot in the primary, according to Secretary of State records.

name: Mississippi Today
title: The MAX set to add five Mississippi music legends to its Hall of Fame
description: The Mississippi Mass Choir was formed in 1988 by the late Frank Williams whose vision of uniting some of Mississippi's finest singers from across the state created a massive gospel powerhouse.
text:
The Mississippi Arts + Entertainment Experience (The MAX) in Meridian adds another batch of star power to its towering Hall of Fame with five new inductees whose lasting contributions further cement Mississippi’s foundational role in American music.
The Mississippi Mass Choir, a world-renowned force in gospel for decades, and bluesman Bobby Rush, who continues to rack up honors and gigs into his 90s, join seminal blues and folk musician Mississippi John Hurt (1893-1966), “Father of the Delta Blues” Charley Patton (1891-1934) and country music icon Conway Twitty (1933-1993) in the 2026-27 inductee class.
Charley Patton Credit: Courtesy of The MAX
“This is what the people wanted,” The MAX President and CEO Penny Kemp said of this inductee class’s all-music lineup. 
Candidate recommendations from the public and votes from the public and from arts and entertainment authorities on the prestigious Panel of Electors combine to balance enthusiasm and expertise in Hall of Fame selections. The rigorous process happens every two years. 
“Candidates must be recognizable icons in their field who have had a lasting cultural impact on Mississippi and beyond, and they have to have a solid connection to Mississippi,” Kemp said, whether by birthright, moving to the state in their early years or spending a significant portion of their career in Mississippi.  
“There are hundreds of people who qualify,” she said, noting Mississippi’s reliably deep bench of creative standouts in literature and visual and performing arts as well as many genres of music. “We produce so many artists and are continuing to do it every day.”
The Mississippi Mass Choir
The Mississippi Mass Choir was formed in 1988 by the late Frank Williams whose vision of uniting some of Mississippi’s finest singers from across the state created a massive gospel powerhouse. Its record-setting debut album hit No. 1 on Billboard’s gospel charts and stayed at the top for 45 consecutive weeks. 
The MAX Hall of Fame nod joins a collection of honors that includes multiple Grammy Award nominations and Stellar Gospel Music Awards, Billboard’s Gospel Artist of the Year, Stellar Gospel Hall of Fame and more.
“We are definitely honored,” Mississippi Mass Choir Executive Director Jerry Mannery said, noting the biblical saying that the prophet does not receive honor at home. That this recognition comes from their own people and home state holds special meaning, he added.
“It’s a testament to longevity,” he said. Thirty-eight years after its debut album, the choir’s current release, the 2024 “We Still Believe,” scored two No. 1 songs. 
“We’re looking to plant new fields. We’re not looking to rest on our laurels,” he said.
For this last project, the choir brought in 42 new members from all over the state (including several new lead singers), bumping up its usual 150-voice strength to a muscular 214. 
“At a time when most folks are kicking back and ready to go into the museum, we’re being inducted into the museum,” Mannery said, chuckling at the distinction. “But we’re  not ready to go into the museum.”
Catch the Mississippi Mass Choir live at the 83rd National Folk Festival in Jackson in November.
Bobby Rush Credit: David McClister
Bobby Rush
The Hall of Fame honor further broadens the spotlight on Bobby Rush’s seven-decade career in a year that also sees the release of the new documentary, “King of the Chitlin’ Circuit” this month and October’s world premiere of “Slippin’ Through the Cracks: The Bobby Rush Musical”  (co-written by Rush and Stephen Lloyd Helper) at New Stage Theatre. 
The legendary blues showman was in his 80s when he won his first Grammy Award, and now he has three. Already enshrined in the Blues Hall of Fame, Rush continues to take his self-defined folk-funk blend to global acclaim.
Mississippi John Hurt
Mississippi John Hurt was a key and a beloved figure in the American folk-blues music revival of the 1960s. Bob Dylan, Jerry Garcia and Taj Mahal were among the generation of musicians influenced by his syncopated finger-picking style and storyteller vocals, and he is hailed as a bridge between the folk traditions of the 19th century and 20th century American acoustic music.
Mississippi John Hurt Credit: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs
“I am absolutely thrilled,” Mary Frances Hurt, the musician’s granddaughter, said by phone from Chicago. She has operated the Mississippi John Hurt Foundation for the last 30 years, criss-crossing the country to accept awards and honors on his behalf.
“I am ecstatic that he’s being recognized in his own home state,” she said of the man she knew as Daddy John. She, too, recalled the Gospel’s words about a prophet and honor at home. “He loved Mississippi and his home so much.” 
That this tribute comes amid such high-profile company in the inductee class, 60 years after her grandfather’s death, “That’s incredible and I’m so grateful for that.”
Charley Patton
Early 20th century Delta blues musician and songwriter Charley Patton’s guitar skills, raw and booming vocals and stage flash proved to be elemental building blocks of blues and early rock ’n’ roll. They exerted a powerful influence on musicians who followed, including such legends as Robert Johnson, Son House and “Pops” Staples. Patton, a Blues Hall of Fame member since 1989, was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as an “Early Influence” in 2021.
Conway Twitty
Conway Twitty Credit: Courtesy of The MAX
Enduring hitmaker Conway Twitty, born Harold Lloyd Jenkins in Friars Point, was actually a rockabilly star and teen idol early on, but scored biggest and longest in the country genre. His record of 55 No. 1 singles held until George Strait broke it in 2006. Twitty penned 11 of those chart-toppers himself. 
From the No. 1 “Hello Darlin’” to the No. 7 “Goodbye Time,” Twitty stayed a star for five decades, selling over 50 million records and earning a spot, too, in the Country Music Hall of Fame.
An induction ceremony for The MAX Hall of Fame will be held Jan. 28 at the MSU Riley Center just down the street. The ceremony will celebrate inductees with entertaining, educational and often moving tributes in performance, followed by a reception back at The MAX. 
New honorees’ bigger-than-life-size portraits will join the soaring, two-story Hall of Fame rotunda that is the centerpiece draw at The MAX, touted as “360 degrees of Mississippi star power.” Interactive kiosks there invite visitors to explore their inspiring stories and achievements.

text:
Sen. Ron Latz, DFL- Saint Louis Park, rises for a point of order while debating a motion to refer a bill to the floor during session Monday, March 3, 2025. Photo by A.J. Olmscheid/Senate Media Services.Most of the sitting Minnesota lawmakers who faced intra-party challengers won their primary elections Tuesday.
Only one incumbent lawmaker was unseated: Sen. Paul Utke, R-Park Rapids, who lost by fewer than 200 votes to Rep. Mike Wiener, who had earned the Republican endorsement in the race. 
Sen. Ron Latz, DFL-St. Louis Park, won out against Lynette Lungay Dumalag, who presented herself as a more progressive alternative to Latz on issues including housing and support for immigrants. Dumalag earned 40% of the vote in the west metro district — not enough to beat Latz, the Senate Judiciary and Public Safety Committee chair who has served in the Legislature since 2002.
In Brooklyn Park, DFL Sen. Susan Pha backed Wynfred Russell, a former City Council member running against one of the district’s House members, Rep. Huldah Momanyi-Hiltsley. Momany-Hiltsley, meanwhile, supported Pha’s challenger, Nehemiah Garley. Both incumbents won their primaries, though Russell came within 7 points of Momanyi-Hiltsley.
St. Cloud City Council President Mike Conway beat out the Republican-endorsed candidate, John Jose, in the GOP primary for District 14A, which includes parts of St. Cloud and Waite Park. Conway will run against Abdi Daisane in the general election, which Daisane lost in 2024 by 13 points.

name: Mississippi Today
title: USM history professor plays major role in Netflix’s ‘The American Experiment’
description: Netflix is featuring a five-part documentary named "The American Experiment," coinciding with the nation's 250th birthday. University of Southern Mississippi professor Andrew Wiest participated in the project.
text:
University of Southern Mississippi professor and military historian Andrew Wiest is among the star-studded cast of Netflix’s “The American Experiment” documentary.
The five-part series chronicles the history of the American Revolution, coinciding with the nation’s 250th birthday. It features commentary, voice-overs and interviews with academics, political figures and more. 
Wiest can be heard reading lines throughout the series, including parts of the Declaration of Independence and playing founding father Patrick Henry. He described what it was like to hear himself in the documentary.
“The narrator says right before you hear us read it that these are some of the most important lines ever written in the English language, and I was like, ‘Wow, and I got to read one of those,’” he said.
Andrew Wiest Credit: University of Southern Mississippi
Christine Cavalieri from Reel2Reel Casting emailed Wiest looking for prominent figures, experts and “extraordinary individuals” for the documentary. He agreed when he learned it was being produced by Playtone, a production company co-founded by Oscar-winning actor Tom Hanks, who have acted, directed and produced multiple projects related to American history, including “Saving Private Ryan,” “Band of Brothers,” “John Adams” and others.
Wiest recorded his lines in the sound booth at USM’s Center for Oral History and Cultural Heritage. Sarah Huisenga from Luminant Media directed him on how to read his lines over Zoom.
He hasn’t seen the full series yet, but he has seen two parts that he voiced. He plans to show parts of the series to his classes.
Wiest considers his role in the documentary a career milestone.
“Most folks don’t read deeply in-depth history,” he wrote in an email. “But a doc(umentary) like this, with the very best historians taking part, condenses the most modern in-depth research into a very watchable whole.”
He continued, “Taking part in this kind of means that I have made it as it were. Wish my mom was around to see it. Her boy done made good.”
A Hattiesburg native, Wiest is in the Hattiesburg Public Schools Hall of Fame and Southern Miss Alumni Hall of Fame. He is a founding director of the Dale Center for the Study of War and Society and co-founder of the Center for the Study of the National Guard.  He received the prestigious Society for Military History’s Samuel Eliot Morison Prize in March.  
Weist was lead historian on “Brothers in War,” an Emmy-winning National Geographic documentary based on his book, “The Boys of ‘67.” He also served as chief historical consultant on the documentary “Vietnam in HD.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lincoln leaders tout $17M youth volleyball complex headed to Nov. 3 general election ballot vote
description: LINCOLN — Lincoln voters on Nov. 3 will determine the fate of a $17 million volleyball facility that supporters say would boost the city’s status as a youth sport destination. Fans tout the proposed N4VB (Nebraska for Volleyball) complex as an economic development project that would generate about $22 million in total annual impact by its […]
text:
Proposed Nebraska for Volleyball (N4VB) youth-centric volleyball complex that is to be financed largely by a state tax incentive, or "turnback tax," requires buy-in from Lincoln voters on the Nov. 3 general election ballot. This is a southwest view of the facility that would rise at 30th Street and Folkways Boulevard. (Rendering courtesy of Davis Design)LINCOLN — Lincoln voters on Nov. 3 will determine the fate of a $17 million volleyball facility that supporters say would boost the city’s status as a youth sport destination.
Fans tout the proposed N4VB (Nebraska for Volleyball) complex as an economic development project that would generate about $22 million in total annual impact by its third year and also serve underrepresented youth through free or reduced-cost programming.
The proposed Nebraska for Volleyball (N4VB) volleyball complex would start with eight courts. (Rendering courtesy of Davis Design)
Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird, nonprofit N4VB and others on Tuesday announced the timing of the general election ballot measure and offered assurances that an affirmative vote would not raise taxes. The vote is necessary for the group to access a state sales tax incentive, referred to as a “turnback tax,” to help finance construction of the privately owned complex. 
“Lincoln is the epicenter of volleyball in America, in the state, and I would dare say the globe when you think about that record-setting attendance that we set over in Memorial Stadium a few years ago,” Gaylor Baird said. “We are taking another step forward in recognition of Lincoln’s preeminent position in volleyball.”
 Earlier resistance 

An earlier hurdle was cleared when the state Sports Arena Facility Finance Assistance Board approved the use of the incentive for the eight-court facility expected to host regional tournaments and year-round activities. It was one of two urban Nebraska projects in May to gain required support of that board after months-long resistance by Gov. Jim Pillen. 
Pillen, an SAFFA board member, ultimately voted for the N4VB project application, submitted in partnership with the City of Lincoln, as well as a $140 million downtown Omaha soccer stadium that is a partnership of the City of Omaha and Union Omaha professional soccer franchise. The state board at the time rejected nine other project applications from across the state.
Pillen-led board approves tax incentive for Omaha, Lincoln sports facilities, rejects nine more 

For larger cities such as Omaha and Lincoln, the financing incentive generally works like this: Up to 70% of new state sales taxes generated within 600 yards of the sports facility goes to help pay off bonds for construction. The “new” tax revenue generated refers to ticket sales or retailers that sprout in the designated area for a certain time after the project is announced. Depending on financing and ownership structure, city voters also might have to approve the turnback tax use. 
The Omaha soccer stadium project differs from the Lincoln volleyball project in that it is to be owned by the city, not privately owned. Deputy City Attorney Jennifer Taylor said Omaha’s 6,500-seat soccer facility, which is to anchor a downtown mixed-use campus and open in 2028, does not require local voter approval.
She said the city of Omaha plans to use revenue bonds to fund a portion of the cost of the soccer stadium and turnback tax revenue will be pledged to pay the debt service on those bonds, when issued.
Aims to ‘open doors’
In September 2025, the Lincoln City Council passed a resolution endorsed by the mayor that authorized the city to issue revenue bonds for the sports complex to be covered by the turnback tax. The resolution said the city would approve bond terms after a green light from city voters at a special election or statewide primary or general election. 
Supporters of the volleyball project have launched a campaign encouraging a “for” vote. They say they are optimistic about the Nov. 3 measure, saying people have been receptive especially after they tell them it is not attached to a tax increase. The N4VB website says the group wants to build a “cutting-edge indoor volleyball complex in northeast Lincoln designed to open doors for the next generation of Nebraska talent without raising local taxes.” 
The turnback tax incentive is expected to finance up to 75% of construction costs of the N4VB complex proposed at 30th Street and Folkways Boulevard, with private funding covering the rest of the project that could grow to 12 courts.
N4VB was founded by former Husker athlete Maggie Griffin, who says a goal is to ensure broad access. Club teams are to lease space to support operational revenue, while time and resources are to be reserved for public clinics, camps and outreach programs that are low or no-cost to area youth.
“Registration fees, travel costs and other expenses can quickly put organized sports out of reach for many families,” said John Goodwin, CEO of the Malone Center, a community-based anti-poverty nonprofit involved in the venture. “The N4VB volleyball complex helps change that.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: McKee nominates Superior Court Associate Justice Luis Matos to Supreme Court
description: Former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi dominated discussion of the open seat on the Rhode Island Supreme Court. But a different applicant made headline news Wednesday as Gov. Dan McKee announced Rhode Island Superior Court Judge Luis Matos as his nominee for the state’s highest court.  “I know his record of his decisions has been […]
text:
Rhode Island Superior Court Associate Justice Luis Matos takes a question from reporters alongside Gov. Dan McKee during a press conference announcing his nomination to fill a vacancy on the Supreme Court on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)Former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi dominated discussion of the open seat on the Rhode Island Supreme Court.
But a different applicant made headline news Wednesday as Gov. Dan McKee announced Rhode Island Superior Court Judge Luis Matos as his nominee for the state’s highest court. 
“I know his record of his decisions has been impeccable,” McKee said of Matos, speaking to reporters at a noon State House press conference called less than one hour beforehand. “There’s a certain sense of camaraderie between me and the judge. We both grew up in boys clubs, we rubbed elbows with every walk of life. I feel as if I know the judge in this sense.”
The 62-year-old Providence resident who immigrated from Portugal in 1969 has served on the Superior Court since 2012. A former federal prosecutor in Rhode Island and in Delaware, he has extensive experience prosecuting health care fraud, white collar crime and public corruption cases, according to his resume. Since its creation in 2020, Matos has served on the Judiciary’s Committee on Racial and Ethnic Fairness in the Courts, helping improve internal policies and public outreach on a fair judicial system. 
McKee repeatedly praised Matos as the “most qualified” of five applicants, though the governor acknowledged that all five contenders met the criteria for the lifetime appointment to the bench.
Yet McKee sidestepped repeated questions from reporters regarding the still-unresolved ethical questions hanging over Shekarchi – which, ironically, now sit before the Supreme Court.
“I’m not on the courts,” McKee said. “The court establishes the law.”
Shekarchi, a Warwick Democrat and land use attorney, applied for the Supreme Court vacancy in May, three days after he stepped down as House Speaker. His bid for the bench prompted instantaneous scrutiny over the ethical implications of leaping from the most powerful position in the legislature to another top spot in a different branch of state government. 
Roger Williams University School of Law Professor Michael Yelnosky, who filed the complaint against Shekarchi, pointed to a clause in the state ethics code that prevents sitting legislators from seeking or taking a job with any state agency for at least one year after leaving elected office. Shekarchi and his attorneys pointed to the exemption in the “revolving door” clause specific for constitutional office — reasoning that the state’s highest court was such an office. A Rhode Island Superior Court judge upheld Shekarchi’s right to apply as within the bounds of state ethics law, but the Rhode Island Ethics Commission has appealed the ruling.



Quotation







There’s a certain sense of camaraderie between me and the judge. We both grew up in boys clubs, we rubbed elbows with every walk of life. I feel as if I know the judge in this sense.


– Gov. Dan McKee



The battle has now landed, ironically, before the state’s highest court. with the Rhode Island Ethics Commission appealing a Superior Court judge’s ruling to allow Shekarchi’s application to advance. The July 27 decision by Superior Court Judge Richard Licht did not prevent the ethics panel from conducting its investigation into Shekarchi, but put the probe on pause ahead of a final court judgment. Court records show the Ethics Commission submitted its notice of appeal to the Supreme Court Tuesday, following a 4-1 vote among commission members to challenge Licht’s decision.
Meanwhile, a separate appointed panel of legal experts reviewed and took public comments on all five applicants, including Shekarchi. Ultimately the Judicial Nominating Commission advanced all five applicants to McKee for consideration — thoughShekarchi and his fellow applicants were still being scrutinized by the Judicial Nominating Commission rather than winnowing the field. But, Shekarchi was the sole applicant to not receive unanimous support from the nominating commission, with two of nine panelists opposed. 
Controversy intensified after it was revealed that four of the seven commissioners who voted to advance Shekarchi’s application also donated to his legislative campaigns, yet failed to disclose their financial support for the longtime legislator prior to the vote. The donations were first reported by GoLocal Prov. 
Matos declined to weigh in on the controversy, proclaiming it would be inappropriate for him to take a stand on any matter pending before the court he may soon join. McKee called on lawmakers to hold a special legislative session before the traditional early January start in order to confirm Matos’ nomination.
House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski and Senate President Valarie Lawson said in a joint statement that they will consider the choice after the Nov. 3 general election.
“We informed the Governor of our shared goal of taking the politics as much as possible out of what has become an overly politicized Supreme Court nomination process,” they said. “We do not believe it is appropriate or prudent for consideration of any nominee, regardless of who it is, to begin until after that date.”
Rhode Island Superior Court Associate Justice Luis Matos takes a question from reporters alongside Gov. Dan McKee during a press conference announcing his nomination to fill a vacancy on the Supreme Court on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
McKee, in contrast, openly acknowledged his looming primary challenge against 
rival Helena Buonanno Foulkes as reason for the timing of his decision — just seven hours before his first televised debate against Foulkes.
“The public is very interested in this issue,” McKee said. “They should know where I stand before they decide this election.”
Ethics Commission to appeal decision that allowed former Speaker to seek Supreme Court seat

Clarity is also the goal of good government advocates and legal experts, who maintain that a Supreme Court review of the appeal on Shekarchi’s ethics case is still of value, even without his advancement as a nominee.
Yelnosky called it a “live controversy,” noting that Licht’s opinion opens new uncertainties into ethical implications on transitions from elected office to all Rhode Island courts. Matos’ nomination, if confirmed, will set off the appointment process anew for his spot on the Superior Court.
John Marion, executive director for Common Cause Rhode Island agreed.
“If taken to its logical conclusion, Licht’s [decision] can be read that no qualifications of any type – including the requirement that someone be an attorney – can be put on the governor’s power to appoint judges,” Marion said in an emailed statement. “We believe that is both incorrect and harmful.”
Jason Gramitt, executive director for the Rhode Island Ethics Commission, confirmed via email that the panel intends to pursue its appeal.
“The last few months have shown us that this is a significant issue of great public concern, likely to repeat itself,” Gramitt said. “Therefore, it is appropriate and necessary to continue the appeal to bring the matter to our highest court for a final resolution.”
Reached by phone Wednesday, Shekarchi declined to comment on the pending court case.
“I want to congratulate Judge Matos on his nomination by the Governor,” Shekarchi said. “I also want to thank everyone who supported my candidacy for the Supreme Court. 
McKee acknowledged that he spoken with Matos Wednesday morning before the press conference but that members of his legal team contacted the other candidates to deliver the news of his decision.
“I did not speak to the speaker today,” McKee said.
The three other applicants on the list submitted to the governor by the Judicial Nominating Commission were Christopher Bush, an assistant attorney general; Laureen D’Ambra, a Family Court judge; and John E. Roberts, an attorney who is a partner with the Boston firm Proskauer Rose LLC.
The lifetime appointment to the court, with a $228,325-a-year salary, fills the vacancy created by the March retirement of Rhode Island Supreme Court Associate Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg.

title: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers gives green light to Line 5 tunnel
description: Canadian energy company Enbridge has secured another permit needed for its Line 5 tunnel project, moving the effort closer toward construction after another critical permit was struck down less than two weeks earlier.  The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced on Wednesday that it had issued a permit for the project, authorizing the company to […]
text:
Ceremonial rock in Mackinac Straits prior to Anishinaabek water ceremony at McGulpin Point, Mackinaw City. May 2021 | Laina G. StebbinsCanadian energy company Enbridge has secured another permit needed for its Line 5 tunnel project, moving the effort closer toward construction after another critical permit was struck down less than two weeks earlier. 
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced on Wednesday that it had issued a permit for the project, authorizing the company to tunnel beneath the lake bed in the Straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet. 
The tunnel would house a four-mile-long pipeline segment intended to replace the dual pipelines running along the lake bed amid ongoing concerns that  the pipelines could rupture, spilling oil and natural gas liquids into the Great Lakes. 
Tribal nations from throughout the Great Lakes region and environmental advocates have pushed to shut down the pipeline for many years, pointing to the 2010 Kalamazoo River oil spill from Enbridge’s Line 6B, and a series of anchor strikes that dented Line 5’s eastern and western segments as warning signs of the potential for a spill. 
Enbridge has pointed to the tunnel project as a preventative measure against any future anchor strikes and oil spill concerns, though pipeline opponents argue that constructing the tunnel carries its own list of harms, including impacts to nearby wetlands and the destruction of several cultural sites and archaeological resources.
This is a breaking story and will be updated

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Supreme Court opinion on privacy law seen as win for data brokers
description: Data brokers allege in court that Daniel’s Law, which allows judges and cops to shield their personal information from the public, is unconstitutional.
text:
New Jersey Supreme Court Justice Fabiana Pierre-Louis authored Wednesday's opinion, seen as a victory for data brokers that believe Daniel's Law is unconstitutional. (Photo by Mary Iuvone/New Jersey Monitor)The New Jersey Supreme Court handed a major victory Wednesday to dozens of data firms that have alleged a state law that shields the addresses of judges and police officers from the public is unconstitutional.
The unanimous ruling comes as the data brokers face a federal lawsuit filed by Atlas Data Privacy, which alleges the brokers did not remove the addresses of people covered by the statute, known as Daniel’s Law, within the required 10-day period after the removal request. The U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals asked New Jersey’s high court to decide whether the law requires a person or company to have acted purposely, knowingly, recklessly, and negligently to be deemed in violation of the law.
On Wednesday, New Jersey’s Supreme Court justices ruled that the portion of the law under which the data firms were sued does not include such a mental state requirement.
“The Legislature included a mental state requirement in the 2020 version of Daniel’s Law regarding actual damages — that ‘a reasonable person would believe that providing’ certain information ‘would expose another to harassment or risk of harm to life or property’ — but deleted that language in 2022,” Justice Fabiana Pierre-Louis wrote in the five-member decision, adding that the 2022 change “suggests that the Legislature intended for Daniel’s Law to require no specific mental state for the imposition of actual damages.”
The ruling notes that it does not represent the court’s view on the constitutionality of Daniel’s Law.
The data firms have argued the law is facially unconstitutional, and the 3rd Circuit said the law may unconstitutionally chill unrelated speech if it does not weigh violators’ intent or mental state.
The Legislature passed Daniel’s Law in 2020 after a disgruntled lawyer fatally shot a federal judge’s son, Daniel Anderl, at their North Brunswick home. It allows active or former judges, prosecutors, police officers, child-protection investigators, and immediate family living with them to stop people from sharing their addresses and phone numbers.
Wednesday’s ruling says a provision in the law allowing individuals covered by the law, or their designees, to sue and be awarded $1,000 if protected information was not removed within 10 days was automatic, rejecting arguments from Atlas Data Privacy and New Jersey’s attorney general that the law implicitly required negligence from those sued.
“The 10-day notice requirement is simply not the same as requiring a mental state of negligence; complying with that time frame is not synonymous with acting with reasonable care,” Pierre-Louis wrote.
In reaching its decision, New Jersey’s Supreme Court noted Daniel’s Law explicitly required “willful or reckless disregard” to award punitive damages but had no similar requirement for actual damages, which run at least $1,000 per violation.
Lawmakers’ removal of language that limited damages to cases where a reasonable person would believe the release of information could expose someone to harassment or harm from a prior version of the law also cut against Atlas’s arguments, the court said.
“Had the Legislature intended to include a negligence standard or require another mental state for the imposition of actual damages, it easily could have included that language in the 2022 iteration of the statute along with the notice requirement and 10-day compliance window,” Pierre-Louis wrote. “It did not.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont doesn’t have a housing shortage. It has an affordability problem.
description:
Vacancies are up and rents are falling, but Vermonters still can't afford housing.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont doesn’t have a housing shortage. It has an affordability problem..
text:
This commentary is by Matt Swenson, the founder of Omnidex Solutions, an independent research and strategic analysis company. He lives in Vermont.
For years, Vermont politics has run on one diagnosis: not enough housing. The prescription never changes: Build more, build denser, permit faster.
Supply matters. But it no longer explains what we’re seeing. In Vermont’s largest rental market, vacancy hit 3.3% this summer, up from under 1% during the pandemic years. More than 1,300 rental units opened in 2024 and 2025. Landlords are cutting rents and throwing in incentives. And working Vermonters still cannot afford what’s available.
The numbers underneath explain why. Between 2019 and 2024, the median value of a Vermont home rose from $233,200 to $352,800 — nearly $120,000 in five years. Household income grew about 15% over the same stretch. In 2019, a Vermonter earning the median income could afford roughly half the homes in the state. By 2024, a third.
That is not a construction problem. That is a gap between what Vermont pays people and what Vermont charges them, and no amount of framing lumber closes it.
Property taxes are a housing cost too. The fiscal year 2027 yield bill, H.949/Act 169, holds the statewide average increase at roughly 3.5% using a $104.9 million one-time general fund transfer. That reduces this year’s property tax bill, but it does not reduce the underlying cost. It pays part of the education bill with other state tax revenue and pushes the pressure into future years. That isn’t structural relief. It’s a bill with the due date moved, and when the one-time money disappears, taxpayers inherit the balance.
Consider what that means when we actually build something. Alice Holway Drive in Putney cost $15 million for 25 apartments — $600,000 per unit, financed mostly through state housing programs, which is taxpayer money. The site made sense: walking distance to the co-op, easy access to Interstate 91. The building doesn’t match the site. Drive past it, and $600,000 per unit is not what you’d guess. I’d put housing on that lot again tomorrow. I would not spend that much doing it, and I would not call it a model for anything.

READ MORE

It also took four years to build. Neighbors appealed to the environmental court, lost, appealed to the Vermont Supreme Court, lost, and appealed again on different grounds. Meanwhile, a subdivision on an open hayfield, requiring new frontage, a new septic system and a permanent increase in car trips draws less scrutiny than a bake sale. We fight density where it’s cheap to serve and shrug at sprawl where it’s expensive, which is precisely backward, and precisely why the fields keep disappearing while the affordability numbers don’t move.
The siting problem is bigger than Putney. Housing in Burlington, Winooski, Rutland and established village centers makes sense where the infrastructure already exists. Pushing that same density into towns like Williston and Hinesburg does not. Hinesburg has studied traffic on Route 116 so many times that the study should qualify for residency. Parts of Vermont increasingly resemble outer Boston. We imported the commute and left the paycheck behind.
Open land is Vermont’s actual asset — the thing in every tourism budget and relocation pitch the state has ever written. Covering hayfields with houses the people working those fields can’t afford isn’t a solution. It’s a trade, and a lousy one.
There’s also a comforting myth in local politics: Build more houses, grow the tax base, ease the burden on everyone else. The data says the opposite most of the time. Cost of community services studies conducted across dozens of counties find that residential development typically costs local governments more in services, chiefly schools, than it generates in tax revenue — commonly $1.15 to $1.50 spent for every dollar collected. Farmland and open land run the reverse ratio, producing a surplus. More rooftops don’t lower tax bills — they raise them, because schools cost money and houses don’t pay for themselves. Every hayfield we convert to subdivisions trades a fiscal asset for a fiscal liability, and the property tax bill in 10 years will show it.
The same math that prices Vermonters out of housing prices Vermont out of the professionals it says it wants. Take a primary care physician at $300,000, near the national average. Federal income tax takes about $68,000, payroll taxes another $17,000, Vermont’s income tax roughly $20,000 — before property taxes. Compare: Colorado’s flat 4.4% rate produces about $12,500. Pennsylvania’s flat 3.07% produces about $9,200. Vermont runs four brackets from 3.35% to 8.75%, with the top rate arriving around $230,000 of taxable income — not yacht money for a state trying to recruit doctors. When a recruiter lays those columns side by side, Vermont’s counteroffer is scenery, and scenery does not amortize.
None of this argues against building housing. It argues against building housing as a substitute for an actual economic strategy. Concentrate development where the infrastructure already exists and make that path fast, not four years long. Stop treating open land as the default site of least resistance. Fix the property tax structure instead of financing it with surplus money. And make the tax code competitive enough that the people Vermont needs choose it on the merits, not in spite of the bill.
Otherwise, the trajectory holds: more homes than Vermonters can afford, more development than the state can carry and a landscape gradually converted into the one thing nobody moved here for.

Elon Poll logoA new poll from Elon University shows a majority of North Carolinians are now opposed to data centers in their communities. 
The increasing resistance comes as data center developers push to add more facilities throughout the state, rolling out an extensive public relations campaign to bolster the industry’s image.  
The latest poll, which surveyed 800 adults in the state at the end of July, found 53% opposed having data centers in their communities, with 20% in support and 27% unsure. That’s a sizable increase since Elon’s March poll, which found 44% opposed to data centers in their communities, 24% in support of them, and 32% unsure. 
Elon Poll director Jason Husser said the growing opposition spans the political spectrum, with the poll showing a plurality of Republicans and men joining a majority of Democrats, independents and women. 
Pro-data center group trying to change opinions in NC with ad campaign

“It’s not just a debate in Raleigh that can be far away for people. It’s a debate in their local county seats,” Husser told NC Newsline. “That sort of local element is important in terms of driving opinion.”
More than 20 local governments have enacted moratoriums on data center development to give them time to study the issue and design local ordinances to regulate them. But other local governments are opting against moratoriums, saying the property tax revenue could help boost tight budgets.
Husser said he’s not surprised the industry’s public relation campaign isn’t working.
“We’ve seen in the past that grassroots NIMBY movements can move the needle more than significant corporate spending, particularly when people are skeptical of those corporations to begin with,” he said.
Voter fraud and confidence in elections 
The poll also shows that the majority of registered voters in North Carolina don’t believe voter fraud is a major problem, but the partisan differences on the issue are starker than ever. 
Out of 717 registered voters surveyed, a little over a third — 37% — said they believe voter fraud is a major problem for U.S. national elections. But more than half  — 54% — said it’s either a minor problem or not a problem at all, and 9% weren’t sure. 
Republicans were far more likely than other groups to see voter fraud as a serious problem. Nearly two-thirds — 64% — said it’s a major problem, compared to 23% of Democrats and 26% of independents. 
Voters overall were a little less certain about foreign interference in elections, but a plurality doesn’t see that as a major problem, either. Among registered voters, 45% said election interference by foreign governments is a minor problem or not a problem at all, while 39% believe it’s a major problem, and 17% weren’t sure. 
Asked about the upcoming midterm elections, 63% of voters said they’re “very” or “somewhat” confident that the overall process will be fair, while 29% said they’re “only a little” or “not at all” confident it will be fair. Eight percent weren’t sure. 
On the other hand, three-quarters of Republican respondents said they believe President Donald Trump was the winner of the 2020 presidential election, compared to 33% of respondents across all parties. 
Husser said the poll was in the field shortly after Trump gave a primetime address reviving his unproven allegations of fraud in the 2020 election. “It seems that Trump has largely had the Republican Party coalesce around his narrative that he was the true winner and was cheated,” he said. 



Quotation







All that ad money is not totally going to waste.


– Jason Husser, Elon Poll director


U.S. Senate race 
The latest poll numbers show former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper holding onto a double-digit lead over his Republican rival Michael Whatley among likely voters. 
The poll found registered voters’ familiarity with Whatley has increased by about 15% since the last Elon survey in March. Both candidates have slightly improved their net favorability. 
“All that ad money is not totally going to waste,” Husser said. 
But Whatley remains underwater on net favorability by -4 compared to 18 for Cooper, so the increase in voter familiarity doesn’t seem to have substantially changed the balance of the race yet. 
However, voters often don’t start paying much attention to campaigns until after Labor Day, and Husser says Whatley is likely to make up some ground as the election approaches.
“Among the roughly half of voters who have heard a great deal or some about Whatley, the race becomes very close,” Husser said. “This leads me to expect some tightening in polls over the next two months.”
Still, he said, it’s an uphill battle for Whatley, especially in a midterm election without a presidential race to draw voters’ attention. 
“Cooper is just so well-known,” Husser said. “It’s pretty hard to stick something to a guy who’s been scrutinized for 20 years. If there was something that was going to stick, they would have figured it out already.”
The margin of error for the poll of registered voters is +/- 4.42%.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Empleados temporales mexicanos de la granja Battle Fish denuncian abusos laborales
description: El Departamento de Trabajo presentó una demanda contra la granja Battle Fish en 2023 por obstrucción de una investigación gubernamental y por medidas de represalia contra los trabajadores agrícolas. Battle Fish negó las acusaciones. Ahora, el ministerio está investigando de nuevo las condiciones en la granja.
text:
TÚNICA COUNTY – El Departamento de Trabajo de EE. UU. está investigando una granja de bagre en el Delta de Mississippi, donde algunos trabajadores temporales denuncian abusos verbales y racismo persistentes, salarios no pagados, condiciones de vida precarias y otras violaciones a sus derechos laborales.
Empleados de Battle Fish North afirmaron que, durante años, la gerencia ha recurrido a amenazas de violencia y a negarles contratos de trabajo temporal para disuadirlos de denunciar los abusos ante las autoridades.
El Departamento del Trabajo también investigó a la granja en 2023 por presuntas violaciones de la Ley de Normas Justas del Trabajo y de las regulaciones del programa H-2A, y posteriormente entabló una demanda a la empresa y a sus dueños por obstruir la investigación. En la demanda judicial, que representa la postura de una de las partes, el departamento afirmó que la granja ocultó alojamientos y vehículos que no cumplían con las normas y amenazó con tomar represalias contra los trabajadores que aceptaran ser entrevistados por investigadores federales.
El caso concluyó con un acuerdo sin conclusiones, y Battle Fish no “admitió ni negó” las acusaciones en el decreto de consentimiento. Sin embargo, en un memorándum anterior dirigido a la corte, los demandados afirmaron que “no obstaculizaron la investigación del Departamento de Trabajo, y mucho menos tomaron represalias contra los empleados que pudieran haber participado en ella”, alegando que “las pruebas demuestran que los demandados de Battle-Magnolia cooperaron de buena fe para facilitar la investigación del Gobierno”.
El juez ordenó a la granja que, en adelante, cumpliera con la Ley de Normas Justas del Trabajo y mejorara el acceso a la información sobre los derechos de los trabajadores.
“La gente que viene contratada pierde las esperanzas, porque la otra vez … fue el Departamento de Trabajo, pero no se vio ningún cambio”, dijo un empleado que salió de Battle Fish pero que sigue en contacto con sus antiguos compañeros de trabajo.
El empleado pidió mantener el anonimato por preocupaciones sobre posibles repercusiones para los trabajadores actuales de la granja.
En relación con la investigación de 2023, Andrew Dulaney, abogado de Battle Fish, declaró a Mississippi Today que “Battle Fish North y Magnolia Processing, Inc. han resuelto con éxito y de manera amistosa los problemas laborales con el Departamento de Trabajo en 2023. Tal como lo estableció el fallo de la Corte y como creemos que todas las partes entienden, hubo un malentendido sobre varios asuntos. Estos malentendidos ya han sido resueltos”.
Mississippi Today analizó archivos judiciales y documentos gubernamentales, se comunicó con agencias gubernamentales y con los representantes legales de Battle Fish, y entrevistó a siete empleados actuales y antiguos que trabajaron en la granja entre 2012 y 2026.
Los empleados son ciudadanos mexicanos que han trabajado en EE. UU. de manera temporal con visas H-2A, las cuales permiten a los empleadores agrícolas contratar a trabajadores desde fuera de EE. UU. de manera temporal. Cuatro dijeron que decidieron renunciar para no seguir enfrentándose a los abusos. Uno de ellos afirmó que la empresa no lo volvió a contratar después de que habló con los investigadores del Departamento de Trabajo sobre las condiciones laborales.
Cinco de ellos hablaron con Mississippi Today bajo condición de anonimato por temor a represalias, y dos exempleados que regresaron a México —Jacob Vargas Huante y Francisco Chávez Barajas— dieron su permiso para que se publicaran sus nombres.
“Yo fui víctima, mañana puede ser otro”, dijo Vargas.
Extrabajadores dijeron a Mississippi Today que la intimidación ha venido principalmente de Houston Battle, uno de los dueños, y de Martín Valencia, un capataz que supervisa las operaciones y se comunica con los trabajadores porque Battle no habla español.
Ni Battle ni Valencia respondieron a solicitudes de comentarios después de que Mississippi Today les dejó varios mensajes de voz y mensajes escritos.
“Durante mi investigación, varios empleados de Battle Fish me informaron que Battle y Martín denigran a los trabajadores amenazándolos repetidamente con hacerles daño físico, así como con despedirlos o hacer que los deporten”, se lee en una declaración de Kristina Espinoza, una de las 10 investigadoras que inspeccionaron la granja en 2023. Según los expedientes judiciales, un empleado les dijo a los investigadores, “Ya no aguantaba en la granja el trato del mayordomo Martín Valencia ni del patrón,… todos los días eran así diciéndonos insultos”.
La exsecretaria de Trabajo, Julie Su, escribió en un memorándum a la corte que la investigación del Departamento de Trabajo había revelado un “patrón amplio y continuo de amenazas e intimidación hacia los trabajadores de Battle Fish”.
En una audiencia de moción, el dueño principal, Bill Battle, negó haber tomado represalias contra los trabajadores.
Una vocera del Departamento de Trabajo, Erika Ruthman, confirmó que hay una investigación abierta en curso sobre la empresa, pero señaló que no podía dar más detalles para garantizar la integridad del proceso. Ruthman se negó a comentar si la investigación en curso es de rutina o en respuesta a una denuncia.
Brandon Davis, un abogado que representa a Battle Fish, dijo que sería “inapropiado” hablar sobre la investigación, pero que Battle Fish “seguiría colaborando con el gobierno federal como nuestro organismo regulador, así como con el público y con nuestros distintos grupos de empleados”.
Un negocio familiar
El equipo agrícola en Battle Fish en el condado de Túnica, Miss., el jueves 9 de julio de 2026. Crédito: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
Battle Fish se encuentra a las afueras de Túnica, en el norte del Delta de Mississippi. Cientos de hectáreas de estanques rectangulares agrupados salpican una extensa llanura de campos que rodea la estrecha Carretera 4.
La granja familiar de bagre y la planta de procesamiento, Magnolia, Inc., se encuentran en el mismo sitio. Son propiedad y están a cargo de miembros de la familia Battle – Houston Battle junto con su hermano y su padre. Los abuelos de Houston Battle fundaron el negocio a finales de los años sesenta, y hoy en día la planta procesa alrededor de 10 millones de libras de pescado al año.
Tanto la granja como la planta de procesamiento contratan a trabajadores extranjeros temporales y fueron demandantes en el caso de la corte de 2023. Anteriormente, una investigación del Departamento del Trabajo había revelado que Magnolia Inc. debía más de 11.000 dólares en salarios atrasados a sus empleados estadounidenses.
El Departamento del Trabajo autorizó a Battle Fish contratar a 14 trabajadores a través del programa de visas H-2A para la temporada 2026, de febrero a noviembre. Cada año cientos de miles de personas trabajan en Estados Unidos con visas H-2A, la mayoría de ellas procedentes de México.
Jacob Vargas Huante, exempleado de Battle Fish, presentó una declaración judicial en la demanda de 2023 y le dijo a Mississippi Today que había trabajado para tres empleadores en Estados Unidos a través del programa H-2A sin problemas antes de llegar a Túnica. “Nunca tuve problemas, nunca fui maltratado… solo ahí con Battle Fish”.
Sin embargo, Noemí Hernández, cónsul general de México en Nueva Orleans, señaló que el consulado recibe con frecuencia denuncias de maltratos laborales por parte de ciudadanos mexicanos que trabajan en Mississippi. “ Hay casos que son lamentables”, Hernández afirmó sobre las denuncias procedentes de todo el estado. “En unos pocos casos, los empleadores incluso recurrieron a la violencia”.
‘Un efecto escalofriante’
Cuando los investigadores del Departamento del Trabajo llegaron a la granja en 2023, informaron que la conducta amenazante de la gerencia generaba un “efecto escalofriante” en los trabajadores y les hacía tener miedo de hablar. Dos investigadores, Espinoza y Jose Berrios, testificaron que tuvieron que hablar con los trabajadores en una gasolinera alejada del lugar de trabajo, e incluso allí algunos trabajadores se escondían detrás de basureros y autos y asomaban la cabeza para ver quién estaba cerca.
En su declaración ante la corte, Battle afirmó que el Departamento de Trabajo “al parecer incluso se llevó a algunos de esos empleados de la granja para interrogarlos en una gasolinera y detrás de un contenedor de basura”, pero un exempleado que habló con Mississippi Today explicó que, cuando los investigadores se le acercaron en la granja, fue él quien sugirió hablar en una gasolinera.
“Sabía cuál era la situación”, dijo el exempleado. “Le dije, ‘¿Tu quieres entrevistarme? ¿Quieres que te diga la verdad? Vamos a la gasolinera donde ellos no me vean y allí platicamos y yo te digo todo lo que está pasando’”.
“Nos prohibieron hablar con ustedes… Martín (Valencia) nos dijo que no podemos quejarnos y si nos estamos quejando nos manda de regreso a México”, afirmó un empleado a los investigadores en una declaración escrita.
Durante la investigación, la gerencia de Battle Fish “amenazaba habitualmente con despedir, deportar o causar daño físico” a los trabajadores que se arriesgaban a hablar con los investigadores, según un memorándum del exsecretario Su dirigido al tribunal.
En su declaración a la corte, Battle negó haber tomado represalias o haber amenazado con tomarlas contra los empleados que hablaron con los investigadores del Departamento de Trabajo, y añadió que “los agentes nos trataron a mí y a Battle Fish North de forma discriminatoria, como si hubiéramos cometido alguna irregularidad”.
Un exempleado le dijo a Mississippi Today que Houston Battle “nos grita porque él piensa que nos tiene en sus manos, porque nosotros no queremos perder una visa de trabajo, porque es difícil encontrar otra”.
“Aquí no nos tratan bien pero tenemos que trabajar. Aquí se gana algo de dinero y en México está bien difícil”, dijo otro empleado a los investigadores del Departamento de Trabajo.
Jacob Vargas Huante en su pueblo natal de Michoacán, México, en 2026. Dijo que el maltrato que sufrió en Battle Fish lo dejó “traumatizado” y reacio a buscar otro trabajo en Estados Unidos. Crédito: Cortesía de Jacob Vargas Huante Credit: Courtesy of Jacob Vargas Huante
Según Vargas, algunos empleados también temen comprometer las posibilidades de que sus familiares obtengan visas a través de Battle Fish debido a la presión de los empleadores.
“Les dicen si tú te quejas ya no te vamos a traer, no te vamos a traer a tu familia, no vamos a querer a tu primo, a tu hermano”, dijo Vargas.
Battle Fish no respondió a las solicitudes de comentarios sobre la no renovación de los contratos de trabajo de los empleados que denunciaron problemas.
Vargas trabajó en Battle Fish alrededor de ocho años antes de irse debido a lo que describió como repetidos abusos verbales y amenazas de muerte por parte de Valencia. Vargas le dijo a Mississippi Today que incluso en su ciudad natal en Michoacán, casi tres años después de renunciar su empleo en Battle Fish, “hay veces que despierto en la noche porque tengo pesadillas, sueño mucho, creo que me esta ahogando, que me electrocutan o que me mata Martín Valencia”.
El trabajo de Vargas incluía el mantenimiento del cableado eléctrico alrededor de los estanques de peces, y en su declaración judicial describió cómo Valencia intentó una vez encender la corriente eléctrica mientras él trabajaba. Francisco Chávez Barajas trabajaba junto a Vargas y recordó el incidente. “Vivimos todos esos maltratos o amenazas, lo vivimos en carne propia”, dijo Chávez.
Los registros de la Corte de Justicia del condado de Túnica muestran que, en 2019, Martín Rodríguez presentó una denuncia por agresión simple contra Jacob Huante. Vargas, cuyo segundo apellido es Huante, afirmó que el Martín que figura como denunciante es Valencia. Vargas se declaró inocente y los cargos fueron retirados en el año 2020. Vargas declaró a Mississippi Today que los cargos eran falsos y que Valencia se había inventado los detalles de un supuesto enfrentamiento. Vargas afirmó que, cuando la policía llegó a la granja, “ sí deseaba que me arrestaran para ponerle una contrademanda, porque era falso todo lo que me estaba haciendo”.
No fue posible contactar con Valencia para obtener sus comentarios, pero en su declaración ante el tribunal, Battle afirmó que ningún empleado le había informado de ninguna conducta abusiva por parte de Valencia.
En la denuncia laboral federal presentada por Vargas que precedió a la investigación de 2023, él afirmó que Valencia lo “intimida” a él y a otros trabajadores, llamándolo “pendejo” y “fucking liar” (“pinche mentiroso”). Un empleado actual describió a Battle como “explosivo” y un exempleado recordó el comportamiento de Battle como “racista” y “arrogante”.
Un exempleado señaló que en ocasiones Houston también regañó y maltrató a Valencia. Valencia “ trata más de defender a Houston que a la gente”, dijo.
En una declaración escrita de la investigación anterior del Departamento del Trabajo, un empleado describió a Battle como intolerante y propenso a enojarse. “Sí Houston se molesta con un trabajador, todos pagamos las consecuencias”, decía la declaración.
La investigadora Espinoza escribió en una declaración judicial que, cuando se disponía a salir del lugar de trabajo, escuchó una conversación entre Battle y su hermano. 
“Creen que soy amenazante, pero no saben lo que es ser amenazante”, citó Espinoza las palabras de Battle antes de que él volviera “enfurecido a la oficina principal”.
Los trabajadores también le contaron al investigador José Berrios sobre un enfrentamiento físico en el que Battle supuestamente agarró a un trabajador, lo hizo dar la vuelta y comenzó a gritarle. Battle negó tener conocimiento alguno de este incidente durante una audiencia sobre una moción en septiembre de 2023 en el Distrito Norte de Mississippi.
El padre de Battle, Bill Battle, también fue interrogado sobre prácticas violentas de represalia durante la audiencia sobre una moción. Admitió haber estado en libertad condicional por romper el parabrisas de un vehículo que conducían dos empleados. Una denuncia afirma que Vargas envió a los investigadores un video de TikTok en el que se veía a Bill Battle rompiendo el parabrisas “después de apuntarles con su arma mientras se iban tras haber ido a recoger sus últimos pagos”.
Sobrecargados y mal remunerados
Un formulario de autorización del Departamento del Trabajo que permite a Battle Fish contratar trabajadores H-2A especifica una jornada laboral de 11 horas, de las 7 a. m. a las 6 p. m., pero algunos trabajadores dijeron que, al llegar, se encontraron trabajando turnos nocturnos de entre 12 y 14 horas sin recibir pago por horas extras.
“Yo nunca descansé en varios años”, dijo un exempleado. Recordó que los investigadores le dijeron que Battle Fish le debía el pago de las horas extras de esos años, que aún no ha recibido. “Nosotros no tenemos un día de descanso”.
“Somos seres humanos, no somos máquinas de trabajo o animalitos”, dijo Vargas.
“ El contrato no dice que voy a trabajar de noche”, dijo un exempleado. “Cuando yo llegué el primer año, solo me dijo: ‘ necesito que duermas en el día porque vas a trabajar en la noche’”.
En una declaración judicial, Vargas escribió que trabajaba al menos tres horas a la semana por encima de las horas establecidas en su contrato sin paga.
Varios trabajadores afirmaron que sólo recibieron reembolsos parciales por los gastos de viaje entre sus lugares de origen y la granja, gastos que el programa H-2A exige que cubran los empleadores. En 2022 el Departamento de Trabajo informó que la planta procesadora no reembolsó en su totalidad los gastos de viaje a sus empleados.
En un correo electrónico enviado a Mississippi Today, Battle Fish negó que no hubiera cubierto completamente los gastos de viaje.
Davis dijo que no tenía conocimiento de los turnos nocturnos, pero afirmó que “Battle Fish cumple con la Ley de Normas Justas del Trabajo en lo que respecta a todos los empleados”. Esta ley federal exige que los empleadores paguen tiempo y medio cuando los empleados trabajan más de 40 horas en una semana.
‘Inhabitable’
La lavandería que comparten empleados en Battle Fish en el condado de Túnica, Miss. en junio de 2026. Crédito: exempleado anónimo Credit: Anonymous former employee
Las normas federales exigen que los empleadores proporcionen a los trabajadores con visa H-2A alojamiento, transporte confiable entre el lugar de residencia y el lugar de trabajo, y acceso a comidas. En Battle Fish, los trabajadores se alojan en pequeños departamentos y tráilers en dos ubicaciones, ambas a unos minutos en auto de la planta de procesamiento.
Una investigadora testificó que, según sus entrevistas, varios trabajadores dormían en el piso y no tenían acceso a agua corriente.
“Las estufas no sirven, ni el aire acondicionado”, se lee en la declaración de un empleado ante los investigadores. “El piso y la regadera se están hundiendo”.
Algunos trabajadores le dijeron a Mississippi Today que vivían en habitaciones hacinadas e infestadas de ratas y cucarachas, donde el piso se estaba cayendo a pedazos.
El exsecretario Su calificó a una de las instalaciones de “inhabitable” para los trabajadores en un memorándum dirigido al tribunal.
En otra declaración, un trabajador dijo, “El transporte está en muy mala condición. No tiene aire acondicionado. Los vidrios están rotos. Las llantas están malas”. Exempleados le dijeron a Mississippi Today que, debido a la falta de vehículos fiables, les resultaba difícil llegar a los supermercados y que, a veces, tenían que ir caminando al trabajo bajo fuertes lluvias.
“Habíamos estado teniendo problemas para comprar comida, era un solo vehículo para todos y eso no da suficiente y a veces no podemos ir a comprar”, escribió un empleado en una declaración.
En su declaración ante la corte, Thomas Cooper Battle afirmó que “contrariamente a lo que sostiene el Ministerio de Trabajo, los vehículos agrícolas se encontraban en un estado de mantenimiento adecuado para realizar las labores agrícolas de Battle Fish North”. También señaló que Magnolia “recurre habitualmente a los servicios de McElhaney Construction para reparar y mantener las viviendas”.
​​Battle Fish no respondió a solicitudes de comentarios sobre las condiciones de las viviendas y los vehículos de los empleados.
Los tractores se encuentran estacionados bajo un cobertizo en Battle Fish en Túnica, Miss., el jueves 9 de julio de 2026. Crédito: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
Vidas en peligro
En un rincón remoto del Delta, a miles de kilómetros de redes de apoyo familiar, los empleados señalaron que el acceso a la atención médica era otro desafío recurrente.
El Departamento de Trabajo exige que los trabajadores con visado H-2A tengan un seguro médico estatal o proporcionado por el empleador que cubra “las lesiones y enfermedades que surjan como consecuencia y en el curso del empleo del trabajador”. Sin embargo, seis de los empleados de Battle Fish que hablaron con Mississippi Today recordaron incidentes en los que ellos o sus compañeros de trabajo sufrieron enfermedades o lesiones graves y su jefe no los ayudó a acceder a tratamiento.
Un empleado que trabajó con Battle Fish por una temporada durante la pandemia de COVID-19 dijo que los encargados lo “abandonaron” cuando empezó a tener una tos que persistió durante días y le impedía dormir porque sentía que se estaba ahogando. Contó que, cuando les pidió a Battle y a Valencia que lo ayudaran a llegar a un hospital, se enojaron y le dijeron que tenía que seguir trabajando. Después de tres días, dijo que “no aguantaba” y terminó pagando 100 dólares de ida y vuelta por un taxi que lo llevó a un hospital en Memphis y 200 dólares por el tratamiento.
Los empleados también denunciaron condiciones laborales peligrosas, incluso manejando tractores sin frenos por la orilla de los estanques por la noche para operar los aireadores que oxigenan el agua. “Arriesgue mi vida varias veces”, dijo un exempleado. “Había riesgo de que uno se fuera a la laguna con todo”.
“Ellos nunca se han preocupado por el bienestar de las personas”, dijo un exempleado. Otro trabajador afirmó en una declaración ante los inspectores: “Si te pasa algún accidente ya no te llevan a veces al doctor”.
Battle Fish no respondió a las solicitudes de comentarios sobre incidentes específicos, pero escribió: “Valoramos a nuestros trabajadores y contamos con un historial de seguridad muy sólido”.
“Estamos orgullosos de ser criadores de bagre en el Delta del Mississippi y de tener la oportunidad de proveer alimentos a Estados Unidos”, afirmó la empresa en un correo electrónico enviado a Mississippi Today.
‘Vale más mi vida’
Houston Battle “los quiere tratar como si fueran esclavos, como si fueran una basura”, dijo un exempleado que ahora trabaja para un empleador en otro estado, donde afirma que las condiciones son mejores.
Vargas, ahora en México, dijo, “Jamás regresaría con Battle Fish… al final pueden dar hasta 2 o 3 millones de dólares que regrese y no regreso, porque para mí vale más mi vida.”
Para un empleado que renunció este año, los mecanismos gubernamentales de rendición de cuentas parecen lentos e ineficaces. Dijo que una abogada asociada con el consulado mexicano le informó que su caso podría tardar años. Corre el riesgo de quedar indocumentado si se queda en EE. UU. mientras espera una resolución. “Yo pienso que ellos quieren que yo me desespere, que yo no sepa qué hacer y que me regrese a México.”
“El Departamento de Trabajo no hizo nada. El gobierno no hizo nada para ayudar. El consulado mexicano es para ayudar a los mexicanos, pero ellos no hacen nada”, dijo.
En respuesta a las declaraciones de los empleados, un portavoz del Departamento de Trabajo señaló que los trabajadores que tengan dudas sobre los salarios pueden comunicarse con la División de Salarios y Horas. La cónsul general Hernández indicó que el consulado brinda orientación a los trabajadores mexicanos sobre cómo denunciar estos problemas ante las autoridades estadounidenses, pero que el consulado en sí no tiene la autoridad para investigar las presuntas violaciones.
El empleado, quien sigue en una situación de incertidumbre semanas después de haber dejado Battle Fish, dijo que durante años había estado manteniendo a sus dos hijos en México con su salario, lo que dificultó la decisión de irse. Pero al final renunció a su contrato a mitad de temporada debido a las condiciones y al trato que recibía. “No pude más. No aguanté más”, dijo. “Quiero que esto pare aquí”.
Georgie Pease se unió a Mississippi Today mediante una beca de 10 semanas con la Escuela de Periodismo de la Universidad de California en Berkeley. Claudia Amendoeira se unió a Mississippi Today mediante una beca con la Escuela de Periodismo de la Universidad de Columbia.

title: University of Michigan selects site for Los Alamos computing center
description: On Tuesday, the University of Michigan took another step toward building a “high-performance research computing center” in Ypsilanti Township, announcing it had honed in on a preferred site for the project.  The university selected a 144-acre site on Textile Road for the facility, with the north side bordering the Huron River. The university says the […]
text:
The university’s planned Research Computing Center, shown in yellow, will occupy a small fraction of the 144-acre site. The majority of the parcel will be preserved as natural space along the Huron River. | Source: The University of MichiganOn Tuesday, the University of Michigan took another step toward building a “high-performance research computing center” in Ypsilanti Township, announcing it had honed in on a preferred site for the project. 
The university selected a 144-acre site on Textile Road for the facility, with the north side bordering the Huron River. The university says the facility, which it is developing with the Los Alamos National Laboratory, will greatly expand its computing capacity, allowing researchers to analyze massive datasets and model complex systems.
According to U-M, the facility will contain an academic computing center supporting university researchers and a federal research computing center supporting Los Alamos National Laboratory’s scientific mission, which will include computational modeling to ensure the safety and reliability of the nation’s existing nuclear stockpile without live testing and national security research into areas like energy infrastructure and cybersecurity.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Universities like Michigan are built by generations willing to invest in discoveries and opportunities they may never live to see,” U-M President Domenico Grasso said in a statement. “We have that same responsibility today – to build for the students, researchers and communities who will follow us. And as we move this project forward, we are equally committed to listening to our neighbors, answering their questions and working with the community to ensure we develop this site responsibly.”
Township officials and residents oppose the project, arguing the university has not engaged with them in a transparent way. The Ypsilanti Township Board of Trustees unanimously passed a resolution in March opposing the development of a facility used for nuclear research within the township.
The community has also raised concerns over the facility’s environmental impacts, and the security of housing a federal research facility in a community with proximity to Willow Run Airport and Detroit Metropolitan Airport.
Following the announcement, U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) criticized the university for choosing to move forward with the project in Ypsilanti Township, despite the community’s protest.
“I have repeatedly urged the University to listen to the impacted community, be transparent, and answer basic questions about the impact of this project. Instead, they have rebuffed these concerns and are ignoring the pleas from residents that do not want this,” Dingell said in a statement. To make matters worse, Ypsilanti Township would see little benefit from an institution that pays no property taxes. You cannot claim to value community input and then ignore the community when you do not like what it has to say. I will continue demanding transparency, accountability, and answers.”
Ypsilanti Township board gives full support to resolution opposing Los Alamos research facility

Douglas Winters, the township’s attorney, told Michigan Advance the decision to site the facility in Ypsilanti Township was a textbook example of environmental racism, noting the economic disparity between Ann Arbor and the eastern side of Washtenaw County, alongside the township’s higher population of Black and brown residents. 
While the university committed to following the principles of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s Michigan Affordability and Responsible Growth Pledge for data centers, Winters says that promise does not offer any relief to the township. 
“It’s not enforceable,” Winters said. “Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts give a pledge.”
Paul Brown, a member of the university’s Board of Regents also issued a statement opposing the choice of a project site.
“When our developments affect communities, we have a responsibility to involve the people who live there,” Brown said. “Here, the University has failed to engage in an adequate conversation with those most affected, and I cannot stand by and support this project being shoved down their throats, in a way that looks like environmental racism. My opposition is driven by the fact that this site is currently in its natural state, is on the Huron River, and most importantly, is opposed by the local residents.”
In its announcement, the university said it would hold a town hall in Ypsilanti Township on Sept. 9 to discuss the project, with additional details on the gathering to be announced.
