title: $188 million headed to organizations to improve rural health in Florida
description: The DeSantis administration Tuesday announced $188 million in grants to organizations across the state to help improve healthcare access to 1.2 million residents of rural areas across the state. “These investments in rural Florida will strengthen hospitals and clinics, expand the rural health care workforce, and help ensure Floridians can access high-quality[...]
text:
Via Florida Agency for Health Care Administration.
The DeSantis administration Tuesday announced $188 million in grants to organizations across the state to help improve healthcare access to 1.2 million residents of rural areas across the state.
“These investments in rural Florida will strengthen hospitals and clinics, expand the rural health care workforce, and help ensure Floridians can access high-quality care in their own communities,” Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a prepared release announcing the grants.
The administration did not make available to the public the grant applications, only a state-compiled list of organizations that received grants and the amount of the grant.
That document indicates nearly 25% of the grant funds were awarded to Community Health IT — about $44 million to support “preventative care and care at home services.” It drew the largest individual grant, $18.5 million to support “preventive care and care at home” in Northeast Florida.
Community Health IT also received a $13.3 million grant, a $3.6 million grant, and a near-$8.2 million grant to support similar services in southwest, southeast, and the northwest regions of the state, respectively. Records show Kendra Siler is the company’s registered agent and president.
The third-largest grant went to Calhoun-Liberty Hospital. It received $11.2 million for “specialty and acute care.”
The DeSantis administration previously announced about $22 million in rural health transformation grants, exhausting what the federal government allotted to Florida in Year One Rural Health Transformation Program funding.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The grants are made possible by  the Rural Health Transformation Program, which provides states access to $10 billion in each of the next five years in grant funding. The grants can support expanded access to care, recruitment and retainment of providers, and for technological innovation, including remote care and emerging delivery models. Dollars cannot be used to reimburse costs of the care provided, though.
The $50 billion initiative is intended to modernize health care in these communities. At nearly $210 million, Florida ranks just above the average grant award of $200 million, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services release

Year Two funding will equal whatever facilities spent by Sept. 30, 2027. That means, for instance, that if Florida spends only $190 million by that time, Year Two grant funding will be $190 million and not the $209 million the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has approved.


There are 67 counties in Florida; 31 are considered “rural” under Florida law. The 2020 Census put Florida’s rural population at 1,183,017 people.

For purposes of the grants, the state is divided into four geographic regions and funds were awarded for projects that fell under one of five broad categories:


Preventive care and care at home; specialty and acute care
Value-based care
Rural and satellite clinics
Workforce initiatives
Health and lifestyles


The Northwest Florida region received $81 million, more than any other areas of the state.
By contrast, the southeast region, which includes heavily populated Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties, received $12 million.
“Every awardee in this round went through a competitive, merit-based review, and it shows in the caliber of the partners we are announcing today,” said Agency for Health Care Administration Secretary Shevaun L. Harris.
“These organizations know their communities, and they have shown us concrete plans to put this funding to work. This is what it looks like to close the gap between rural and urban health care access, one community at a time.”

name: Delaware
title: Audit Finds Gaps in Delaware’s Oversight of Dual Public Employment
description: State auditor says fragmented systems make it difficult to verify whether employees are ever paid for overlapping taxpayer-funded work; University of Delaware disputes auditor’s authority over records from 2023-25 DOVER, Del. — Delaware lacks a reliable statewide system for identifying and monitoring public employees who hold more than one taxpayer-supported[...]
text:
State auditor says fragmented systems make it difficult to verify whether employees are ever paid for overlapping taxpayer-funded work; University of Delaware disputes auditor’s authority over records from 2023-25
DOVER, Del. — Delaware lacks a reliable statewide system for identifying and monitoring public employees who hold more than one taxpayer-supported position, limiting the state’s ability to determine whether workers are ever paid twice for overlapping hours, according to a new performance audit from the Delaware Office of Auditor of Accounts.
The audit, covering fiscal years 2023 through 2025, does not conclude that widespread improper payments occurred. Instead, State Auditor Lydia York’s office said incomplete records, disconnected payroll systems and inconsistent procedures prevented auditors from fully determining whether agencies and other covered organizations complied with Delaware’s Dual Employment Law.
The law, enacted in 1986, is designed to prevent public employees from receiving compensation from multiple taxpayer-funded employers for the same hours. It also requires covered organizations to maintain appropriate time records, verify hours and adjust compensation when necessary.
“The State cannot reliably identify individuals engaged in dual employment or effectively determine whether statutory requirements have been met,” the auditor concluded. The report said those weaknesses create a risk that improper concurrent compensation could occur without being detected.
No Central System to Track Dual Employment
Auditors attempted to identify potentially dually employed workers using records from Delaware’s Payroll Human Resource Statewide Technology system, financial disclosure filings, legislative records and information from individual agencies.
But no state agency maintains a complete list of people subject to the dual-employment requirements, according to the audit. Delaware also uses multiple payroll systems that are not fully integrated.
The Public Integrity Commission, which has oversight responsibilities under the law, relies heavily on annual self-disclosures and manual processes and does not have an automated system that can identify people simultaneously employed by multiple public entities, auditors found.
At individual agencies and organizations, auditors also found inconsistent procedures for documenting employees’ hours, obtaining supervisory verification and making payroll adjustments when work schedules overlap.
The report recommends creating a centralized system capable of identifying and tracking dual employment, improving integration among payroll systems, strengthening internal controls and recordkeeping, clarifying oversight responsibilities and providing the Public Integrity Commission additional resources.
Auditor and University of Delaware Disagree Over Records
One of the audit’s most significant limitations involved the University of Delaware.
The Auditor of Accounts requested personnel, payroll, timekeeping and scheduling information involving selected university employees who also held other taxpayer-supported public positions during the audit period.
UD did not provide the requested records. As a result, auditors said they could not determine whether the selected individuals received compensation from multiple taxpayer-supported positions during overlapping work hours.
The disagreement centers on whether the Dual Employment Law applied to the university during fiscal years 2023 through 2025.
UD maintains that it did not.
In its formal response, the university said it is a privately governed, state-aided institution rather than a state agency or political subdivision and argued that the version of the law in effect during the audit period did not cover university employees.
The university pointed to House Bill 38, signed into law in 2025, which established specific dual-employment reporting requirements for institutions of higher education receiving state funds. Those requirements took effect May 22, 2026. UD contends the legislation demonstrates that those obligations did not previously apply to the university.
UD said it recognizes its obligations under the new law and intends to work with the auditor on records required after the law’s effective date. However, the university said it would not release confidential employment records for fiscal years 2023-25 when, in its view, no statutory requirement existed to do so.
Auditor Rejects UD’s Interpretation
York’s office disagreed with the university’s legal interpretation.
The auditor acknowledged UD’s unusual status as a privately governed, state-aided institution and said the audit was not attempting to regulate university personnel decisions.
Instead, the auditor argued that its authority extends to determining whether state-appropriated money was spent in compliance with Delaware law.
“Public funds do not lose their character as State funds merely because they are disbursed through a state-aided institution rather than directly through a state agency,” the auditor wrote.
The auditor also cited a 2008 Delaware attorney general opinion concerning application of the dual-employment law to state-funded salaries at UD.
York’s office characterized House Bill 38 differently from the university, saying the legislation clarified reporting procedures for higher education institutions but did not create the auditor’s underlying authority to examine how state appropriations are spent.
The dispute remains unresolved for the years covered by the audit.
15 Individuals Affected by Records Dispute
The missing UD records affected the auditor’s testing involving 15 people who held positions associated with the General Assembly, courts or other state offices during the audit period.
The report identifies them as Sherry Dorsey-Walker, Melissa Minor-Brown, Madinah Wilson-Anton, Sophie Phillips, Michael Smith, Sarah “Tizzy” Lockman, Marie Pinkney, Martin O’Connor, Sheldon Rennie, Monica Horton, Janell Ostroski, Peter Burcat, Bethany Hall-Long, Cora Scott and Evan Park.
The audit does not find that those individuals were improperly paid or violated the Dual Employment Law.
Rather, the auditor said it could not determine whether the law was followed because it did not have the university records necessary to compare work schedules, payroll information and timekeeping records.
That distinction is central to the finding: the names appear because auditors were unable to complete their testing, not because the report established wrongdoing by any of the individuals.
Some Previous Problems Remain
The audit also followed up on findings from an earlier review covering fiscal years 2020 through 2022.
Auditors said a previous finding involving UD remains open because the university had not taken action to address it for the period reviewed. A finding involving the City of Dover also remains open, although Dover has drafted a policy that was awaiting City Council approval when the audit was completed.
Previous findings involving Delaware State University, Eastside Charter School and Delaware Technical Community College were considered resolved after the institutions provided evidence of new policies or controls.
Accountability Problem, Not Finding of Fraud
The broader conclusion of the audit is less about documenting fraud than about the state’s ability to detect a problem if one occurs.
Auditors cautioned that government performance audits are not designed to uncover every instance of fraud, waste or noncompliance. In this case, the larger obstacle was that records and systems were often insufficient to provide reasonable assurance that the law was being followed statewide.
Until Delaware develops integrated reporting, standardized recordkeeping and clearer responsibility for monitoring dual employment, the auditor said the possibility that improper overlapping compensation could occur without detection will remain.
To Go Box:

What is dual employment? Holding a public job while also serving in another qualifying elected, appointed or taxpayer-supported position.
What does Delaware law prohibit? Receiving taxpayer-funded compensation from more than one covered position for the same working hours.
Did the audit find widespread double payments? No. The auditor said the state lacked sufficient systems and records to fully determine compliance.
Why is the University of Delaware involved? Auditors sought UD payroll and timekeeping records for selected employees with other public positions. UD declined, arguing the law covering the 2023-25 period did not apply to the university.
Were the 15 people named in the report accused of wrongdoing? No. Auditors said they lacked sufficient records to determine whether dual-employment rules were followed for those individuals.
What happens going forward? A law that took effect May 22, 2026, establishes specific dual-employment recordkeeping and reporting requirements for state-funded institutions of higher education. UD says it will comply with those requirements prospectively.

Source: Delaware Office of Auditor of Accounts, Dual Employment Performance Audit for Fiscal Years Ended June 30, 2023-2025.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Federal appeals court protects longer petitioning time for South Dakota ballot questions
description: A South Dakota group won another victory Tuesday in its effort to preserve adequate time for petitioning questions onto statewide ballots, but a state official immediately pledged to continue the fight in court. A federal appeals panel upheld a lower court’s ruling that state lawmakers violated the First Amendment when they moved up the deadline […]
text:
The Warren E. Burger Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse on Jan. 9, 2025, in downtown St. Paul, Minnesota. The courthouse hosted oral arguments in June 2026 in a South Dakota lawsuit over ballot-question petition deadlines. (Photo by Ellen Schmidt/Minnesota Reformer)
https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/petition-signatures-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
A South Dakota group won another victory Tuesday in its effort to preserve adequate time for petitioning questions onto statewide ballots, but a state official immediately pledged to continue the fight in court.
A federal appeals panel upheld a lower court’s ruling that state lawmakers violated the First Amendment when they moved up the deadline for submitting petition signatures by three months. After the three-judge appeals panel issued its ruling, South Dakota’s attorney general said he will request a review by the entire 11-member 8th Circuit Court of Appeals.
Petitioners need 17,508 signatures from registered voters to put a proposed law on the ballot in South Dakota, and 35,017 signatures for a proposed state constitutional amendment. South Dakota lawmakers approved legislation last year that moved the deadline for filing signed petitions in a general election year from the first Tuesday in May to the first Tuesday in February.
A group that’s been involved in numerous ballot questions, Dakotans for Health, challenged the law in federal court. Last August, a district court judge ruled the law violates the First Amendment, writing that moving the deadline three months earlier “arguably goes beyond merely inconvenient and enters the realm of severe.” The state appealed that ruling.
Judge blocks South Dakota from enforcing earlier ballot question petition deadline

During arguments heard by the three-judge appeals panel in June, the state’s lawyer, Paul Swedlund of the state Attorney General’s Office, said a shorter deadline gives more time for potential litigation over ballot questions to play out.
“The more time that you have to litigate a case, the better chance it is that you’re going to get it finished,” Swedlund said then.
Judge Raymond Gruender disagreed with that assertion, writing in Tuesday’s opinion that “even if that were the case, however, nothing in the record indicates that the new deadline advances that interest in any meaningful way.”
Gruender added that the state didn’t provide “sufficient factual or legal support” for its argument that pre-election litigation on petitions would bolster the confidence of voters in the initiative and referendum process. Judge Jane Kelly joined Gruender in the decision.
In a dissenting opinion, Judge James Loken wrote, “the Constitution does not authorize this federal court micromanagement of state elections.” The now-unenforceable law would have furthered South Dakota’s “interest in election integrity by extending the time for pre-election petition litigation,” Loken added.
Republican South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley highlighted Loken’s comments Tuesday in a news release.
“While we respect the panel’s decision, we still believe the South Dakota Legislature reached a fair solution to our petition process, without infringing on the First Amendment,” Jackley said.
Law and litigation affect petitioning efforts
Rick Weiland of Dakotans for Health told South Dakota Searchlight in June that his group was still collecting signatures for two potential ballot questions. He believed there was no enforceable deadline, because state lawmakers had not passed any further legislation regarding the petition deadline as the lawsuit played out.
Though the group is still collecting signatures, the effort may be winding down soon, Weiland said. Counties face a Sept. 16 deadline to have ballots printed for the Nov. 3 general election.

Rick Weiland, of Dakotans for Health, answers a question from moderators during an election town hall at Dakota Wesleyan University in Mitchell on Sept. 19, 2024. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)

“We’re really far away from being able to close this loop in a quick, fast way,” he said. “I think it’s very unlikely we’re going to be able to submit.”
The law “did have a chilling effect on our ability to raise the funds we needed, and to basically get volunteers engaged,” Weiland said. “It takes a well-funded, well-coordinated effort to be successful, and with that bill hanging over our heads and tied up in the courts, it’s very difficult to get that kind of support.”
His group is circulating two potential constitutional amendments that Weiland said would be a check on the power legislators have in Pierre.
The first of those amendments would protect voter-approved ballot measures from being changed by state lawmakers for seven years. Then, lawmakers would need a supermajority vote in both chambers and would still need voter approval.
The second would require that changes to the initiated ballot measure process that are approved by the Legislature — like regulations on how organizations or individuals collect signatures — would automatically be referred to voters at the next general election.
Legislators have placed four of their own proposed constitutional amendments on the ballot this year. Those amendments would allow the state to withdraw from expanded Medicaid if federal funding for it declines, clarify that a voter must be a U.S. citizen, establish a trust fund for unclaimed property proceeds, and require that future state constitutional amendments receive 60% support from voters rather than a simple majority.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska State Board of Education unanimously approves North Omaha girls school
description: LINCOLN — After a four-day delay, the Nebraska State Board of Education unanimously passed conditional approval of a nonpublic girls school in North Omaha. The board voted 6-2 Friday to postpone its vote until Tuesday to give members time to question the school’s founder and CEO, DérNecia Phillips, Ph.D. The school, Identity Preparatory Academy, is […]
text:
State Board of Education President Elizabeth Tegtmeier, left, and state Education Commissioner Brian Maher. March 8, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — After a four-day delay, the Nebraska State Board of Education unanimously passed conditional approval of a nonpublic girls school in North Omaha.
The board voted 6-2 Friday to postpone its vote until Tuesday to give members time to question the school’s founder and CEO, DérNecia Phillips, Ph.D.
The school, Identity Preparatory Academy, is set to open in the Hope Center for Kids and is looking to serve fourth through eighth grade students in North Omaha, starting with fourth and fifth grade in its first year and adding grades each year after. Its website says enrollment is closed for the 2026-27 school year.
Board member Kirk Penner had asked to postpone the vote because of concerns with wording that had been temporarily posted on the school’s website, including “abolitionist framework” and “liberatory practices.” Board President Elizabeth Tegtmeier elaborated Tuesday that the worry was how an abolitionist framework fit into state law on American civics.
Phillips, who was present at both the Friday and Tuesday meetings, said Tuesday that the term “abolitionist framework” was referring to the school’s goal of abolishing the school-to-prison pipeline that she said is a prevalent concern in the North Omaha community. Though the school still holds that goal, she said, the words were removed and replaced with an “appreciative framework” that was developed by the community.
On Tuesday, both Penner and the board’s Vice President Liz Renner said if the board had not approved Penner’s motion to postpone the vote, the four conservatives on the eight-member board would have voted no on the conditional approval, leading to the motion’s failure.
“While I thought the additional scrutiny and request for more conversation at the last minute was unfair, I could also recognize it wasn’t ‘no,’” Renner said. “It was still a request to learn.”
Penner said he, alongside board members Sherry Jones and Maggie Douglas, met with Phillips at Identity Prep on Monday for about 90 minutes, and he asked her directly about the past website language. He said Phillips’ responses were consistent with her testimony Friday and Tuesday and in previous correspondence, which left him with enough confidence in the school’s mission.
“Identity Preparatory Academy is going to change education for young scholars in North Omaha,” Penner said. “I am such a believer that I have sent a check to help support their mission.”
Phillips and several other testifiers Tuesday noted the delay in approval hurt Identity Prep’s fundraising efforts, and Phillips said some families rescinded their student’s enrollment because of the uncertainty about whether the school would open. Multiple testifiers called the timing of the vote “harmful” and “disrespectful,” as the school plans to open Aug. 19.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Eighteen people testified at Tuesday’s meeting, virtually and in person, all of whom supported Identity Prep’s conditional approval. Board member Deborah Neary noted that roughly 250 people watched Tuesday’s meeting remotely, in addition to about 20 in-person attendees.
Testifiers largely called out the board for using different criteria to justify their concerns that were not used in the approval process for other nonpublic schools. Several testifiers spoke about the positive impact they expect the school to have in North Omaha and said they wished such an option was available for them when they were growing up.
State Sen. Terrell McKinney, who represents North Omaha, said watching Friday’s meeting was disappointing.
“We hear of all these other negative narratives about young people that come from our community,” McKinney said. “But when we take the initiative to try to educate ourselves and educate our kids, we still receive pushback, and that is a sad reality that we’re in in America and in the state of Nebraska.”
Regarding the concerns about “abolitionist framework,” McKinney said people tend to “weaponize words” to fit a narrative they believe.
“Individuals on the board, I assume, feel some type of way about young black girls being educated by black women in our community,” McKinney said.
Lisa Schonhoff, who chairs the board’s planning and evaluation committee, spoke to the timing concerns shared by testifiers. She said Identity Prep submitted its application on June 4 — nearly a month after its May 7 deadline — and because the board did not meet in July, there was limited time to discuss possible concerns.
“I know it’s a bummer, that it’s close to the start of school, and can be a little bit difficult,” Schonhoff said. “But I think the public needs to understand that that’s how the timing worked out.”
Schonhoff also expressed appreciation to board members that “refrained from seeking out social media and the press to cause more hate and division,” likely in reference to Neary who made statements at Friday’s meeting and on social media saying that she believed the hesitance to approve Identity Prep was based in racism.
Penner also called out Neary by name, telling her to “stop the bull—” and argued that the four conservative board members “are not group thinkers like those on the left.”
Neary stood by her statements Tuesday, saying she had been hearing for a month behind the scenes that Identity Prep might not be approved due to racist concerns. She accused the four conservative board members of intentionally blindsiding the board with last-minute issues that weren’t brought up in committee, contributing to the board’s dysfunction.
Though the delay brought some negative impacts to Identity Prep, Phillips said she was excited to show board members what the North Omaha community has built for its girls. She added that she felt that Penner, Jones and Douglas had truly listened to what she had to say.
“I appreciate the fact that our community has shown up in a mighty way today, and that we’re having these important conversations about education,” Phillips said. “And what I would say to our community is, don’t let that stop here.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Outside of Little Rock, Arkansas counties and cities move ahead on data center moratoriums
description: Little Rock and Pulaski County haven’t paused approvals of data centers — despite months of trying — even as they’ve faced community pushback over two major facilities planned in the area. But across Arkansas, other cities and counties aren’t having the same problem. Independence County’s quorum court unanimously passed a five-year moratorium on Monday, the[...]
text:
The construction site for the Serverfarm data center in Clarksville, Arkansas on July 13, 2026. Construction on it began earlier this year. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Little Rock and Pulaski County haven’t paused approvals of data centers — despite months of trying — even as they’ve faced community pushback over two major facilities planned in the area. But across Arkansas, other cities and counties aren’t having the same problem.
Independence County’s quorum court unanimously passed a five-year moratorium on Monday, the latest — and longest — adopted in the state. Russellville passed a six-month pause on approving the facilities last month. Union and Carroll counties each passed a one-year pause in June.
“We would not be able to support the needs of a data center, nor would we want to,” Independence County Justice of the Peace Brad Covington, a Republican, told the Advocate. “It’s not something that the citizens want or need, and it doesn’t do anything for the citizens of Independence County.”


The county’s moratorium was first reported by White River Now.
While there are no known data center projects planned for the area, Covington said a recent wind turbine development “absolutely” contributed to the quorum court’s decision this week. The county passed a three-year ban on wind turbines in October 2025 — only to find out about two months ago that a company had dozens of contracts to build turbines that predated the court’s measure, he said. 
“It just raised our eyebrow as to all these things that can be going on behind the scenes, that there’s not anything in place that requires these companies or people to come before any local authorities,” he said of the wind turbine situation and how it related to the data center pause. 
“They can just, willy nilly, sell land and build data centers or crypto mines or any of this stuff.”



We want to hear from you
Click here to submit information about regulations, moratoria or data center projects in Arkansas. Advocate reporters will fact check the information provided and update the map as needed.



That realization, combined with worries about water and power and what Covington said was a relative lack of jobs and money that would accompany a possible data center, prompted the county to act.
While efforts to halt data centers have been more successful in areas of Arkansas where Republicans are dominant compared to Democrats, the pushback nationally has been bipartisan. Texas’ Republican governor ordered a temporary halt on the approval of new data centers, weeks after New York enacted the first statewide moratorium in the nation. 
Meanwhile, Americans have flooded local government meetings and social media with messages of opposition to data centers.
The advent of artificial intelligence sparked a boom in announced data center projects across the country. Companies like Google and Meta are racing to build out the computing capabilities required by the most advanced AI models, which in turn have resulted in larger and more energy-intensive data center projects. 
The move by the quorum court in Independence County and other Republican-leaning counties comes as Little Rock and Pulaski County have repeatedly failed to pass moratoria on data centers since May. 
The latest votes highlight the political dynamics surrounding data centers in Arkansas. Republicans hold a majority of seats on the Carroll, Independence and Union county quorum courts. Democrats hold a majority on Pulaski County’s quorum court while Little Rock’s city board seats are technically nonpartisan.
Mixed opinions, limited information about $6.6 billion data center in Arkansas River Valley

Proposals for regulating the facilities have seen warmer reception among the local governing bodies for the state’s capital city. Little Rock passed regulations in June after fierce social media blowback, while regulations were on the agenda for the county quorum court’s agenda committee on Tuesday night.
Meanwhile, Fayetteville passed regulations on data centers in June, while Fort Smith’s city council planned to discuss them Tuesday night.
There are currently six large data center projects proposed in Arkansas — two of which are already under construction. 
Independence County doesn’t have any proposed centers, according to County Judge Kevin Jeffrey, but he said the quorum court was following the developments around the country and state. 
“The question marks, or the questions, seemed to have gotten more intense than the answers,” he said.
The Republican judge said he believes the outstanding questions about the facilities in other parts of the state and the country warranted the pause. 
“It’s responsible, for the citizenry, to not have regrets but rather be on the front end of it and be prepared. I think over time, a lot of these questions should be answered,” Jeffrey said. “In the meantime, it just gives us some breathing room to take everything in.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA child welfare deaths continue to drop after spiking last year
description: Deaths and critical injuries in Washington’s child welfare system continued to decline this spring, after a record high in 2025 that had lawmakers considering changing state law. Six children died and five more nearly died from April through June, according to new data from the state Department of Children, Youth and Families, which runs the […]
text:
(Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)Deaths and critical injuries in Washington’s child welfare system continued to decline this spring, after a record high in 2025 that had lawmakers considering changing state law.
Six children died and five more nearly died from April through June, according to new data from the state Department of Children, Youth and Families, which runs the child welfare system. In this period last year, the total of the two types of incidents was 14. 
Through the first six months of this year, 10 children died and eight more suffered critical injuries. This is half of what the state saw from January through June 2025. 
Department of Children, Youth and Families Secretary Tana Senn said she is “relieved to see the number of cases continue to decline,” while noting “every critical incident is a tragedy.”
Washington state officials attribute the dramatic drop at least partially to the recent overall decrease in opioid-related overdoses. In the first quarter this year, fatal opioid overdoses were down over 9% from late 2025, according to preliminary state data. Meanwhile, emergency department visits for suspected opioid overdoses were up 10%. 
“This underscores the impact of the broader ecosystem on the families we serve,” Senn said.
Of the 18 incidents so far this year, four were related to fentanyl. Last year, 27 of the 57 were tied to the synthetic opioid.
(Graphic courtesy of the Washington state Department of Children, Youth and Families.)
The numbers only cover children involved in the state child welfare system in the year before the maltreatment-related death or critical injury.
The cases this most recent quarter included ones related to drowning, opioids and safe sleep. The sleep incidents often involve parental substance use, according to the Department of Children, Youth and Families.
Several recent moves by the department may also be contributing to the downturn. 
For example, starting in June 2025, child welfare staff were mandated to conduct “safe child consults” for cases involving opioid use and a child younger than 3 before they could be closed. By the end of the year, over 23,000 had been completed, with nearly 40% involving high-potency synthetic opioids, like fentanyl.
“Over the past year, we have made some internal shifts in our practice, strengthened partnerships, and are heartened by the public health data showing a decrease in overall drug overdoses,” Senn said.
State legislators earmarked money this year to help with the issue. 
This included a few million dollars to hire more caseworkers; $876,000 for a public health nurse program in some high-need communities to serve families with a child under age 3 where drug use is a factor; $188,000 for a referral program to family resource centers for parents with children older than 3; and $252,000 to expand a program that helps coordinate care and navigate resources for expecting mothers and newborns with prenatal drug exposure.
State agencies, including the Department of Children, Youth and Families, will make requests in September to Gov. Bob Ferguson for funding in the next budget. But money is tight as the state faces another budget shortfall. Agency officials have said they see a need for additional staff training specific to parents with substance use disorder to keep infants safe while sleeping. 
The current budget also funded a new workgroup focused on addressing last year’s rise in injuries and deaths through increased drug treatment options.
Also helping the situation potentially is a 2023 law directing judges deciding on whether to remove children from their parents to “give great weight” to the presence of synthetic opioids. 
The policy was a fix to the earlier Keeping Families Together Act that lawmakers passed to raise the standard to remove children from their homes and keep them with other relatives instead of foster care. Conservatives have blamed this law for the spike in fatalities in recent years.
The Legislature considered several bills this year to address the rise in deaths and injuries, but all stalled.

text:
Delaware players have until 9:45 p.m. Wednesday to buy tickets for one of the largest lottery prizes offered in 2026
DOVER, Del. — Delaware lottery players have until 9:45 p.m. Wednesday to get a ticket for a Powerball jackpot that has climbed to an estimated $1 billion, putting the prize among the biggest lottery jackpots offered this year.
The jackpot for the Wednesday, Aug. 12, drawing carries an estimated cash value of $433.1 million before taxes, according to the Delaware Lottery.
The advertised $1 billion prize would be paid as an annuity, while a winner choosing the cash option would receive a one-time payment. Final jackpot amounts can increase depending on national ticket sales.
No ticket matched all six numbers in Monday night’s drawing, allowing the jackpot to cross the $1 billion mark.
Monday’s winning numbers were 6, 37, 54, 55 and 64. The Powerball was 10, and the Power Play multiplier was 3.
Although there was no jackpot winner, two tickets sold in California and Maryland matched all five white balls to win $1 million each. A Tennessee ticket matched the five white balls and included Power Play, making it worth $2 million.
Jackpot Has Been Growing All Summer
The Powerball jackpot has been growing since May 2, when tickets sold in Florida and Texas split a $20 million jackpot. By late July, Powerball officials were already calling it the largest Powerball prize of 2026.
The continuing roll has now pushed the jackpot into the rare $1 billion range, likely generating increased interest at Delaware Lottery retailers ahead of Wednesday night’s cutoff.
Powerball drawings are held Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays at 10:59 p.m. Eastern time. Delaware Lottery retailers stop selling tickets for that night’s drawing at 9:45 p.m.
How Powerball Works
Powerball tickets cost $2 per play. Players select five numbers from 1 through 69 and one Powerball number from 1 through 26.
Power Play, which can increase most non-jackpot prizes, costs an additional $1.
The odds of winning the Powerball jackpot are approximately 1 in 292.2 million, while the odds of winning any Powerball prize are about 1 in 24.9.
Delaware requires lottery players to be at least 18 years old. Winners should check tickets carefully after the drawing and follow Delaware Lottery requirements for claiming prizes.

name: Maryland Matters
title: ‘Enough is enough’: Activists push back as BGE requests another rate increase
description: Consumer advocates, environmental groups and workers’ unions rallied Tuesday against the latest rate hike proposal from Baltimore Gas & Electric, calling it unjustified, particularly after the Exelon utility earned a record-setting $578 million in profits last year.
text:
An advocate holds a sign opposing Baltimore Gas & Electric's rate increase request during a news conference Tuesday in Baltimore. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Consumer advocates, environmental groups and workers’ unions are pushing back against the latest rate hike proposal from Baltimore Gas & Electric, arguing that it is unjustified, particularly after the Exelon utility earned a record-setting $578 million in profits last year.
BGE estimates that, if approved by Maryland regulators at the Public Service Commission, its proposal would raise customer bills by $8 per month. The request would increase the monopoly utility’s “return on equity” — essentially its guaranteed profit margin for capital investments — from 9.5% to 10.4%.
“After six years of annual rate hikes and record-breaking profits, BGE has come forward not with solutions, but with more problems. Enough is enough,” said Emily Scarr, a senior adviser with consumer advocacy group Maryland PIRG. “We’re calling on the Public Service Commission to reject BGE’s rate hike, and to lower BGE’s already excessive profit rate.”
BGE’s latest request comes with rising utility costs squarely in the political limelight. During the past two legislative sessions, Maryland lawmakers have passed legislation aimed at lowering bills. They believe their most recent attempt will lower customer bills by at least $150 annually, with new rules for utility companies and cuts to an energy efficiency program subsidized by customer bills. As of March 2026, about 290,000 BGE customers are behind on their payments.
Advocates unfurled a banner calling during a Tuesday news conference in Baltimore, opposing a rate increase request from Baltimore Gas & Electric. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
The distribution rates that BGE charges for electricity have increased at about twice the rate of inflation since 2010, according to data from the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel, which represents ratepayers in rate proceedings before the PSC. BGE’s gas rates have increased three times more than the rate of inflation during that same timespan, according to the office.
BGE has said that its July request for a $156 million increase is based on “bare bones” spending that it must undertake in order to maintain the electric system, which serves about 1.3 million Marylanders.
“We hear from customers all the time: Their No. 1 priority right now is affordability,” said Nick Alexopulos, a spokesman for BGE. “They are facing increased costs of all life essentials. Energy is one of them, but it’s food, it’s housing, it’s transportation, it’s childcare.
“This rate case from BGE is the bare minimum to keep the lights on,” he said. “We did that for a reason. We did that because we heard our customers.”
But for the BGE customers who gathered Tuesday in downtown Baltimore outside of BGE’s headquarters, frustrations remain.
Angel Nuñez, who serves as a bishop at the Bilingual Christian Church in East Baltimore, said his church hears from numerous parishioners struggling with high utility bills. The church itself recently received a $3,000 bill, Nuñez said.
“They bring it to the church and ask us to help them out to pay these bills, these crazy bills that are going on,” he said. “But there’s a problem. We can’t help them. You know why? Because we’re getting these bills in the thousands.”
Poll: Utility costs, the economy and taxes top of mind for voters

Tuesday’s news conference also attracted representatives of a few local unions, who said their members are feeling the pinch from high utility bills, in addition to higher costs at the gas pump, the grocery store and more.
“The people caring for our communities are struggling to take care of themselves,” said Ricarra Jones, the political director for 1199 Service Employees International Union United Healthcare Workers East.
The Public Service Commission has said that a decision in the case is not expected until early 2027. During a brief hearing in Baltimore on Tuesday, commissioners were presented with a possible schedule that would involve evidentiary hearings in November and a final decision by the end of January.
The commission operates almost like a jury at a trial, said Chairman Kumar Barve, who represented Montgomery County as a Democrat in the legislature for decades before taking the post.
“The burden of proof is on the company, BGE, to prove that they’re correct and that they need higher rates,” Barve said.
BGE’s profit rate, storm costs debated
BGE, which was acquired by Chicago-based Exelon in 2012, argues that its return on equity must be competitive — compared to alternative investments with comparable risks — in order for it to attract investors who can provide capital to cover its costs. If BGE struggles to attract those investors, consumers can face other cost increases.
Angel Nuñez, a bishop at the Bilingual Christian Church in East Baltimore, speaks against a rate hike request Tuesday. Nuñez said his church recently got a $3,000 BGE bill, and parishioners are often asking for help from the church for their bills. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
During its last rate case, BGE also requested a 10.4% return, but received 9.5% instead.
“We propose what is — in our opinion — what we need to finance our investments, to make sure that the immediate impact to customers is as low as possible and that we recover it over time,” Alexopulos said.
During this year’s legislative session, Del. Andre Johnson (D-Harford) sponsored a bill that would have required the PSC to compare requests from investor-owned utilities such as BGE against the average expected 10-year U.S. equity market return.
Johnson withdrew the bill before its hearing, citing concerns with the way it was drafted. But consumer advocates like PIRG say they plan to fight for the legislation to make a return in 2027.
“We expect that [legislation] to come back, to direct the PSC to make sure that rate … is in line with the amount of money it actually costs to attract investors, and not a penny over that,” Scarr said. “Because every penny over that is just adding to their profits.”
In February testimony filed in support of Johnson’s bill, the Office of People’s Counsel argued that, because BGE is a monopoly utility and investors’ risks are low, it should receive a far lower return on equity.
The office pointed to one study, which showed average 10-year U.S. equity market return forecasts from large investment firms in early 2025 was at 6.7%. If BGE were held to a 6% rate, customers would have saved $282 million from 2024 through 2026, the office found.
Scarr also expressed concern that one component of BGE’s rate request may violate “the spirit” of the energy bill passed by the General Assembly this year, which set a one-year ban on the use of “forecast test years.” That’s when utilities request rate increases based on future projections, rather than asking for reimbursements for past spending.
Maryland Public Service Commission Chair Kumar Barve speaks during Tuesday’s hearing on a $156 million rate increase request from Baltimore Gas & Electric. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
BGE is seeking a certain amount of storm recovery costs in advance, by calculating a historic average for storm costs, and adding it to rates automatically each year. In traditional ratemaking, utilities incur costs, and then request reimbursement from regulators, who determine whether their costs were reasonable and prudent.
“They’re asking for more money for expenses for 2026 when they already got a rate increase for this year. That doesn’t seem to go with the spirit of that law,” Scarr said.
But the company argues that it needs the advance storm cost payments in order to be more nimble, especially as storms increase in frequency and intensity amid a changing climate. And the customer base would be reimbursed if they overpay, Alexopolus said.
“If the weather isn’t as bad and we don’t have to spend as much to do storm restoration, rates will go down because of this rider in the future,” Alexopulos said. “Now, if the weather is much, much worse and we have to spend more money to do storm restoration, then rates will adjust accordingly based on that. But we need a baseline.”
Also facing scrutiny is BGE’s proposed FlexPay program, which BGE advertises as a flexible, optional program that would let customers prepay for their energy use.
But advocates say the customers who sign up for the program would be waiving traditional termination protections, allowing BGE to shut off their power more quickly after late payments.
Olivia Wein, a senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, said she worries the program would place families on a “hamster wheel of stress.”
“[It] should really be called StressPay, because what this means is that you will have to keep an eye on the meter — and when it starts ticking to zero, you’re about to be disconnected,” Wein said. “This is going to result in faster and more disconnections, and constant stress.”
