title: Despite Trump order, Maine to stick with current childhood vaccine guidance
description: Maine will continue to follow guidance from trusted medical and public health organizations in light of President Donald Trump’s executive order reshaping childhood vaccination recommendations, the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday. “President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are playing politics with the lives of our nation’s children.[...]
text:
A nurse gives vaccinates a teenager at the Latino Community Development Agency on July 9, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)Maine will continue to follow guidance from trusted medical and public health organizations in light of President Donald Trump’s executive order reshaping childhood vaccination recommendations, the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday.
“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are playing politics with the lives of our nation’s children. Vaccines are safe and effective and save lives,” said Gov. Janet Mills in a statement, which noted the state would continue to follow the guidance of the American Academy of Pediatrics on childhood vaccine recommendations. “Maine will continue to follow the science and the facts, and our approach to vaccines remains unchanged by yesterday’s executive order.” 
Foreseeing the tension between the Trump administration’s efforts to pare down immunization requirements and evidence-based recommendations from other organizations, Maine lawmakers passed legislation this spring to detach the state’s vaccine policy from federal guidance, allowing Maine to also accept recommendations from the American Academy of Family Physicians and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
The new laws also protect pharmacists who administer vaccines from liability and grant more authority to prescribe certain vaccines to children and adults, expanding access to immunizations.
Trump’s executive order — which calls on federal programs and funding to “support maximal parental choice over childhood vaccines” — came as the president continued to erroneously connect vaccines to autism during a White House event on Monday. His administration has attempted to de-emphasize childhood vaccinations’ importance, and with Monday’s executive order, wants to reduce the number of routine vaccines kids receive or, in some cases, space them out.
Healthcare experts and politicians from both sides of the aisle opposed the order, saying it will cause confusion.
Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, called the executive order — which comes as the country reaches a 35-year high of measles cases — dangerous. “There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance,” Racine said in a statement.
“Dozens of studies involving millions of people show there is no link between vaccines and autism, and yet federal leaders continue to promote this outdated, disproven idea to scare families,” Racine added.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Democrats repeat calls to shut down Delaney Hall
description: Three House Democrats appeared in Morristown Tuesday to criticize the conditions inside New Jersey’s two migrant jails.
text:
Reps. Frank Pallone, Analilia Mejia, and Rob Menendez exit Delaney Hall after visiting the detention center in Newark on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Democratic lawmakers met in a Morristown church Tuesday to repeat calls to shut down Newark immigration jail Delaney Hall and raise alarms about medical care for detainees held there.


Their appearance came 10 days after the death of Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo, a Salvadoran man who was held at Delaney Hall for six weeks and whose family said was denied diabetes and blood pressure medication. Families of others who died at Delaney Hall also spoke with Rep. Analilia Mejia, Rep. Rob Menendez, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, along with local leaders from Morris County.


“Three deaths at Delaney Hall — completely and totally unacceptable. Fifty-five deaths in ICE custody since the beginning of Donald Trump’s time in office, over the last 17 months or so,” said Jeffries. “That means one death in ICE custody every six days. That is not America.”


Lopez Cornejo was the second Delaney Hall detainee to die in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody since the facility opened in May 2025. Jean Wilson Brutus, a 41-year-old Haitian man, died within a day of arriving at the facility in December. Menendez said last week there was a third death of a person who was having a medical episode while being processed at Delaney Hall but was released from custody before they died at a local hospital.


The three lawmakers said they also heard from former detainees who said they suffered medical neglect while held at Delaney Hall and the state’s other migrant jail, the Elizabeth Detention Center.


A woman named Margarita who said she was detained for two months at the Elizabeth facility following a raid in Dover described being pepper-sprayed and watching immigration agents pin her husband to the ground, despite her son shouting in English that he recently had spinal surgery. It was an experience that left her “traumatized,” she said.


Inside the facility, she said, detainees were served spoiled food. A pregnant detainee missed her prenatal appointments, and another detainee waited five days to see a doctor for a toothache, she said.


Mejia said that when she visited Margarita in detention, she found that Margarita was being given a quarter of her diabetes medication. Her medication was only restored after pressure from members of Congress who conducted oversight visits, Mejia said.


“I want you to think about what our government is doing to human beings, that we would treat each other with such callousness, that we would allow a human being to suffer, knowing that they are deteriorating in a preventable way. Her doctor was not contacted, her pharmacy was not contacted, and her family was ignored,” she said.


Menendez, who has made repeated oversight visits to Delaney Hall, said Geo Group, the private company that runs the facility under a 15-year contract with the federal government worth over $1 billion, staffs the site with only one physician who is not present around the clock.


He said no physician was at the jail on the day Lopez Cornejo died. If someone has a medical emergency when the physician is not there, the people attending to that individual are either nurses or physician assistants, he added.


“These are the types of things that we have raised over and over again,” Menendez said, “and you are seeing the dire consequences of them not being able to adequately provide healthcare to the individuals that they are bringing through Delaney Hall and Elizabeth Detention Center.”


The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has disputed that medical care inside Delaney Hall is lax.


“All detainees are provided with proper meals, water, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers. In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens,” a recent, unsigned statement from the department reads. “It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody. This includes medical, dental, and mental health services as available, and access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee governor refuses clemency for death row inmate; execution set Thursday
description: Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee is declining to stop Thursday’s scheduled execution of death row inmate Darrell Hines, even as his attorneys claim he could suffer cruel and unusual punishment because of an “under-skilled” physician. “After deliberate consideration of Anthony Darrell Hines’ request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding[...]
text:
Gov. Bill Lee will not grant a reprieve to a Tennessee death row inmate asking the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in on his case.  (Photo by Mike Simons/Getty Images)Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee is declining to stop Thursday’s scheduled execution of death row inmate Darrell Hines, even as his attorneys claim he could suffer cruel and unusual punishment because of an “under-skilled” physician.
“After deliberate consideration of Anthony Darrell Hines’ request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the state of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene,” Lee said in a statement Tuesday.
Attorneys for Hines, who was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 stabbing death of motel maid Catherine Jean Jenkins in Kingston Springs, said the physician likely to oversee the execution is unqualified to insert the IV to administer lethal drugs, based on the botched execution in May of Tony Carruthers. Lee called off that execution after the doctor and execution team struggled for about an hour to apply a central line, leaving the inmate in what one witness described as a “bloody mess.”
“It would be a grotesque spectacle for Tennessee to move forward with the execution of Darrell Hines given his debilitated medical condition and the many unanswered questions following the botched execution attempt of Tony Carruthers,” attorney Kit Thomas said in a statement.
Thomas said the Tennessee Department of Correction violated its own protocol by hiring Dr. Mark Fowler to handle the Carruthers execution even though he was unqualified to set the central IV line.
Hines’ attorneys petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court to postpone his execution and review a Tennessee Supreme Court decision against allowing a special master to determine whether his Eighth Amendment rights could be violated. They contend he could suffer the same problems as Carruthers because of two strokes that left him partially paralyzed.
The attorneys also sent a second letter to the Department of Correction, governor, attorney general and warden of Riverbend Maximum Security Institution asking the state to disclose the results of the lethal injection drug it plans to use on Hines.
WKRN reported that Jenkins’ daughter, Melissa Jenkins, previously said “justice will be served” by the execution but that closure “doesn’t exist” because most of the focus is placed on the person convicted of committing the crime, rather than the victim.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Pricey campaign launched to assist with ‘ridiculous’ federal Medicaid requirements
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: Starting this week, Healey said, notices are being mailed to MassHealth members about how the federal changes could affect them and what actions they need to take to stay covered.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY accused President Donald Trump of inflicting administrative obstacles on vulnerable Medicaid recipients to trigger potential insurance coverage losses, as she visited Haverhill Tuesday to tout a new public outreach campaign aimed at mitigating the impact of those federal policy changes.
Beginning in less than five months, more than 300,000 MassHealth members will need to satisfy work and education requirements to maintain their coverage as a result of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Trump signed in July 2025.
“They’re intentionally making it really burdensome to be on MassHealth because the whole point is if you kick people off of MassHealth, you’re going to lower the amount that the federal government has to pay out,” Healey said at a press conference. “And they’re going to take that money that they save covering people with healthcare, and they’re going to use it to cover the tax cuts for the wealthy. That’s essentially what’s going on.”
Through the federal law, Trump and congressional Republicans have set their focus on eliminating what they describe as fraud, waste and abuse in public benefit programs like Medicaid and SNAP. In a New York Times opinion piece last year, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other Trump administration leaders said “that too many able-bodied adults on welfare are not working at all” and implementing work requirements will “prioritize the vulnerable, empower able-bodied individuals, help rebuild thriving communities and protect the taxpayers.”
Tax provisions in the federal law will disproportionately benefit the richest 10% of Americans, according to a Center for American Progress analysis. The White House last month celebrated the one-year anniversary of Trump’s “widely popular” tax breaks — including no taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security, as well as “Made in America Car-Loan deductions” — and said that nearly 70% of filers who got a tax cut earned below $100,000.
Healey unveiled the MassHealth public outreach campaign at Make It Haverhill, a workforce and digital access program run by Community Action, Inc. The nonprofit is among nearly 50 community-based groups joining with Health Care For All to spread the word about the work requirements. The Legislature appropriated $10 million to Health Care For All for the campaign.
The effort largely mirrors the playbook that Health Care For All deployed during the sprawling MassHealth redetermination process in 2023 and 2024, after eligibility checks were paused during the pandemic.
“The success of that effort showed that trusted, collaborative, community-based outreach is essential to helping people stay covered,” Health Care For All Executive Director Jennifer Lemmerman said.
Starting this week, Healey said, notices are being mailed to MassHealth members about how the federal changes could affect them and what actions they need to take to stay covered.
MassHealth has a new website about eligibility changes that take effect Jan. 1 and largely impact adults ages 19 to 64. It offers information on how to report changes to MassHealth, access help from community organizations, find enrollment assisters and visit enrollment centers. There’s also a screening tool that people can use to determine whether they may be exempt from the requirements, including if they’re pregnant, parenting children ages 13 and younger, have a disability or are managing certain health conditions.
Lemmerman said a targeted advertising campaign will start “very soon” across the state, spanning social media, billboards, and messaging on buses and at MBTA stations.
Healey bristled at the federal law during the press conference and said “many” MassHealth recipients are working people.
“Gig workers — think about the person doing the delivery to your door. You know, they’re working, but they don’t make enough, and therefore they’re on Medicaid,” Healey said. “I think about students, in college, out of college, past 26, people who have gone back to school. They’re not making money or consistent income, and they’re on MassHealth, as well. I know a lot of people that are on MassHealth so that they continue to get mental healthcare, and services, and therapy that they need.”
The campaign features a communications toolkit to alert members about changes with flyers, posters and social media graphics available in English, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, Haitian Creole, Vietnamese, Khmer, Simplified Chinese, Arabic and Cape Verdean Creole.
MassHealth estimates that 360,000 members will need to comply with the monthly, 80-hour work and education requirement. Members can also satisfy the requirement if they earn at least $580 monthly, regardless of how many hours worked.
“I want to emphasize these are people that deserve to be in MassHealth, but because of the incredible paperwork barriers that the federal government is imposing, are at risk of losing that coverage for themselves and for their families,” Health and Human Services Secretary Kiame Mahaniah said. “The federal government would rather bury us in paperwork rather than make sure that eligible members can receive the care that they need. As a physician at a community health center, this hits particularly close to home, and it is something that is just immoral in terms of the approach the federal government is taking.”
Assistant Secretary for MassHealth Ryan Schwarz said Massachusetts will ultimately end up with fewer people enrolled in health insurance “given the frankly completely ridiculous paperwork requirements and administrative hoops that the federal administration is requiring individuals to jump through to retain their coverage.” Healey warned coverage losses across Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act marketplace will “hurt everybody” in the form of higher premiums. 
MassHealth members will also need to deal with more frequent eligibility renewals. Healey urged members to open all MassHealth communications, including blue renewal envelopes, and ensure the agency has their current contact information. Mahaniah held up a blue envelope and acknowledged he’s heard from patients who are fearful to open it and receive bad news.
“This is not one of those cases. This is a case where you really want to open the blue envelope,” Mahaniah said. “This is what guarantees that we continue covering you with MassHealth.”
Mahaniah said officials are working to automatically exempt people who are not subject to the work requirements, including those who are pregnant or have dependents. He also said the state is using data matching to automatically verify people who are already complying with the work and education rules.
Schwarz said his team has been scrambling to digest guidance that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid published on June 1 for implementing the work requirements. Schwarz became the MassHealth chief a week later.
“That guidance was surprising, if not just downright shocking, to every single state in the country that had been working, based on guidance from our federal partners, from staff at CMS throughout the last 12 months, as to what we were expected to do,” Schwarz said. “And they changed a lot of that in the guidance that was issued on June 1. As a result, our team has had to change a lot of our plans and operations, and we’ve been working literally day and night for the last nine weeks to try and understand how we can best retain coverage for every single eligible member in the state.”
During her visit to the Merrimack Valley Tuesday, Healey also held a campaign meet and greet in Methuen alongside Mayor DJ Beauregard, Sen. Pavel Payano and Rep. Ryan Hamilton.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico House Democrats announce plans to overhaul CYFD in 2027 legislative session
description: Democratic leaders in the New Mexico House of Representatives on Tuesday announced their child well-being priorities for next year’s legislative session, most of which centered around reforming the state’s troubled child welfare agency.
text:
New Mexico Rep. Michelle Paulene Abeyta (D-To'Hajiilee) speaks alongside fellow Democrat state representatives — from left to right: Meredith Dixon of Albuquerque, Pamelya Herndon of Albuquerque, House Speaker Javier Martínez of Albuquerque, Christine Chandler of Los Alamos, Eleanor Chávez of Albuquerque and Janelle Anyanonu of Albuquerque — at an Aug. 11, 2026, news conference about their child well-being priorities for the 2027 legislative session. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Democratic leaders in the New Mexico House of Representatives on Tuesday announced their child well-being priorities for next year’s legislative session, most of which centered around reforming the state’s troubled child welfare agency.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At an Albuquerque news conference, House Speaker Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) and several Democratic state lawmakers outlined their plans to sponsor legislation in the 2027 session that would create a three-member commission to oversee the state Children, Youth and Families Department, revise confidentiality protections in the state Children’s Code, ban congregate care for foster youth under the age of 12 and equip the recently formed Office of the Child Advocate with subpoena power.
What to do with CYFD has become a key issue in the race to become New Mexico’s next governor. That has intensified after recent reports that alleged CYFD staffers dropped a foster teen at the U.S.-Mexico border and instructed him to walk alone into Ciudad Juárez to reunite with his estranged mother.
“The time to talk about the problem is over,” Martínez said. “It’s time for action, and it’s time to take care of our most vulnerable children.”
Tuesday’s announcement came just weeks after the New Mexico Department of Justice gave lawmakers on the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee dozens of legislative and policy recommendations to reform CYFD. Many of the proposals for the 2027 legislative session mirrored the NMDOJ’s recommendations.
The group of lawmakers at Tuesday’s news conference said they had not yet decided whether to present these proposals as an omnibus bill or as several pieces of legislation. The 2027 legislative session will be a 60-day session, meaning lawmakers are freed up to tackle issues beyond the state budget.
But even the state budget will focus on child welfare, Rep. Meredith Dixon (D-Albuquerque) said.
Dixon, who serves as vice chair of the standing House Appropriations and Finance Committee, said that CYFD’s funding requests in the next state budget will be “carefully reviewed” to make sure they reflect healthy staffing levels, vacancy rates and more.
“As we develop the upcoming state budget, we will prioritize investments in services for at-risk youth,” Dixon said.
State lawmakers acknowledged that many of the proposals were not necessarily new. Rep. Michelle Paulene Abeyta (D-To’Hajiilee), for example, said her 2025 legislation to create the Office of the Child Advocate was significantly pared back before it became law. Namely, she said, the state Senate removed provisions in the office’s guiding legislation to give it subpoena power.
“Today, we are back to restore its teeth,” she said.
A new governor will preside over the 2027 legislative session as Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is term-limited. Martínez, for his part, said he stands ready to work alongside New Mexico’s next governor on these issues, whether it’s Democratic nominee Deb Haaland or Republican nominee Gregg Hull.
New Mexico Senate Republicans are set to hold a half-day task force meeting, titled “Reimagining CYFD,” at Central New Mexico Community College in Albuquerque on Wednesday. Former cabinet secretaries are scheduled to speak before the Republican lawmakers, according to an agenda for the event.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Who else is willing to debate in Nebraska this midterm cycle?
description: Nebraska 2nd District will likely have three debates, while the governor race likely won’t – or at least not with Pillen.
text:
Nebraska TV station cameras before a news conference on Aug. 19, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A Nebraska tradition returns as the Senate race between registered nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts will likely have only one debate at the state fair. 
Some Nebraska elected officials have avoided debates in recent years. U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer didn’t debate Osborn in 2024. Nebraska Gov Jim Pillen didn’t participate in any debates on his way to the governor’s mansion in 2022. 
Although Pillen is seen as vulnerable by some, with national polling showing Nebraska is led by one of the nation’s least popular incumbent governors, Pillen told the Examiner earlier this year that he won’t debate because he has been consistent about not doing debates. 
“I don’t know why I would ever change that,” Pillen said. 
Voting booths at the Lancaster County Election Commission office on April, 24. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Pillen’s 2022 campaign called debates “political theater.” 
The current Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Lynne Walz, and Legal Marijuana NOW’s gubernatorial candidate, Rick Beard, both said they would “absolutely” participate in a debate.  
Former Omaha state Sen. Brett Lindstrom, who turned in signatures to appear as a nonpartisan gubernatorial candidate, told the Examiner he would “welcome” a debate. 
“Four years later, Nebraskans still haven’t heard from their governor. Let’s fix that,” Lindstrom said. 
While the details are still being ironed out, Democratic nominee for the 2nd congressional district, Denise Powell, and Republican nominee, Brinker Harding, have agreed to three debates.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As in other cycles, election analysts view the 2nd District as a top pickup opportunity for minority Democrats hoping to take over Republicans’ slim majority in the closely divided U.S. House. Outgoing Republican Rep. Don Bacon debated his opponents as the incumbent in 2024, 2022, 2020 and 2018. 
In Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District, incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Flood’s campaign team said debates will happen, but details are not set in stone. Democratic nominee Chris Backemeyer’s spokesperson said they agreed to two debates. The 1st District comprises 12 counties, including Lancaster County, which is home to heavily Democratic Lincoln, a city whose blue voters are often drowned out by the region’s more conservative smaller cities and rural areas. 
Flood has won his past two U.S. House elections by 20 and 16 percentage points, respectively. Analysts, including the nonpartisan Center for Politics, The Cook Political Report and Inside Elections, consider the 1st District seat safely Republican — though national Democrats see the race as competitive.
The state’s 3rd Congressional District, which includes central and western Nebraska and much of the state’s northeastern and southeastern edges, is among the nation’s most conservative by political party registration advantage and voting record. 
That race has two nonpartisan candidates, one Democrat and a Legal Marijuana NOW candidate, David Else, trying to beat incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith.
One nonpartisan candidate, Mark Cohen, said he was approached about doing a debate. Macey Budke, the other nonpartisan candidate, said she hasn’t heard anything about a debate but would be open to one. 
The Smith campaign said, “Congressman Smith regularly connects with constituents by holding tele-townhalls, traveling the district to visit main street businesses, schools, health care providers and family farms, and meeting with Nebraskans in their communities throughout the district.” 
Becky Kelly Stille, the Democratic nominee, didn’t respond to a request for information about debates in the 3rd District.

The general election is Nov 3.

name: VTDigger
title: When disaster strikes Vermont, where is Washington?
description:
As floods, wildfires and other disasters devastate communities, Washington's response has been political spectacle rather than action.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  When disaster strikes Vermont, where is Washington?.
text:
Dear Editor,
Every night, the news brings us stories of families losing their homes to floods, tornadoes, wildfires and other disasters. The scale of this natural devastation reflects a growing national crisis. Yet where are the reports of our government responding to the enormous needs of people who are clearly suffering?
Are the Federal Emergency Management Agency, the Red Cross and relief organizations expected to shoulder the growing burden of helping hundreds of families whose homes have been destroyed or damaged, while businesses are left wondering how they will survive and entire communities struggle to rebuild their lives?
We are facing a crisis that is, in part, the consequence of years of neglect of our environment and failure to adequately prepare for the consequences of a changing climate. Yet too often, it seems that Washington is more focused on political battles and spectacle than on the people who are suffering.

READ MORE

I am genuinely curious to know how our legislators view this crisis and what they believe our government should be doing to address it. More importantly, I would like to know how they intend to respond.
Alis HeadlamRutland, Vt.

name: VTDigger
title: At the polls, Vermont primary voters seek change
description:
Voters are casting their ballots in competitive Democratic governor and lieutenant governor races and several crowded local races.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  At the polls, Vermont primary voters seek change.
text:
A voter carries ballots past a booth in Shelburne on Primary Day, Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Across the state, voters are hitting the polls on Tuesday to decide who will challenge Vermont Republicans come November in competitive Democratic governor and lieutenant governor races as well as several crowded local races. 
“I’m just hoping for change, and that no matter what party orientation, that our legislature and the governor can work together to really make positive change in the state,” said Susan Gerreston, a Montpelier resident, outside of the city’s polling site, at City Hall, on Tuesday. 
For Gerreston, that change is represented by Democratic candidate Amanda Janoo, who is running for governor. The economist and first-time candidate won over Gerreston’s vote because of her progressive platform. However, the Montpelier resident said she has also “heard good things about” Janoo’s competitor, Aly Richards, who ran a successful campaign for affordable child care as the former CEO of Let’s Grow Kids, a prominent education lobbying group in the state. 
“I don’t think we can lose either way,” Gerreston said, referring to the faceoff for the Democratic nomination for governor, which will determine who will challenge Republican Gov. Phil Scott in the general election this fall. Scott, who’s in his 10th year in the office, is considered the nation’s most popular governor but has recently seen his job approval ratings diminish, with a University of New Hampshire poll finding him at a four-year low, slipping by 10 points.
Hartford voter Jen Durgin voiced that waning popularity: despite falling to the political left, she voted for Scott twice in the past, in part to show that Vermont can support moderate Republicans, she said. 
But after Scott vetoed a bill that would have lowered insurance charges for public school employees, and has put up “unreasonable obstacles to greenhouse gas reporting,” she has lost faith in the incumbent governor, she said. 
Gerreston, the Montpelier voter, also cited Scott’s vetoing of progressive bills passed by the Senate as a reason why she believes change is needed in the seat. This summer, Scott has vetoed bills targeting healthcare reform, energy development and AI data center regulations. 

Weston Bird, 8, accompanies Kristen Bird as she fills out a ballot in Essex Junction on Primary Day, Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

For Marilyn and George Albrecht, in Hartford, school funding was top of mind. Their children and grandchildren all attended Hartford High School, which they said was the reason they chose to settle in Vermont 40 years ago after George Albrecht’s military job stationed him there.
“Property taxes go up, and the quality of education goes down,” said George Albrecht, who declined to say how he voted Tuesday. “If taxes go up any more, they will tax us right out of here.” 
Hartford voter Joe Dombroski’s property taxes have doubled in the past few years, he told VTDigger in an interview outside the polls Tuesday. Keeping taxes low was one of the biggest issues on his mind. 
“Just lower the prices,” he said. He knows that school consolidation can be unpleasant, but having attended a merged high school across the border in rural New Hampshire, he believes  it’s possible and thinks it yielded better educational outcomes than a small rural schoolhouse. He hopes Vermont lawmakers heed that example, though he declined to say how he voted.
Education took center stage during the last legislative session, as Scott and the Legislature agreed to an education reform compromise that seeks to facilitate voluntary school district mergers.
In Norwich, Liz Blum, 84, turned out with enthusiastic support for Amanda Janoo’s governor candidacy and Elizabeth Burrows’ bid for state senate, in the crowded six-person Windsor County primary for three seats representing the district. She donned a Burrows for Senate shirt that she buttoned over before heading into the Tracy Hall polling place.
“I am so thrilled with Amanda Janoo. She has a great chance to beat Phil Scott, who has been in office 10 years too long and hasn’t improved anything. I see Amanda as a whole-picture person, with really sensible solutions for saving small communities and taxing the wealthy,” Blum said.
This story will be updated.

title: Maine child food insecurity remains highest in New England, latest data shows
description: Maine continues to have the highest rate of food insecurity among children in New England, according to the latest data from national nonprofit Feeding America in its annual “Map the Meal Gap” report and data collection. That means that 20.7% of Maine children, or roughly one in five, were food insecure in 2024. It’s the […]
text:
Good Shepherd Food Bank distribution center in Hampden, ME (Photo courtesy of Good Shepherd Food Bank)Maine continues to have the highest rate of food insecurity among children in New England, according to the latest data from national nonprofit Feeding America in its annual “Map the Meal Gap” report and data collection.
That means that 20.7% of Maine children, or roughly one in five, were food insecure in 2024. It’s the highest rate in all of New England — a ranking Maine has topped for years — with Connecticut coming in second, with 18.8% of children experiencing food insecurity. 
But as Maine’s population has grown, the year-over-year rate of growth in child food insecurity has slowed. 
“Food insecurity touches every community in Maine,” Heather Paquette, president of Good Shepherd Food Bank, said in a statement. “These numbers represent our neighbors — children, older adults, working families, veterans and people doing everything they can to make ends meet. While the data show the scale of the challenge, they also reinforce the importance of continuing to work together to ensure everyone in Maine has reliable access to the nutritious food they need to thrive.”
Because of delays in federal data reporting, data for 2025 and 2026 isn’t expected to be available for several years.
In 2024, the number of overall people in Maine who are food insecure surpassed 200,000 for the first time.
And while the rate of overall food insecurity has not changed significantly in recent years — growing from 10.5% in 2021 to 14.5% in 2024 — the number of Maine residents who are considered food insecure has grown by more than 50,000. 
The statewide numbers put Maine just above the national average of 19.5% of children and 14.4% of people overall who were food insecure, according to the report.


Within Maine, Washington County has the highest rate of overall food insecurity at 18.8%, followed by Piscataquis County with an 18.1% overall rate. 
Androscoggin County had the highest child food insecurity rate at 26.3%, closely followed by Washington County at 26.1%. 
Food insecurity is compounded by the increasing cost of food, which because of inflation and other factors has continued to rise since the data in the report.
The average cost of a meal in Maine in 2024 was $3.92, a 16 cent increase from the year before. 
The report found that food insecure households reported that they needed an additional $23.60 per person each week to pay for enough food. Over the course of a year, that leaves all of Maine’s food insecure households $151 million short of what they need for food costs. 
Just under half (46%) of food insecure Mainers in 2024 were estimated to be above the income threshold for federal food assistance, which means that while they have limited or uncertain access to adequate food, they are ineligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
The USDA has canceled its Current Population Survey Food Security Supplement, one of the data sources Feeding America uses in its food insecurity analysis. That change did not affect the 2024 data, but may not be available for 2025 or future years. 
But Feeding America plans to incorporate alternative data and research in its future reports. 
The delay in data means the report can’t show the impact of recent changes to government food assistance programs during President Donald Trump’s second term. Last year, Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which reduced benefits by restricting what factors can be taken into account when determining a household’s allotment, capping future program funding increases at the rate of inflation and imposing stricter work requirements. 
It also requires states to pay for portions of SNAP, which had exclusively been funded by the federal government since it began many decades ago. How much each state has to pay will depend on its payment error rate — a measure of how often households receive too much or too little in benefits.
Maine’s payment error rate of more than 10% in 2025 means the state would be responsible for 15% of SNAP benefit costs, or $50 million per year, beginning in 2028.
Last session, the state Legislature worked to address some of the federal changes. Lawmakers passed a law helping immigrants who have been cut out of the federal SNAP program to maintain access to state-funded food assistance, and approved funding through the budget to decrease the state’s payment error rate in an attempt to reduce the amount of cost-sharing Maine is responsible for in future years.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bethany families tell of Mastrangelo’s betrayal on day of sentencing
description: Anthony Mastrangelo will spend 4 years in prison for sexually abusing girls at a town-run camp in Bethany, the result of a plea deal.
text:
Anthony Mastrangelo, the 27-year-old Bethany man who pleaded guilty in May to sexually abusing girls at a town-run camp after-school program and while babysitting, was sentenced to 20 years in prison, suspended after he serves four years, the result of a plea deal.
He was handcuffed and taken into custody after a sentencing hearing in New Haven on Tuesday.
Mastrangelo’s crimes prompted a firestorm in the small town where he was once considered a trusted friend and caretaker for local children, resulting in his incarceration and modest changes to state laws regarding municipal programs for children, which run with no state oversight.
The case also led to the resignation of former Bethany First Selectwoman Paula Cofrancesco, who was found in an independent investigation to have deceived residents and resisted efforts to make programs for children safer.

Former Bethany First Selectwoman Paula Cofrancesco during a board meeting on Oct. 1, 2024. Credit: Shahrzad Rasekh / CT Mirror

But on Tuesday, the most significant impacts of Mastrangelo’s crimes were heard in victims’ statements that expressed the trauma, anger and confusion left in the wake of his actions. Parents who said they’d experienced a nightmare scenario also expressed disillusionment at the negligence of Bethany’s municipal programs.
The first statement came from the father of one of the girls abused by Mastrangelo when she was 9. Identifying himself as A.A., he said that he couldn’t believe such events could have transpired at a municipal program, which he expected would have oversight. In the extended period after her abuse was investigated and before Mastrangelo’s arrest, he said, the family avoided town events for fear that they would see Mastrangelo “or the people that enabled him.” He said he was haunted by memories of Mastrangelo hugging his child in the parking lot and approaching him to say he wanted to babysit his kids because he liked them so much.
“I feel horrible. Horrible he did this to our daughter. Horrible he did this to our friends. Horrible I didn’t see the signs,” he said. 
Statements by victims reflected the inability of children as young as 9 to comprehend the nature of the abuse or how to stop it. In one statement, a victim said she’d been abused when other camp staff were in the room and hoped someone would notice.
The theme of grooming was repeated during the sentencing hearing, including by Judge Tracy Lee Dayton, who wondered if there were other victims: “It’s hard for me to believe that these are the only five people that you hurt.”
“This behavior is shockingly predatory,” Dayton said. Dayton said she was “revolted” when she read through court documents and saw that Mastrangelo enrolled in Quinnipiac University to pursue a degree in elementary education when he was already under investigation for sexually assaulting “little girls.”
“I could think of one reason why you’d want to be in a school — the same reason you’d want to work in a camp,” she said. “Unfortunately, a lot of young ladies and a lot of their parents have had to learn very, very difficult lessons because you think your child is going to be safe at school, your child is going to be safe at home, you think your child’s safe at camp — community camp.”
Dayton said she was torn about the length of the sentence, part of a plea deal agreed upon by another judge in her absence, but said that completing sentencing on Tuesday would ensure that the families didn’t have to return to court.
Dayton also commended Amy Lestinsky, the mother of one of the girls, who has publicly fought for justice over the past two years even as the identities of most of the families have remained private.

Amy Lestinsky, Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff and Sen. Jorge Cabrera spoke at a news conference in May 2025 in support of the passage of Senate Bill 6. Credit: Jessika Harkay / CT Mirror

Lestinsky’s daughter spoke briefly to the court, and then Lestinsky spoke at length. She said that the experience had left her slow to trust other people and that she has been called a bad mother for so publicly speaking about her daughter’s assault. Lestinsky addressed Mastrangelo directly, wondering whether he was grooming her family to trust him. 
When Mastrangelo abused her daughter while babysitting, more than a year had passed since he’d been investigated for abusing four other girls. He had lost his job at the Bethany school and Parks and Rec program but had not yet been arrested, and the investigation was not widely known.
“You chose the wrong child to sexually abuse, because this victim, my daughter, has a mother who will not be quiet. A mother who will fight ’til the very end and make sure justice is served,” she said. She wished him and his family to endure suffering like her family. “No child ever deserves to be treated the way you treated the victims. You took advantage of their innocence, you took advantage of the trust they had in you. I hope you see yourself for the piece of garbage you are every time you look in the mirror.”
Lestinsky also addressed his mother, saying she swept the accusations against her son “under the rug.” 
“I hope you remember every day what an atrocious mother you are,” she said. 
Some of the statements on Tuesday reflected the betrayal felt by parents who assumed that municipal camps, like the one where Mastrangelo worked in Bethany, would be safe environments for kids. As Mastrangelo’s actions came to light, so too did revelations about the lack of licensure and state oversight for such camps. The state has little idea about how many such camps exist, how many children attend them or what rules and regulations govern them.
Towns and cities across the state have repeatedly argued that no such regulation is needed because there is built-in oversight from local governments and that creating licensure requirements would prove expensive, forcing some camps to close their doors and depriving families of safe and affordable childcare options. 
Some proposals to regulate camps failed in recent years, but this year, a modest bill was passed that creates new mandated reporter requirements for camp staff and requires a report by the Office of Early Childhood and other stakeholders on the landscape of such programs in Connecticut.
In addition to his prison sentence, Mastrangelo was also sentenced to 10 years of sex offender probation, a more restrictive form of probation that requires therapeutic treatment. When he is released from prison, Mastrangelo will also have to register as a sex offender. Dayton also issued restraining orders that bar Mastrangelo from coming near the victims or contacting them for the next 50 years.

text:
Clarke University will use a grant from the Network for Vocation in Undergraduate Education to explore the interplay of vocation and mission. (Photo courtesy of Clarke University)Clarke University plans to use a professional development grant to explore and strengthen its community ties in Dubuque and the surrounding area, bringing together college and community officials.
The Dubuque university has announced it the award of a $20,000 grant from the Network for Vocation in Undergraduate Education, or NetVUE, for professional development and the formation of a mission and vision-focused group of both faculty and employers.
NetVUE is a country-wide network of colleges and universities created by the Council of Independent Colleges to support vocational exploration among undergraduate students, according to its website.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to a university press release, this cohort will “discuss vocation and mission” to help inform Clarke officials in future curriculum changes and developments. Clarke faculty and staff will also have opportunities to participate in panel discussions and other activities focused on the same topics as the cohort, and NetVUE will participate in the university’s annual opening workshop.
Gina Burkart, director of learning services and assistant professor of first-year studies at Clarke, said in the release the initiative will “foster deeper and more tangible connections between Clarke and the community” and help create more opportunities for students and university partners. Burkart led the proposal for the grant.
“It is my hope that this project creates more capacity for students to engage in vocational endeavors with community partners—while also weaving the spirit and core values of the Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary into the fabric of the Dubuque community,” Burkart said in the release.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Appointment of Muslim judge in tiny Mississippi town brings social media attacks
description: Ridgeland attorney Assma Ali
text:
A municipal judge’s appointment in a small Mississippi Delta town has drawn social media backlash, from internet trolls and a few Mississippi politicians, because she is Muslim.
But those who know Assma Ali, including a law professor, say the U.S. native is qualified and an upstanding member of Mississippi’s legal community.
“We have people from out of state who just see a woman in a hijab and they say action must be taken. These attacks against Ms. Ali are about her religion,” said Frank Rosenblatt, an attorney and professor at Mississippi Christian University School of Law, who has known Ali for years and spoke highly of her willingness to mentor young lawyers.
In recent days, people including some Mississippi politicians attacked Ali online for what they claimed are radical beliefs – without any substantiation. They accused her of fabricating the judicial appointment and speculated she would institute Islamic law. Social media posts falsely claimed she was appointed as a judge in Ridgeland or in Lumberton. 
“Mississippi appoints first Yemeni Sharia Hijabi judge,” Amy Mekelburg of New York, founder and editor-in-chief of the Rise Align Ignite Reclaim Foundation, wrote in a post on X that has over 1 million views. Mekelburg incorrectly claimed that Ali had made up the appointment, calling it an “Islamic scam.”
Ali, an immigration lawyer with nearly 10 years of experience, was appointed last week as the municipal judge for Benoit, a town of fewer than 400 people in Bolivar County. She is an American citizen of Yemeni descent. She runs her own private practice in Ridgeland. She earned her law degree from Mississippi College School of Law, now Mississippi Christian University, in 2017 and was admitted to the state bar the same year.
Ali, in a statement on social media, said she will uphold the U.S. Constitution and Mississippi law.
“I was born in the United States, and as both an attorney and a judge, I am committed to upholding the United States Constitution and the laws of the State of Mississippi,” Ali wrote. “I am grateful for the opportunity to serve the people of Benoit and will approach this responsibility with fairness, integrity, impartiality, and respect for the law.”
On Monday, Ali shared her signed oath of office and Benoit’s meeting agenda showing her appointment in a post on social media for “clarity and transparency.” 
Mississippi has more than 200 municipal judges, who are appointed by the city’s governing body, not the state, and who only have jurisdiction over that city. They deal with city ordinance violations, traffic violations, misdemeanor crimes and some initial appearances, according to the Mississippi State Judiciary’s website.
In cities with a population below 20,000, a municipal judge is not required to live in the area where they serve, according to an attorney general’s opinion. Some seats are part-time appointments and judges can continue private practice.
“Ms. Ali is a very well liked and popular member of our community,” Rosenblatt said. 
Some people on social media have called for her to be removed because she is Muslim. Rosenblatt pointed out that the U.S. and Mississippi constitutions expressly prohibit disqualifying someone from public office because of their religion.
“I think some of the things we’ve seen from some state officials are incredibly disrespectful to Ms. Ali, and they are in direct contradiction of the U.S. Constitution and the Mississippi Constitution,” Rosenblatt said. 
Some, without documentation, claimed that Ali would implement Sharia law in Mississippi. 
Sahar Aziz, a professor of law and Middle East Legal Studies Scholar at Rutgers University Law School, said there is no one Sharia law and called it “a very complicated and multi-jurisprudential legal system” subject to a multiplicity of interpretations across time, countries and cultures. She compared it to the differences of opinions and interpretations in the Catholic church.
“The accusation they’re making is a very serious one. They’re saying that simply because you are a Muslim we just presume that you are going to violate the separation between church and state. And you are going to impose whatever your interpretation is of Islam upon everyone that goes before you as a judge,” Aziz said, adding that similar accusations have been leveled against other public officials across the U.S.
“It’s not relevant at all to the United States,” Aziz said. “No more relevant than the question: Will an Orthodox Jew impose Jewish law in the U.S. if he or she is a judge? Will an orthodox, practicing Catholic impose canon law on the parties which they’re adjudicating?”
In 2015, the Mississippi Legislature passed a law banning any foreign law from being enforced in Mississippi, which at the time was billed as being an anti-Sharia law measure. There had been several previous unsuccessful attempts to pass similar measures, with opponents pointing out it seemed to be a “solution in search of a problem.”
In a 2024 post about a proclamation from Republican Gov. Tate Reeves celebrating Arab American Heritage Month, Ali wrote, “This means the world to the Arab community, my children, and future generations. This is why I love this state!”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY lawmakers move ahead with expanded bobcat hunting despite population concerns
description: FRANKFORT — Regulations to expand bobcat hunting, including at night with thermal equipment, moved forward Tuesday, despite bipartisan concern from some lawmakers about the status of Kentucky’s bobcat regulation. The state legislature’s Administrative Regulation Review Subcommittee has the authority to vote to declare a regulation as “deficient” if lawmakers[...]
text:
A bobcat is seen at the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources' Salato Wildlife Center in Frankfort. (Provided by Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources)FRANKFORT — Regulations to expand bobcat hunting, including at night with thermal equipment, moved forward Tuesday, despite bipartisan concern from some lawmakers about the status of Kentucky’s bobcat regulation.
The state legislature’s Administrative Regulation Review Subcommittee has the authority to vote to declare a regulation as “deficient” if lawmakers disapprove of it or recommend changes to a regulation. The committee Tuesday took neither action on regulations proposed by the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources.
Sen. Steve West, R-Paris, a co-chair of the committee, told the Lantern lawmakers decided to defer to the department’s decisionmaking with the understanding that “if there’s some type of impending doom with a collapse of the bobcat population” the department can come back to lawmakers with revised proposals. 
“Anecdotally across the state if you talk to hunters, the bobcat population seems to be pretty strong,” West said. “If we felt that there was harm to the overall population, or that they were endangered in any way, or things of that nature, we probably would have acted, but the members of the committee didn’t feel that way today.” 
The proposed regulations from the wildlife management agency would expand the bag limit — the number of bobcats that a hunter or trapper can kill during a season — from five to 10 bobcats and allow, for the first time, a hunter to kill one bobcat at night. The Kentucky Fish and Wildlife Commission, a volunteer board that votes on hunting regulations, approved the bag limit expansion last year and approved the nighttime hunting of bobcats in June. 
But two Louisville lawmakers on the committee echoed concerns from the state’s own wildlife biologists, trappers and some members of the Fish and Wildlife Commission about increasing opportunities to kill bobcats while not having solid population data on bobcats. 
“It’s curious to me that we would hunt something that was not overpopulated, that we don’t have a definite number of them in the state, and that it seems to me that we have biologists that are not in lockstep on this,” said Sen. Julie Raque Adams, R-Louisville. “It would be my opinion that we would have more of a unified opinion on this before we tackle this issue. But that’s just my opinion.”
In May, the department’s director of wildlife and the manager of the state’s furbearer program told the Fish and Wildlife Commission they haven’t been able to get adequate tooth samples from hunters and trappers to estimate the state’s bobcat population, along with having concerns over the safety of nighttime hunting. The chief executive of the department, Commissioner Rich Storm, worked with a powerful state lawmaker to legalize the nighttime hunting of bobcats through the passage of a last-minute bill, Senate Bill 39, during this year’s legislative session. The department’s deputy commissioner Gabe Jenkins told the Fish and Wildlife Commission it was the “intention” of Senate Bill 39 that the board move forward with regulations for hunting bobcats at night.
Sen. Julie Raque Adams, R-Louisville, questioned why the department was expanding hunting of an animal when wildlife biologists were not in “lockstep” on the decision. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Rep. Mary Lou Marzian, D-Louisville, told department representatives she was concerned that people could wipe out bobcats and that “it’ll be another species that’s going to be gone forever in Kentucky.” 
Todd Blevins, the state director of the animal welfare and protection group Humane World for Animals, also told the committee it would be a risk to expand the bag limit for bobcats and allow the nighttime hunting of bobcats when “we simply just don’t have the numbers.” 
“You’re not going to find the trappers and organizations like mine on the same page very often. But when you do, I think that tells you that there’s something wrong with the policy,” Blevins said. 
But representatives for the department defended the decisions to move forward with the bobcat hunting expansion. Jenny Gilbert, the legislative liaison for the department, said there had been requests to “increase the harvest” of bobcats before this year’s legislative session. 
She also said the department and commission took “the most conservative approach” to complying with changes to state law. Despite the increase in the bag limit to 10 bobcats, the proposed regulations limit hunters to only killing one bobcat at night during the season. Hunters can kill only three bobcats out of the 10 overall, both daytime and nighttime hunting, Hunters are allowed to kill the remaining bobcats in their bag limit with other weapons such as bows or traps. 
Benjamin Monarch, the general counsel for the department, said “the process of informing our decisions is one of methodology that we take very seriously and is very comprehensive.” 
“Does that mean that you’re always going to have perfect information? Certainly not.” Monarch said. “We do the best we can to gather data and extrapolate from that data to make reasonable conclusions.” 
West told the Lantern that wildlife management issues get “very complicated” and “there’s a constant struggle” over hunting seasons with various interested groups. 
“We have to call balls and strikes and just be an umpire, and that was our call today on this one,” West said.
The proposed regulations will now go before the Interim Kentucky Natural Resources and Energy Committee, where lawmakers on that committee will consider the regulations before becoming finalized. The department will also hold a Sept. 30 hearing collecting public comments on the regulation allowing the nighttime hunting of bobcats at its department headquarters.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Cattle producers cope with ‘gut-wrenching’ losses from July heat wave
description: George Kenzy said he did all he could to prepare his family’s feedlot for extreme heat and humidity. That included extra water tanks, covering the ground with light-colored bedding to reduce heat absorption, and keeping the ground as wet as possible. “And it seemed like Mother Nature just had the upper hand on this one,” […]
text:
A cow on a ranch near White River, South Dakota. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/cattle-die-off-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: Scroll down for a downloadable version of this story with a host intro script.
George Kenzy said he did all he could to prepare his family’s feedlot for extreme heat and humidity. That included extra water tanks, covering the ground with light-colored bedding to reduce heat absorption, and keeping the ground as wet as possible.
“And it seemed like Mother Nature just had the upper hand on this one,” Kenzy said.
Thousands of cattle in South Dakota died of heat stress last month. Though locations across the state experienced unusually high temperatures, data from the Rapid City office of the National Weather Service help illustrate the historic nature of the heat wave: It was the city’s second hottest July on record, according to several indicators, and the city experienced its highest-ever recorded temperatures on July 25 downtown (110 degrees) and at the airport (112 degrees).
July was also the warmest month on record for the contiguous United States, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, with an average temperature of nearly 77 degrees.
Days of heat, high humidity, a lack of wind and cooler nighttime temperatures created a dangerous mix, according to Warren Rusche, a South Dakota State University Extension feedlot management specialist.
“Heat stress is one of those issues we have to be ready for all the time in South Dakota,” Rusche said. “What’s different is we haven’t seen widespread death losses like we saw in quite a few years. Normally the approaches we’ve taken have been successful enough that we’ve avoided some of these larger scale death-loss events.”
Rusche estimates at least 2,000 cattle deaths across the state, though he said that’s “likely too low.” No official count is available and likely won’t be for weeks as producers document their losses, he said.
Individual and overall financial impacts
South Dakota ranks seventh in the nation with 3.6 million cattle, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Brule County, which includes Chamberlain and Kimball, lost between 1,500 and 2,000 cattle from heat stress, Rusche said, which equates to about $6 million of financial losses.
“As devastating as this is for individual ranchers, it’s going to have minimal effect on our beef industry as a whole, just because a lot of producers didn’t get hit with significant death loss,” Rusche said. “The drought, probably, is going to play more of a role in cow numbers than the actual death loss events that we experienced.”
Cattle producers should report their losses to their local Farm Service Agency office, Gov. Larry Rhoden said in a statement on social media. The U.S. Department of Agriculture offers livestock indemnity payments to producers who face “livestock deaths in excess of normal mortality caused by adverse weather.” Those payments are equal to 75% of market value of the livestock lost.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Financial impacts are not the only thing on the minds of producers like Kenzy.
“Initially, it’s shock and awe,” he said. “It’s the absolute gut-wrenching loss of life of the cattle that you’ve cared for so much, put so much work into and then, yeah, you have to clean up the carnage and move on.”
Much of the impact spread through central and southeast parts of the state, including Kenzy’s operation near Gregory. He did not specify how many cattle he lost.
Feeding operations were more heavily impacted by the heat than cow-calf operations, according to Warren Symens, past president of the South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association.
“When you get a 1,500-pound animal that’s been fed to gain fast and grow fast and be ready for consumers, they suffer a lot more because they’re much bigger and they’re in a different environment,” he said. “They can’t go stand in a water pond like a cow on a pasture can.”
The nation’s cattle herd is at a 75-year low, Symens said, “so, anything that’s removing pounds of cattle from the system has an effect,” including on the already high price of beef.
Rising temperatures across the state
South Dakota’s average temperatures are climbing, according to State Climatologist Laura Edwards.
“Most of those increases are driven by warmer nights,” she said. “So, really, that’s not unusual to see warmer nights, but that stretch in July was really unusual, even for the trend that we’re on.”
Report cites 2-degree rise and urges South Dakota leaders to act on climate change, renewable energy

The state’s also seeing increased humidity levels due in part to a difference in row crops in recent decades, Edwards said. Some farmers have transitioned from spring wheat, which is usually harvested by this time of year, to corn and soybeans, which are continuing to pump water into the air, creating humid conditions, Edwards said.
“We see that it may be affecting humidity on a local scale, which could be a contributing factor to the cattle,” she said. “But it’s not enough on its own to really make that much of a difference, when we’re talking about livestock issues that we’ve seen all across the region.”
Larger-scale weather patterns, like hot air being pushed north from the Gulf of Mexico, creates more humidity than regional crop changes, Edwards said.
A Sioux Falls-based nonprofit, South Dakota Green Project, reported earlier this year that the state’s average temperatures have increased by two degrees since 1900. Days with extreme heat are becoming more frequent, according to the report. Compared to the 1970s, Sioux Falls now experiences 10 more heat warning days per year and Mitchell experiences 16 more.
“As our climate continues to warm, bouts of extreme heat become longer, more frequent, and more intense, increasing the risk of heat-related illness and mortality,” the report reads.
Encouraging producers to ‘check on each other’
Symens, of the Cattlemen’s Association, noted producers might have disagreements about issues affecting the industry, “but we’re all in this together.”
“With these losses, give your friends and neighbors a call and see how they’re doing and just check on each other,” he said. “We’re pretty notorious for not asking for help when we need it. There’s nothing wrong with reaching out to each other.”
Andrea Bjornestad, a professor and mental health Extension specialist at SDSU, said cattle deaths and financial losses could cause chronic stress and anxiety for ranchers that manifest as physical symptoms — chest tightness, shakiness, rapid heart rate — and emotional symptoms such as feelings of hopelessness, guilt and shame.
Chronic stress can also push people to isolate themselves to avoid talking about their struggles with friends and family, and to avoid social activities.
“All of these things can contribute to stress on the body, the mind, as well as stress within relationships, whether it’s family members or friends,” Bjornestad said, “and contribute to a decline in mental health.”
Bjornestad’s been researching the mental health of farmers and ranchers for more than a decade. She’s worked with producers during past major losses such as the ongoing avian flu outbreak that’s killed millions of birds and during the COVID-19 pandemic when large pork packing plants closed, forcing farmers to reckon with euthanizing their pigs.
“The ranchers talk so much about their connection with their animals and how their animals actually help them have positive mental health,” Bjornestad said. “So, I think to significantly lose animals in itself is such a huge loss, not just financially, but emotionally, because that connection is lost.”
Counselors can be a “neutral party” for producers who want to talk about their struggles, Bjornestad said. SDSU offers a grant-funded agricultural behavioral health voucher program for five free counseling sessions for producers and their immediate family members.
